This realm is not above the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; furthermore, there are further realms above it, such as the wind-wheel, the gold-wheel, and the various triple-worlds, all of which are infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
Question: Since pure lands must exist in all directions, why do you specifically praise the Western Quarter?

Answer: This, too, is not a well-posed question. Suppose one were to praise the land of Akṣobhya Buddha; you would again suspect a partiality toward the Eastern Quarter. To expand: [the same logic applies to every direction].
Turning away from conceptual proliferation. Question: Why does it not universally take the dharma-realm as its object? Answer: There are three reasons.

First, so that beginners may easily direct their minds toward it. Second, because Amitābha’s original vow is supreme. Third, because the Buddha has a particular affinity with the sentient beings of this land.

Generally speaking, when the Buddha delivers sentient beings and they receive his transformation, whether the process is difficult or easy, shallow or deep, depends entirely upon these conditions (*pratyaya*). As for the nature of these conditions...
The depth of their benevolence is vast and profound. Through various teachings and expositions, they are able to inspire joy and lead others to enter with faith;
they are able to stir latent seeds from the past; they are able to render demonic obstacles impossible to obstruct; and they are able to cause the essential nature to unfold.

All Buddhas originally descend from the Dharma-body to manifest traces and firmly bind the seeds of conditions. Whether mundane or supramundane, these matters are entirely inconceivable. They are most exalted.
The vehicle of the teachings is proclaimed throughout the ocean-like assembly; it penetrates deeply into the sea of suffering and accords with compassion within the realm of tranquil light.

Thus, ten thousand virtues are reverently received, and all spirits look toward the Pole Star. One should know that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions, and these conditions are none other than the Dharma-realm.

A single thought encompasses all thoughts; a single birth encompasses all births. Whether it be a single fragrance, a single flower, a single sound, or a single color—even down to the acceptance of repentance, the bestowal of predictions, or the placing of hands upon the crown of the head—there is nothing throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time that is not universally integrated.
Therefore, this superior causal condition is called the "Dharmadhātu-dependent Origination. This is precisely what is meant by "universally conditioning the Dharmadhātu."

Those at a shallow stage of practice may resolve their will to seek [the Pure Land] with single-minded devotion. Those at a deep stage of practice need not abandon the Western Paradise to seek elsewhere for the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

To claim that the Western Paradise is provisional while the Flower Treasury World is real, or that the Western Paradise is small while the Flower Treasury World is great, is to fall entirely into the pervasive conceptual attachments of sentient beings;
it arises from failing to realize that the provisional and the real are one body, and that the small and the great are non-dual.
Because they lack intrinsic nature. △ Second, the inquiry and explanation of the title of the sutra:
"Śāriputra, what do you think? (The praise of its merits has already been explained in detail above.

Those who uphold this sutra and those who hear the names of these Buddhas— all such sons and daughters of good family shall be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas,
and they shall all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Therefore,
Śāriputra, you and all others should faithfully accept my words and the words of all the Buddhas.
It is said:
"This sutra alone elucidates the supreme essence of the mind; the names of all Buddhas likewise elucidate the supreme, perfect, and ultimate ten thousand virtues.
Therefore, those who hear it shall all be protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Furthermore, upon hearing this sutra and upholding it, one immediately grasps [the truth]."
"Holding the name" refers to the fact that the name of Amitābha is protected and kept in mind by all Buddhas. Question:

If one merely hears the names of the Buddhas but does not yet uphold the sutra, will they still receive protection and mindfulness such that they do not regress? Answer: This principle has both a restricted and a universal application.
According to the *Zancha*, even if one recites my name with a confused and defiled mind, it does not constitute "hearing. This is because such a state cannot give rise to decisive conviction.
With settled conviction and understanding, one merely attains mundane rewards of goodness, yet fails to obtain vast, profound, and wondrous benefits.

If one reaches the Samādhi of One Practice, then one accomplishes a mind of vast and subtle practice, which is called attaining a semblance of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
It is likewise necessary to hear the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions; therefore, having heard them, one must uphold them.
To reach the state of "one mind not distracted" is to truly hear the names of the Buddhas and receive their protective mindfulness; this is the restricted meaning.
As for the universal meaning: the compassion of the Buddhas is inconceivable, and the merit of their names is likewise inconceivable.
Therefore, upon hearing a Buddha’s name even once—regardless of whether one possesses a focused mind or not, or whether one has faith or not—all [hearers] achieve [the goal].

If this is true even for those with the conditions of the seeds [of enlightenment], how much more so for the Buddha, who delivers sentient beings without weariness toward enemies or kin? If one merely hears his name, he will surely protect and mind them;

why then should there be any doubt? However, according to the *Vajraśekhara Tri-śāstra*, it is bodhisattvas whose roots are matured who are protected and minded by the Buddha, situated at the stage of the distinct ground (*bhūmi*) or the perfect dwelling (*pariniṣṭhita-vihāra*).
This is because, relying on their own power, they must enter the nature of co-arising (*sahaja-gotra*) before they can be protected and minded. Now, we rely on the power of others...
By virtue of this power, those at a similar stage immediately receive protective mindfulness; even those at stages lower than that likewise possess the principle of universal protective mindfulness.
Down to the point of hearing the Buddha’s name but once, there is a power of inspiration within the dharmatā of identical essence.
One will also obtain the distant cause and shall never regress. *Anuttara* means "unsurpassed.

*Samyak-saṃbodhi* means "perfectly equal and perfect enlightenment," which is the fruit-enlightenment of the Mahāyāna. The threefold non-regression in its perfection is another name for attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime;
therefore, it is urged that Śāriputra and others should all believe and accept this. Such is the merit of hearing the name.
Thus it is. Śākyamuni and all the Buddhas of the ten directions have proclaimed this in unison; how could one not believe it? This concludes the first section:
Encouraging Faith and Circulation. II. Encouraging Aspiration and Circulation.
Śāriputra, if there are those who have already made a vow, are now making a vow, or will make a vow,
desiring to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, all such persons shall attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Whether they have already been born, are currently being born, or will be born in that land, for this reason, Śāriputra—
"Whosoever among sons and daughters of good family has faith should make a vow to be born in that land.

Those who have already vowed have already been born; those who vow now will be born now; and those who shall vow shall be born then. This clearly demonstrates that the vows made based on faith are never in vain.
Without faith, one cannot make a vow; without a vow, faith does not lead to birth [in that land]. Therefore, it says "If..."
Those who possess faith should make a vow. Furthermore, a vow is the warrant for faith and the pivot of practice;
it is an especially vital matter. When one raises a vow, faith and practice are contained within it. This is why I have earnestly exhorted you three times.
Moreover, the aspiration to be born in that land constitutes the two gates of joy and revulsion: revulsion toward Saṃsāra (Sahā) and reliance upon the two truths of Suffering and its Origin.

It is associated with two kinds of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). Because it is associated with the two kinds of great vows—those arising from the aspiration to seek Sukhāvatī and those arising from the two truths of cessation and the path (*mārga-nirodha-satya*)—one attains non-retrogression on the path to Great Bodhi. Question:

When making a vow now, one should simply say "I shall be born [there]. Why is it called "being born in this life"? Answer: This also has two meanings. First, regarding a single lifetime (*eka-janman*):...

"Name-Now" (ming jin) means that by making vows and holding the Name in this present life, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land at the time of death. Second, regarding "Name-Now" in terms of *kṣaṇa* (moments):
with one thought-moment of resonance, one is born in one thought-moment; with every successive thought-moment of resonance, one is born in every successive thought-moment.

This wondrous cause and wondrous fruit are not separate from the single mind, just as the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale are simultaneous. Why wait for the exhaustion of retribution in Saṃsāra before [attaining birth]?
The Pool of Nurtured Treasures. Now, by means of faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name, the lotus buds will attain glory and the shadow of the Golden Terrace will appear;
one is then no longer a person within the realm of Saṃsāra. This is the ultimate perfection and the ultimate suddenness—difficult to discuss and difficult to conceive.

Only those of great wisdom can truly believe it. △ Third, the exhortation to practice and circulate [the teaching] has two parts: first, the praise by all Buddhas; second, the conclusion by the Master.
[The Buddha] sighed. Now, first:
"Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable merit of all Buddhas, so too do those Buddhas praise my own inconceivable merit, saying: 'The Buddha Śākyamuni...'"
They are able to perform what is most difficult and rare: to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within the five turbidities of this Sahā world—
the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life—
and to preach for the sake of all sentient beings this Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
Although the merit and wisdom of all Buddhas are equal, there are differences in the ease or difficulty of their transformative teachings.
It is easy to attain enlightenment in a Pure Land, but difficult in a defiled world. It is easy to preach the Dharma for sentient beings in a Pure Land, but difficult for those in a defiled world.
Even for sentient beings in a defiled world, it is relatively easy to teach the gradual Dharma, but difficult to teach the sudden Dharma. For the sake of sentient beings in a defiled world...
It is relatively easy for sentient beings to speak of other sudden teachings; however, it is even more difficult to speak of the Pure Land teaching of horizontal transcendence, a sudden method.

For it is already no small matter to teach sentient beings of this degenerate age the wondrous contemplation of sudden cultivation and sudden realization through the horizontal transcendence of the Pure Land.

To speak of this—which requires no arduous labor of cultivation and realization, but allows one to ascend directly to the stage of non-retrogression simply by holding the Name—is truly extraordinary, supreme, and wondrous.

This supreme skillful means transcends all thought; it is the most difficult among the difficult. Therefore, among the Buddhas of the ten directions, there is none who does not extol me, Śākyamuni, as being uniquely courageous.
Regarding the "Dust of the Kalpa" (kalpa-kaṣāya): it is a time when defiled dharmas gather together.

Within such a kalpa-dust, one cannot cross over unless one practices the path of transverse emergence beyond karmic constraints. Regarding the "Dust of Views" (dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya): the five... [text fragment]

The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) increase and flourish, namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Because they are dark, obscure, and submerged, they are called "turbidity. Within this turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*), one cannot cross over without relying on skillful means.

As for the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*), the five dull secondary afflictions increase and flourish, namely: greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), and [doubt].

Because doubt, affliction, agitation, and turmoil cause confusion, they are called "turbidity. Within the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), it is not that the ordinary mind itself is the practice of the Buddha-mind;

one must necessarily transcend them. As for the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*): one perceives that the coarse and inferior five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) produced by afflictions are combined and given the provisional name "sentient being.
Since both their physical form and their mind are base and deficient, it is called "turbidity. This is the turbidity of sentient beings.
Within the age of turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*), those whose conduct is neither joyful nor loathing cannot cross over.
Those in the turbidity of life have both cause and effect that are inferior; their lifespans are short, not even reaching a hundred years. Therefore, it is called "turbidity.

Within this turbidity of life, one cannot cross over without spending eons of time and without practicing a path of diligent effort. Furthermore, it is solely through this adornment of faith and aspiration—first...
Reciting "Amitābha Buddha" once transforms the turbidity of the kalpa into a pure sea assembly; transforms the turbidity of views into immeasurable light;
transforms the turbidity of afflictions into the light of eternal tranquility; transforms the turbidity of sentient beings into birth by transformation within lotus flowers;
and transforms the turbidity of lifespan into immeasurable longevity. Therefore, a single recitation of "Amitābha Buddha" is the fundamental teaching of Śākyamuni, the Original Teacher.

The Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained in this world of the five turbidities is now bestowed in its entirety as a realized fruit upon sentient beings in this turbid and evil age. This is the sphere of practice of all Buddhas;
it can be fully exhausted only by a Buddha communicating with a Buddha. It is not something that the nine realms can believe or understand through their own power. O sentient beings!

The former refers specifically to those of the five turbidities and evil persons; the latter refers universally to the four lands—the vessel world (*bhājanaloka*) and the nine realms of the sentient world (*sattvaloka*)—within all worlds.

△ Second, the conclusion and praise by the Master of the Teaching. The previous exhortation to believe and propagate [the teaching] was the entrustment of all Buddhas; this [exhortation] is that of the Original Teacher.
Regarding the entrustment (*parindanā*): while the specific wording of the instructions varies slightly, they generally refer to "all worldly beings.
This is just as the previous Buddhas addressed "you, all sentient beings"; one should understand that Mañjuśrī, Kāśyapa, and others are all included within this entrustment.
Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of the five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task:
having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I preach this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of all the world. This is truly most difficult.
The single practice of upholding the Name with faith and aspiration does not involve worldly activities, yet it revolves perfectly within the five turbidities. Only through faith can one enter;

it is not a realm traversed by discursive thought. Had it not been for the Original Teacher coming into this evil world to manifest the attainment of Bodhi, and seeing, teaching, and proclaiming this practice through his great wisdom and great compassion, by what means could sentient beings have received it? Nevertheless...
We dwell amidst the turbidity of the kalpa; we are certainly confined by time and oppressed by suffering. We dwell amidst the turbidity of views; we are certainly entangled by false wisdom.
We dwell amidst the turbidity of afflictions; we are certainly mired in craving and stung by evil karma.
We dwell amidst the turbidity of sentient beings; we are certainly settled in foulness and impurity, unable to...
One awakens to this truth, yet remains complacent in one's own inferiority and weakness, unable to exert oneself toward flight [from suffering].
Dwelling amidst the defilements of existence, one is inevitably swallowed by impermanence; like a spark from a stone or a flash of lightning, there is no time to react.

If one does not deeply realize the extreme difficulty of this situation, one will falsely assume there are other methods for escaping the turbulent house of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Thus, frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) abounds; only through profound [insight]...
Knowing it to be exceedingly difficult, one is only then willing to die in order to exhaust the thieving mind and treasure this single practice.

This is why our Original Teacher spoke of its extreme difficulty with his whole mouth and gave such profound instructions; we should understand this. The first part, the general exhortation, is concluded.
△ Second, the concluding exhortation.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, and others—
hearing what the Buddha had said, rejoiced, accepted it with faith, paid homage, and departed.
This Dharma-gate is inconceivable; it is difficult to believe and difficult to know, such that not a single person was able to pose a question.

The Buddha’s wisdom discerns the capacities of beings, and knowing that the conditions for the assembly to attain Buddhahood have ripened, he speaks spontaneously without being asked, so as to bring about four benefits.

Like the transformation brought by a timely rain, they rejoice; they derive benefit from the *loka-prasiddha-tantra* (the standpoint of worldly convention). To be free of all doubt is called "faith" (*śraddhā*); it is the act of receiving and internalizing [the teaching].

"Non-forgetfulness" is called *vedanā* (reception). From this, one gains benefit as an antidote to being human. "Casting oneself down in refuge" means entering into the *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination;

this is called "prostration. From this, one gains benefit from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). However, within each individual benefit, all four benefits are mutually present; this is merely a provisional distinction.
The above constitutes the four benefits of self-practice, which for the time being ensure non-retrogression. [This is] the retribution.
The flow of grace circulates; it is called "departing" because it continues until the end of the future limit, inexhaustibly benefiting others through the four benefits of transformation.

As the Sūtra says: "In the age of the Dharma-ending period, among billions upon billions of people who practice, scarcely one attains the Way; only by relying on the mindfulness of the Buddha do they attain deliverance."
Alas! Now is precisely the time for this. Were one to abandon this inconceivable Dharma-gate, how could one possibly attain excellence?

When I, Xu, first entered the monastic life, I prided myself on the School of the Ultimate Vehicle (Zongmen) and held the scriptural teachings (Jiaodian) in contempt, falsely claiming that the practice of chanting the Name was intended only for those of middling or inferior capacity.

Later, due to a severe illness, I resolved to return to the West [to seek the Dharma]. Thereupon, I again studied the *Miaozong chao*, the two commentaries on the *Yuanzhong lun* (*Yuanzhong shu* and *Zhongguan shu*), and the works of Master Yunqi.
Having consulted such works as the *Qishu chao*, I have finally come to realize that the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation is truly the unsurpassed king of jewels.

Only then did I dare to set my heart upon it with total resolve, holding fast to the Name so firmly that ten thousand oxen could not turn me back. My friend Qubing has long been devoted to the practice of Pure Land;
wishing to make the essential meaning of this sutra clear and radiant without excessive verbiage, he requested that I compose a brief commentary for him. I, for my part, desired—
That all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm may be born together in Sukhāvatī is a principle that cannot be overturned.
I began writing this on the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month of the Dinghai year and completed the draft on the fifth day of the tenth month; it was finished in nine days.
May every single phrase and every single word serve as a provision for the path, and may all who see or hear it attain the stage of non-retrogression. Whether through faith or doubt—
All shall plant the seeds of the Way; those who praise or revile alike shall attain liberation. I reverently entreat all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to accept me with their compassion and bear witness.
May my fellow students and friends rejoice in this and grant their blessings. This concludes the postscript, written by the monk Ouyi Zhixu of the West, at the age of forty-nine.
The Original Postscript to the Essential Explanation of the Buddha-spoken Amitābha Sūtra states:
The sūtra says, "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. An ancient said, "Meditate on the Amitābha of one's own nature, and you shall be born [in the Pure Land]."

"The Land of Purity is Mind-Only. When one contemplates this in conjunction [with other teachings], the meaning becomes clear: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha"; that outside the mind there is no Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no mind.

Later generations failed to understand this. They abandoned the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to speak separately of a "Land of Purity that is Mind-Only," and they abandoned the World-Honored One of Compassion endowed with myriad virtues to speak separately of a "Maitreya of Self-Nature. Is this not nearly [the same as] seeking outside the mind?
Is there a mind outside of the Buddhas? The Great Master Lingfeng deeply realized that the essence of the nature of mind has nothing external to it;

he specifically extracted the essential commentary for this sutra. Upon opening and reading it once, those who possess faith, aspiration, and the name [of the Buddha] may personally hold their own warrant.
Not only are the words concise and the meaning comprehensive, but it also causes this rare and most difficult school to appear as if it were manifest before one's eyes.
The sounds of drums and gongs resounded as the entire treasury of scriptures was opened, with nothing remaining hidden away; this is truly something unprecedented in the annals of past and present.

It is titled *Yaojie* (Essential Explanations); could this not indeed be the supreme essence of the mind? I, Zhengzhi Qubing, a disciple of the Pure Land school from ancient Wu, respectfully record this.

Master Jue has now revealed his heart and soul in this translation. Indeed, the treasury of secrets is destined to be opened wide in this present age;

Preface: I have heard that to have practice without the teachings inevitably carries the peril of falling into pits and ravines; yet to have the teachings...
To practice without [adhering to] the teachings would be like the proverb of "counting jewels while eating one's meal. Therefore, the teaching is itself practice, and practice is itself the teaching.
When teaching and practice do not diverge, the ultimate principle is revealed. Thus, teaching, practice, and principle—these three—are all called "sūtras.
When these three sūtras are complete, it is the Buddha’s teaching; to the contrary, it is the teaching of Pāpīyas, not the Buddha’s teaching.

I now receive this teaching and respectfully present the *Wǎngshēng Jìngtǔ Chàn Yuàn Yí* (Ritual for the Vows and Repentance of Rebirth in the Pure Land) and the *Juéyí Xíngyuàn Èrmén* (Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Cultivating Practices),
both composed by the Compassionate Cloud Repentance Master Zūnshì, following them after the *Mítuó Yàojiě* (Essential Explanation of Amitābha).
After the practitioner has attained the essential point, if they can further devote their whole heart to this,
then this inconceivable King of Sutras will not only be free of superfluous words, but its meaning will no longer be a mere path of concepts; rather,
the subtle and wondrous essential exposition will reside not in the Buddha, nor in a spiritual teacher, but in the person themselves, according to their own practice of the teachings.

One approaches the depth or shallowness of accord with principle; according to the depth or shallowness of this accord with principle, the distinctions among the stages of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) are established.

Yet these distinguished stages of fruition all necessarily involve the perfect realization of the three non-regressions (*avaivartika*), and in a single lifetime, they collectively enter the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.
Therefore, difference is itself non-difference, and sequential positions are themselves not sequential positions. Who would say there is "one"?
Beyond the practice of samādhi, there is a further matter pertaining to the Dharmakāya. This practice is the most vast; other practices are limited. This practice is the most swift and miraculous;
other practices are sluggish [the characters *tai* and *ti* both have the pinyin *tì*; it means to be obstructed or stagnant]. This practice is the most inconceivable;
other practices can be compared or measured against it. For this reason, it is called the "Treasury King of Samādhis."

Indeed. The *Xingyuan yi* (Ritual of Vows and Practices) is traditionally known as the Great Sūtra on the Repentance for Rebirth in the Pure Land. The ritual methods within its two sections are traditionally known as the Small Sūtra on the Repentance for Rebirth in the Pure Land.

Furthermore, the ten recitations at dawn, the practice of binding the mind to the object, and the two practices of the multitude of blessings—all these are indispensable for those who cultivate the path of the Pure Land.
The former [the *Xingyuan yi*] was composed by [Tan]luan, while the latter [the *Jingtu wangsheng zhuan*] was described by [Dao]cho.
In the future, how could we ever dare to abandon ourselves? *The Ritual for Repentance and Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land* (Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zunshe,

Tracing the origin [of this teaching], we see that the Buddhas, out of compassion for beings who are deluded and blind, have established many skillful means to guide and lead them.
Yet, the practice of the Pure Land through pure karma is the most direct and straightforward; all Mahāyāna sūtras proclaim this essential point.

Whether they be bhikṣus of the fourfold assembly or virtuous men and women—whether their faculties are impaired or complete—if they wish to swiftly shatter the darkness of ignorance and seek to extinguish the five heinous crimes, [they should take up this path].
Regarding the ten evil acts, transgressions of prohibitions, grave offenses, and other minor faults, one desires to restore both the major and minor precepts;
to attain the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) in the present life and to be fully endowed with all the bodhisattva gates of the pāramitās;

and at the time of death, to be free from all fears, with body and mind peaceful, comfortable, and joyful as if returning home, while light illuminates the dwelling and extraordinary fragrances and sounds arise.
One will joyfully behold Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing before one.

They shall escort one upon a purple-golden pedestal, extending their hands to receive and guide one across the five realms of existence and through the nine grades of rebirth. One shall cast off feverish affliction and find rest in cool serenity;

having first departed from worldly toil, one immediately reaches the stage of non-retrogression. Without passing through long kalpas, one attains the realization of non-arising. If one wishes to cultivate even a small portion of the Dharma—
They receive wondrous retribution; the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously praise them and bestow predictions of enlightenment before their very eyes.

In a single thought-moment, they make offerings to countless Buddhas and immediately return to their own lands to sit and eat with Amitābha. They engage in discourse with Avalokiteśvara and walk alongside Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Their vision penetrates all and their hearing is thorough; the dimensions of their bodies are boundless. They travel freely through the air, possess clear knowledge of their past lives, and perceive everywhere.
The five realms of existence are like reflections in a mirror; in every thought-moment, one realizes the inexhaustible samādhi.
Such descriptions could never be fully exhausted. One should practice this sublime Dharma; all that has been spoken is true and not false.
The Buddhas of the ten directions extend their broad and long tongues to praise this matter, thereby demonstrating its truthfulness.
How could we dare not believe the Buddha? We now establish these ritual practices based on the various sūtras concerning the Pure Land;
for those who wish to know them in detail, they may consult the sūtras for further benefit. For now, I shall explain them according to ten categories.
First, to adorn and purify the site of enlightenment, select a secluded and quiet hall or room and remove the old earth. In a clean place, take fresh soil free of tiles and stones to fill the ground.
Anoint it with fragrant paste until it is utterly pure. Above, suspend a new jeweled canopy; from within the canopy, hang five...

Various banners: hang silk streamers and flowered banners throughout the room (as there are no other offerings of playthings). Select fine ornaments and install the Buddha image facing east, seated in the west.
Avalokiteśvara attends to the left, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta attends to the right. Before the images, arrange various excellent flowers, lotuses, and the like.
It is best to install nine images of those destined for rebirth; however, it is not a hindrance if they are absent. Other matters of adornment follow.

Arrange them according to one’s capacity (ensuring they are in accordance with the Dharma and treated with gravity). Spread mats and seats all around, mindful of low-lying or damp ground (as there is no mention of *kūṭha* rugs;

this is because the *Buddhottamasiddhi Sūtra* prohibits them). The practitioner must wear fresh and clean robes; if none are available, one should wash and dye the upper garment worn next to the body.

Only after bathing and donning these should one enter the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*). When entering or exiting through the side entrances on the left and right of the door, one’s shoes and sandals must be kept orderly and neat.
It is chaotic. When going there, one must change into old clothes. After bathing—where "bathing" refers to washing the head, face, neck, and arms afterward—one puts on clean clothes;
this is to be done daily in this manner. One should exhaustively provide various offerings to the Triple Gem.

If one does not give all that one possesses, the practice of the Dharma will not be single-minded and there will certainly be no response or descent [of blessings]. Only when one has nothing left of one's own may one seek from others.

(Alternatively, if the fruit lacks its own substance, and if the fruit is not something that can be sought, then there is no fault even if one lacks various offerings. When ten people have returned, more than that is not permissible;
it is appropriate to begin on a six-fast day (*ṣaḍvarṣā*).

Second, regarding the method of skillful means for entering the *maṇḍala*: if the body and mind are distracted, one must first practice preparatory skillful means. One should prepare a separate room for seven days that is not in the same location as the *maṇḍala*.
If there is no separate building, it is permitted to share a single chamber; day and night, one should train and test oneself according to the prescribed rules.

Furthermore, they recited the texts for the five repentances and other liturgies with such extreme proficiency and mastery that all other activities—dyeing, washing, sewing, and miscellaneous household affairs—were immediately suspended.
They focused their thoughts solely on being born in the Pure Land before long. With single-minded devotion, they sought repentance without hindrance;
each set a specific deadline for themselves, disregarding even their own bodies and lives, determined to achieve the pure karma of rebirth in that very moment.
One must not entertain a single thought of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Reprove and cast away craving and desire; diligently pacify anger and delusion.

Each practitioner possesses beginningless evil habits; one should swiftly seek to abandon them and not engage in them. When practicing right repentance for obstacles, one should observe which habit is most predominant.
Reprove and discard it, then balance and harmonize them so that they are restored to equilibrium, ensuring that the practice of the Dharma does not result in wasted effort.

Regarding the third stage, the "Proper Cultivation of Intention" (*samyak-prayoga-citta*), there are three periods: the Great Assembly of Seven-Seven-Day Periods, the King Drum-Sound Great Amitābha’s ten days and ten nights, and the Sixteen Contemplations of the Lesser Amitābha’s seven days and seven nights.
One should adopt these three levels as the duration; they must absolutely not be reduced. This is the "Proper Cultivation of Intention."

Regarding this, those who achieve the five gates of mindfulness through the faith described in Vasubandhu’s treatise will ultimately attain birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss and behold Amitābha Buddha.
These are: first, the gate of prostration; second, the gate of praise; third, the gate of making vows; fourth, the gate of contemplation;
and fifth, the gate of dedication. "Dedication" refers to the merit and goodness accumulated through acts such as prostration.
Through skillful means of dedication based on the faculties, one attains three types of gates conducive to enlightenment:
first, the undefiled pure mind, because one does not seek various pleasures for oneself; second, the peaceful pure mind, because one uproots the suffering of all sentient beings;
and third, the joyful pure mind, because one causes all sentient beings to attain great enlightenment through gathering them [into the path].
Because sentient beings are born into that land, I shall take the treatise in its entirety as the primary intent here.
However, I have added the practice of repentance to eliminate obstacles to rebirth, so as to accord with the Buddha’s compassion and swiftly deliver sentient beings.

Whether sitting or walking, do not allow the mind to become distracted. One must not, even for the duration of a finger-snap, think of the five worldly desires or engage in conversation, chatter, or laughter with outsiders.
One should not use excuses to delay practice, nor indulge in negligence or sleep.

Rather, one should maintain an uninterrupted focus of mindfulness with every breath and movement, practicing with single-minded diligence to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. Question: Since the practices are so numerous, how [should one proceed]?

What is single-mindedness? Answer: There is single-mindedness in principle (*li*) and single-mindedness in phenomena (*shi*). This means that when one engages with worldly affairs at the site of practice (*daochang*), all things are without intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing;
they share the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), in accordance with the conditions of the Dharma-realm—this is called single-mindedness in principle.

When prostrating to the Buddha, not thinking of other matters but focusing solely on prostrating to the Buddha, and likewise when reciting sutras or practicing the Way, this is called single-mindedness in phenomena.

"For the sake of sentient beings, I have resolved to attain Bodhicitta and seek the Pure Land; therefore, I universally prostrate to the Triple Gem and extensively cultivate offerings. With all reverence, single-mindedly prostrate to the Buddhas who eternally abide throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm (when performing this general prostration, there is no need to visualize them according to specific directions; as you bow down, form this mental visualization):

One’s own body and the true reality-body (*dharmatā-kāya*) of all Buddhas of the ten directions are fundamentally devoid of subject and object. Therefore, there is neither one who worships nor one who is worshipped. Contemplating this absence of subject and object is called the "Ocean of the Dharma Realm. May all sentient beings see and enter it together.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the eternally abiding Dharma of the ten directions and the dharma realm (visualize as above).

With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the eternally abiding Sangha of the ten directions and the dharma realm (when visualizing, change "all Buddhas" to "sages and saints"). [After prostrating, kneel with palms joined and hold flowers. The leader addresses the assembly:]
All these assemblies, each kneeling in turn, solemnly holding incense and flowers, make offerings according to the Dharma.

The Eighth: The Method of Repentance and Vow (There are five methods in total; here, citing the first and the last, the method of repentance and vow is explained). First, Clarifying Repentance:

Repentance involves both the phenomenal and the noumenal, which should be practiced in tandem. Phenomenally, one exhausts the three karmas without sparing body or life, shedding blood and tears like rain to lay bare the roots of transgression, never daring to conceal or deny them.

Noumenally, one contemplates the true mark of transgression, wherein both the one who repents and that which is repented of are entirely quiescent, as explained at length elsewhere. Having understood the phenomenal and the noumenal, one should with an impartial mind universally repent on behalf of all beings.
Contemplation on the Clouds:
"I and all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been constantly obstructed by the heavy offenses of the three karmas and six sense organs.

We have failed to see the Buddhas and do not know the essential way out. We merely follow the cycle of birth and death and do not understand the wondrous principle. Although I now know this, I am still [bound] together with all others."

Sentient beings are equally obstructed by all manner of grave transgressions. Now, before Amitābha and the Buddhas of the ten directions, we universally take refuge and repent on behalf of all sentient beings.
We pray only that you will grant your protection so that these obstructions may be extinguished. (Having visualized this, say:)

For the sake of all sentient beings throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*, I vow that they shall all sever the three obstructions. With utmost sincerity, I repent. (Hold the incense burner and strike it downward. Contemplate the ten minds of reversal and conformity.

Initially turning one's back on the True and pursuing the deluded is called the ten minds of conformity; now, turning one's back on the deluded and facing toward the True is called the ten minds of reversal.
One should contemplate these carefully in terms of both phenomena and principle. From the beginning up to "denying cause and effect" constitutes conformity.)

The following is the inverse [order]. When arriving at the time for the formal confession (*pratikramana*), one must likewise support this sense of the inverse and the conforming [order]. (Visualize as follows:
"From beginningless time until now, I and all sentient beings, due to craving and views, have internally reckoned a self and persons, and externally added evil [to them]."
Friend, he does not rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of another’s virtue; instead, he extensively commits grave offenses through all three karmas.
Although his actions are not numerous, his evil intent is pervasive, continuing day and night without interruption.
He conceals his faults and does not wish for others to know them. Fearing neither the miserable realms nor possessing shame or remorse, he denies the existence of cause and effect.
Therefore, on this day, I deeply believe in cause and effect; I give rise to profound shame and remorse, and I give rise to great fear.
I reveal and repent my transgressions, severing the continuity of such thoughts. I resolve to attain Bodhicitta, abandoning evil and cultivating goodness.
Diligently exerting oneself in the three types of action to reverse the grave transgressions of the past; rejoicing in even a hair’s breadth of virtue performed by ordinary beings or sages;

and recollecting that the Buddhas of the ten directions possess great merit and wisdom, capable of rescuing and delivering myself and all sentient beings from the ocean of the two deaths and establishing us on the shore of the three virtues.
Since beginningless time, I have failed to realize that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent, and have extensively committed manifold evils. Now...
Knowing emptiness and stillness, for the sake of seeking Bodhi and for the sake of sentient beings, I extensively cultivate all virtues and universally sever all evils.
I only pray that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the World-Honored One Amitābha will compassionately accept me and grant me leave to repent.

Having thus reflected, [I, disciple] (so-and-so), repent with a sincere heart. The Buddhas of the ten directions truly see and know that my own nature and that of all sentient beings are fundamentally pure.
The dwelling place of the Buddhas is called the Light of Eternal Quiescence (*nitya-śānti-prabhā*), which pervades every moment and all things.
The Dharma. Yet I do not understand it, falsely imagining a self and persons; within the Dharma of equality, I give rise to discrimination;
within the pure mind, I produce defiled attachment. Due to these inverted causes and conditions of the five desires, I circulate through birth and death, traversing the three realms.
Seated upon this continuity, I do not contemplate the time of liberation, and furthermore, I create extremely evil karma therein. 4.

They commit the five heinous crimes and are icchantikas; they revile and slander the Mahāyāna, disparage and destroy the Triple Gem, deny the existence of all Buddhas, sever their study of Prajñāpāramitā, misappropriate the property of the Sangha of the ten directions, misappropriate the property of Buddha-stūpas, defile those who practice the pure life, and habitually associate with evil dharmas.

They mutually praise and protect those who violate the precepts; they revile practitioners of the Three Vehicles in various ways; they conceal their internal faults while externally manifesting dignified deportment;
they constantly use the five types of improper means to solicit the four requisites; they preach the Dharma with impurity and instruct others in what is contrary to the Vinaya.
Having left the household life because of the Buddha, they instead destroy the Buddha-dharma; they oppose their teachers and elders, disregarding their lawful instructions;

they act wantonly out of greed and anger, devoid of shame or remorse. By these causes and conditions, through the power of such evil karma, at the end of their lives they shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
Amidst the blazing of fierce fires, they undergo immeasurable suffering; for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, there is no prospect of liberation.

Only now do they begin to realize this and give rise to great shame and profound fear. The World-Honored Ones of the ten directions and Amitābha Buddha have long since conceived great compassion for me.
For countless kalpas past, in order to deliver me, they have cultivated the Bodhisattva path without sparing their own bodies.
Life. Now that you have attained Buddhahood with the fulfillment of great compassion, you are truly able to provide protection and refuge for all.

As I have committed evil deeds, I am certain to fall into the three miserable realms; I pray that you will arise in pity and accept my repentance, so that my heavy offenses may be extinguished and all evils eliminated, until the causes for rebirth in this Sahā world are forever exhausted, and I may be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas according to my wish. At the moment of death—
At that time, there is no obstruction whatsoever. (Rising, say:
Having completed the repentance, I take refuge in and pay homage to Amitābha Buddha and all the Triple Gem. (Prostrate three times on the ground, performing the triple prostration:

Second, the explanation of the exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*). (Visualize yourself kneeling before all the Buddhas of the ten directions and making the exhortation. The World-Honored One’s intention also lies in preaching the Dharma. With the power of their Dharma-eye, the Buddhas of the ten directions know my exhortation and request: "We pray that you will abide long and turn the wheel of the True Dharma; wherever you may be born, may you always be able to accept our requests.

I now entreat you all to turn the unsurpassed, wondrous wheel of Dharma. If the Buddhas...
When he intends to manifest parinirvāṇa, I shall with all sincerity entreat him, praying only that he remain for as many eons as there are motes of dust in a buddha-field,

Rejoicing in the Essence of the Threefold Knowledge (The merit of even a single hair’s breadth of goodness performed by ordinary or noble beings throughout the ten directions—I too rejoice in it. May these roots of goodness and merit cause those who see them to give rise to joy;

The Fourth: The Dedication of Merit (Dedicating every iota of merit from the beginningless past until now toward the three realms of existence; therefore, I now repent and vow to seek Bodhi). I, [Name], disciple, with a sincere heart, dedicate all roots of goodness:
the merit of prostrations, praises, and offerings; the request for the Buddhas to remain in the world and turn the wheel of Dharma;
and the merit of sympathetic joy and repentance. I dedicate these to all sentient beings and to the path of Buddhahood.
Having performed the dedication, take refuge in and pay homage to Amitābha Buddha and all the Triple Gem.

Formulate the aspiration for the five knowledges (in general, this must involve the extinguishing of sins and the removal of obstacles, supporting the Four Great Vows, rejoicing in Bodhi, and forming the thought of seeking birth in the Pure Land,

I, [Name], disciple, make this vow with a sincere heart: may all the various virtues produced by the three karmas of myself and my fellow practitioners of purity adorn this pure vow. May merit and wisdom manifest before me.
May the World-Honored Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta compassionately accept me, appearing in person for my sake, emitting pure light to illuminate my faculties.
The two obstacles are pacified and eliminated; one delights in cultivating pure conduct, and both body and mind are moistened with clarity.

In every thought-moment, one does not lose the roots of goodness for the Pure Land, and within dreams, one constantly beholds the various wondrous adornments of that land. This brings comfort and joy to my heart, causing me to give rise to diligence.
I vow that at the time of death, I shall know in advance that the moment has arrived; all hindrances will be completely removed, and wisdom and mindfulness will increase in clarity.
With no physical illness or mental distress, and with a mind free from delusion, one will behold Amitābha Buddha and his retinue face-to-face, filled with joy and happiness.

In a single kṣaṇa, one attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). Upon arrival, one sees for oneself that one has been born within a lotus flower and receives a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) from the Buddha.
Having received this prophecy, one gains mastery over manifesting transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) in as many buddha-fields as there are atoms of dust, acting in accordance with sentient beings.

May my birth be for the benefit of others; may I cause sentient beings as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field to resolve upon bodhicitta, and may they simultaneously leave suffering behind and together be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

May such practices and vows manifest before me in every thought-moment, continuing without interruption until the end of the future, and may my actions of body, speech, and mind constantly perform the work of the Buddha. (Thus making this vow)

One should give rise to right practice and fulfill it completely. There are three different ways of reciting [the precepts]. (The first four involve repentance according to the occasion, whether extensive or concise).
Having made the vow, one takes refuge in and pays homage to Amitābha Buddha and all the Triple Gem.

Homage to the Noble Assembly. (The leader kneels and says:)
I address the assembly: listen to these verses of the Tathāgata from the sutra.
Why do you not strive to do good? Contemplate the naturalness of the Way. Each of you should be diligent and energetic; exert yourselves to seek it for yourselves.
You will surely attain transcendence and be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, crossing directly over the five evil paths.
The evil realms naturally close, and the path to ascent is without end. It is easy to travel, yet no one does;
why not abandon worldly affairs? Diligently practice to seek the Way and its Virtue, so that each may attain ultimate longevity and life-joy without end.
The tenth method of sitting in meditation:
one should sit at a single location on a rope-couch facing west, because this facilitates visualization and symbolizes the correct direction.
Sit upright in the full lotus posture with the neck and spine aligned, neither leaning back nor hunching forward. Regulate the breath and settle the mind; then, observe.

Although there are many gateways [to visualization], I shall now briefly indicate two types based on essential and easy-to-visualize methods, according to what is appropriate for each individual; these need not necessarily be used together.
Those who have already become proficient in other visualizations may proceed as they wish, provided they do not depart from the Pure Land—all such practices should be cultivated.

As for the two types mentioned: first is the "Universal Observation of the Mental Image," which is the practice undertaken at this very moment; by calculating its merit, one will surely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
In that world, he immediately gives rise to the thought of being there. Within a lotus flower, he sits in the full lotus posture.

rather, let the breath reach its natural limit as the measure. The sound should be neither too high nor too low, neither too slow nor too hurried, but maintained in perfect equilibrium.
In the interim, the ten breaths are linked together to prevent the mind from scattering; applying oneself with single-minded diligence in this manner is what is called "ten recitations.
This is to rely upon the breath to bind the mind. Having performed these recitations, one makes a vow and dedicates the merit, saying:
I, [Name], disciple of the Buddha, single-mindedly take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. May his pure light illuminate me;

May these ten recitations enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows; by riding upon the power of the Buddha’s compassion, may all my transgressions be extinguished and purified.

In a single thought-moment, one will be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Upon the blossoming of the lotus flower, one shall behold the Buddha, immediately hear the Buddha-vehicle, and suddenly open the wisdom of the Buddhas.

Regarding the gate of binding the object of focus: whether in public affairs or private life, throughout one's daily activities and engagements, even in moments of haste, one should never forget the Buddha nor lose sight of the Pure Land.
Just as one’s mind is bound to a pressing matter, one should maintain this secret recollection even while performing various tasks.

The preceding practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is also like this. If one loses mindfulness, one repeatedly gathers it back; after a long time, it becomes one's nature, and one constantly remembers it spontaneously.

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "For example, there are two people: one is single-mindedly intent on remembering [the other] (analogous to the Buddha mindful of sentient beings), and the other is single-mindedly intent on forgetting [him] (analogous to sentient beings mindful of the Buddha).
These two people may encounter each other and yet not encounter each other, or see each other and yet not see each other. Thus it is with these two people.
Their mutual remembrance is deep and profound; thus it continues from birth to birth, like a form and its shadow, never diverging.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. Yet if the child runs away, what can the mother’s remembrance do?
If the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers him, then mother and child will not be separated throughout their successive lives.
[The Buddha is] far away. Yet, if sentient beings keep the Buddha in mind and recite His name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future;
they will not be far from the Buddha. Without relying on expedient means, their minds will spontaneously open. It is like a person who has been smeared with incense, whose body retains its fragrance.
By binding the mind in this way, one proceeds naturally, constantly warding off all evil thoughts. Even if one should wish to commit evil, because of the mindfulness of the Buddha—
Evil cannot be accomplished. Even when one follows evil and performs evil deeds, the mind remains constantly humble and soft; it is like a body with fragrance that naturally sheds its stench.
Furthermore, if one perceives the mind giving rise to even a slight evil thought, one immediately recollects the Buddha.
