they receive a Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), which is not a birth through the stages of segmentation (*bheda-utpāda*). Third, the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction is the dwelling place of exclusively Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas.

Having shattered ignorance (*avidyā*) and manifested the Dharma-nature, they attain the true fruit; yet, because their ignorance is not yet exhausted, it moistens their untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).

The Dharma-nature Reward Body (*dharmatā-niṣyanda-sambhogakāya*) is also called the Land of Fruitional Retribution (*vipākaphala-kṣetra*). This refers to what is stated in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing): "The Three Worthies and Ten Sages abide in the land of fruitional retribution.
Because one contemplates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), the resulting fruition is termed "real" (*satya*).
Because the cultivation of causes is not fixed and matter and mind are unimpeded, it is termed "unobstructed. This is the Indra’s Net world-system (*indrajāla-lokadhātu*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, regarding the fourth, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light: it is the principle of the *tathatā* dharma-realm illuminated by the ultimate wisdom of wondrous enlightenment;
this is termed a "land" (*kṣetra*) and is also called the "Dharmatā-body. It is simply the Buddha-nature of *tathatā*, which is neither body nor land, yet is spoken of as body and land.

Apart from the body there is no land, and apart from the land there is no body. To designate them as "body and land" is one phenomenon with two meanings. (From the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*).
The dwelling place of Vairocana is named "Eternal Quiescent Light" (Nityapraśāntaprabhā). The first two lands are *nirmāṇakāya* (response bodies); they are the abodes of the *nirmāṇabuddhas*.
The third is both *nirmāṇa* and *saṃbhoga* (recompense); it is the abode of the *saṃbhogabuddhas*. The fourth is solely true purity; it is neither *nirmāṇa* nor *saṃbhoga*;

it is the abode of the *dharmakāya*. "Eternal" (*nitya*) is the *dharmakāya*; "quiescent" (*praśānta*) is liberation (*vimukti*); "light" (*prabhā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). It is like the syllable *I* of the world.
The three points—neither vertical nor horizontal—are each individually named the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). It is the dwelling place where all Buddhas and Tathāgatas roam;

it is the ultimate, true, and eternal, and is the most supreme pure land. Viewed through the lens of the aforementioned three bodies and four lands, the lands as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions are solely the lands of my own mind.
The Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the three periods of time are solely the Buddhas of my own mind.
There is no land that is not established by my own mind; there is no Buddha who does not manifest from my own nature.
How could the Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond ten million *billion* worlds not be the Pure Land of the Mind-only?

Is the Teacher within that Land of Ultimate Bliss not the Amitābha of one's own original nature? Furthermore, this single mind alone encompasses the ten realms, such that body and land are interfused.

Layer upon layer, they are unimpeded. Furthermore, the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are without distinction. Sentient beings and Buddhas manifest within one another; every thought-moment intersects with every other. Therefore it is said:

"Within the minds of all Buddhas, sentient beings are in every atom of existence the Land of Ultimate Bliss; within the minds of sentient beings, all Buddhas are in every thought-moment Amitābha. It is also said:
"The pure and defiled lands of the ten directions are gathered and contained within a single kṣaṇa; the forms of a single thought-moment..."
The mind arrays itself, universally encompassing the entire dharma-realm; all is inherently and spontaneously present from the beginning, not newly formed through conditions.
As it is with a single thought-moment, so it is with a single speck of dust. Thus, within each and every speck of dust are all lands, and within each and every mind are all minds;
each mind and each speck of dust further interpenetrate one another, layer upon layer, infinitely and without obstruction, manifesting all at once and instantaneously.
It is neither hidden nor manifest; all things are perfectly accomplished, neither superior nor inferior. Thus, when the spirit migrates to billions of lands, it is truly born within one’s own mind.
How could the physical form be conceived within the nine lotuses and yet escape the span of a single *kṣaṇa*? It is further said: "The Land of Ultimate Bliss pervades all places;
taking up one part, the whole is contained within it. This is like the net of a thousand jewels atop Śakra’s palace, where the light and shadows of the thousand jewels enter [one another].

There is one jewel. The light and shadow of this one jewel pervade all thousand jewels. Although each jewel mutually pervades the others, this jewel cannot be that jewel, and that jewel cannot be this one;
they interpenetrate without being confused, and remain distinct without being divided. Each one manifests its universal presence, yet has no fixed location.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss is but one among these thousand jewels, and each of the ten million *koṭi* lands is likewise one of these thousand jewels.
First: From the beings of the three vehicles down to those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras, there is not one who is not a single bead within the thousand beads.
Amitābha Buddha likewise directly reveals one bead from among the thousand beads. To see one Buddha is to see all Buddhas of the ten directions;

it is also to see the sentient beings of the nine realms throughout the ten directions, the oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust, and the ten periods of time, past and present, all suddenly perfected within a single seal. There is no...
This applies to all other dharmas as well. Thus, it is not only in the various lands of Sukhāvatī; in every single atom, every atom is a Sukhāvatī that is solely mind-only.
Every atom is a Buddha, and every Buddha is the Amitābha of one’s own original nature.
These are the clear instructions successively propagated by the Buddhas, patriarchs, sages, and worthies above; how, then, can there be any doubt?
Question: Since the pure and the defiled are mutually integrated, such that every dust mote is a Land of Ultimate Bliss, why is it that only the Sahā world is defiled? Answer:

To the deluded karma and afflictions of ordinary beings, even the pure appears defiled; yet to the vision of the Buddha’s eye, all that is defiled is pure. How could the realm of Śākyamuni’s fruition-body be anything but pure?
Question: You have encompassed all things without exception; I believe that "Mind-Only" is vast indeed. It is perfectly interfused and unimpeded; I believe that "Mind-Only" is wondrous indeed.

Yet, why do you still remain mired in deluded emotions and fail to leave behind defiled karma? By what means can the land of Mind-Only be purified? Answer: When the mind is defiled, the land is defiled;
when the mind is pure, the land is pure. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "If one wishes to obtain a pure land, one should purify one's own mind."
Mind. According to the purity of one’s mind, so too is the Buddha-land pure. For one who purifies their own mind, there is no cultivation of a pure land;

what else could there be? Question: May I hear the details regarding the method for cultivating the Pure Land? Answer: There is no cultivation in the Pure Land; cultivation arises from the delusion of existence.
The Dharma has no high or low; high and low arise from the faculties [of sentient beings]. Since faculties vary in many ways, the categories of practice are likewise manifold.
To subsume these manifold types, there are generally three gates: first, visualization and contemplation (*guanxiang*); second, recollection (*yiniàn*); and third, various practices (*zhòngxíng*).

All of these take the Land of Ultimate Bliss and Amitābha as their primary focus. Regarding visualization and contemplation, the *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas are the body of the Dharma-realm; they enter into one..."
Within the mental conceptions of all sentient beings, when one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, that very mind is the thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary signs.
This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Tathāgatas’ correct and universal knowledge arises from the mind’s conception.
One should single-mindedly bind one's mindfulness and contemplate that Buddha with clarity. The Tiantai Commentary states: "The Dharma-realm body..."
This refers to the *dharmatā-kāya* (Dharma-nature body) of the Buddha. Because the minds of sentient beings are pure, the *dharmakāya* manifests with mastery; hence it is called "entering.
It is like the rising sun in the sky, its reflection appearing in a hundred rivers, illustrating that the Buddha-body possesses mastery and can manifest according to the objects before it.

Furthermore, the *dharmadhātu-kāya* is the Buddha-body; there is nowhere it does not pervade, as the *dharmadhātu* is its essence. By attaining this Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, one understands and enters [this state].
Because they correspond [to one another], it is said that "the mind enters into the Buddha. Regarding "this mind makes the Buddha": the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent;

because the mind is pure, he exists. Regarding "this mind is the Buddha": having heard that the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent, and that he exists because the mind is pure, one might then consider them to be entirely separate.

Therefore, it is said: "In the beginning of study, it is called 'making' (作); at the end of accomplishment, it is simply 'is' (即). The *Miaozongchao* states: "If one wishes to conceive of the Buddha’s body, one should..."

The essence of clear contemplation is the essence itself, which is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*). When it arises, it becomes the capacity for contemplation. Original enlightenment is the body of the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas;

there is no separate object of realization for a Buddha, for they fully realize the fundamental nature of sentient beings. If initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) exerts its function, original enlightenment then becomes manifest.
Therefore, it is said: "The *dharmakāya* arises from the mind and thoughts. Furthermore, Amitābha and all other Buddhas are one body and one wisdom.
The application is likewise so. The manifestation of Amitābha’s body is the bodies of all Buddhas; the clarity of the marks of all Buddhas is the essence of Amitābha.

Therefore, the general elucidation of all Buddhas serves as the essence of the visualization of Amitābha. From the passage "the Dharma-realm body" onwards, the explanation is given in terms of the mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus.

From the passage "furthermore, the Dharma-realm body" onwards, the explanation is given in terms of the correspondence between understanding and entry. Rongxin’s commentary states: "If there were no..."

Regarding the first interpretation: it is that contemplation is not the contemplation of the Buddha. If the second interpretation were absent, then the essence of the practitioner and the Buddha would be distinct. These two interpretations complement one another;

this is the method of contemplation for the present. The *Chao* further states: "The mental contemplation of the present does not merely contemplate the Buddha of original nature within the mind of the aggregates."

Thus, by entrusting [the realization] to another Buddha, one manifests one's own original nature. Therefore, it first clarifies that the response-Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) enters the mind that conceives of a self;

next, it clarifies that the Buddha-body is entirely original enlightenment (mūlapratyavekṣā). Thus, through the manifestation of the response-Buddha, one comes to know one's own original nature. This clarifies the meaning of relying on the external, thereby establishing the contemplation of "Mind-Only" (cittamātra).

If one speaks of "establishing" or "acting," this refers to the three inconceivable contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). To speak of "refuting" or "establishing" is termed "acting," which refers to the two contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Not refuting and not establishing is termed "being such" (*tathatā*), which refers to the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

To act while being entirely "such" means that all three truths are simultaneously refuted and simultaneously established. To be entirely "such" while acting means that all three truths are neither refuted nor established; this is the emptiness within the Middle Way.

It is a provisional designation. It can destroy the three delusions and establish the three dharmas; therefore, it evokes the perfect response of the three bodies of other Buddhas and enables the realization of the three bodies within one’s own mind.
This is precisely what is meant by the names "emptiness," "provisionality," and "the middle" regarding the fruit. Thus, delusion is entirely wisdom, and hindrance is entirely virtue.
Therefore, the mind is the responsive Buddha, and the mind is the resultant Buddha. Know that this activity is the one mind; cultivate this.
The Three Contemplations constitute the essential body of all contemplations and the sublime core of this sutra. It is further said:

"This contemplation can purify the lands of the four Buddhas; only in this way does it become the ultimate purpose of this sutra. This is truly because the subtlety of these contemplations is able to destroy the three delusions.

It is not merely that the Shared Land (*sahā-loka*) is purified; rather, according to the depth or shallowness with which one’s delusions are severed, one naturally attains the three lands, such as the Land of Residual Existence (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*).

Although Vaidehī originally desired to abandon the defiled for the pure, the Buddha showed her the method of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); thus, the abandonment of the defiled is brought to completion and the manifestation of the pure is left nothing lacking.

As for those whose delusions have not yet been destroyed who are born into the Shared Land, by relying on the superior [land] and increasing their cultivation, the three pure lands may be expected. For now, this is the teaching.

It is said: Regarding the relative gravity of the five turbidities, the shared residence (*sahā-loka*) may be pure or defiled. However, when one contemplates with perfect completeness (*pariniṣpanna*), the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) of that shared residence—though produced by light turbidity—are far more pure than those lands produced by other wholesome causes;
their characteristics are thus vastly different. Second, regarding "recollection": it may involve taking the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) as the object of focus.

Whether one holds the name or recollects it, both are termed "recollection" (*anusmṛti*). This involves both a principle and a phenomenon. As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s Liberation of the Householder states:
"If one wishes to see the Tathāgata Amitāyus of the Land of Peace and Bliss, one shall see him at will.
I am able to fully know all matters concerning the adornments and spiritual powers of the lands of all Tathāgatas; they come from nowhere and go nowhere."
There is a location, yet there is no place of abiding. Just as one's own body has no coming or going and no place of movement or dwelling, so too that Tathāgata does not come here, nor do I go there;
for I know that all Buddhas and my own mind are like a dream. As that which is seen in a dream arises from conceptualization, I see that all Buddhas arise from my own mind. Furthermore...
I know that my own mind is like water in a vessel, and all phenomena are like reflections in that water. My own mind is like a magical illusion, and all Buddhas are like illusions.
All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas produced by my own mind are entirely like echoes; they are, for example, like the sound of an echo arising in an empty valley in response to a voice.
I have realized and understood that my own mind perceives Buddhas according to its thoughts. Thus do I know; thus do I recollect. What...

"One sees that all Buddhas arise solely from one's own mind. The Zhenyuan Commentary states: "From the passage 'coming from nowhere' onwards, it correctly distinguishes that 'mind-only' is precisely the mind itself.

When there is no [deluded] mind, one immediately enters True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is because one realizes that those [apparent] marks are empty, as they are manifested solely by the mind. Once one has realized mind-only..."
When the mind is realized, it is itself the Buddha; therefore, whatever one contemplates is none other than the Buddha.

The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* teaches the cultivation of the "Buddha-standing Samādhi," wherein one focuses single-mindedly on Amitābha. This is like dreaming of gold, jewels, and kinsmen with whom one enjoys themselves. Yongming said:

This metaphor illustrates that which is produced by mind alone: it exists yet is empty, like an illusion that is not real. Thus, when both mind and Buddha are forgotten, the illusory marks are nonetheless not absent;
one does not destroy the mind and Buddha, and emptiness and existence are unimpeded. There is then no coming or going, yet this does not hinder universal perception.
To perceive is non-perception, always in accord with the Middle Way. (In the *Amitābha Sūtra*, from "upholding the name" to "single-mindedness...")
Regarding "undisturbed" (*wúluàn*), Jingjue said: "One-mind undisturbed" (*yīxīn bùluàn*) has both a principle (*lǐ*) and a practice (*shì*) aspect.

If one realizes this mind of nianfo, such that the four modes of being (*sìxìng*) do not arise, this is the "one-mind of principle. If one applies the mind to maintain mindfulness, with every thought uninterrupted, this is called the "one-mind of practice.
Zhenxie said: "The one-mind of practice can be practiced by all people, because by holding the name, the mind is not disturbed; it is like a dragon obtaining water."
It is like a tiger relying on a mountain. If you take the principle of "one mind," it is not some other method;
simply take up the four characters of Amitābha Buddha and recite them directly throughout the two periods of six hours [day and night].

Understand that the mind which is capable of reciting is fundamentally neither having a thought nor lacking a thought, neither having both presence and absence of thought, nor being neither present nor absent. Since the reciting mind is thus, the object of recitation is likewise.

Furthermore, as stated in various sutras: whether one focuses the mind for a single lifetime, for three months, for ten recitations at dawn, for seven weeks, or for six periods during ten days and ten nights;

or if one maintains uninterrupted and exclusive mindfulness for a single day and night—provided it is augmented by the power of deep faith, the power of pure vows, and the power of the Buddha’s grace—one will all be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This applies even down to those who have committed the five grave offenses.

Even an evil ordinary person who has ten recitations at the time of death can attain birth [in the Pure Land]. As for the three groups of practitioners, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* sets forth ten great vows, namely:
paying homage to all Buddhas; praising the Tathāgatas; extensively cultivating offerings; repenting of karmic obstacles; rejoicing in merit;

requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma; requesting the Buddhas to remain in the world; constantly following and learning from the Buddhas; always acting in accordance with sentient beings; and universally dedicating [all merit].

Dedication: For each and every vow, it is said: "As long as the realm of space is not exhausted, as long as the realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, as long as the karma of sentient beings is not exhausted, and as long as the afflictions of sentient beings are not exhausted, may my vows likewise not be exhausted.
Yet, since the realm of space and the karma and afflictions of sentient beings can never be exhausted, this King of Vows of mine shall have no end.
May it continue from moment to moment without interruption, through the actions of body, speech, and mind."
Without weariness or fatigue, until the very last moment of life when all the sense faculties completely dissolve and all power and majesty are utterly lost—
when ministers, high officials, palaces, inner and outer chambers, elephants, horses, chariots, precious treasures,
and hidden hoards no longer follow one— only this King of Vows does not abandon or depart from one, throughout all...
At that time, led before him, in a single kṣaṇa he was reborn in the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
There he immediately beheld Amitābha Buddha. That person saw for himself that he had been born within a lotus flower;

having received the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) from the Buddha, after the passage of countless kalpas, he universally benefited sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions according to their minds by the power of his wisdom, even unto...
He rescues sentient beings from the great ocean of the suffering of afflictions, causing them to transcend it and all attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
In the *Mahāratnakūṭa*, ten kinds of minds are set forth: first, to give rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of great loving-kindness that is free from harm;
second, to give rise to a mind of great compassion that is free from oppression and vexation; third, regarding the Buddha’s true Dharma, not to begrudge one’s own body or life.
1. A mind that delights in guarding [the precepts]. 2. A mind that gives rise to supreme patience toward all phenomena and is free from attachment.
3. A mind of pure intention that does not crave gain, honor, or respect. 4. A mind that seeks the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes and never forgets it at any time.
5. A mind that respects and honors all sentient beings without any sense of inferiority. 6. A mind that is unattached to the world.

The treatise states that one generates a mind of certainty regarding the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma). Ninth, there is a pure mind free from defilement regarding the nine types of roots of goodness.
Tenth, there is a mind of recollection that arises by relinquishing all signs regarding the Tathāgatas. These ten minds, when brought together, constitute a single mind.

If one desires to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) and yet does not attain birth there, such a thing is impossible. [This concludes] the cultivation of the three [contemplations] according to the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
There are three blessings: first, filially supporting one’s parents, serving one’s teachers and elders, maintaining a compassionate heart so as not to kill, and cultivating the ten wholesome karmas;

second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, fully observing the various precepts, and not violating dignified conduct; third, generating the bodhicitta and having deep faith in cause and effect.
Reading and reciting the Mahāyāna, and exhorting practitioners to do so—these three types of karma are the primary causes for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, as clarified in the *Mahāvaipulya* regarding the three grades of those who resolve upon Bodhicitta, and in various sūtras and śāstras, they include:

reciting sūtras, upholding mantras, building stūpas, fashioning images, prostrating, offering praise and hymns, observing the precepts, burning incense, scattering flowers, and hanging silk banners and streamers.
In general, whatever practice or deed is supported by the power of faith, aspiration, and dedication, there is none that does not arise. Nevertheless,
as vows and practices vary in magnitude and principle and phenomenon differ, the resulting environments and beings, the Buddhas one perceives,
and the Dharma one hears must necessarily be vastly different.
Question: Sudhana attained his goal in a single lifetime; why, then, is he not born in the Flower Treasury World (Huāzàng) but instead exhorted to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Jílè)?
Answer: This question appears in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra Commentary* (Huáyán shū). Its response states: "Because there are karmic conditions; because their minds are unified;

because they do not depart from the Flower Treasury World; and because [Amitābha] is his original teacher. It further states: "When Samantabhadra leads the ocean-like assembly of Sudhana’s followers to take refuge in the Land of Ultimate Bliss..."

This is because, in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), one enters the wisdom of Mañjuśrī and cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra; thus, both merit and wisdom, as well as phenomena and principle, all accord with the Dharma-realm.

Although such a person of great resolve has wondrously realized original luminosity and is suddenly equal to the various sages, their power and function are not yet fully perfected, and they have not yet reached the stage where they can universally benefit sentient beings like the Tathāgata.
Therefore, by relying on the Pure Land and approaching Amitābha until reaching Buddhahood, the underlying intent is as follows:
This is so. Question: Regarding the two methods of visualization and recollection, their practices differ; are the results they induce the same or different?
Answer: They are all different. Yongming said: "The nine grades of rebirth are not of a single level; some may travel to the Land of Transformation and behold [the Buddha]."

Regarding the Buddha’s response body (*nirmāṇakāya*): some perceive the Buddha’s true essence in the land of retribution for birth; some ascend to the stages of the bodhisattva grounds in a single night, while others take eons to realize the Lesser Vehicle;

some possess sharp faculties and others dull faculties; some have concentrated minds and others distracted minds; and some have slow or swift awakening on the Path—thus their spiritual capacities differ.
Or perhaps there are differences in the timing of when the flowers bloom. Ciyun said: "The nine grades are merely a rough classification; if subdivided, they would be immeasurable. Question:

"Is it not the case that Ultimate Bliss is only the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*)? Why then do you say that some are born in the Land of Reward (*vipākabhūmi*) and behold the true body of the Buddha? Answer: "I thought so..."
Is there a separate land of true retribution (sambhoga-kāya) outside of the land of common residence (sahā-loka)? One should know that the three lands do not depart from the land of common residence;
they differ only in the successive variations of body, environment, and enjoyment. Jingxi said: "If one directly contemplates this land, the four lands are fully present.
It is like the oceanic assembly in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which does not depart from the Jeta Grove, yet the great śrāvakas neither know nor see it. This is precisely of that category.
Question: Since the four lands are fully present in this land, one need only practice by progressing through them here. Answer: Alas, defiled karma is difficult to eliminate.
To eliminate defilement and cultivate purity, it is necessary to seek rebirth in that land. Siming said: "The turbidity in this land is heavy; [the ten evils...]"
Faith alone enables one to emerge from the wheel of suffering. That land is supreme in its realm; those of the nine grades all ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.

Have you not heard that among the disciples who received instruction during the era of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, there were those who remained on the level of a Śrāvaka for kalpas as numerous as the atoms of dust?

This was entirely because they retrogressed, thereby requiring such a long duration. Even Śāriputra, having realized the sixth mind, still fell back through the five paths of rebirth—how much more so for those who are merely indolent! This is surely due to...
In this land, conditions for regression are numerous; hence it is said: "The seeds of fish and the flowers of the mango yield few fruits despite many causes.

If one is born in Sukhāvatī, relying upon those superior conditions, even an ordinary person of the broad ground immediately attains the stage of non-regression. For this reason, one should seek birth there.

Question: There are many types of beings who dwell together in pure lands. Why is it that you now specifically point to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and exclusively praise its superior environment and superior conditions?
Answer: It is precisely because of the environment and conditions that we point specifically to it. A sutra states: "In that land there are no manifold sufferings;
there one experiences only various joys. Now, let us contrast this with the Sahā world: here, this physical body of flesh and blood is suffering for all who are born. In that [land], however...

Those born by transformation from lotuses have no suffering of birth. At this time, the seasons alternate and senescence daily encroaches; for them, there is no suffering of aging as they are not subject to cold or heat.
Here, the four great elements are difficult to harmonize and give rise to many illnesses; for them, their transformed bodies are subtle and wondrous, and there is no suffering of disease.
Here, those who reach seventy are rare and impermanence is swift; for them, their lifespan is immeasurable and there is no death.

This is suffering. Here, there is affectionate attachment among kin; where there is attachment, there must be separation. There, having no parents, wife, or children, there is no suffering of being separated from those one loves.
Here, there are enemies and adversaries; where there is enmity, there must be meeting. There, gathering with the most virtuous, there is no suffering of meeting those one hates.
Here, there is hardship, hunger, and cold, and a greedy pursuit that knows no satisfaction. There, clothing, food, and precious treasures are all received in abundance.
[This world] is accomplished [as such]. This foul and defiled physical form has many deficient and ugly features; those [beings there] possess dignified appearances and all have radiance.

This [world] revolves in birth and death; that [realm] eternally realizes non-arising. This [world] has the suffering of the four destinies; that [realm] does not even have the name of the three evil paths.
This [world] is filled with hills, mounds, pits, ravines, forests of thorns, and mountains of earth and stone—all impure and evil. That [realm] is made of gold.

The precious trees upon the earth reach toward the heavens, and towers soar with the seven treasures; flowers bloom in four colors. Here, the Śāla grove has already passed away, and the Dragon Flower [Buddha] has not yet appeared;
there, the Honored One Amitāyus currently preaches the Dharma. Here, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta can only look up to their illustrious names.
There, the boundless Superior Person personally acts as a supreme friend; here, the host of Māras and externalists disturb right practice.

There, the Buddha’s transformation unifies all, leaving no trace of Māras or externalists; here, seductive forms and lewdness delude practitioners. There, the retribution for past deeds is pure and truly devoid of women;
here, evil beasts and *chi-mei* spirits together fan the flames of perverse sounds. There, the water birds and forest trees are all...
He proclaims the sublime Dharma. Although the conditions and environments of these two lands differ vastly when compared, the excellence of the Land of Bliss cannot easily be fully enumerated.
Its environmental excellence can satisfy the sentient beings' aspiration to attain purity; its causal excellence can assist those born there in the power of their practice.
It is from this that the three stages of non-retrogression are perfected, distinguishing it from other pure abodes where there are differences in ascent and descent.
Question: The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are all accessible for veneration; why then do you single out Amitābha? Answer: There are three reasons for this.
First, his vows are profound and grave. Second, there is a karmic affinity with the Sahā world. Third, his path of transformation is closely related [to our realm].
During his causal stage, Amitābha made various vast and great vows, which may be summarized as follows: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings wish to be born in my land, or if they hear..."
"If those who cultivate the roots of all virtues and invoke my name—even for as few as ten recitations—should fail to be born [in my land], I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
Once they have been born in my land, if there should be any regression or lack of certainty regarding their attainment of Buddhahood, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
Thus, the *Huayan chao* states: "The vows of Amitābha are profound; he specifically receives and guides the sentient beings of this Sahā world. As for Śākyamuni...
In this age, there are already many who have heard the Buddha’s teaching and turned toward Amitābha.

Among the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) era—whether monastic or lay, male or female, noble or humble, rich or poor—there are none who do not believe and take refuge in him. Even those who have not yet heard the Buddha’s teaching will eventually recite his name.

Those who are stubborn, foolish, violent, wicked, and devoid of faith may, when encountering calamities, hardships, or dangerous situations, or when uttering sounds of lamentation and resentment, involuntarily call out "Amitābha Buddha" with their lips; or even during moments of playful jesting with children.
One may gather sand or knead clay to build walls or paint murals, thereby creating images of Amitābha Buddha.
Even those whose conduct is not yet stable and whose speech is not yet formed can naturally chant "Amitābha Buddha. All of this arises without being exhorted and occurs without being taught.
As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "I preach this sūtra so that they may see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and his..."
In this land, whatever you ought to do may be sought therein. Do not harbor further doubts or perplexity after my parinirvāṇa.
When the future teachings of the sūtras are extinguished, out of my compassion, I have specifically retained this sūtra for a hundred years.

Sentient beings who encounter it shall all attain deliverance according to their wishes. Furthermore, the sūtra states: "After this sūtra is extinguished, the Buddha-dharma will be entirely non-existent."
He left behind only the four-character name of Amitābha Buddha to save sentient beings.
Those who do not believe and instead slander him shall fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering. Thus, Tiantai said: "That Buddha has a particular affinity for this degenerate age.
The sages of the two lands manifest dwelling in both pure and defiled realms, using the two gates of subduing and gathering to discipline sentient beings.
Those born here are broken by impurity, suffering, brevity, and manifold demonic afflictions, so that they may come to know weariness [with saṃsāra].

Those [in the Pure Land] are sustained by purity, bliss, longevity, and non-retrogression, so that they may come to know joy [in liberation]. Once there is both weariness and joy, the path of transformation proceeds.
Furthermore, regarding those who have not yet been fully delivered beyond the three vehicles of Śākyamuni’s dispensation, their deliverance lies with Amitābha.
Therefore, the various Mahāyāna sūtras repeatedly and earnestly exhort one to go [to the Pure Land]; this is indeed because the path of transformation is interconnected with it. Question:

Is there not the fault of attachment and aversion, or subject and object, in this process of rejoicing in and detesting, or accepting and rejecting? Answer: This is not the worldly kind of attachment and aversion, or subject and object;
rather, it is the universal method by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transform ordinary beings into sages. Without detestation and relinquishment, how could this be achieved?

By transforming the ordinary, how could one become a sage without joyfully embracing [the path]? An ordinary person enters the stage of the sages, and from that sage-stage up to Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), there is nothing that does not involve joyful aspiration and aversion.
Only at the ultimate stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (Suyojana) do grasping and rejecting finally cease. Therefore, it is said:

"If grasping and rejecting reach their limit, they are no different from non-grasping and non-rejecting. Furthermore, the Dharma of the Pure Land is intended solely for those of a single type of spiritual capacity. This...

Pointing toward the past, the sounds of ten thousand streams fade away; receiving that which comes from the future, the tide of sound arises. Thus, through wearying of and relinquishing, one accords with true emptiness;

through delighting in and grasping, one establishes wondrous provisionality. When delighting in and wearying of are thus extinguished, emotions vanish; when there is no grasping or relinquishing, practice flourishes.
This accords with the perfect Middle Way. When the flower blooms, one beholds the Buddha. Thus, can it be said that love and hatred, or subject and object, have been transcended?
Question: Does rebirth in the Pure Land not contradict the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*)? Answer: Tiantai Master said:

"To ardently seek birth in the Pure Land while realizing that the essence of birth is unattainable is itself true non-arising. This is what is meant by: "Because the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. The foolish person...
Those bound by birth, upon hearing "birth," immediately form the understanding of birth; upon hearing "non-birth," they immediately form the understanding of non-birth.
They do not know that birth is itself non-birth, and non-birth is itself birth. Changlu said: "To take birth as birth is the view of permanence (śāśvata-dṛṣṭi);

to take non-birth as non-birth is the view of annihilation (uccheda-dṛṣṭi). Birth yet non-birth, and non-birth yet birth—this is the primary truth (paramārtha). I shall further explain this in detail.
I shall explain this according to the meaning of nature (*prakṛti*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is fundamentally unborn;
it is only through the conjunction of causes and conditions that the characteristic of birth arises. Because the nature is capable of manifesting characteristics, non-birth is itself birth.

Because characteristics arise from the manifestation of the nature, birth is itself non-birth. To know this is to know that birth in the Pure Land is produced solely by the mind. How could this principle be contradictory?

Question: The doctrine of rebirth in the Pure Land is clear in its intent; yet scholars today fail to comprehend it, all harboring doubts that the distance of ten quadrillion lands is too vast and that it will be difficult to reach at the moment of death.
Answer: You have heard much about how there is no land outside the mind and no mind outside the land, yet you still say you do not understand.
This is for no other reason than that you mistakenly identify your own mind as being confined within the physical body.
Within the space of a single square inch of the heart, one fails to realize that the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*) is signless and fundamentally vast.
Indeed, the empty space of the ten directions and the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are infinite and boundless; yet the measure of my own mind pervades each and every one of them.
Viewed in this light, the myriad nations are extremely close within my mind—how could there be any distance? At the end of life, [one] is born within my mind. How could it be far?

It is easy. What difficulty could there be? The *Ten Doubts Treatise* speaks from the perspective of the birth-and-death mind and the physical eye of ordinary beings regarding ten million billion lands.
However, for those sentient beings who have perfected the karma for the Pure Land, the concentrated mind at the moment of death is itself the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land;
the very movement of thought is the moment of being born in the Pure Land. For this reason, the *Contemplation Sutra* says: "Amitābha Buddha..."
The land is not far from here. Furthermore, the power of karma is inconceivable; one is reborn there in a single thought-moment. You need not worry about the distance.
It is like a person dreaming that while their body remains on the bed, their mind and consciousness travel everywhere to other lands.

Rebirth in the Pure Land is exactly like this; you need not have any doubts. As a sutra says: "In the mere twinkling of an eye, one attains rebirth. It is also said: "In the time it takes to bend and extend the arm."
Regarding the phrase "in the space of a moment," the *Shinxilu* states that the reason ten trillion lands are reached in a single moment is simply because one's own mind is fundamentally wondrous.
These various layered metaphors merely express that [the destination] arises within one's own vast mind; it is exceedingly near and exceedingly easy.
For example, traveling from here to India, a distance of over one hundred thousand li, involves passing through many kingdoms along the way.
In the past, there was a person who heard it said that memory resides within the mind. Later, while sitting or lying down, he suddenly gave rise to a thought and contemplated that land.
Thinking of a thousand *li*, he immediately reached a thousand *li*; thinking of ten thousand *li*, he immediately reached ten thousand *li*.
Contemplating India, he immediately arrived in India. Rebirth in the Pure Land is precisely this principle. Without cultivating pure karma, one cannot reach it.

It is extremely difficult. Once pure karma is perfected, it becomes extremely easy to reach [the Pure Land]. However, if you simply apply a resolute mind, you will certainly not be deceived. Question:
It is said that failing to cultivate pure karma makes reaching [the Pure Land] extremely difficult. Why, then, are ordinary people of perverse evil reborn there even at the moment of death? Answer:

In the *Contemplation Sūtra*, regarding the lowest grade of rebirth: those who have committed unwholesome deeds, such as the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten evil acts—such foolish people ought to fall into the evil realms and undergo inexhaustible suffering for many kalpas.

Yet, at the moment of death, they encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who provides various consolations, expounds the wondrous Dharma, and instructs them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Though this person is oppressed by suffering and has no leisure to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, the virtuous friend...
He said: "If you are unable [to do otherwise], you should invoke the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. In this way, with a sincere mind, let the sound not cease.
By fully reciting 'Namo Amitābha Buddha' ten times, in every thought-moment, the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death will be eliminated.
A golden lotus flower, like the orb of the sun, will appear before that person; in the space of a single thought, he shall go [to the Pure Land]."
One is born in the World of Ultimate Bliss; only after twelve great kalpas have passed does the lotus flower finally open.

Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with voices of great compassion, extensively expound the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and the methods for extinguishing karmic offenses. Upon hearing this, one rejoices and immediately resolves upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Because the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra* states that mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*) extinguishes the obstacles of karmic offenses, it regards mindfulness of the Buddha as supreme.

This is the condition (*pratyaya*). To clarify this further, let us examine it by consulting the commentaries (*vyākhyā*). First: A mind that exerts itself for even a short time can surpass one that commits evil throughout an entire lifetime.
Although the duration is brief, its power is fierce and sharp; because this mind is courageous and resolute, it is called a "great mind" (*mahācitta*).
This is because the matter of abandoning the body is urgent. It is like a person entering battle who does not spare their own life or limb; such a person is called a "hero. Second: Alternatively...

If one’s observance of the precepts is lax while their practice of the vehicle is urgent, then at the moment of death, the encouragement to recite the Buddha’s name will easily bring about a concentrated mind.

Even if one has not cultivated samādhi in the present life, this is because past seeds have now ripened; for the power of past wholesome karma is so strong that one encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) at the time of death, whereby the merit of ten recitations is accomplished.
Third, when practicing the mindfulness of the Buddha, one must earnestly repent and awaken. Thus Yongming said: "Good and evil are not fixed."

The essence of causes and conditions is empty, yet their manifestations involve rising and sinking; phenomena possess degrees of excellence and inferiority. A single ounce of pure gold surpasses a hundred ounces of layered blossoms;
the faint glow of a torch consumes ten thousand fathoms of piled grass.

Question: In this world of the five turbidities, all people possess transgressions. Even if one has not committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), who among them is free from other karmic offenses?
If these have not been repented and extinguished, can one still attain rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha’s name at the moment of death?
Answer: One may indeed attain rebirth. This is entirely due to the inconceivable power of Amitābha’s great vows. As stated in the *Nāgasena Sūtra*: "A hundred large..."

A stone placed upon a boat does not sink due to the power of the boat; yet without the boat, even a small stone will sink. The boat is a metaphor for the power of the Buddha, and the stone is a metaphor for evil karma.

Therefore, there is the teaching of "birth in the Pure Land while carrying one's karma. Those possessed of afflictions and defilements can attain birth in the Land of Common Residence (Sahā-buddhakṣetra).
Seng Xiongjun was a native of Bingzhou and Fenzhou; he worked as a butcher of oxen. At the moment of his death, he saw a herd of oxen.
Having been tormented by such agonizing pain, Zhang Zhonggui made it his business to slaughter chickens.
At the moment of death, he saw a divine being drive a flock of chickens that pecked out both his eyes until blood filled his bed. By invoking the name of the Buddha, he was reborn in the Pure Land.

How could this be anything other than the power of the Buddha? To clarify this further through an analogy: it is like a person who has committed a crime and ought to be imprisoned by the authorities, yet seeks the protection of a king.
The King issued a summons, but the official could not detain him; he thus reached the imperial capital once more. The *Xizi Chao* states:

"To attain birth in the Pure Land is to rely upon the power of others—the embrace of Amitābha’s vows, the exhortation and praise of Śākyamuni, and the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. It is like crossing a great ocean:
having obtained a massive ship, there is also a skilled guide, and furthermore, a favorable wind; one will surely reach the other shore swiftly. If one is unwilling..."
Embarking upon the boat, one lingers in a land of evil; whose fault is this? Question:

If one is born while still carrying karmic burdens, can one avoid falling back? Answer: All such persons do not fall back. As the Sūtra says: "Those who are born all abide in the assembly of those fixed in right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
furthermore, those who are born are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive). The *Ten Doubts Treatise* states that there are five causes and conditions for [this].
First, one is sustained by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s great compassionate vow. Second, the Buddha’s light constantly shines upon them, and their bodhicitta always increases.
Third, the sounds of water, birds, trees, and forests, as well as the resonance of music, all proclaim suffering and emptiness;
those who hear them constantly give rise to the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Fourth, they have only bodhisattvas as virtuous friends and no adverse conditions.
Externally, there are no ghosts, spirits, or malevolent demons; internally, the afflictions such as the three poisons never arise at all.

Furthermore, one constantly draws near to and makes offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions. Fifth, one’s lifespan lasts for eternal kalpas, shared with the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas.
Therefore, one does not fall back.

Question: If one who has committed evil throughout their life can attain birth [in the Pure Land] by reciting the Buddha's name at the end of life—carrying their karma with them and yet without falling back—then may I simply attend to worldly affairs and wait until the end of life to recite the Buddha’s name? Answer: Alas! You would deceive yourself and you would also deceive Heaven.

The phrase "inferior monastics and laypeople, both male and female" refers to all such individuals. That ordinary, evil persons who have committed transgressions are able to practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection) at the moment of death is because they possess roots of goodness from previous lives;
thus, they encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and attain the practice of *nienfo*. Such fortunate occurrences are as rare as one in ten thousand.

In the *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts), it states that there are ten types of people who cannot practice *nienfo* at the time of death: first, they may not necessarily meet a virtuous friend who can exhort them.

1. Preoccupation with worldly principles; 2. Being so entangled by karma and suffering that one has no leisure to mind the Buddha; 3. Losing the power of speech due to a stroke; 4. Losing one’s mind through madness;
5. Encountering water or fire; 6. Meeting with jackals or wolves; 7. Having one’s faith destroyed by evil friends; 8. Dying in a state of delusion;
9. Perishing in battle; 10. Falling from a high cliff. These are all common occurrences seen and heard; they concern both monastics and laypeople alike.
It exists. Summoned by past karma and induced by present karma, it suddenly manifests before one, leaving no room for avoidance.
Once you suddenly encounter such a state, you will be unable to act or maneuver; even a living Buddha as your spiritual friend cannot save you.

You will then follow your karma toward the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties to undergo suffering. Even if you wish to hear the name of the Buddha, you will not hear it. Even were it so...
Even if one lacks such evil conditions and dies of illness, one cannot escape the wind-blade dismemberment of the body and the separation of the four elements.
Like a living turtle being pulled from its shell, one is oppressed by agony and overwhelmed by terror and panic; thus, one is unable to recite the Buddha’s name.

Furthermore, even if one dies without illness, worldly attachments remain unresolved and worldly thoughts do not cease. One is agitated in the breast by the craving for life and the fear of death, compounded by—
Household affairs remain unsettled; funeral matters are not yet arranged; wife weeps and children cry; one is tormented by a hundred kinds of anxieties and cannot focus on the Buddha-name.

Furthermore, even before death, while still in this body, one cannot avoid enduring pain and suffering through moaning and groaning, seeking medicine and physicians, and performing prayers and repentance;
as distracting thoughts fly about in confusion, one cannot focus on the Buddha-name.
Furthermore, even before one falls ill, it is simply that as one grows old, the signs of decay manifest; one becomes exhausted, frail, and burdened by sighs, sorrows, and anxieties.
Amidst this state of senility, with the body left in disarray and right in disorder, one is unable to recite the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even before one has grown old, while still in the prime of youth, if the wild mind has not yet ceased and one remains entangled in worldly affairs—
clinging here and there, wandering in confused thoughts, and drifting in a vast ocean of karmic consciousness— one will be unable to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Moreover,

even if one is free from busyness and possesses the resolve to cultivate practice, if one cannot clearly discern through the phenomena of the world, if one cannot let go, and if one cannot maintain composure, [the same obstacle persists].

If you do not sever [delusions] while sitting, even a slight境 (object-condition) appearing before you will cause the one master to follow along in delusion; thus, you will be unable to recite the Buddha’s name.
Observe this: whether it be at a time of old age and illness, or during days of youth and leisure, if even a single matter hangs upon the mind, [the practice is lost].

It is already difficult to practice the Buddha’s name at this early stage; how much more so at the time of death? To further say, "Just attend to worldly affairs," is truly for a fool to speak the words of a fool;
I can only assure you that you have applied your mind wrongly. Moreover, worldly affairs are like a dream—what real efficacy do they possess?

Which single thing among them can take the place of [preparing for] birth and death? Even if one builds monasteries, increases the permanent endowments, seeks fame and status, or forms alliances with the powerful and noble—it is all in vain.

One might think that one has performed many good deeds; yet little is known that one has instead violated precepts such as failing to realize the fundamental nature of the Way and extensively constructing monasteries.
Conditioned merits harbor many faults; before the heavenly realms are attained, hell is already established. Before birth and death are clarified, they all become the root of suffering.
Only when the light of the eyes falls to the ground and one undergoes suffering will one finally realize that everything done throughout one's life was in vain.
This adds further shackles and fetters; it increases the firewood and charcoal in the cauldrons of boiling water; it assists the swords and spears upon the trees of blades.
Having lost one’s human body beneath the *kāṣāya*, it will be difficult to recover for ten thousand kalpas. Even an iron-hearted man would shed tears upon hearing this.

If the Patriarchs spoke with such bitter urgency, how could they have permitted one to wait until the moment of death to practice mindfulness of the Buddha? Master Sīxin said: "The wealth and treasures of worldly people..."
Like a mountain, with wives and concubines before one’s eyes, enjoying day and night in pleasure—what can be done? The path ahead is narrow; the secret tally has arrived in the dark.
One cannot linger for even a moment. Old King Yama does not yield to sentiment; what face has the Lord of Impermanence?
For now, let us rely on what is within everyone’s own sight and hearing: those in the streets before and behind, our kinsmen, relatives, friends, brothers, the strong, and the young.
How many have already died? The people of this world mostly say, "I will practice nianfo when I grow old. Let me teach you to know: on the road to the Yellow Springs, there are neither old nor young.
An ancient said: "Do not wait until you are old before practicing nianfo; most solitary graves belong to the young."
It is further said: "From my early years, I sought a wife, raised children, and managed the household affairs, enduring myriad hardships.

Yet when the three-inch breath is severed, all ceases at once. If one is a filial descendant, offering a bowl of soup and rice on the third day of spring and the ninth day of autumn, and weeping a few times, this is still a way of remembering one's parents.
But as for an unworthy son, even before the bones of his parents have grown cold..."
They squander their wealth and indulge in music at will. Compared to this, what is there to be so anxious about? An ancient worthy said: "The wealthy old man is as busy as an arrow;
his rice breeds worms and his coins rot through their strings. He weighs them on scales and counts them by lamplight—like puppets on a string."
Do not let it be interrupted. Master Sīti (Dead Heart) was so bitter in his admonitions; did he ever permit one to wait until the moment of death to practice mindfulness of the Buddha?
How much time does a human life possess? It is like a flash of lightning; in the blink of an eye, it passes away.

While you are still young and free from illness, shake yourself to your core, cast aside worldly affairs, and for every day’s duration, recite the Buddha’s name; for every moment of effort, cultivate the purity of the Pure Land.
Karma! Since another’s life has come to an end, my funeral provisions have been prepared in advance; my future path is now secure.
Had it not been so, repentance would be difficult to pursue later.
Question: The human mind is prone to advance and retreat with ease. Upon hearing a single word of exhortation, one may become courageous and diligent;

yet, when suddenly encountering obstacles and difficulties, one’s thoughts immediately shift, claiming that Pure Land practice is merely for the afterlife and offers no benefit or relief in the present moment.

Is it not natural, then, that such a sentiment arises? Answer: Your vision is not yet broad enough. By receiving and upholding the names of the Buddhas, one obtains ten benefits. First: day and night...
First, all the great powerful divine generals of the heavens, with retinues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, protect them by concealing their forms.
Second, twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, along with all bodhisattvas, constantly follow and protect them.
Third, all Buddhas guard and mind them day and night, and Amitābha constantly emits light to receive and sustain them. Fourth, no evil spirits can harm them.

Five: Noxious snakes, venomous dragons, and poisonous drugs shall all be unable to cause harm. Six: One shall not suffer from fire, water, enemies, thieves, swords, arrows, imprisonment, shackles, or untimely death;
prior karma shall be extinguished, the lives of those who bear grudges shall be liberated, and there shall be no further opposition or retribution.
Seventh, one’s dreams at night will be upright; or one may see the sublime and wondrous form of Amitābha.
Eighth, the mind is constantly joyful, the complexion is radiant, physical strength is abundant, and all undertakings are auspicious.

Ninth, one is always respectfully honored, provided with offerings, and joyfully prostrated to by all people of the world, as if they were honoring a Buddha. Tenth, at the end of life, there is no fear, and right mindfulness manifests before one.

One shall behold the holy assembly of Amitābha holding golden lotus flowers to welcome and lead one to rebirth in his land, where one will experience supreme and wondrous bliss throughout the bounds of the future.
These ten benefits, as listed above, are fully recorded in the sūtra and proclaimed from the Buddha’s own mouth; they bring benefit both in the present life and in future lives.
One should simply practice with diligence and harbor no doubts.
Question: One must shake off the body and mind and cast aside worldly affairs; this can only be practiced when external conditions are favorable and the body and mind are at ease.

If, however, worldly affairs cannot be discarded, how should one be instructed? Answer: If one truly and deeply contemplates impermanence with sincere application of mind, then regardless of suffering or pleasure, favorability or adversity, stillness or clamor, leisure or busyness, one may freely attend to public or private duties, welcoming guests and attending to visitors.
Guest: When myriad conditions intersect and disturb one, and one must respond to challenges from all directions, these do not hinder the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name.
As it is said: "In the morning it is Amitābha; in the evening it is Amitābha. Even if one is as busy as an arrow, one does not depart from Amitābha."
It is further said: "Though the bamboo be dense, it does not hinder the flow of water; though the mountain be high, how could it obstruct the flight of white clouds?
For those whose worldly ties are heavy and whose strength is light, one must likewise steal moments of leisure amidst busyness and seek stillness within the clamor.

One should establish a daily recitation quota of thirty thousand, ten thousand, three thousand, or one thousand repetitions, never allowing a single day to pass without it. Furthermore, even when one is extremely preoccupied...
There is not a moment of leisure. Every morning, one must perform the ten recitations (*daśanāma*). If practiced for a long time, the merit will be perfected and will not be in vain.
In addition to reciting the Buddha’s name, one should recite sutras, prostrate before the Buddha, repent, make vows, and engage in various forms of creating karmic connections and accumulating merit.

One should cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds according to one's capacity to assist this practice. Dedicate every iota of goodness toward the Western Pure Land. By applying effort in this way, not only...
One will certainly attain rebirth there, and furthermore, one’s level of spiritual attainment will be enhanced. Question:
You have spoken generally about *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation), but you have not yet provided its specific method. Moreover, the practice of the ten recitations with dedication has not been explained.

I would be grateful for a detailed exposition. Answer: Regarding *nienfo*, some practitioners focus exclusively on the thirty-two marks [of the Buddha] to bind the mind and achieve concentration. Upon opening their eyes...
With eyes closed, one will constantly behold the Buddha; or, by merely reciting the name and maintaining it without distraction, one shall likewise behold the Buddha in this very life.
Among those who behold the Buddha in this world, for the most part, the superior method is to recite the Buddha’s name. Regarding the method of reciting the Buddha’s name:

one must restrain the mind so that it does not become distracted, maintaining a continuous succession of thoughts, binding the object of focus to the name of the Buddha, and using the mind to attend to each syllable as it is pronounced.
It is clear: regardless of how many times one recites the name, one must maintain single-mindedness and continuity of thought from heart to heart.
Only in this way can a single thought-moment extinguish the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. Otherwise, it is truly difficult to extinguish such sins.
As for the "ten recitations," every morning one should face west, stand upright with palms joined, and recite "Amitābha Buddha" continuously until the end of the session.
One breath constitutes one recitation (*nian*). Thus, ten breaths constitute ten recitations. One follows the length or shortness of the breath without limiting the number of Buddha-recitations;
the limit is reached when the breath is exhausted. The voice should be neither too high nor too low, neither too slow nor too hurried, but balanced and moderate.

Ten breaths should be connected in succession so that the mind does not scatter, making this single-minded concentration the primary practice. What is called "ten recitations" refers to using the breath to bind the mind. This is to be maintained until the end of this life.

One must not abandon this practice for even a single day. Upon finishing the recitation, one says: "I, disciple [Name], with single-minded devotion take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
May your pure light illuminate me; may your compassionate vow embrace me. Now, with right mindfulness, I invoke the name of the Tathāgata for ten moments of thought.
For the sake of the path to Bodhi, I seek birth in the Pure Land. According to the Tathāgata’s original vow..."

If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in my land and, with a sincere heart of faith and joy, recite the name even ten times, yet do not attain birth there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment—except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma.
I now recall that since this life began, I have committed no heinous crime nor slandered the Mahāyāna; I pray that these ten recitations may enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows.
Relying on the compassionate power of the Buddha, all my transgressions shall be extinguished and the causes for purity shall increase. When the time of death approaches, may I know it myself;
may my body be free from the suffering of illness and my mind free from attachment. May my consciousness remain undisturbed and unscattered, as if entering meditative absorption.

May the Buddha and the assembly of holy ones come to welcome me, holding a golden platform in their hands. In the space of a single thought-moment, may I be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where upon the opening of the lotus flower, I behold [the Buddha].
The Buddha immediately hears the Buddha-vehicle and suddenly awakens to the Buddha-wisdom, extensively delivering sentient beings and fulfilling the vow for Bodhi.

Having made this reflection, one should then cease. This essential method of instruction bequeathed by the former sages has been widely transmitted for a long time; it should be followed and practiced.
Question: "We who dwell in the world beyond—how should we augment our practice? Answer: "Did I not say before that there are many types of cultivation, which are subsumed into three gates?
These three gates are each accessible; one may enter them either individually or in combination, taking whichever suits one's inclination."
Question: The cultivation of universal contemplation and the mindfulness of the mind-only seem to be the practice-gates for those of superior capacity.

The ten vows of the *Avataṃsaka* and the ten minds of the *Ratnakūṭa* are likewise the functional applications of those with great roots. If one’s faculties do not correspond to these practices, it is difficult to achieve their merit and conduct.
Now, when I examine myself, I find that my own preference is simply to single-mindedly hold the Name, supplemented by prostrations and repentance. How should the Master regard this?

"What is it? [The Master] replied: "Excellent! You have understood the proper measure. It is fitting that you should skillfully guide others in the teaching of exclusive practice without interruption.

As for 'exclusive practice,' this means that sentient beings have heavy obstructions, their objects of perception are subtle while their minds are coarse, and their consciousnesses are drifting and their spirits are flying; thus, meditative contemplation is difficult to accomplish.

Out of great compassion, the Great Sage directly exhorted them to exclusively recite the Name. Because reciting the Name is easy, if it is continuous, birth [in the Pure Land] occurs immediately, moment after moment."

Continuing: taking one's life as the limit for the vow, ten [recitations] result in ten births, and a hundred result in a hundred births. Why is this? Because one attains right mindfulness through the absence of external, distracting conditions;
because it accords with the fundamental vows of the Buddha; because it does not contradict the teachings; and because it follows the words of the Buddha.

If one cultivates mixed practices while seeking birth [in the Pure Land], one may hope for one or two out of a hundred, or three or four out of a thousand. This is because the mind is disturbed by diverse conditions, causing one to lose right mindfulness.
Therefore, because it does not accord with the original vows of the Buddha, because it contradicts the teachings, because it does not conform to the Buddha’s words,
because mindfulness is not continuous, because the mind does not continuously repay the Buddha’s kindness, because although there are karmic practices they are always associated with fame and profit,
and because one delights in frequenting distracting conditions— thereby obstructing oneself and others from being born in the Pure Land— for those who practice without interruption, the body...
Devote yourself exclusively to venerating Amitābha Buddha; recite the name of Amitābha Buddha with your mouth exclusively; and contemplate Amitābha Buddha with your mind exclusively.

Furthermore, whenever greed, anger, or delusion arise, repent immediately upon committing them, ensuring that no day, night, or moment passes without doing so, so that you remain constantly pure and uninterrupted.
Master Shandao was renowned in the Indian tradition as an emanation of Amitābha; observing him now...
The essential point is that mindfulness must continue in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment. Yongming said:
"One must single-mindedly take refuge and cultivate diligently throughout one's entire life. Whether sitting or lying down, always face the west.

While practicing the Way and performing prostrations, or when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, be earnest and sincere, free from all distracting thoughts, as if facing execution or imprisoned in a jail by enemies."

Pursued by enemies or pressed by water or fire, one should single-mindedly seek salvation, praying to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly realize non-arising (*anutpāda*), extensively deliver all sentient beings, perpetuate and glorify the Triple Gem, and vow to repay the four debts of gratitude. Only through such ultimate sincerity will these aspirations not be in vain. However, if one’s words do not accord with one’s deeds, if faith and aspiration are slight, and if there is no mind of continuous mindfulness but rather frequent interruptions— [The following is the concluding portion of the prayer: May the Buddhas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, out of their great compassion, receive my sincere invocation. May I, by the power of this merit, be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. When my life comes to an end, may the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas come to welcome me; may I cast off this defiled body and be born among the lotus flowers. Once born, may I immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression, and thereafter, together with all beings, benefit and transform the world, never ceasing until the end of the future. May all the Buddhas of the ten directions bear witness to this vow. May it be so! May it be so! May it be so! Amity! Amity! Amity!

This is the underlying meaning. Relying on their own indolence, they hope for rebirth at the moment of death; however, being obstructed by karmic hindrances, they fear it will be difficult to encounter virtuous friends.
As the winds of death and the fires of dissolution press upon them, right mindfulness cannot be established. Why is this? The present is the cause, and the moment of death is the effect.
If the cause is real, the effect will not be in vain. When the sound is harmonious, the echo follows suit; when the form is straight, the shadow is upright.

Question: To have thoughts succeed one another in an unbroken stream is surely not what you aspire to. Yet, as your power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not yet perfected, your mind lacks a master.
Sometimes old learning has not been forgotten; sometimes perverse thoughts arise in disorder; sometimes when sensory objects and conditions meet, your vigilance is not firm;
or sometimes emotional conceptions fly about, impossible to suppress. Unaware, your thoughts run east and west; in the blink of an eye, they have traveled a thousand miles.
Ten thousand *li* away! Furthermore, if one is entangled by even a hair’s breadth of worldly affairs, one cannot extricate oneself for five days, ten days, half a month, or even a full month.
It is not merely a matter of interruption; it is something to be ashamed of when spoken of and to be lamented when reflected upon.

How, then, can this be remedied? Answer: Alas! This is a universal malady among students. When such interruptions occur, if one does not lash oneself with a severe whip, [the affliction will persist].

If you practice exclusively [for the Pure Land] without interruption, yet never achieve success, there are three "stinging whips" from the ancients: first, repaying kindness; second, resolving the will; and third, seeking verification. Regarding repaying kindness:
having cultivated the Pure Land, one must remember to repay kindness. For instance, the nurturing of one's parents—is this not a profound kindness?
The instruction and formation provided by one's teachers—is this not a profound virtue? From the moment you first left the household life, you were already to repay them.

This is a profound debt of gratitude. Later, when you travel as a wandering monk (*paryaṭaka*), you must likewise repay this great virtue. For twenty or thirty years, you have left your hometown and parted from your well;
you have disregarded all the hardships and sufferings of your parents and teachers, and you have not even cared for them in their old age or illness.

Even when they die, you do not return. Now, they may be suffering in the three miserable realms (*trāya-patha*); you look to me to save them and deliver them, yet your mindfulness is interrupted moment by moment. Purify [your mind].

The land is not purified; the Pure Land is not realized, and one cannot even save oneself. Since you cannot save one another, you are people who forget kindness, betray righteousness, and are profoundly unfilial.
As the Sūtra says, "The sin of unfiliality shall cause one to fall into hell. Thus, a single moment of interruption is itself the karma of hell.
Furthermore, you wear clothes without raising silkworms and eat food without plowing the fields, yet you lie in monastic quarters.

The Patriarchal Way teaches that when one possesses the full realization of the manifestation of enjoyment, yet the benefactor’s wife and children have diminished their portion, and one’s insight into the Way remains unclarified, then even a drop of water or an inch of thread must be repaid by pulling the plow and dragging the harrow before one may attain it.

If you, however, allow your mindfulness to be interrupted moment by moment, the Pure Land will not be realized; if the Pure Land is not realized, there is a debt to be repaid. Thus, it is said: "If for even a single thought-moment there is interruption..."
This is indeed the karma of a beast. As for "resolute determination": if you study with single-minded cultivation, your resolve must be decisive. You have spent your entire life practicing Chan;
yet, having failed to awaken to Chan, when you turn to the teachings, you do not understand them either. Having played with these things until now, your deluded thoughts remain undying;
you wish to utter a few words of Chan, utter a few words of the teachings, write some characters, and compose [writings].

A few verses: Sentiment hangs between two ends; thoughts branch into four paths. The Patriarch said: "To let a thought linger for even a hair’s breadth is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms;
for a fleeting emotion to arise is to be bound by shackles for ten thousand kalpas. Yet you lack resolve in your will, and your sentiments and thoughts are manifold.
For these many reasons, one’s right mindfulness is interrupted. Thus, even a single moment of interruption constitutes the karma that binds one to the three miserable realms.
Furthermore, if one’s resolve to guard the roots of the precepts is not firm, or if one’s body and speech are driven by constant seeking, the scriptures state:
"It would be better to pour molten copper into one's mouth and wrap one's body in hot iron than to receive the offerings of others with a body and speech that have broken the precepts."
Regarding food and clothing, you have failed to maintain strict discipline due to the false movement of a deviant mind.
Because of these false movements, your dedicated cultivation has been interrupted. Thus, even a single moment of interruption is not merely the karma of hot iron or molten copper; it is far worse.

Furthermore, when attachment and aversion arise and your resolve is indecisive, you fail to break through the illusions of empty fame and floating profit. When fame and profit accrue to you, greed and craving immediately take birth. Fame...
When one’s own benefit falls to others, resentment and envy arise. An ancient said: "Those who crave fame and profit share the same destination as the hungry ghosts;
those who pursue love and hatred fall together into the fiery pit. Yet, it is precisely through these feelings of love and hatred that the Pure Land is interrupted.

Thus, a single moment of interruption is itself the karma for the hungry ghosts' fiery pit. To verify this: having already studied the practice of exclusive cultivation, you should seek spiritual efficacy.
Examination: Now that your hair has turned white, your face is wrinkled, and the signs of death have appeared before you, how many days do you know remain until your end?
You must seek to see the Buddha right now. Master Yuan of Mount Lu received the Buddha’s hand upon his head three times;
Master Huai-gan called upon the Buddha’s name and immediately beheld the Buddha; Master Shao-kang chanted the Buddha’s name once, and a Buddha followed him.

They emerge from the mouth like a string of pearls. Such miraculous responses are tens of thousands upon tens of thousands. If your mind remains uninterrupted, it will not be difficult to see the Buddha.
If a mind of interruption arises, you will certainly not see the Buddha. Since you do not see the Buddha, you lack the affinity for him and will find it difficult to be born in the Pure Land.
If you are not born in the Pure Land, you will inevitably fall into the evil realms. Thus, a single moment of interruption is precisely [the cause of this].

Mind and object are of one substance; sentient beings and Buddhas share the same source. To seek that Buddha is to seek one’s own mind; it is not an external seeking. One must investigate one’s own mind.
One must seek that Buddha; how could it be anything else? If one were thus, then grasping and rejecting, delighting and loathing, would burn with attachment to signs.

How could there be anything external to the mind?
