Because the mind is capable of encompassing all—enveloping all environments and beings, matter and mind, the pure and the defiled, the causes and effects of Buddhas and sentient beings, and the three periods of time and the ten directions—it contains everything within itself without exception. It is a single, unified experience. To seek an external appearance is to be deluded.
It cannot be attained. One should seek it in this manner; how could one seek it within the deluded mind? Such a prayerful seeking is what the Buddha has certified.

It is utterly remote from those in the world who do not recognize their own fundamental mind—those who are foolish and ignorant, who seek the Buddha of Western Sukhāvatī within the shadows of the physical body and its sensory reflections, claiming that this is the Pure Land of Mind-Only and the Original Nature Amitābha. Truly, they are far removed from the truth.

Far removed is the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the body of Amitābha; they are not the same as the aggregate-body (*skandha*) of sentient beings. If the body and mind were subject to arising and ceasing, the Buddha would likewise arise and cease.

Because the Buddha would arise and cease, samādhi could not be accomplished. Even if one were to seek an arising-and-ceasing Buddha, one would be born into an arising-and-ceasing land and fail to achieve right practice.
For with a samsaric mind one produces samsaric views, and thus that nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) would likewise undergo cyclic revolution. That is to say—

This is the meaning. If one seeks the Buddha Amitābha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond ten million *koṭi* lands in the western direction, and contemplates it with the wondrous contemplation that accords with the nature as it truly is, the marks and signs of the Tathāgata’s original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) will manifest, and the true mind of the sentient beings’ initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) will be revealed.

When the initial and original enlightenments merge in mutual resonance, and sentient beings and Buddhas respond to one another, samādhi is thereby accomplished and correct practice is established. Not...
Only in the land of arising and ceasing can birth truly occur. This mind pervades all places, not even excluding the hells, let alone the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Yet, in places of suffering, beings follow their nature by seeking escape; in realms of bliss, they follow their nature by seeking rebirth.

Although one seeks to leave suffering and attain bliss according to the teachings of the Sūtras, in reality, nothing transcends our own mind-nature. Therefore, it is called the Pure Land of Mind-Only.
The original nature is Amitābha. Since the deluded mind has no substantial reality, how could it be the "original nature that is solely mind"?

Those who seek within the deluded mind of reflected conditions take the physical body, as well as the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the oceans of lands of the ten directions, to be external objects.
Those who seek within the unmoving true mind take the oceans of lands of the ten directions, the great earth, and the mountains and rivers to be the internal mind. Know this.
Thus, within the internal mind, one may arbitrarily abandon the defiled and grasp the pure, feeling aversion toward the east and joy toward the west.

Because one’s own mind truly possesses the great vow that bears fruit as a Buddha capable of drawing others in, whatever is sought shall not fail to be attained. If, however, one treats it as an external object, then it will be split into two separate pieces.

As soon as one stirs a thought, one deviates from the essence of the Dharma and fails to attain one's own mind. Because there is only the Buddha-nature inherent as a cause, which lacks functional power, though one seeks it, nothing is found.
Furthermore, the deluded mind is merely a false reflection of conditions; by mistaking it for being within the physical body, one thinks there is no land where birth can occur.
The true mind, however, nurtures all lands and worlds; it inherently possesses the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, both its environment and its inhabitants. One need only seek it therein.
They must arise. When the deluded mind abandons the external and turns inward, the true mind takes the external as internal.

Thus, while the objects of the deluded mind appear distinct from the mind itself, the true mind is such that mind and object are one and the same. The deluded mind undergoes birth and extinction without foundation; the true mind is unmoving and unshakable.

While the deluded mind exists within the cause without manifesting the fruit, persisting in birth and extinction from beginning to end, the true mind’s cause and fruit are consistent, such that cultivation and realization penetrate one another. This is the distinction between the True and the Deluded.

The mind seeks [the truth], yet their differences are such that when discussed, they exceed the disparity between a day and an eon; when discussed in terms of location, they are not merely as far apart as heaven and earth.
If one discusses its essence, the true [mind] envelops the ten voids, while the deluded [mind] dwells within the body.

If one discusses its function, the true [mind] cuts through the Sahā world to directly transcend birth and death, whereas the deluded [mind] is like boiling sand for rice, which remains unaccomplished even after kalpas. Thus, the practitioner must resolve to give rise to the bodhicitta.

To seek birth in the Pure Land while falsely seeking a true Buddha is truly lamentable; it is like mistaking a thief for one’s own son, whereby the family’s wealth and treasures will surely be squandered.
The Great Master of Siming spoke of the contemplation of the Buddha and the contemplation of the mind as "pointing to the false to reveal the true."

It is not that the actual reality of the Pure Land’s environment and its inhabitants is denied; rather, how can we lament that in later generations, false views have arisen like swarms of bees and demonic cohorts have blazed forth?
They extinguish the eye of the True Dharma and sever the lineage of the Buddhas. Clinging to delusive mental images, they refuse to seek the West.

Even commoners in the streets and alleys have not heard the correct teaching, yet they secretly transmit these false views from one to another. If you truly seek liberation from birth and death, you must rely on the correct [teaching].
This is said to be correct. If one’s hindrances are heavy, one should further examine the objects of the deluded mind that perceives shadows.
How is it that the deluded mind has no substance? It falsely recognizes itself as dwelling within the physical body; the body dwells in the world; the world dwells in space.
Space is vast and all-pervasive, containing within it all lands and atoms. Thus, the great realm of space is vast while the small mind is inferior to the body. In a single thought-moment, it turns—
It is so subtle that it cannot be pointed out; it is sought though it cannot be sought. Is this not utterly bewildering?

Once this principle is understood, one knows that the boundless nature of emptiness does not exist outside my Great Enlightened, Pure Mind. How much less do the various worlds exist outside of empty space?
How much less does the form-body exist outside of the worlds? How much less does the deluded mind exist outside of the form-body? Thus, the deluded, subtle body clings to the realms.
The great emptiness is perfectly round; it does not exist outside my mind. My mind is vast and expansive.

As for the physical bodies, deluded thoughts, and all sentient beings of the ten directions and the three periods of time, if one seeks even a single dharma existing outside the mind, it is utterly unattainable. The Sūtra says:

"To recognize the confusion within enlightenment—the turbid and agitated appearances—as the nature of the mind; to take this single delusion as the mind, and to be certain that it is deluded regarding the physical body..."
Internally, they do not realize that their physical bodies, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all things within the wondrously luminous true mind.
It is like discarding a clear ocean hundreds of thousands of miles wide and recognizing only a single bubble, taking that bubble to be the entirety of the tide.
To exhaustively explore the oceans and seas is merely to double one’s delusion. It is further said:

"The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind pervades the worlds of the ten directions, containing and nurturing the lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions—the pure, jewel-adorned realms of the Wondrously Enlightened Kings. It is also said:

"The empty space of the ten directions is born within your own mind, like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky; how much more so, then, are all the worlds contained therein?"

Is it empty? Since the lands of the ten directions—both the environment and its inhabitants, matter and mind—are my own original possession, and I now seek birth in that originally possessed land to behold the originally possessed Buddha, this is precisely to overturn and shatter beginningless ignorance and not to follow delusion.
When that Buddha manifests for me, it is precisely the Buddha of my own original mind manifesting. When my mind manifests, that Buddha manifests.
My mind is the mind of that Buddha; that Buddha is the Buddha of my mind. They are of one essence and non-dual; their nature is fundamentally interfused.
How could one abandon the Buddha of the inner mind within the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, falsely calculating that there exists elsewhere a "mind-only" apart from this?
[The Buddha said: "It is the Buddha. Someone asked: "Does the deluded mind not also possess the dharmas of the environment and its inhabitants? He replied:

"Even if the deluded mind possessed the environment and its inhabitants, would it not also possess the Land of Ultimate Bliss? If the Land of Ultimate Bliss were a real realm like that of Sahā, one could seek it and say that the mind possesses it.
However, if there is no real realm and it is merely a false imagination, what reality is there to claim that the mind possesses it? One should know this."

The mind that is identical with the object is called "true"; the mind that is separate from the object is called "delusory. Although truth and delusion are the same in essence, they differ in terms of identity and separation.
To be identical is to attain; to be separate is to lose. The meaning of this is clear.

Annotated Explanation of the Diagram of the Minds and Objects of Reality and Delusion The large square on the left symbolizes the Great Awakened Mind of non-arising and non-extinction. Since the mind cannot be illustrated by analogy, it is provisionally represented by a square shape.
The large circle symbolizes the boundless void of the ten directions. The ten small squares symbolize the infinitesimal [realms] within each of the ten directions.
"Worlds as numerous as motes of dust. The character "mind" (心) is a metaphor for the shadows of the six sense-objects (ṣaḍ-viṣaya) harbored within the chest.
These delusive shadows reside within my own body; the body resides in the world; the world resides in space; and space resides within the heart-mind of Great Enlightenment.

Therefore, one knows that the distinction between the East as defiled and the West as pure consists of two forms of actual reality, separated by ten trillion lands. The Buddhas and Patriarchs said: "The Pure Land is fundamentally Mind-only."

The Amitābha of intrinsic nature resides precisely within the great awakened mind that encompasses the ten voids. To claim that he exists within the illusory shadows of deluded thought would be to say one is profoundly deluded.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "To cast aside hundreds of thousands of great oceans and instead recognize a single floating bubble as the entirety of the tide—this is a person who is doubly deluded.
This is exactly what that means. Furthermore, it is like empty space arising within the great awakening, as vast as the ocean.
A single bubble arises; all the subtle dust-motes of lands with outflows are produced in dependence upon space. Thus, pure and defiled lands alike do not depart from the true mind.
To realize the distant is to find it near; to seek is to find no seeking, for one naturally accords with the principle of reality.
The Diagram of the True and the False Mind-Object, with an Appendix: The Discourse on Refuting Delusion through Nianfo (also titled *Direct Pointing to the Essential Heart*).
The Great Hero (the Buddha), observing that the Sahā world is subject to the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and bondage by karma, taught people to recite the name of Amitābha.
As people seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the time since the Sage departed has grown ever more distant and human society has become increasingly corrupt.

Misinterpreting the teaching that "all dharmas are in the mind," they instead identify the mind with the shadows of the six sense-objects arising within the chest. Claiming that the Pure Land exists within, they do not seek rebirth there.

These six objective shadows all belong to external conditions; they have no inherent substance of their own. If those external conditions do not exist, this mind will immediately cease. How can it be said...?
How could there be any land within this? Some claim that upon awakening to the Way, the Buddha-land is simply within the mind.
Once one has seen one's nature, how could it be reasonable to instead cling to the shadows of conditioned objects? Even demons, heretics, and evil thieves transcend such views;

in this world, such a view is the most inferior of all. If you wish to awaken to your true original mind, you should contemplate the shadows of conditioned objects within the six sense-fields that you currently recognize.
This mind has always been within your chest. The chest resides in the body; the body dwells in the land;
the land and all oceans of pure and impure lands are entirely within empty space. Empty space is boundless, and the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—reside entirely therein.
Although this space is vast, my unmoving true mind is neither large nor extremely large. That space is contained within my true mind, just as...
A small fragment of cloud appears within the Great Clarity; how could the pure and defiled oceans of lands not reside within the fundamental mind?
Thus, when the Buddha says that all dharmas reside in the mind, he does not mean within the illusory shadows of conceptualization in the chest, nor within the deluded mind of conditioned reflections;

rather, they reside within the fundamental true mind of the present single thought. This mind is detached from cognition and transcends hearing and seeing; it has forever severed [all dualistic attachments].
All phenomena of arising and ceasing, increasing and decreasing, are neither beginning nor present; they are fundamentally True Suchness (*tathatā*), containing all wonders.
This is the source of delusion and enlightenment within the ten realms, whose vastness is beyond the reach of discursive thought.

Since all bodies and lands are entirely contained within the Great Enlightened True Mind and are realized as identical to the Buddha, one knows that the actual realms of Sukhāvatī, Sahā, and so forth, are entirely my own.
When the mind acts according to its own whims—abandoning the east and grasping at the west, loathing impurity and delighting in purity—it burns with attachment to signs and seeks them out;
yet all such states do not depart from my own mind. Therefore, when the marks and signs of Amitābha appear in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they are the manifestation of one's own mind.
When one's own mind manifests, that Buddha appears. My mind is the Buddha’s mind, and the Buddha’s mind is my mind. They are of one essence, non-dual.

Therefore, it is said that the Pure Land is solely the mind and Amitābha is one's original nature. This does not mean that there is no land or Buddha in the West and that one need not seek rebirth there;
rather, it means that within your own arising-and-ceasing, conditioned reflections, these are termed "the mind-only original nature.
To seek that Buddha is to seek one's own mind, and to seek one's own mind is to seek that Buddha. Why, then, do you now destroy the Dharma and disperse the Sangha?

Those who idly wander among the Confucian path or superficially engage with the principles of Chan do not realize that one must seek the principle of non-obstruction within the very realm and the very mind.

Instead, they divide the non-dual Dharma into internal and external, distinguishing between realm and mind. They teach people to abandon the external and grasp the internal, turning their backs on the realm and heading toward the mind.
This causes hatred and attachment to increase and discrimination to become even more extreme; for as soon as one divides the realm...
They regard the Land of Ultimate Bliss as external and teach that one need not seek rebirth there.

Dividing their own minds, they falsely point to the illusory shadows of the six sense-objects—the empty and false discursive thoughts—as being the mind itself, claiming that the Land of Ultimate Bliss exists within.

Furthermore, they contemplate this mind as having no substance, asserting that it is fundamentally devoid of all dharmas of cause and effect, good and evil, cultivation, or realization. From this point on, they act according to their whims, recklessly entangling themselves in worldly conditions, and thus they teach.
People need not perform prostrations to the Buddha, burn incense, light lamps, recite sutras, or offer vows; this is called "clinging to signs" (*nimitta*).
Those who are superior should cause the bound mind to remain unmoving, like a block of dull stone. [Otherwise,] they will disrupt the methods of meditation (*dhyāna*).

In extreme cases, they even advocate for unrestrained spontaneity, claiming that the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are all but empty flowers that do not hinder the Path. Because of such false views, they proceed directly—
They dwell facing the very lowest layer of the Avīci Hell, remaining there until this view is repented and that hell itself perishes accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding external objects, although they see them as truly existent, they do not dare to say they are non-existent; they likewise designate them all as "external things," splitting reality into two poles.
Thus, they are unable to achieve the identity of mind and object, doing nothing but putting on clothes and eating meals, for fear of violating their physical desires. They do not dare—

They dismiss these as external matters; yet, although they have heard the names of the heavens, hells, and the lands of bliss within the dust-motes of the universe, because they have not seen them, they flatly declare them to be non-existent.
Instead, they claim that mere pleasure is heaven and mere suffering is hell—how base is their vision!
The Tathāgata calls such people objects of pity; therefore, my heart is truly one with the Buddha’s.
The mind and the principle are one and the same; therefore, the power, majesty, and radiant light of Amitābha reside within my heart.
Relying on the power of my own deluded mind, he performs all buddha-activities for me, never failing to guide me at any time.

My mind, likewise, dwells within the vow-mind of Amitābha, cultivating the wholesome practices of mindfulness of the Buddha and the aspiration for rebirth; there is no practice that is not fully contained therein.
Regarding the virtues of the Buddha: by realizing those Buddha-virtues, one accomplishes my samādhi.
Therefore, one knows that from the initial aspiration to the ultimate consummation, not a single dharma of Amitābha’s vow-power fails to proceed directly toward my own mind.

Since my own mind is the Buddha-mind, I too—from the beginningless past until the end of the future—cultivate all samādhis, such that not a single dharma fails to be gathered and returned to the Buddha.
The ocean is originally the Buddha, because the Buddha-mind is identical to my own mind.

Thus, although the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, cause and effect, and the pure and the defiled are all of one mind, there is in reality no hindrance to each remaining in its own respective position.
Because they are of one mind, although the pure and the defiled differ, that which is sought does not transcend the true mind. Because they are their own distinct parts, although they are one...

The mind must necessarily abandon the defiled and take up the pure. When one abandons the defiled and takes up the pure, the Way of resonance and response intersects, and one beholds the Original Nature Amitābha.
Upon realizing that all is One Mind, purity and defilement are naturally distinguished; thus one can awaken to the Pure Land as being solely Mind.
Cultivating in this manner is like casting a single drop into the ocean, where it becomes of one flavor; only then does one know that the great ocean is oneself. How could it be otherwise?

There is one practice that is utterly wasted and fails to bring about merit or virtue. A foolish couple from a village, though ignorant of principle, possessed the sincere faith that those lands truly exist;

thus, at the time of their deaths, they were instead able to attain rebirth there. Conversely, those who fear existence and fall into emptiness mistake the shadows of conditions for the mind, asserting that there is no external land; therefore, even though they cultivate the path, they continue to undergo birth and death. This is so.

Therefore, all who seek rebirth therein should, with a profound mind, give rise to superior vows and practices: whether by reciting the name or holding mantras, or by circumambulating, prostrating, burning incense, and scattering flowers;

by repenting during the six periods of the day and night, casting aside all worldly concerns, and single-mindedly focusing on the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows without allowing the mind to slacken or abandon its effort—then at the end of life, one will be reborn there.
Furthermore, one should be able to filially support one's parents and serve one's teachers and elders.
With a compassionate heart, one refrains from killing; cultivates the ten wholesome actions; upholds the Three Refuges; fulfills all the precepts; does not violate dignified conduct;
has deep faith in cause and effect; does not slander the Mahāyāna; and encourages practitioners to proceed. By cultivating such dharmas as these, one will likewise be born there.
To seek birth in every thought-moment in this manner is precisely non-thought, non-seeking, and non-birth. Why is this? For diligent cultivation is itself non-cultivation;
it is not that one does not cultivate that constitutes non-cultivation. Human life is impermanent; with each breath, one passes into the next world.

Mundane affairs are like a continuous chain, a link after link never severed. If one cannot, amidst the oppressive entanglements of worldly toil, bring one’s ambitions to rest and cease one's efforts, [one will remain bound].

"Though one may be severed limb from limb, if one gives rise to the vow and establishes practice with all one's strength in a single leap, how could one fail to be reborn there in accordance with that thought?

I now prostrate and exhort the children of the Buddha: you should practice with a single mind. (Self-note: Written at the request of Layman Li of Dafang, who composed an exhortation on the Land of Bliss, asking for my commentary.
Thus recorded on the twentieth day of the ninth month of the Yihai year of the Hongwu era.)
Refuting Misinterpretations, Part Three (A Sigh from a Worthy Patriarch):
The *Nianfo Samādhi* is of profound scope and is difficult to master in its entirety. Throughout past and present, the oral transmissions of various masters have differed from one another.
As for Tiantai, its teachings are fully complete; Ci'en and Xianshou each drew upon its strengths.

Our own Chan school is also extremely clear, yet later students, being shallow and limited, find no point of orientation. With many divergent views and numerous paths, they seek the entrance but do not find it.

Regarding the passages in the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* that speak of the Pure Land, people secretly speculate and give rise to interpretations based on the literal words, claiming that there is fundamentally no Pure Land and thus no need to seek rebirth there.
They do not realize that the Master’s teaching accords with the intent of the sutras; even if one follows his phrasing, he does not say that the Pure Land does not exist.
Since the Pure Land exists, the principle of seeking rebirth is self-evident. Why is this? Because beginners are attached...
Pointing at the moon, the Great Master said: "If the minds of people in the East are pure, they are without sin;

if the minds of people in the West are impure, they likewise have [innumerable] offenses. If those in the East commit sins and then recite the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the West, then when those in the West commit sins and recite the Buddha's name, what land would they seek for rebirth?
This is an extreme statement intended to show that one must purify the mind and must not commit sins. How could it be that the West is truly..."
Is there such a thing as a person who commits sins and is impure? As it is said: "If the mind is pure, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is a Buddha;
if the mind is not pure, a Buddha is an ordinary person. How could there truly be an impure Buddha who then becomes an ordinary person?

Therefore, it is further stated that the distance to the Pure Land merely follows the differences in the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of sentient beings; how could the Buddha-land itself possess any distinction of distance? It is essential...
Sentient beings forever sever the ten evils and the eight heterodoxies; they fully cultivate the ten virtues and the eightfold noble path.

If they awaken, they are able to practice kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, and can purify such wholesome qualities as impartiality and rectitude; these are Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Śākyamuni, and Amitābha.
If they are deluded, they differentiate between self and others with heterodox minds and false, weary afflictions; these are Mount Sumeru, the waters of the ocean, dragons, and ghosts.
Regarding the hells: now, examining the Master’s intent, it follows that as the mind is pure, so the Buddha-land is pure. Is this not in accord with the Buddha’s own mind?
However, when the Sages teach the Dharma, their methods of negation (*paryudāsa*) and affirmation (*vidhi*) differ. Negation excludes everything as "not"; affirmation affirms everything as "is.

Though both issue from the Buddha’s mouth, their meaning is no different. If, in the result, one does not necessarily have to abandon the defiled to attain the pure, then simply purifying the mind is sufficient.

One need only purify the mind; it is not necessary to specifically abandon evil and cultivate good. Since one abandons evil and practices good among people, one must likewise relinquish the defiled and grasp the pure within the land;
thus the meaning becomes even clearer. Therefore, when the Buddha taught negation (*paryudāsa*), he was truly manifesting affirmation (*vidhi*) to lead beings toward birth;
when he taught affirmation, he was truly relying on negation to make known non-birth. Caoqi [Huineng] instructed people that because the mind is first purified, [the land is purified].
The Pure Land of the Buddha’s recompense is inherently pure; it does not require one to seek birth there. This is through *paryudāsa-pratiṣedha* (negation by exclusion).

At Mount Lu, they teach that upon entering the purity of the Buddha’s recompense, the causal mind becomes naturally pure. This is through *vidhi-vākya* (affirmative expression); it necessarily requires seeking birth there. The teaching of the Dharma is neither before nor after; these two meanings have never been separated.
Alas, how can one, upon merely hearing the negation (*paryudāsa*), claim it is the truth, and then declare the affirmation (*vidhi*) to be false, thereby giving rise to regression?

This is truly a cause for lamentation. Throughout the various sections of the Buddha’s lifetime teachings, he spoke extensively because he wished to respond to the capacities of beings and eliminate their doubts.

In this Dharma-ending age, when upholding the school and establishing the teaching, how could there not be times for suppression and exaltation? It is precisely at such a time that one must encompass all things without exception;

how can one recklessly give rise to dualistic views? Furthermore, the Great Master said: "If the mind is level, what need is there to labor over keeping the precepts? If conduct is straight, what need..."
"Use this to practice dhyāna. If one follows these words, it would seem that one need not maintain the precepts to practice dhyāna. However, if the mind is equanimous, one does not kill others;
this self-benefit encompasses the distinctions between male and female. True preceptual conduct is entirely contained therein.

How could one who is completely devoid of maintaining the precepts—such as those who plunder or murder—be said to have an equanimous mind? Thus, we know that what need is there to labor over [external] maintenance? This precisely reveals the Great Precept.
"Dhyāna" is translated as "quiet contemplation" (靜慮), or "right concentration" (正定), or "the samādhi of one practice" (一行三昧).

How could there be one whose conduct is upright yet whose contemplation is not quiet, whose concentration is not right, or whose practice is not unified? This makes it clear that what is being manifested is profound dhyāna; for what use would there be in practicing otherwise?

The Master feared that later students would become mired in the Dharma and attached to its traces; thus, within the context of the essence of the precepts, he asked, "What is the use of maintaining the precepts?

and within the context of the realm of meditation, he asked, "What is the need for practicing meditation? Following this logic, one might conclude that within the teachings on the Pure Land, it is unnecessary to seek rebirth there.

Later students became further mired in this, claiming that it is truly unnecessary to seek rebirth. This is the height of folly. In fact, what the Great Master said was intended as an exhortation to the contrary.
The teachings of the various patriarchs consist of both conforming praise and inverse admonition. Without conformity, there would be no way to open the path for cultivation and progress;

without inversion, there would be no way to demonstrate the severity of vigilance and self-restraint. These inverse exhortations and conforming praises all respond to the needs of the times; they contain no fixed, substantial dharma.
If one merely follows the words of the ancients without seeking their true intent, it is like encountering those who value the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) [only as a mere name].

It would instead become a poisonous medicine. The Master refers to the Perfect and Wondrous Three Truths: where there is birth, he speaks of non-birth; where there is no realization, he speaks of cultivation and realization.
Both extremes are unattainable, and the Middle Way does not exist. This accords with the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate, being straightforward and clear.
How could one then claim that the Chan school has failed to exhaust the essential meaning of the Pure Land?
As for Master Daochuo of Hexi, Shandao of Chang’an, Chan Master Xinyuan, Zhijue, and Cijue—were they not those who followed in his wake?

All of them were able to receive the distant echoes of his legacy and diligently propagate this Way. Daozhen and Huaiyu’s virtuous conduct was particularly manifest, as was that of Yuanzhao and others.
The Master’s efficacy became increasingly manifest, and his legacy remains to this day; how could one be further deluded? Section Four:
Contemplating the Buddha and Mind through Wisdom (This is the fundamental Dharma-wheel of the Pure Land school. Those who hold the name must also enter into principle through this "holding").

Regarding the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, it has had its origins from ancient times until the present. Yet, among them all, the principle of the Threefold Contemplation of Tiantai stands preeminent.
The Sūtra transcends all other doctrines. As for the "three contemplations," in a single thought-moment, one is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.

Being empty, all things are empty; being provisional, all things are provisional; being the Middle, all things are the Middle. They are simultaneously negated and established, and simultaneously neither-nor.
Negation and establishment are perfectly interfused and free from dependence. The Great Master Siming elucidated this principle through the Perfect and Subtle Three Contemplations.
This explains the sixteen contemplations. First is the contemplation of the setting sun. It first indicates the method for directing the visualization.

Although a practitioner at the initial stage understands that both the sense organs and their objects are the Dharma-realm, their mental conceptions are weak and inferior, making it difficult for the sublime realm to appear. Thus, the Tathāgata establishes this extraordinary skillful means.

One should immediately take the setting sun as the object of contemplation, causing the sun within meditative observation to arise. A person of wondrous understanding realizes that the mind capable of visualization inherently possesses all environments and beings.
Now, with a mind already endowed with the sun, one takes as the object the very sun that is the mind itself, causing the sun of the original nature to manifest before one.
Using the *dharmadhātu*-mind to take the *dharmadhātu*-object as its focus, one gives rise to the sun of the *dharmadhātu*. Since all are the *dharmadhātu*...
The realms are they not themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle? Furthermore, when the faculties and their objects are empty and quiescent, the mind becomes daily unimpeded.

Because they are provisionally established through dependent origination, defiled thoughts arise daily; yet since both the mind and the days are the Dharma-realm, they manifest as they are in their very essence. Once the daily contemplation is perfected, [the practice is complete].

The three contemplations exist simultaneously; they are neither one nor three, yet they are one and three—an inconceivable mystery. As it is with the contemplation of the sun, so it is with the other contemplations by analogy.

Furthermore, the title of the sutra, "Contemplation of Amitāyus Buddha," mentions the primary retribution (the Buddha) to include the secondary fruits (the Pure Land), and describes the teacher of transformation to encompass his followers;
thus, one simply contemplates that Buddha. One enters the contemplation of the Buddha through a single mark or excellence, contemplating only this.
The white tuft of hair between the eyebrows becomes exceedingly clear and distinct. The eighty-four thousand marks and signs will naturally manifest.
To see Amitāyus Buddha is to see all the Buddhas of the ten directions; this constitutes the universal contemplation of all physical forms and marks. The tuft of hair is like five Mount Sumerus.

In the *Shu* (Commentary), the practitioner is instructed to contemplate the tuft of hair of the "inferior response" [body], as it is suitable for contemplation by those at the initial stage of the path. —Ciyun.
The Dharma Master instructs [the practitioner] to visualize Amitābha Buddha with a sixteen-foot golden body seated upon a lotus flower.
Focus single-mindedly on the single mark of the white tuft of hair between his brows. The tuft is fifteen feet long, five inches in circumference, and has eight facets;

it is hollow both internally and externally. It curls to the right in elegant spirals between the brows, so pure, brilliant, and translucent that its qualities cannot be fully described. Make it manifest.
The golden countenance is reflected with distinct clarity. When forming this visualization, remain firm and do not waver; once this visualization is perfected, samādhi will manifest before you.
As the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas are the body of the Dharma-realm; they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings."
When one brings the Buddha to mind, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics. This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.
The ocean of the Tathāgatas’ perfect and universal knowledge arises from the mind’s contemplation. Therefore, one should contemplate that Buddha with focused attention.

Indeed, the body of the Dharma-realm is fundamentally and originally in profound accord with its manifestations, capable of giving rise to responsive applications; yet it cannot be evoked except through the resonance of the practitioner's devotion.

How could the Buddha not respond? His capacity to be moved is like water; his capacity to respond is like the sun. Therefore, when initial awakening (ādikṣaya-bodhi) merges with original awakening (mūla-bodhi), it is like the rising sun entering the pure sky.
Like reflections appearing in a hundred rivers, the interaction between stimulus and response is such that he enters the mental conceptions of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Buddha-body is omnipresent, taking the Dharma-realm as its essence. If one attains this contemplation of the Buddha’s three [bodies]...
When [the mind] is obscured, the contemplative understanding enters into the Buddha-body, and the Buddha-body enters into the contemplative understanding.

This is the initial enlightenment (śikṣā-bodhi) realizing original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi); therefore, original enlightenment enters into initial enlightenment. When understanding and entry correspond, this constitutes entering the mental conceptions of sentient beings.
One should know that the present contemplation does not merely contemplate the Buddha-nature within the mind of the aggregates (skandhas), but rather relies upon another Buddha.

This reveals the original nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, it first clarifies that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body Buddha) enters the mind that conceives of a self; next, it clarifies that the Buddha-body is entirely the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

Thus, the *nirmāṇakāya* manifests, making known the clarity of the original nature. Relying on external objects, [the teaching] is established; through the contemplation of "mind-only," it is founded.

These two meanings mutually support one another; this is the present method of contemplation. Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. This clarifies the nature.
Cultivating the principle of non-duality, there are two meanings for becoming a Buddha. First, a pure mind can evoke the responsive Buddhas of other directions.

This means that while the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is fundamentally devoid of form and characteristics, through the pure minds of sentient beings—which, based upon the karmic consciousness, perfumes the Buddhas' Dharma-bodies—one perceives the superior form and characteristics of the responsive Buddhas. Second, samādhi can accomplish one's own fruition-Buddha. This means that sentient...
One gives rise to the thought of purity and accomplishes the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, thereby ensuring that one will ultimately become a Buddha oneself.

Regarding these two meanings: first, one acts as another Buddha; second, one acts as one's own Buddha. One should know that the resultant Buddha arises from realization and is not something that occurs spontaneously;

it is precisely through this process that cultivation is perfected within the fundamental nature. This reveals that the qualities of the nature are not inherently Buddhas by themselves. These are the two meanings of "Buddha."

First, the mind is identical to the Responsive Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*). It was previously stated that the Buddha is fundamentally without marks; yet, because the mind is moved by resonance, he appears.
Thus, the existence or non-existence of the mind and the Buddha were previously seen as entirely distinct and eternal. Now, this view is obliterated;

therefore, the very mind of sentient beings is in its entirety the Responsive Buddha, for apart from the mind there is no further Buddha. Second, the mind is identical to the Fruitional Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*), because the Tathāgata already exists within the minds of sentient beings.
Having arrived, he sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). How could he wait for a future time before becoming a Buddha of fruition (*phala-buddha*)? Regarding these two meanings:

the former refers to the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (response-body Buddha), and the latter refers to the *dharmakāya* (fruition-body Buddha). One should know that the Buddha of fruition is primordially possessed; he is not established through conditions. He is "that which acts" (*kriyā*) and yet is "that which is" (*sat*).

This reveals that Buddhahood is not achieved through the causes and conditions of cultivated virtues. That which is empty destroys what is provisionally established; both are termed "action" (*kriyā*). It is not...
To negate without establishing is called "is. To act with total affirmation is such that the three truths are both negated and established;
to act with total affirmation is such that the three truths are neither negated nor established. This is the functioning of emptiness and provisional names within the Middle Way.

Thus, one can negate the three delusions and establish the three dharmas, thereby eliciting the perfect response of the three bodies of other Buddhas and enabling the fulfillment of the three bodies as the fruit of my own mind. This is precisely emptiness.
If one takes these provisional names as being real, then delusion is entirely wisdom and hindrances are entirely virtue. Thus, the mind is the Responsive Buddha;
the mind is the Fruitional Buddha. Therefore, know that those who practice this single mind cultivation are practicing the inconceivable three contemplations. Someone may say:

"Why is it that you do not consider that by focusing solely on the conceptualization of phenomena (*vastu-saṃjñā*), one instead manifests the contemplation of wisdom (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*)? This would cause those at the initial stage of practice to find entry difficult. Answer:

"Whether it be the contemplation of wisdom or the conceptualization of phenomena—even down to the slightest merit—if one attains single-mindedness (*ekacitta*), all shall be born in the Pure Land. Yet, there are vast differences in their excellence. This is truly because the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhigama*) is entirely different from that of the Hīnayāna.
The Hīnayāna is deluded regarding 'mind-only' (*cittamātra*), perceiving the Buddha as existing externally. The Mahāyāna knows that my own single mind is fully replete [with all things]."
Regarding the nature of all Buddhas: by taking the observation of Amitābha’s environment and its inhabitants as a condition, it perfumes the mind-nature (*cittatā*).

The Pure Land environment and its inhabitants, which are inherent within the mind-nature, arise through this perfuming; they are born because the mind possesses them. How could they be separate from the mind-nature?

The entire mind is Buddha, and the entire Buddha is mind. One observes the mind all day long, and one observes the Buddha all day long. Furthermore, one should understand that the *dharmadhātu* is perfectly interfused and inconceivable.

The essence of this principle is that my single thought-moment likewise manifests its entire substance as sentient beings, as Buddhas, as the support, as the correct [teaching], as the faculties, and as the objects.
Even down to a single atom, there is nothing that is not the total manifestation of the entire Dharma-realm.
To manifest even one such thing is to manifest the entirety of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm. Since it is the entire Dharma-realm, what single object could fail to possess all phenomena?
Furthermore, the perfectly luminous essence of the resultant Buddha is the inherent nature-virtue possessed by ordinary beings from the very beginning.

Therefore, this gate of contemplation relies upon the environment and inhabitants of that Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), employing subtle and wondrous observation to focus specifically on Amitābha to reveal the true body of the Buddha.

One must understand that the environment and the inhabitants coexist within the single mind; the nature of the mind is all-pervasive, such that there is no phenomenon not created and no phenomenon not possessed. If even a single phenomenon...

If it arises outside of the mind, it cannot be called Mahayana contemplation. Furthermore, the Sutra states that images of one zhang and six chi or eight chi in height are provided to accord with those of inferior capacity, enabling them to contemplate the small and perceive the great.

All sublime and extraordinary conceptions arise from cultivation based on the nature; the distinct forms of the small and the great are all manifestations of the trace descending from the fundamental source.
Since the nature that can contemplate is fundamentally without differentiation, how could the objects contemplated possibly [be different]?

Regarding the measure [of these teachings]: the discourse on the Perfect and Sudden is universally encompassed by a single sound. It reveals the sequential path without being gradual; it accords with the capacities of beings without being partial.
It simultaneously opens the gates of contemplation and fully manifests the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). How could the source of the Semblance Dharma not lie herein?

Chapter Five: The Contemplation of the Honored Image in the Practice Hall through Nianfo Now, the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the mind and its principle, are one and the same in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The sacred images and magnificent ritual implements within the practice hall are, in essence, identical to the environment and inhabitants of that Pure Land. Thus, although the practitioner has not yet departed from this Sahā world, they are as if already born in the Pure Land.

At the time of death, there is nothing that does not respond to such practice. Furthermore, even when the ritual of repentance consists of but a single incense stick or a single flower, how could this not be the principle of the Three Truths?
If one does not use these truths to observe every matter with right mindfulness, then the path of the Mahayana’s sudden and perfect enlightenment cannot be revealed.
This is like the immeasurable adornments of a Buddha-land, all of which arose from the causes of that Buddha.

The manifestations resulting from practice—such as the adornments of the site of enlightenment—are all without distinction, being the manifestations of the Buddha. Furthermore, these very ornaments constitute the wondrous marks of the [Buddha’s] body.
Through the mutual fusion of the environment and the embodied, the principle of the Dharma-realm is revealed. How could these be regarded as mere objects composed of earth and wood?
Therefore, one should know that mind, environment, body, and land are a single, unified enjoyment, sovereign and unimpeded. As the Sūtra says: "Pāramitā..."

From all jeweled canopies arises the mind of pure understanding regarding all objective realms; from all flower curtains arises the mind of the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
from all robes arises the mind of unimpeded entry into the vajra-dharma; from all networks of bells arises the mind that understands all phenomena to be like illusions;
and from all solid fragrances arises the mind of the Tathāgata’s seat, pervading the entire realm of the Buddhas.
The birth of all kinds of precious and wondrous seats arises from the mind that never tires of making offerings to the Buddhas.

The birth of all precious banners arises from the mind of joy that understands all phenomena to be like dreams. The birth of precious palaces where all Buddhas dwell arises from unattached roots of goodness.
The birth of clouds of all precious lotuses and so forth arises from these same principles; for this reason, incense, flowers, lamps, candles, banners, and canopies [all arise].
From ritual implements down to clothing, bedding, food, drink, medicine, and even a single mote of dust—there is nothing that is not samādhi and nothing that is not a Dharma-gate.
All are capable of inspiring in people a mind of wondrous understanding and realization of the holy;

they are also the very non-obstruction of body, environment, and wisdom of all living beings and Buddhas. Furthermore, they can walk with me as true Dharma companions, giving rise to wondrous awakening together.

One will be born in that land. The Sūtra says: "Maintain the mind through meditative concentration so it is always focused on a single object; through wisdom, realize that objects are identical to samādhi.
If one can perform this contemplation, then the faculties and their objects become unified. How could it be that my three karmas alone are the means of cultivation?
Just as the instruments of suffering in hell—swords, staves, blades, and fire—are all capable of shaking and transforming beings into snakes by the power of those evil causes.

Even dogs, insects, and birds, by piercing through bone and marrow, perform various acts of suffering; how much more so should the ritual implements of the *bodhimaṇḍa* not all fail to attain liberation and together accomplish *samādhi*?

Furthermore, regarding the honored images one reveres and makes offerings to, if one exhausts one's heart and will as if toward a father or mother, how could they not enable me to be swiftly reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*)? Moreover, even with just one Buddha and two Bodhisattvas—
An image—through the power of supernatural faculties and vows—is identical to the Buddha’s true body; it is efficacious when struck and responsive when sought. What difference could there be?

How can you harbor the view that it is merely wood, earth, glue, lacquer, gold, or pigment? Why not cultivate the visualization of the True Buddha with the marks and signs of the Great Vows of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?
If the image is not perceived as real, the mind will not be unified, samādhi will be difficult to achieve, and the loss will be profound indeed.

Indeed, the Buddha’s compassion is universally pervasive; within his non-dual body, he manifests according to the capacities of sentient beings, appearing as either the true body or the transformation body, or manifesting in various forms and images.
Because my own eyes are shrouded by deep obstructions, I perceive differences within a single dharma and mistake the Buddha’s true body for a mere image. Yet how could this image truly be an image?
It is like the Buddhas who welcome and guide those of the three grades, who appear differently according to the varying degrees of excellence or inferiority in their spiritual rank. I...
The images I see are indeed as they should be seen by me; how could it be that the Buddha’s compassion is not universal such that he does not manifest these images to me?

Yet, there are differences in what is perceived, all of which are the single essence of Amitābha. On the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the great bodhisattvas perceive the Buddha’s vast and immeasurable body adorned with a celestial crown as Vairocana.
The followers of the Three Vehicles perceive him as being born in a royal palace, aging, and so forth.
"O Bhikṣus, because we are ordinary persons, we should perceive these [images] as being composed of earth and wood. In ancient times, people carved wood into the form of a mother;
when someone borrowed it, the image could manifest joy or anger. If such was the power of filial piety in this world, how much more so for those made by the Buddhas of the past and present!

The evidential manifestations of image-making are manifold: from radiant auspicious responses to even śarīra relics that remain unharmed by water or fire—all of which are recorded in the historical annals."
It cannot be fully described. A sutra states: "The Buddha’s pure body pervades all places; there is not a single dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma.
How could this image alone be anything other than the Buddha? Question: "To be free from all marks is itself to be the Buddha.
Since even the Buddha-body is not [ultimately real], how much more so this image? Answer: "If everything were not the Buddha, then everything would be the Buddha. How could it not be the Buddha?"
Yes. If one understands this meaning, one realizes that the honored image is not separate from the ocean of vows;

it possesses great supernatural power capable of gathering and receiving all powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities, great kindness and great compassion, permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as the marks, signs, and radiance, being entirely equal and without distinction from the whole body of Amitābha. Within this, I shall perform the practice of repentance. When...

Just as a beggar who has gained access to a sovereign king constantly harbors a mixture of shame, trepidation, fear, and affection, thirsting for the Master’s acceptance and hoping for liberation—how much more so when encountering one who is difficult to meet throughout kalpas?
Having now met him, how could one treat him with negligence, fail to advance in superior practice, and create obstacles for oneself?
Furthermore, one should reflect that it is because that Buddha takes pity on me that he has manifested this semblance body to receive me.
I repent. All grave offenses shall certainly be extinguished; one will surely be born in the Pure Land and the mind will attain joy.
Suddenly, it is as if the heavens are vast and the earth is clear, and one obtains the Dharma-eye. That Land of Ultimate Bliss can then be seen as if before one's eyes.

Thus, one knows that the teaching of the ultimate identity between the true and the image is not at all shallow. Students should exhaust their sincerity and not give rise to divergent interpretations.
Section Six: Refuting the Heretical Teachings of Annihilationist Emptiness.

The entire body of the Holy Teachings of this one epoch is fundamentally based on the correct doctrine of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Even those phrases that transcend the hundred negations—how could they ever depart from the Dharma of dependent origination?
Nowadays, there is a certain class of people who have severed their roots of goodness, who are the most evil *icchantikas*, and who do not recognize the Buddha.
The Patriarch’s discourse on shattering attachments, eliminating doubts, untying adhesions, and removing fetters follows the footsteps of others;
yet you falsely claim that, apart from this mind, all conditioned phenomena are empty, that there is neither Buddha nor Dharma, and that there is neither good nor evil.

You mistakenly identify deluded consciousness as reality, asserting that no dharma can be found outside this mind. Consequently, you negate cause and effect and repudiate sin and merit, even speaking of the Buddhas...
Bodhisattva images are but lumps of earth and pieces of wood; the vast treasury of the teachings is merely worn-out, unclean paper.
All virtuous deeds and merits are said to be nothing more than a path of attachment to signs (*nimitta*). To speak of others' shortcomings and display one's own长处 (longs) is futile;
even to maintain a *kōan* (hētou) is said to be an act of stubborn clinging. It is better, therefore, to leave people utterly empty and bare within and without.
Having attained a state of expansive openness, they then secretly commit various evils while claiming that these do not obstruct the Way; thus they deceive themselves and others.
Such views are exceedingly numerous. Since they are incompatible with both the Teachings and the Vinaya, it is utterly improper for them to indiscriminately enter our school.

This must surely be Pāpīyān, whose ancient resentment has not yet been extinguished. He has sent one who assumes a form and attire identical to my own to destroy my Way and Dharma until nothing remains.
Alas, how painful! As the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas preach the Dharma of emptiness for the sake of delivering beings from existence;

yet those who become attached to emptiness cannot be transformed by any Buddha. It further says: "It would be better to speak of an 'existence' as large as Mount Sumeru than to speak of an 'emptiness' that leads to attachment."
It is said that there is not even so much as a mustard seed’s worth [of self]. Even the realization of the emptiness-view of the Hīnayāna is discarded by Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas;

how much more so when the Buddha reveals that existence itself is emptiness, and that emptiness does not depart from existence—this is what is called "true emptiness. People today speak of emptiness as being empty only after departing from existence;
such emptiness becomes a nihilistic view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), like falling into a pit from which one can never emerge. Yongjia said: "Abandoning existence to cling to emptiness."
The same applies to illness; it is like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into a fire. Shanxing falsely preached that all phenomena are empty, while Baolian secretly indulged in sexual desire;
both fell into the hells. Later generations, failing to exercise restraint, have again trodden in their footsteps—like the blind leading the blind.
That both the master and his disciples willingly sink into such depths is truly most lamentable. Even a son cannot bear to witness the transgressions of his father;

how much more so for us, the sons of the Śākya, who have received the grace of transcending the world, yet instead of honoring the formal teachings and the words of the Dharma, we indulge in their reckless disparagement?
Such people will surely head toward the five realms of the Avīci Hell, amidst its great heat and fierce flames, each individually reaping the fruit of their own erroneous interpretations today.
This report—how could it be empty talk? Even Deshan and Danxia were like Mañjuśrī wielding his sword, at once destroying the attachments of others for their sake.
How could these be treated as mere subjects for casual discussion or instruction? That the Buddha-dharma endures for a long time depends entirely upon the scriptures and the images.
If one merely practices the external forms, robes, and dignified deportment of the Dharma, what basis is there for such conduct to endure for long?

The Buddha taught that even failing to show proper respect toward the sutras and images incurs great transgression; how much more so, then, for those who treat them with contempt or derision—their sins and rebelliousness are evident.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught the emptiness of dharmas, desiring that people realize the emptiness of the person to sever evil. How can it be that they fail to understand the Buddha’s intent and, instead, become stagnant in their attachment to emptiness?

To abandon the wholesome—how could this not be a perversion? Furthermore, since you say that even unwholesome states are unimpeded, I do not understand what impedes the wholesome dharmas such that you wish not to cultivate them.
Moreover, you compare those who eat vegetarian food to oxen and sheep, while you dismiss those who preach the Dharma as having "empty understanding."

One does not realize that wisdom and understanding are like the eyes, while the practice of the Way is like the feet. Without feet, though one sees, one cannot travel; without eyes, though one travels, one cannot see.
Because of not seeing, one will inevitably fall into pits and ditches; because of not traveling, how can one reach the place of treasure?
Mañjuśrī understands the profound and serves as the teacher of all Buddhas; Samantabhadra’s practice is vast and acts as the father of all sentient beings.
Even the Zen school of Nanyue still regards the practice of "not being without cultivation and realization" as the essential principle for entering the path to enlightenment.
If the false views of people today are so deep-seated, will they not swiftly fall into places of extreme suffering? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

"One may claim to be already sufficient, and suddenly a groundless and great arrogance arises in the mind; one even treats the Tathāgatas of the ten directions with contempt, let alone those below them."

They rank themselves as śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, they are said to suddenly turn toward eternal extinction (*parinirvāṇa*), repudiating cause and effect, and entering exclusively into emptiness.
When the mind of emptiness manifests before them, they even give rise to the view of perpetual annihilation. They do not pay homage to stupas or temples, and they destroy scriptures and images.
Addressing donors, they say: "These [images] are merely gold, copper, earth, or wood; these scriptures are merely tree leaves or paper."
"O Flower! To fail to respect one's own physical body—which is truly eternal—and instead to venerate earthenwood images is, in truth, a profound perversion.
Those with deep faith should destroy such objects; those who harbor doubts and mislead sentient beings will enter the Avīci Hell. Having lost right concentration, they shall surely fall into ruin.

The World-Honored One has already forewarned those who speak falsely of the emptiness of dharmas, or who claim to have attained what they have not attained, or claim to have realized what they have not realized."
He bestowed upon him the record of his entry into hell. How could a person of today possibly escape what the Buddha has recorded?
The Dharma-gate of Non-duality of Chan and Buddhism is the seventh;
the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-Recitation encompasses all capacities within the Dharma-realm without exception. It is truly that which Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra [uphold].
This realizes the realm of the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). It belongs to the same category as the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras; its flavor is that of the *amṛta* (the finest essence).
Yongming said: "There is Pure Land without Chan; of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go. Once you have seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
This is truly the path that leads upward, and even further upward. Nowadays, people, because their ambitions are not fulfilled, sigh and say: "Throughout my life..."
"Enough! Zen practice is not what I hope for; it is better to simply recite the Buddha's name. Thereupon, he instead grew indolent in his body and never deeply reflected upon himself.
Should he happen to encounter some slight success, immeasurable evil deeds would once again manifest before him. If this is how one recites the Buddha's name, what benefit is there?
He says that Zen practice is subtle and difficult, like constructing a ten-thousand-pillar mansion, whereas reciting the Buddha's name—

This is coarse and easy. It is like making a small opening in a grass hut; seeing the ground as it is, one encounters royal cuisine in times of hunger yet mistakes it for wild herbs, or views the king of wish-fulfilling jewels as a mere fish eye—how lamentable this is!

One does not realize that while the practice of the two gates of Chan and Buddhism differs, their arrival at the destination is the same. In Chan, whatever is brought forth is it; do not seek it in the Buddha. If you yourself...

One possesses right knowledge and vision, yet does not encounter a person of right knowledge and vision; even if one does not fall back, one mostly enters the path of Māra because there is no power of the Buddha to provide rescue and protection.
One does not take anything at all as a basis for mindfulness, but mindfully contemplates only that Buddha.

Even if one lacks correct understanding or the guidance of teachers and friends, by simply having direct faith in the existence of the Buddha’s body and land and resolving to be born there, one will be reborn—even if one remains stuck in heterodox or Hinayana views.
They likewise return to the correct path because they are rescued and protected by the power of Amitābha’s vows; this is called a difference in the practice of cultivation.
As for the depth or shallowness of the Dharma gates, Zen meditation is precisely the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and the recitation of the Buddha’s name is precisely Zen meditation.

Without Zen, one cannot attain rebirth in the Pure Land; without Zen, the Buddha-recitation lacks contemplative wisdom. How could there be two different approaches to reciting the Buddha’s name and practicing Zen? If one understands this—

In principle, one should seize the opportunity when one's aspirations are realized; with a single stroke, one must sever all attachments. Resolutely generating the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), one should practice this Way with vigor.

Regarding all worldly things—wives, children, treasures, wealth, even one’s head, eyes, marrow, brain, and even life itself—one should not be stingy or sparing. One must resolve to seek birth [in the Pure Land];
how could one, out of necessity, treat this supreme Dharma-gate as a mere grass hut or a "fish-eye" minor path, acting with such expedient negligence?

To practice in such a manner is truly a great pity. If you could follow the Master’s example, cast aside the view that there is a "Great Vehicle" as a precious destination, and resolve upon a mind of certain non-retrogression, then to row with oars and poles even further as the wind and current carry you along—how fortunate would that be! Question:
How can saying "The Buddha is a dry piece of dung" or "Strike him dead with a single blow" be the same as reciting the Buddha's name with reverence, longing, and devotion?

Answer: The six characters of the Great Name bring about peaceful harmony through effortless ease. Should one engage even slightly in discursive thought, one cannot avoid the various refinements of the "many-mouthed" masters.
It is simply this: the body of Amitābha Buddha is the land, and the land is the body; body and land are without obstruction, and mind and environment are perfectly interfused.
Whether "that" or "this," they are a single enjoyment. This extends even to the aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and spheres (*āyatana*).
All dharmas, right up to unsurpassed bodhi, are at all times and in all places unobstructed and unhindered;
they are neither bound nor liberated. Whether horizontal or vertical, adverse or favorable, they are all the pure form-body of Amitābha.

Even lust, anger, and ignorance do not interrupt this Brahma-conduct; the host of worldly afflictions are companions in the Dharma. How much more so, then, a dried piece of excrement? Since this is already...
Buddha! Why must you dig into the pure ground to carve out flesh and create sores?

You give rise to the thought of saving sentient beings, yet within the impartial Dharma that is free from arising and ceasing, you proclaim birth and proclaim death, performing a thousand tricks to vex all and cause countless "dead people" upon the level ground.
Eh! At this point, you must take care not to misunderstand. If you misunderstand, you will surely receive the heavy blows from my staff.
If you claim that this is something one can touch upon at the "heap of refuse" under the gate of Caoxi’s school, you have not yet seen it even in your dreams.
Question: I fear that such deliberation is not permissible. Answer: It is none other than this very deliberation.
Do not say that deliberation has a mind or that deliberation is without mind; when have I ever engaged in deliberation? Question: But you have already deliberated.
Answer: What did I just say? The questioner did not understand. After a long silence, he asked again: "Everything is Buddha. Even a dung-scoop?"
"Even a willow twig or a broom can serve as an answer. Why then do you answer with a dried excrement-stick? [The Master] replied: "All things are the Buddha.

One may ask about doors, windows, gates, or lattices; why then do you choose to ask about the Buddha? Thus, one should know that the questioner's approach was too high-minded. My answer was intended merely to shatter their attachments."

How can it be said that because the words differ, one falsely recognizes Zen and the Buddha-dharma as distinct practices? Question: The Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation is thus; how does one attain correspondence with it? Answer:
One sound of the Buddha-name corresponds with one sound; every sound of the Buddha-name corresponds with every sound.

As the ancient masters have refined this through the aforementioned methods, what more remains unclarified? It is simply a matter of being willing to put it into practice; what need is there for further anxiety?
This is not so. It is like an empty valley where every sound is answered: a loud voice echoes loudly, and a faint voice resounds faintly.

The Land of Bliss gathers in sentient beings through the three ranks and nine grades, guiding them according to their faculties without missing a single opportunity. For those who can apply themselves with diligent effort, nothing will be in vain.
For this reason, it is not only that the Buddhas of Dhyāna and Śākyamuni are non-dual; this applies throughout the entire lifetime of Śākyamuni’s teaching.
The path of transformation does not go beyond the single dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha (nien-fo). I exhort future worthies: do not give rise to divergent views.

Regarding the eighth dharma-gate of the Buddhas’ methods of subduing and gathering, when practitioners hear of the aforementioned realms of the environment and its inhabitants, they realize that this land is truly suffering while that land is truly blissful. Although they contemplate...
The Dharma-gate of wisdom is perfectly integrated and subtle; one directly perceives that both lands are, in their very presence, the actual reality.

This is not like the shallow faith which claims that the other land exists when the mind is present and does not exist when the mind is absent, being a mere illusion of light and shadow, empty and unreal.
If one possesses this wisdom, one will not be turned back by erroneous interpretations, biased views, or evil associates. Then...

One should correctly contemplate the suffering and happiness, and the purity and defilement, of these two lands. With respect to these objects, one should give rise to two kinds of mental states as skillful means;
for without these two minds, one cannot be born there. First, cultivate weariness toward the Sahā world, following the "Gate of Refutation" taught by Śākyamuni.
Second, cultivate joyful aspiration for Sukhāvatī, following the "Gate of Gathering" shown by Amitābha. Through these two gates, practice with diligence...
Advance in the practice of the *nien-fo* samādhi; you will certainly achieve success. What is meant by the "gate of reduction"? The Sahā world is suffering; there is not a single joy to be found.
The three miserable realms burn day and night, beyond endurance. The asuras engage in wrathful battle; how can humans find peace? The faculties and sense objects seethe with the eight sufferings.
Through cause and effect, beings rise and fall through the four modes of birth. There are seasons of cold and heat; the environment is but sand and mud. By day...
The night passes away; impermanence does not abide. Furthermore, one receives a body that is foul and filthy, with male and female forms distinct from one another.

The clothing and food required are difficult to obtain and coarse and poor. One’s lifespan is not long, and various sufferings arise in succession. Even if one is born in a celestial palace, when the retribution is exhausted, one returns once more to extreme suffering.

Moreover, one does not know that pleasure is itself suffering, nor that those closest are precisely the source of enmity. With inverted perceptions and clinging to objects of perception, one seeks no liberation.
The Path: From karma arises karma, revolving without ceasing. Such suffering and affliction cannot be fully described;
therefore, one should cultivate weary detachment. What is meant by "gathering the gates"? In the precious land and jeweled ponds of Ultimate Bliss, there are no three evil realms.

Its adornments are wondrously superior to those of the ten directions. There is no shifting of cold, heat, day, or night. There is no birth, aging, sickness, death, or the accumulation of karmic bonds. It consists purely of males and has no females.

One is born by transformation within a lotus flower; food and clothing appear spontaneously; one is able to achieve the joy of the Dharma; one’s lifespan is immeasurable; and the radiance of one’s body is inexhaustible.
Upon hearing the sound of the Dharma, one immediately knows where to turn for refuge; upon beholding the marks and signs of excellence, one awakens to the Way in an instant.
Such various forms of happiness are immeasurable; therefore, one should rejoice in them. If one can follow the Buddha's teachings day and night without ceasing, then—
In this land, one should regard all objects of sound and form as a hell, as a sea of suffering, and as a burning house; one should regard all precious things as instruments of torment;
one should regard food, drink, and clothing as pus, blood, and iron skin; and one should regard all kinsmen as yakṣas, rākṣasas, and man-eating ghosts.
Regarding the adornments of that Buddha’s land through the power of his vows, one should, in every thought-moment, accord with that principle.
One should conceive the thought of peace and security; the thought of a treasure; the thought of one's own household affairs; and the thought of a place of liberation.

One should regard Amitābha Tathāgata and the assembly of Bodhisattvas as a compassionate father and a compassionate mother. One should conceive the thought of being welcomed and guided, the thought of a bridge and a ford, and the thought that upon calling his name in times of fear or urgent distress, he will immediately come to provide protection and rescue.
One should maintain the thought of mindful renunciation. If one feels weary and seeks detachment regarding the gates of conditioned existence...

If [one's practice] is not profound, one will not be liberated from the karmic bonds of this Sahā world. If one’s aspiration for the gates of gathering [the roots of goodness] is not earnest, it will be difficult to ascend to the supreme realm of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
Without the first step of putting the teachings into practice, although one may understand the purport of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*), it will result in nothing but empty understanding;

even if one wishes to be born there, because one lacks both joy [in the pure land] and revulsion [for this world], there is no cause by which that can be attained. If one cultivates these two gates [of aspiration and practice] without recognizing the essence of contemplative wisdom, [the effort will be in vain].

However, because this is merely a conceptualization of phenomena, its stage is not that of the superior class. If one can cultivate with fervent joy and revulsion in a balanced manner, once contemplative wisdom has arisen, it will further become of the superior grade.
Someone may say: "If all conditions are set aside, the mind accords with principle and the environment merges with the spirit;

one naturally accords with the Dharma. Why must there be such joy and revulsion, or such grasping and abandoning? I answer: If you claim that setting aside all conditions is the Way, [you have not yet understood].
If you give rise to even a single thought of letting go, your mind immediately turns away from and becomes distant from the Way. Guoshan said: "Do not merely forget emotions and let your heart die;
this is a most difficult-to-cure illness and the deepest of all. If you remain silent and idle like a fool, know that you do not yet understand how to apply yourself to practice.
Furthermore, when it says "let go," one lets go of worldly karmic conditions; how could it mean letting go of the essence of diligence?
This is the mind of the Way! Sitting within the armor of non-action, how could one attain a mind that understands the environment and merges with the Way?

If you know that not letting go is itself letting go, then even while actively engaging in joy and aversion, or acceptance and rejection, you are in fact free from joy and aversion, and free from acceptance and rejection.

To practice non-practice and to be mindful of non-mindfulness is called "effortless action" (*anābhoga-caryā*). Since this is the unconditioned, wondrous mind, how could it be difficult to swiftly realize the principle of the Middle Way?
Furthermore, because one practices, one is free from annihilationism; because one does not practice, one is free from eternalism.

Once annihilationism and eternalism are both abandoned, one differs from what was previously asked and is born directly into the Land of Peace and Bliss. There, one takes the two Great Beings as fellow practitioners and dwells together with Amitābha.
True. What dharma is there that cannot be questioned? What practice is there that cannot be learned? What doubt is there that is not eliminated? What is there to be sought that is not attained?
Thus, are not this joy and this aversion not themselves the great causal practices for accomplishing unsurpassed enlightenment?
Exhortation to Practice, Part Nine:

Now, the pure and the defiled share the same essence, and the sentient being and the Buddha are of one principle. Since all dharmas are fundamentally equal, why should there be a need for exhortation to practice?

Yet, alas, when the deluded mind creates objective realms, the pure and the defiled are thereby divided. Through mutual opposition they come into being, and bondage and liberation become vastly different. Thus, one remains entangled for many kalpas.
It is easy to perceive and understand; therefore, one must diligently exhort sentient beings in the ocean of suffering to seek rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.

Once a practitioner has deeply realized that the distinctions between the pure and the defiled, and between suffering and bliss, are true and unerring, they will proceed like a farmer rushing toward profit, whom it is impossible to stop.

Yet, farmers labor day and night without rest for the sake of a single year’s sustenance against hunger and cold, never growing weary even after many years. Those who travel [the path] transcend the sufferings of kalpas;
