how could they stop at merely avoiding the hunger and cold of a single year? To ascend to the security of the nine grades is far more than merely attaining warmth and satiety for one year.

Between the two gates of *zhé* (restraint) and *shè* (gathering), it is like gold and jade versus sand and stone. Even if there were three feet of sand and stone, a child would surely discard the stones to seek the gold. This does not need to be urged.
One should take this for oneself: that this land is suffering while that land is bliss; that one is submerged in the cycle of birth and death here, whereas there one enjoys sovereign liberation.

These are matters that even a child can discern; one must certainly abandon the defiled and seek the pure with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire. If one hears the teaching and acts upon it immediately, what need is there for further exhortation?

That these two lands—one of suffering and one of bliss—are the words of the Buddha, one should believe them with certainty and without doubt; through practice, they will be attained of their own accord.
When people today see excrement or urine, they pinch their noses and knit their brows; loathing its foulness and impurity, they wish to depart from it as quickly as possible.
When they see brocade or fine silks, they broaden their faces and break into smiles; coveting their brilliance and purity, they wish to obtain them as quickly as possible.

Even toward these transient objects of beauty and ugliness, they cannot endure them for even a moment, yet their hatred and love burn fiercely. How much less could they fail to feel joy and aversion swiftly toward long kalpas of ultimate bliss or ultimate suffering?
How extreme is their folly! How deep is their delusion! Furthermore, in this realm, Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet appeared;

the worthy sages are hidden from view, and sentient beings rush headlong through the sea of suffering like children who have lost their father. If one does not take the King of Vows of Sukhāvatī as one’s refuge, who will provide protection?
Even if a divine immortal has not yet left the mundane world, it is still difficult for them to attain the three grades of the ten wholesome acts.

Due to these causes, one is born into the heavens of the triple world; yet from the inferior to the superior, each must pass through many kalpas, making it exceedingly difficult to fulfill one's aspirations.
Success is as rare as a drop in the vast ocean. In the interim, one may encounter the factions of evil Māras, leading to permanent regression and total loss.

How could one dare speak of escaping the triple world and attaining the four fruits and four stages of the path? Much less could one traverse the various stages of faith, abiding, practice, and realization to transcend this realm.

Yes. If one cultivates the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, one will not remain within the ordinary stages; in a single lifetime, one will cross directly through the three realms and five paths.

Received by the Buddha’s welcoming hand, one will be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*). Upon the opening of the lotus flower, one will see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and awaken to the Way, all without departing from the present thought-moment.
One will stride boldly across the Great Square, making offerings to all the Triple Gem and transforming all sentient beings. When Maitreya is born...

Having come to this place, you shall instruct all those encountered throughout kalpas—parents, wives, children, brothers, sisters, enemies, and kin—in the factors of the Path (mārga-aṅga) and inform them of their past causes, causing them all to realize the fruits [of the path]. Would your conduct and vows then not be truly vast?

Such meritorious virtues, if lost through a single moment of negligence in practice, will belong to future lives. How can one afford to be lax? Moreover, worldly affairs are manifold and continuous like an unbroken chain;
the mind does not abide for even a single thought-moment, and the body never rests wherever it goes.
These serve to cause my rise and fall and obstruct my original nature; from kalpa after kalpa until now, they have never ceased. Impermanence and transformation cannot endure for long.
Remain! Though a lifespan may last a hundred years, it does not exceed the snap of a finger. Today and tomorrow cannot guarantee one's continued existence.

Suddenly, when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one is unaware that in an instant one has become another being. According to the causes of one’s karma, one receives a form among various classes of beings—some with fur and horns, some walking upon the earth, and some flying through the air.
Today’s understanding is entirely forgotten in a state of daze; drifting aimlessly through the three miserable realms and the six destinies is much.
The kalpa does not know its own end; even if Maitreya is born, where is my place of birth certain?

I have not yet heard the names of my parents or the Triple Gem, let alone the perfect discourse of the scriptures. Though I receive this different body and cherish it deeply, I create karma through karma and enter darkness from darkness.
My fear of death and greed for life are no different from today. If one does not [awaken] in this very moment—
In the interim, emulating those previously awakened great men, you have vigorously generated the Great Mind and established a resolute will.

With the power to lift a cauldron and pull up a mountain, you have severed [delusions] once and for all. How could your meritorious conduct not be so manifest as to illuminate and move gods and humans?

May all beings receive your grace and be protected by the Buddhas; may the three evil realms be closed and the gate of *dhāraṇī* be opened, without waiting for the full exhaustion of retribution in this Sahā world.

Thus, one attains rebirth there. If, however, one waits for a place that is secure and convenient, where food and clothing are abundant and sufficient, and where incense, flowers, and all matters accord with one's wishes—calculating past and future to select an auspicious time to settle accounts of both kindness and enmity, and to bring this virtuous undertaking to completion.
Thereafter, one should set forth in practice. Even if the realm of empty space were exhausted, there would be no end to this [practice].
*The Direct Pointing to Mind through Nianfo of the Jewel-King Samādhi*, Volume II.
*The Direct Pointing to Mind through Nianfo of the Jewel-King Samādhi* (Lower Volume).

The Tenth [Chapter], "Exhortation Against Killing," states in the Preface to the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*: "All things possessing vital energy and blood must possess consciousness. All that possesses consciousness necessarily shares the same essence.

Viewed through this lens, even the wriggling insects and crawling creatures are of one true purity with the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas of the ten directions. [This is true of] both sentient beings and Buddhas."
Since they are the same, how could humans—who are indeed most sentient—not also be equal? We all receive the substance of the five elements and are born together within heaven and earth.
Like the "rat of Xu" or the "swallow of Wei," which correspond to celestial phenomena and resemble the sun and moon, they are even able to preside over human calamities and blessings;
how then could they not be equal to humans? That which distinguishes them from humans is due to beginningless deluded thoughts and evil.
Dragged by karma, one changes form and appearance without realizing it or knowing it. People merely have not yet encountered their karmic retribution;
how could they truly be superior to me? When those [beings] reach the end of their retribution and are destined to become humans or devas, I am obstructed and do not recognize them.
Suddenly, when my own human karmic retribution is exhausted, I find myself inferior to them. How can you say that because I devour them, they must necessarily be inferior to me?
How much more so when, in the past, we were of the same kind as them, mutually serving as parents, brothers, wives, children, sisters, and various relatives and kinsmen;
to kill and eat them now is to kill and eat one's own former kin. The Buddha said: "All sentient beings possess buddha-nature."
Because they will certainly attain Buddhahood in the future, to kill them is to kill a future Buddha. How can one not stand in awe of this? Alas for those who kill today!

They do not recognize their prior causes; when their parents were alive, they committed many acts of rebellion against them. From their parents they incurred resentment, and from that resentment they formed hatred.
This enmity and hatred continue through successive generations without ceasing, leading to mutual killing as they revolve through the cycle of rebirth.

It does not stop there. Therefore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra prohibits taking one's own life, as well as inciting others, employing expedient means, praising killing, or making vows and incantations for the sake of killing.

Furthermore, it strictly enjoins the permanent severance of all karmic actions resulting from such causes and conditions; this is a sincere admonition. Moreover, those various creatures are endowed with innate foreknowledge;
they avoid danger without waiting for the right moment and flee without selecting a location. Heaven and earth are vast enough for them to sustain themselves on their own. Yet now—
That one can cause it to arise for oneself, and that when two [causes] happen to meet, it inevitably falls into the hands of a person, is because the prior causes cannot be escaped.
Since they cannot be escaped, I should contemplate the suffering and exercise restraint. As the Sūtra says: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the conditions and causes converge, one must receive the retribution oneself. Therefore, the World-Honored One manifested the pain of a headache and the golden spear.
He replied: "If even the Buddha is like this, how much more so should it be for ordinary people?

In this world, those who have been friends throughout their lives will still harbor a grudge until death if they are rebuffed by a single word or wronged by a single object; how much less could one forget such deep resentment when one's flesh has been eaten with a white blade?"

The secular classics do not permit surrounding [animals for slaughter], nor do they allow the netting of flocks; one does not fish with nets, nor shoot at prey while it sleeps, nor eat animals upon hearing their cries.
This is quite similar to the permission granted in the Tripiṭaka teachings to consume the "three kinds of pure meat.

Although this does not equal the complete cessation of the karma of killing found in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, it is nonetheless a gradual step toward such cessation. Even this gradual step toward cessation carries the reputation of extending virtue to the birds and beasts. Furthermore—

Even with regard to a dry bone that possesses no consciousness, my heart still cannot bear it; how much more so for a living being endowed with flesh and blood and a shared spirit—how could such a thing be killed and eaten?

Laozi said: "Hunting and racing about cause the mind to go mad. Furthermore, shooting at birds in flight and chasing fleeing beasts, disturbing those emerging from hibernation and startling those in their nests, indulging in violence and slaughter, and cooking and slaughtering against reason—the officials of the Lord of Fate in the void record every detail, whether great or small, and cause those [beings]...
While alive, one’s lifespan is diminished and one encounters all manner of unfavorable circumstances; upon death, one falls into hell and undergoes every form of suffering.

There, one is subjected to being hacked and minced on mountains of knives and trees of swords, boiled and roasted, with entrails pulled out and lungs extracted, skin flayed and flesh devoured, bones sliced and marrow scraped, heads strangled and eyes gouged, feet burned and hands set ablaze.
One passes through every great hell without exception, enduring as much as the dust and sand swept away by the wind. There is no end to it.

This serves as a metaphor for their lifespan. When their retribution is exhausted, they fall again into the realm of hungry ghosts for such eons; furthermore, they fall among animals. Within the animal realm, they must kill one victim to repay each debt.
If the intent to kill is grave, one act of killing may result in a retribution of ten thousand or even a million deaths, continuing until it is inexhaustible.

Only then will they encounter the person they previously killed, meeting them as before. They shall kill and eat to repay their debts, with not even a grain’s weight of discrepancy, just as it was originally ordained.

Even those who, through slight merit, are born among humans still adorn themselves with hundreds of thousands of sufferings—such as poverty, solitude, misery, many illnesses, short lifespans, epilepsy, loss of will, blindness, deafness, muteness, scabies, ringworm, carbuncles, and pus and blood—and are surrounded by all manner of hostile conditions that gather upon their bodies.
Their kinsmen abandon them, and they endure what is unbearable; all of this is the result of killing.

Because their karma is so profound, they undergo such extreme suffering. Furthermore, even among different species there are hearts of benevolence; by principle, they should not be killed. Lambs kneel to suckle their mothers;

crows return to feed their parents—these possess the rites of filial piety. Dogs protect their masters; the *zhài* (unicorn-like creature) does not bend—these possess the capacity for loyalty and uprightness.

Bees and ants have the relationship of ruler and subject; mandarin ducks have the bond of husband and wife; wild geese fly in formation as brothers; and birds warble in harmony as friends. Observe this...

How do those multitudes of living beings differ from humans? Humans, on the contrary, cannot extend compassion based on our shared essence; instead, they kill others to nourish themselves—can this truly be called being "spiritual"?
When the secular world entertains guests or performs seasonal sacrifices, is it not possible to maintain one's fast and precepts by using water-moss, pond-weeds, melons, and fruits?
Formerly, there was a butcher’s son who refused to kill. His father placed him, along with a knife and a sheep, in a secret room, saying that he would not...
"The sheep that was to be killed shall be you. The son then took his own life; by this cause, he was reborn in heaven and enjoyed celestial bliss for many kalpas.
Thus we know that one who refrains from killing will be born in a favorable realm and will surely find their person virtuous.

Life after life, they will receive the retribution of longevity, and they will certainly be able to extend their virtue far to their descendants. Now that the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, there are many who act for—

The disciples of the Buddha are unable to embody the Buddha’s compassion; they eat and drink as they please, yet when they see those who abstain from meat, they instead slander them for having "too poisonous" hearts.
With all manner of flowery speech, they expose their faults. When the celestial deities behold such evil people, they are filled with wrath.
How can it be that worldly people, upon encountering such types, conversely call them upright? It was only when Zichan obtained his rightful position that he could do so.

Ah! King Qi’s lack of injury to the art of benevolence is understandable; even the *Daiji* (Book of Rites) considers the killing of animals to be unfilial, let alone the fourfold assembly of the Śākya school.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Because humans eat sheep, when the sheep dies it becomes a human, and when the human dies they become a sheep. You repay my life, and I repay your debt.
By these causes and conditions, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas one remains constantly in birth and death, coming and going back and forth through life after life."

They devour one another; their evil karma arises together and persists until the end of the future. Furthermore, a verse says: "If one wishes to kill living beings, one should practice self-observation.

One's own body cannot be killed, for the life of a creature is no different from it. There are perverse people who claim that sentient beings are born and die in delusion, and that sin and merit are fundamentally empty;
thus, they say there is no retribution for killing. Why do they not also say that I, too, am falsely seeking and falsely eating?
The tongue and flavors are fundamentally empty; there is no benefit in eating them. Since one possesses a greedy mind, how could there not be karmic retribution?
What has been described above is an examination of oneself by analogy with others. To refrain from killing with equanimity is the path that benevolent people ought to follow.

One who cultivates the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection truly desires to purify the three karmas, resolve the knots of resentment, and be reborn in the Pure Land; how, then, can one fail to cease killing and eating? At the point of death...

At the time of death, one obstructs oneself. The Great Canon contains extensive teachings and principles; this is true for all three teachings without exception. How could a mere scrap of paper possibly cite them all?

I pray that you will hear the purport of this meaning: embodying the Way and cherishing life, may we all ascend together to benevolence and longevity, and each reach the full span of our natural lives.

One will be freed from all enmities and resentments. Furthermore, by being able to transform others according to the Dharma, one fulfills the compassionate salvation of the sages, causing both self and others to fully realize a mind of loving-kindness;
thus, one will surely together attain birth in the realm of the Lotus and achieve Perfect Enlightenment.
Chapter Eleven: Encouraging the Observance of the Multitude of Precepts (All are the True Causes for Pure Karma).
Question: All evils ought to be restrained; why is this expressed so briefly? Answer: The sūtras contain teachings on the complete observance of the multitude of precepts.

Why stop at merely refraining from killing first? One should rather sever the act of killing so that all the precepts may be fully possessed. If the virtue of the precepts is not cultivated, upon what can one rely to establish one's practice?

It is like a vessel containing clarified butter (*ghṛta*): one must first wash away the impurities. Cultivating *samādhi* is also like this; only when the various precepts are pure can it be accomplished.
Even if past karma is deep and heavy such that it cannot be severed instantaneously, one should employ skillful means to restrain it and exhort oneself.

Reflect upon your own mind, examine yourself, and repent of your transgressions. Cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). Understand that worldly pleasures are few while sufferings are many;

that all things are impermanent, subject to decay, and will soon be extinguished. All phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally impure; therefore, employ every skillful means (*upāya*) to ensure their definitive cessation.
How could one lose control by following after discursive thoughts? Furthermore, regarding worldly skills, various arts, and even all forms of virtue—

As for those whose thoughts are divided by evil: if they do not cast them aside, how can they attain the samādhi of single-mindedness? Without such single-mindedness, how can they attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]?
How could it be otherwise for sentient beings? The ignorance and karmic consciousness pervade the entire Dharma-realm;

should even a single thought of worldly concern arise, one is immediately dragged away by such hosts of dust-like afflictions and demons. One’s entire being becomes submerged, and there is no prospect of escape. It is like a fish...

A single strand [of negligence] can bind one; the harm is not small. If it is thus even with a mere thought, how much more so with physical action? One should cultivate samādhi as swiftly as an arrow hitting its mark.
Without waiting for the exhaustion of karmic retribution, one desires to leap out of the dense forest and resolutely take birth in the Pure Land.

How could one afford to lose the precepts, let the mind wander toward external objects, or allow one's practice to become lax, thereby causing oneself to enter the evil realms once again? If one hears this teaching and yet does not observe the precepts, when the time comes—
In the end, there will be no proof. Do not say that the power of the Buddha lacks responsive efficacy.
Chapter Twelve: Exerting the Power of Diligence.
As for diligence, it is not being discouraged by the eight worldly winds, nor being affected by the various views or the great and small ailments of body and mind.

One may become negligent in one's practice due to these conditions. When a practitioner seeks to enter samādhi, they may be disturbed by all manner of internal and external delusions caused by both the powerful and the subtle Māras.

At such times, one should fortify one’s resolve and intensify one’s diligence, making it indestructible like a vajra-banner, immovable like Mount Sumeru, and unassailable by any poison like the great ocean. Even if...

If the Buddha says, "You shall not be reborn there," you should immediately reply: "I have previously received the prediction from Śākyamuni Buddha that all sentient beings should make a vow to be reborn in that land, even those who do not refrain from the ten evil deeds or the five heinous crimes.

I have not committed the five heinous crimes and have recited the name more than ten times; I shall certainly attain rebirth there. How could the Buddha deceive himself by daring to violate his own original vow? Moreover, [the merit of] ten..."
Just as all Buddhas manifest their broad and long tongues to bear witness to this matter, one must certainly seek birth in the stage of non-retrogression.

This constitutes the adamantine, enduring, and heroic power of the practitioner. If even the Buddhas’ own prophecies cannot cause one to retreat from their initial resolve, how much less could the hosts of Māras and evil associates, the elements of water and fire, thieves and robbers, powerful and perverse states, or the attachments of wife and concubines ever move them?

"I shall practice my vows. Someone asked: "If worldly people practice yet do not attain birth [in the Pure Land], why is this? The answer was: "Because their views are heterodox and their conduct is not dignified.
He asked again: "In that case, would their merit be lost in vain? The answer was: "No; they will certainly rely upon the power of Amitābha’s vow.

If they are not born in this life, they will surely be born in the second life; if they are not born in the second life, they will surely be born in the third life. By directing one's thought toward it for even a single moment, one will be born in the future."
One will certainly attain rebirth there; this is called "never falling back. Yet, one has merely endured the suffering of saṃsāra for many kalpas in vain.
Therefore, one must resolve to achieve it in this single lifetime. How could one allow one's own resolve to be divided, thereby falling into those who attain rebirth in future lives?

If, however, driven by past karma, one’s vows and practices have been deficient, one should single-mindedly recite the [mantra] that "extracts all light and heavy karmic obstacles" to attain [rebirth].
The Dharani for Rebirth in the Pure Land: Reciting it once extinguishes all five heinous crimes and ten evil deeds within one’s body.
Reciting it one hundred thousand times ensures that the bodhicitta is never lost or forgotten. Reciting it two hundred thousand times causes the sprout of bodhi to emerge.
Reciting it three hundred thousand times, Amitābha Buddha will dwell perpetually upon one’s crown, and one will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. This mantra...
In the *Shiben*, the phonetics, phrases, and readings are largely erroneous. The translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Śālarabha of recent times is the most detailed and essential;
therefore, one should recite it as the direct instruction for correct practice. The mantra is as follows:
Namo Ratnatrayāya | Namo Āryāmitābhāya Tathāgatāyārhate Samyaksaṃbuddhāya | Oṃ Amitāye Amitābha Utpala ||
Vīre amṛte svāhā | Amṛte karbure amṛte śvete | Amṛte tejini amṛte vikalpaṃte | Amṛte vikalpaṃte gamini svāhā ||
Amṛte gagane kṛtike amṛtodbhave svarasvate sarva-ārakte sattvasāre gauri māṅgalye kṛtye kṛte svāhā.
"Hō" (homophonous with "nai") is also known as the Root Mantra of Amitāyus Tathāgata. By reciting it, one attains great diligence and is swiftly reborn in the Pure Land.
The thirteenth [chapter], "Right Practice," Part One:

The aforementioned methods for seeking birth in the Pure Land are all sublime, yet they do not yet constitute right practice. The practitioner must resolve their will to enter the *maṇḍala* (place of practice).
First, they should contemplate themselves and all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space as constantly dwelling within the great ocean of birth and death.
Through kalpas without end, they have wandered aimlessly and sunk into the six realms of existence, without refuge and without rescue.

If one does not cause them to be universally liberated, how can it be called "right practice"? Thereupon, one contemplates the objects of both enemies and kin with equanimity, giving rise to a heart of great compassion as vast and all-encompassing as space.
Furthermore, one reflects: "My own body is a mass of sores, afflictions, karmic debts, and suffering; if I do not [apply this to others]..."
To bestow gifts upon sentient beings and cultivate samādhi merely for their liberation would contradict the Buddha’s admonitions and violate my original vow.
How deeply pitiable it is that sentient beings suffer! Now I resolve my mind like a lion-king emerging from its cave;
seeking no companion and seeking no protection, I shall roar with a thunderous cry to subdue all, and will certainly not yield to the evil Māra.
When the faction has retreated, once such a great resolve has been established, one should then carefully examine the correct practice of mindfulness of the Buddha as practiced by the ancient sages.
One should select a naturally tranquil site that has never been defiled. As for expenses, one should exhaust all that one possesses before seeking anything from others.

One should establish the *maṇḍala* according to the Dharma, making it exceedingly pure and solemn. All offerings and services must be fully prepared and rendered brilliant, subtle, and exquisite. There should be no...
One should universally dedicate all roots of goodness from the beginning toward the practice and vows for the adornment of the Pure Land.
If one does not dedicate them in this way as the cause for rebirth, how could such a state be attained?

With the three minds fully aroused and the five limbs cast in prostration, one contemplates the Buddha’s marks and signs while kneeling with palms joined, directing the mind to universally encompass all sentient beings throughout the boundless oceans of lands.
"This body of mine, wandering from antiquity until now without returning, is deeply pitiable. Weeping with tears and lamenting, I pray that the Buddha will bestow his compassion.

Unconsciously, my body felt like a great mountain collapsing. Taking refuge in the Triple Gem, I held incense and flowers in my hands; visualizing them throughout the entire Dharma-realm, I prostrated with sincere devotion.
I cut open my own belly and washed out my intestines to confess and reveal my transgressions and sins, practicing this through the six periods of day and night."

One should vow to practice until the end of one's days, even if obstacles are deep and the response [of rebirth] has not yet been felt. During this time, one must not entertain a single momentary thought of the five worldly desires.
If, despite this, one does not attain rebirth there, then the Buddha would be a speaker of great falsehood.

Therefore, the efficacy of this samādhi is such that it is praised by all Buddhas and followed by all sages. Regarding the ritual procedures for this samādhi, only Ciyun (Zhiyi) attained the middle way; it is appropriate [to follow his method].
Taste this thoroughly. This is the foremost superior practice; its realm is profoundly deep. Students should exert all their strength within it and must not abandon this to pursue that.
If one’s faculties are unequal and it is difficult to perfect these supreme practices, one must still dwell in a pure chamber to ensure both the interior and exterior are solemn and clean.
One should establish a practice according to one's inclination, performing prostrations to the Buddha and repentance, determining a fixed number of times each day to present [these offerings].

With single-minded diligence, one vows never to regret this in the interim. One may either specialize in reciting the sutras, specialize in upholding mantras, or simply maintain the holding of the Name.
If one obtains a favorable sign, it is known that the transgressions have been extinguished and the conditions are profound.
The sutra states that one cannot be born in that land through roots of goodness, merit, or causal conditions that are meager. Upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, one should uphold his Name.
From one day up to seven days, by maintaining single-mindedness without distraction, one will immediately attain rebirth there.
Thus, we know that upholding the Name is itself the cause and condition for many roots of goodness and much merit.

Furthermore, there are those who have not yet been able to completely sever worldly ties and still cultivate worldly virtues, yet who possess sincere faith and harbor no doubt regarding the Land of Ultimate Bliss; they long for it in every thought-moment and do not forget their previous practice.
Cultivate this according to your inclination. Within the four modes of deportment, take this as your refuge. Upon encountering sensory objects, penetrate their profound source;

when facing circumstances, exert yourself in the practice of skillful means. At the time of death, you will surely be reborn there. However, while various practices differ, the power of the Dharma is fundamentally equal.
It depends solely on whether one’s resolve is slow or swift; thus, the Buddha responds with either delay or immediacy. Students must not fail to understand this. Furthermore, there is...
Regarding the Dharma Gate of Ten Recitations by Ciyun: every morning, after washing and rinsing the mouth, one should practice facing west in a quiet place.
This is the primary cause for rebirth in the Pure Land and must never be neglected. Someone asked: "How can one apply the mind so that it does not become distracted?

The answer is: "One should simply direct the mindfulness of body and speech; do not concern oneself with whether it is distracted. As long as there is no interruption, the mind will naturally become single-minded, and this may indeed be called 'single-mindedness'."
The measure is simply to practice without ceasing; there is truly no need to worry about distraction. It is like a mother who has lost her beloved child, or a dragon who has lost its life-pearl:
the mind becomes one-pointed not by expectation, but spontaneously; how could it be made one through forced restraint? The mind cannot be constrained.
In truth, it depends solely on whether the practitioner is diligent or indolent.

Regarding the fourteenth [section], "The Samādhi Cultivated While Traveling Abroad," a traveler who was performing prostrations asked: "I was born late; my faculties are dull and my learning meager. From the past until now, I have wandered in hardship."

Regarding Lake Hai: while dwelling in stillness and advancing in practice, you have not yet attained [mastery] by assessing your own capacity. If you were to remain at your current lodging without relying on a formal dharma hall, the three karmas during the six periods of the day could all be practiced.
I prostrate and pray that your vast compassion will graciously grant me the skillful means to respond to the world.

If one wishes to cultivate samādhi, one must first have all hundred matters fully prepared before setting forth in practice. Now, your aspiration stands out above the common; you must recite the Buddha’s name.

Samādhi universally encompasses all capacities; within the four modes of deportment, every action serves as a function of the Way. If you would practice with vigor, you must first establish a heart that does not deceive others.
Conceal your virtues and reveal your flaws; be careful never to boast or display yourself. From the very foundation of your being, you will then be secure both inwardly and outwardly.
Read the Pure Land sutras, dharanis, and methods of repentance thoroughly until they are mastered, and practice the prescribed modes of deportment so that they become habitual.
With a demeanor that is dignified and refined, one should give rise to true faith as previously described, mobilizing the wisdom of great compassion for the sake of all sentient beings.
One should contemplate, according to principle, the purity and defilement of the two lands, and realize that the two retributions of suffering and joy are truly objects of aversion and aspiration.

Purifying body and mind, one should wear clean clothing according to one's means. On the six days of the fast, one should prepare modest offerings of incense and flowers before the Three Jewels and prostrate with bowed knees and forehead touching the ground.
[He] established vast and great vows, taking this as his refuge wherever he was born throughout his lifetimes, never again feeling regret.
From this day until the end of his life, he practiced this Dharma during the six periods of each day. As for whether incense and lamps were present or not, he did not insist upon them.
Question: Samādhi requires a single-minded focus, yet human affairs involve myriad complications. How can one practice so that they do not obstruct one another? Answer: It is like...

A bird enters a cage; its body is within the cage, yet its mind remembers the garden. Neither of these two constitutes an obstacle: the cage binds the body but cannot bind that heart seeking liberation;
external circumstances constrain the body but cannot restrain my will to go forth. The three realms are like a cage.
This body is like a bird; when it seeks release, it aspires to go to the groves, which are the Pure Land. Thus one knows that the myriad strands of delusive conditions do not obstruct the true mind.

Three times a day and three times at night, whether there is an image present or an image naturally accompanies the person, one should recite aloud and prostrate with the body, or recite silently and prostrate with the body. If there is no Buddha image, one may face a scripture or face west.

One may perform prostrations from afar, or, if facing east is not possible, perform them according to the direction one is facing. However, when traveling on a road, boarding a boat, or engaged in activities for maintaining the body, these matters must not be neglected;

thus, spiritual practice and worldly affairs proceed together. One should reflect that these worldly tasks are fundamentally for the sake of sustaining the body, and as one’s own person practices the Way, worldly affairs are of the same essence as samādhi. Question: Since the mind cannot have two simultaneous functions, how can this be?

Question: "If two matters are performed simultaneously, how is this possible? Answer: "In a single mind, there is no obstruction to seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, acting with the body, and recollecting with the mind.

Since its application is inexhaustible, why stop at two matters? Thus, amidst these active functions, one may recite one scroll of the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, or the 'Superior Grades' chapter, or the section on Śrī Avalokiteśvara and Śrī Bhadrapāla from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, as well as reciting the Pure Land dhāraṇī three, seven, or even up to a hundred times."
Recite the Buddha’s name one hundred, three hundred, five hundred, or up to one thousand times. This serves as the preliminary rite for entering the repentance ceremony;

only after dedicating the merit (*pariṇāmanā*) should you enter the repentance. Following the textual divisions and meanings, visualize yourself reverently facing the Buddhas of the Pure Land, or before an image of the Buddha.

Prostrate, gaze upon them, and circumambulate them, clearly perceiving each detail without allowing your mind to become dull or confused. Once the prostrations are completed, contemplate the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*).

Stop when the allotted time has passed. Recite the sutras, dharanis, and the Buddha’s name as before, and perform the dedication of merit. This visualization-based prostration is identical to the ritual methods for the practice hall described previously;
the only difference is that it is performed with the body. The tone of the recitation should be adjusted—either light or heavy—according to the person and the quality of the environment.

One should ensure that speech and silence are balanced so as to honor the profound and dignified tradition, allowing others to hear only when necessary. One must never engage in excessive conversation with many people.
First, burn a single incense stick before the Buddha, or take up an object to represent incense; at that time, simply direct one’s mental attention toward it.

At other times, one should remain in solitary sitting or solitary walking, staying far removed from clamor and distraction, as well as from gathering with others for idle chatter, jesting, or derision.
One must avoid jesting, laughing, singing, lamenting, chanting, or using pens and inkstones—activities that cause one to lose right mindfulness and other such matters.

At night, when the human mind is settled and the environment is tranquil, the application of effort should be different [from daytime]. Since the matter of birth and death is of great importance, how can one indulge in sleep through laziness?
Even at the extremes of cold or heat, be careful not to remove your robes. Your dharma robes and prayer beads should be kept within reach, as should your hand-towel.
Pure water should never be absent from the corner of one's seat; whatever may be required should be prepared in advance.
Furthermore, one should observe whether the other’s faculty of faith is thick or thin, ensuring that one does not cause them distress or weariness, remaining unobstructed in this regard.
Then, one should produce a sound like that of a lute or a harp—subtle yet resonant, grand yet not weak—so as to delight the devas and be heard by the spirits and animals.
The merit of this practice is profound. Whether on a boat or in the humble, secluded corners of another’s home, one must always examine the environment and the people.
With single-minded diligence and skillful means, one should adapt and persevere until the practice is exhausted. One must by no means give rise to faults regarding others or expose their evils.
Furthermore, one must not exhaust another's joy or diminish another's excellence. When at leisure, one should simply...
If there are other matters or if one is hindered by others, one should likewise choose a secluded place and sit upright facing west with palms joined at the chest.

Whether speaking aloud or remaining silent as appropriate, one should perform the visualization and prostrations as before. Furthermore, when engaged in work, one should perform one prostration for each phrase until the recitation is complete.
When the task is finished and the body is at leisure, one should perform the prostrations with the body until they are complete.

If, while prostrating before the Buddha, an urgent matter suddenly arises and one cannot finish even a single prostration for each phrase, one should imagine that the prostrations are complete according to the point reached.

One must by no means enter into a repentance ritual and then, having performed only a small portion, start the repentance over again from the beginning. Furthermore, these prostrations performed through visualization are intended for times of necessity; one should not perform them through visualization during times of leisure. Nor...

One can imagine that while one observes the ritual during times of labor, one might instead waste it in vain during times of leisure. Those with shallow faith should not be urged toward practice too abruptly;
those with deep faith should not fail to be secretly initiated so as to lead them to consent of their own accord. Furthermore, one must not allow the merit to accrue to oneself;
rather, like spring nurturing all things without its own merit being seen, one should rely on the *dōjō* for cultivation, following what is easy to practice according to the Middle Way. From...
Cultivating while traveling among others; practicing with ease amidst adversity. When one practices with ease amidst adversity, the merit becomes even more manifest.
Question: Is mental visualization the same as the body? Answer: The mind is the master of body and speech. Once the master directs its visualization, how could it fail to reach the body and speech?

It is like when one carries incense and flowers—the body and mind arrive everywhere. Is this not also merely a matter of mental visualization? Question: If that is so, would it not be possible to dispense with the movement of body and speech?

Question: Although mental karma is superior, if one fully employs both body and speech, it is called the "perfect cultivation of the three karmas. Question: Outside of the six periods of practice, how should one apply the mind? Answer:
One should perform such practices as contemplating the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), reciting mantras, chanting sutras, invoking the Buddha’s name, and prostrating.

One must never abandon these thoughts from moment to moment, vowing to be reborn [in the Pure Land]. It is like a traveler on a road: if one's steps are swift, one arrives quickly; if one's steps are slow, one arrives late. One should act accordingly.

This is how one should apply the mind. If the strength of body and mind is weak such that one cannot fully practice during all six periods [of the day], one should simply fix upon a certain number of periods each day.
Although it is not to be resented if more can be added, one must not increase or decrease even a single period and thereby alter the practice as originally established.
Question: If this is so, is the practice performed at the place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) not necessarily required? Answer: It is like a person who has fallen into the sea and seeks...
The boat had not yet been obtained when he suddenly encountered a floating log; seizing it, he reached the shore. How could one who possesses a boat necessarily seek out that log?
Moreover, while traveling as a guest, one’s staying or departing follows the master’s preferences and aversions; thus, there is no obstruction. Should one not advance in one's practice?
As described above, this samādhi cultivated on the road for a traveler has an extremely profound realm; among the four types of samādhi, it is called the "neither-walking-nor-sitting samādhi."

It is also called the Samādhi that Accords with the Four Modes of Deportment. It perfectly accords with those of great capacity; those of small wisdom and small faculties may also receive its benefits according to their respective portions.
I observe that people of the world, upon hearing what is easy, immediately form the notion that it is easy and falsely claim to have attained realization;

yet when they hear what is difficult, they give rise to discouragement and lose their resolve entirely. Those whose faith is earnest, moreover, fall into false views and transmit secret signs, thereby misleading many.
The methods of its transmission take on a thousand forms and ten thousand manifestations; there are even those that cannot be heard, yet all are capable of ensnaring the human mind.

If one does not gradually expand their practice, both teacher and disciple will fall into ruin. How could it be otherwise than this, given the earnestness with which you inquire from me with a rectified mind?
Since this can indeed be cultivated, then for all those who rush about with worldly affairs, wandering in the four directions; those in shops, markets, and among the various artisans and craftsmen;
those who are slaves, eunuchs, or subject to the service of others; and even those confined in prison—there is no time when they cannot cultivate it.
How much more so for the fourfold assembly of the ordained and the four classes of the laity, who have dwellings and leisure, and whose needs are fully provided? They have attained...
How could a person of such autonomy fail to advance in their practice? The guest’s name was Xingyi and his courtesy name was Zixi.

He said that he had read Master Zhijue’s *Wanshan tonggui ji* (The Collection on the Common Return of Myriad Good Deeds) very thoroughly. Later, while traveling to Mount Lu, he visited the remains of Master Huiyuan and consequently made a vow to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, saying:
The Fifteenth Chapter: Rituals for Samādhi and Rules for the Maṇḍala.
These are as detailed in the texts such as Venerable Ciyun’s *Repentance Ritual* (Chanyi) and others; they shall not be set forth here again in full.

One must ensure that body and mind are tranquil and settled, with the aspiration that within the period of repentance all obstacles are exhausted and practice is perfected. For three days or seven days prior to the commencement, [one should prepare] incense...
One must not be negligent regarding offerings such as flowers, incense, and pure water. This place has already been descended upon by the Buddhas and devas with solemn majesty;
they have expelled demonic activities and obstacles such as defilement and evil, so that the practitioner may achieve *samādhi*.

Therefore, one should conceive of the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) as a pure land, as a place of liberation, and as a treasury of jewels. One will certainly attain rebirth there; do not look down upon it. Furthermore, one should contemplate:

The sufferings of the world are endless. Just as one who has escaped an enemy must never enter their presence again, you must not harbor within your mind matters that are difficult to relinquish during your ordinary life.
Letting such residual thoughts remain will create obstacles at the time of repentance, causing your sublime practice to fail to progress and its merit to be wasted in vain.
Fearing that you may not meet [the opportunity] again, the ritual manual states: "One must not for even a single moment entertain thoughts of the five worldly desires."
When ten practitioners have returned, more than that is not permitted. One must examine these individuals carefully: whether in their daily conduct they have committed no major transgressions;
whether their faculty of faith is pure and thick, free from all impulsiveness; whether their voices are harmonious and elegant, and their deportment is dignified;

whether they accept instructions and do not give rise to regret or distress for the sake of birth and death; and whether they are willing to maintain humility and do not crave fame or profit. If [these qualities] are lacking...
Such persons—four, three, or even two—are excellent; one alone is especially sublime. One must not fail to examine them, lest they cause the destruction of the rules and disturb pure cultivation.

Among them, let one person of honored virtue and mature practice, or someone who has been separately invited as a long-standing master, serve as the presiding host of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) ritual arena.
The entire assembly shall observe the rites and listen to his expositions, taking him as their great reliance.
Whether appearing to act in opposition or conformity, do not look for faults. Such a person may also examine themselves and speak with humility;

whether proceeding or halting, in the rituals of worship, recitation, bowing, kneeling, sitting, or standing, and in every instance of joining the palms, circumambulating, and so forth, one should be upright, dignified, and solemn.

Withdrawing the gaze from external objects and ceasing to listen to distractions, one should gather the sensory realm back into the mind. Those who have not yet attained realization should consult those who are already awakened; be careful never to rely on your own strength. Thus it should be done.
The body and mind may be restless, swaying or leaning.

Having bathed, rinsed the mouth, and changed one's robes and footwear overnight, one should prepare the ritual implements according to the prescribed rites. The repentance leader leads the assembly into the *maṇḍala*;
with the exception of two inner attendants, no others are permitted to enter. Each person circumambulates while burning incense and performs three prostrations according to their assigned position.
To pray for their descent through inspiration. When the rites are completed, they stand in a circle.

The Master of Repentance steps forward from the assembly and recites a prose text to invoke the protection and witness of the Triple Gem, so that there may be no obstacles to the body and one will surely be reborn in the Pure Land. Thereupon, he invokes the name of the past Buddha, Samantaprabhāsa.
Recite the Mantra of Praising Great Compassion, the Cintāmaṇicakra Mantra, and the Vairocana Consecration Mantra seven times each.

When the presiding penitent raises the mantras, they should hold a water vessel over the incense burner to request its fragrance; this should be passed to the person on the right after approximately half a roll has been recited.

Next, the sand, the incense, and the flowers are treated in the same manner. Thus, circling to the right three times and completing the three recitations of the mantra, one again raises the Great Compassion Mantra and sprinkles water for purification around each location.
First, regarding the lamps: at the very front, a lamp is lit to illuminate the path;

next, one holds a basin and sprinkles water; next, one carries a tray and scatters sand; next, one lifts an incense burner and walks while offering incense; finally, one scatters flowers at each respective spot. From...
He circumambulated the Buddha’s seat three times to the right, ensuring that the sand was spread evenly along the water’s edge.
Next, he circumambulated once the area outside the *dōjō*, the place for providing offerings to living beings, and the Hall of Dhyāna Joy.

Then he went to the clean kitchen, followed by the eastern purification bathhouse, the places for changing clothes, the resting areas, secluded spots, and major thoroughfares. In all places where practitioners passed, or around those buildings, he performed the circumambulation. All [of these].
Sprinkling [incense water] once around is called "binding the boundary" (*sīmābandha*). The boundary is like a diamond (*vajra*) city wall. Furthermore, scattering sand binds the earth boundary;
sprinkling water binds the boundaries of the cardinal directions; performing the incense rite binds the space boundary; and scattering flowers adorns the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

All these aforementioned rites are performed through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of this Great Compassionate Holy Lord and his divine mantra. Wherever the sand and water reach, they become [the purified site].

In the Buddha’s Jewel Land, demons and enemies cannot enter, and heterodox outsiders cannot destroy it; thus, samādhi can be accomplished. One must be careful not to violate the boundaries of the realm (*dharmadhātu*).
To violate these boundaries is a great omen of misfortune; furthermore, it causes the path-practice of the entire assembly to be difficult to accomplish and beset by many obstacles.

Regarding the characteristics of these boundaries, there are internal and external ones. The internal boundary marks are the four sides and limits of the *bodhimaṇḍa*. The external boundary marks are...

Regarding the area outside the roofline in the eight directions where sand and water reach: if an insider goes outside and stops within the boundary, it is not a breach; however, if they cross beyond the boundary, it is called a breach. If an outsider comes inside and stops outside the boundary, it is not a breach;

however, if they cross beyond the boundary, it is called a breach. If a person performing ritual duties inserts their finger, the hem of their robe, or the like, into the interior boundary by even a fraction of an inch—such as the width of a curtain—it constitutes a breach of the boundary.
If a person who consumes pungent foods, is impure, or is otherwise wicked enters the exterior boundary for even a brief moment, it also constitutes a breach of the boundary.
When one rebuilds the site of practice (dojang), it constitutes a distant breach of the boundaries of the sacred precinct; how can one not stand in awe?
For those whose strength of body and mind is insufficient and who wish to practice during five periods, they should cease at midday.

For four periods, they should further cease during the night. For three periods, they should again cease after the afternoon. For two periods, they remain only in the morning and evening. Thus, the established discipline remains unchanging; one need only increase [the duration].
Do not diminish [your practice]. Even amidst the conditions of illness or official affairs, you must maintain mindfulness.

How can you allow your practice to rise and fall according to your diligence or laziness, establishing it in the morning and abandoning it by evening, thereby causing your correct conduct to be impure? One who cultivates this path should repeatedly examine whether they are truly capable of practicing it.

It is like crossing a river with one's body floating: one observes the depth and distance of the water so as not to become exhausted before reaching the other side; the practitioner is likewise. Thus one should observe.
Exert yourself with diligence; observe whether the dharma is extensive or concise, and then adopt it. You should not establish a practice for a single moment and then abandon it immediately.
Furthermore, you must not have a separate intention for recitation while your mind lacks concentration.

Just as an arrow shot by one whose mind is focused hits its mark, when practice is pure and the mind is one-pointed, realization arises in accordance with the thought. How could the merit obtained in a single such moment be easily measured?
Chapter Sixteen: Praising the Power of the Buddha’s Descent to Transform.

The above descriptions concern the sentient beings’ aspiration to seek upward; however, the World-Honored One’s vow-power to descend and transform exceeds the sentient beings’ upward-seeking by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond all analogy. As the Sūtra says: "The compassion of Amitābha Buddha..."

His radiant light shines universally throughout the Dharma-realm, providing universal protection so that no one shall fall. His power of compassionate vows pervades the entire Dharma-realm, universally embracing all so that none shall be lost.
His aggregates, sense bases, elements, and body are entirely identical to the Dharma-realm, causing all to awaken to this realization so that none shall regress.
Therefore, all sentient beings of the ten directions are the objects of my Amitābha’s vow-power.

He upholds [this vow] and does not abandon it from lifetime to lifetime. For this reason, within my Buddha’s great vows, the mere single recitation of his name can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
Amitābha is ever present in the world to save suffering sentient beings;

if sentient beings can but remember him, how could he not respond swiftly? When a mother rescues her child from danger, why wait for the child to call out for help? It is simply that one must not flee.

One who passes away shall certainly receive salvation. Even for one who has committed all five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and whose mind is filled with the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*), such that at the end of life the signs of the Avīci Hell appear—if they repent for even a single thought or recite the Buddha’s name ten times, they can transform the hell into a pure land and attain rebirth there.
Question: As clarified in the sutras, those who enter hell are rescued and liberated by the Buddha; however, is this not a matter of causes and conditions?
"Few. Yet why is it that there are some who can ultimately never be saved? Answer: "Within a slaughterhouse, living beings are gathered and killed day and night without ceasing.
Among those, there are some for whom the killing can be stopped, and some for whom the killing can ultimately never be stopped. It is exactly like this regarding the inability to be saved from hell.

Furthermore, it is like a person who knows the meaning of the scriptures and accords with the Buddha’s wondrous mind, yet whose three actions of the body and four actions of speech [are not in harmony]."

Because they inherit past habitual tendencies, they are unable to eliminate their evils. Thus, at the time of death, they do not encounter virtuous friends to exhort them to mindfulness of the Buddha;

they enter directly into hell. Although they undergo various sufferings, the seeds of their wholesome causes are not extinguished. Amidst these painful circumstances, they perceive the mind as it contacts its objects.
Once they know this is the mind, they also know that the living being and the Buddha are of one essence. Because they are of one essence, they immediately realize that this is precisely [the Buddha].
The Tathāgata’s subtle, wondrous, and pure body, by virtue of being able to realize that sentient beings and Buddhas are one, experiences all sensations of suffering as if they were dream-events.
He realizes that the very characteristics of suffering are themselves bodhi; for this mind is fully matured and free from error.

Furthermore, one can shorten the retribution for many kalpas of extreme suffering so that it is experienced all at once as something light. Although such a person undergoes manifold sufferings, they perceive no sign of suffering;

instead, they give rise to a heart that wishes to undergo suffering in another's stead.
