Like ice and snow reflecting the heavens and men, they are like the two wings of a bird, or like a chariot.
The two wheels: their fundamental conditions arise from the Buddha; their merit resides in the true mind. No longer perishing amidst the frost, this person is the lotus flower.
How could there ever have been divergent paths within the secret [teachings]? Their distinctions are all Vairocana; the vajra emerges prominently and transforms into suchness.

The wish-fulfilling jewel of the mind: wherever one travels, one sees the Buddha. To contract the earth [to shorten the distance] requires no talisman. In the Red Lotus Pond of Sukhāvatī, the ocean of kalpas in this Sahā world shall dry up.
(Yunzong) Yunzong was a man of the Way; he plowed for his food as his own provision. He could learn from Shen Guang’s awakening; it is fitting to follow the good.

Guiding cultivation: one has been preoccupied with the fields. Turning back, one sees that coming and going have ceased; this single expanse of golden ground—through diligent management, there will surely be an autumn harvest.
(Yogācāra) When a disciple is engaged in practice, how could they not serve their teacher? Much remains untranslated throughout ancient and modern times; it is profoundly deep and far-reaching.
Inconceivable. When the jade verses are proclaimed anew, when the golden bells ring out alone—this entire body is Amitāyus; it seems as if he has never known [otherwise].
(The Daoist Nun) Long I have remembered Lü Chunyang, who deeply mastered the Twelve Chapters. The Daoist Nun diligently recites the Buddha’s name; the elixir of the immortals is further...

Seeking the Way, it surpasses Mount Penglai in its entirety; one hears only the fragrance of the lotus. Fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of excellence, his countenance possesses the majestic radiance of a Buddha.
(Exoteric School) The city gates open toward the four directions; from north and south, all come to court the King. Without departing, the mind is pure and clear; all become Buddhas.

At the site of enlightenment, the vase and the platter were fashioned together with gold; the branches and leaves shared the same fragrance. He befriended all spiritual teachers, his diligent efforts beyond measure.

Wen Long’s *Pure Land Text* [states]: "His recitation of the Buddha's name was most earnest and diligent; he was widely learned, mastering both the ancient and the modern, and his eloquent discourse was profound."

Seeing and hearing, one must contend with the delusions of heterodox speech; instead, firmly grasp the incense of the Dharma. The Buddha within the mind requires no many words—I pour out my heart and speak it to you.
Many people are fierce and courageous; by reciting the Buddha's name, they leave the *saṃsāra* and pass directly through to the path of *nirvāṇa*, able to eliminate birth and death.

The Mara of Death is conquered; the Pure Land’s peaceful world is reached. The winds and waves of the sea of suffering have subsided. Having performed the rites of prostration at that time, he returns to sing the song of victory.
The Buddha as Physician is called the Great King of Physicians; people return to the land of immortality. Whatever is taken up becomes a wondrous medicine; all that is manifested is [healing].

A wondrous method: Within the tangerine, heaven and earth are vast; within the alchemical vessel, years and months are long. Since the conditions for illness have no place to arise, the feverish afflictions are naturally cooled.
Relying on the Buddha as one’s divining stalks and tortoise shell, one must not be parted from Him for even a moment. A lotus flower issues from the mouth, and the shadow of the sun turns toward—

Rushing westward. The place where one rests upon the seat; the time when listening to the Dharma in the forest. Jūnping, you need no longer practice divination. Teacher of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
A man need not mock the helmeted warrior. Is there no impermanence, old age, or sickness? When governing the people, one must recite the Buddha’s name. Entering the sea requires...

Boarding the boat, there are plenty of golden palaces; it is not that white jade towers do not exist. When the Buddha of Awakening preaches the wondrous Dharma, the dust-mote worlds are all contained within a single hair.
Fields and gardens pervade the ten directions; do not let the tilling and weeding fall into neglect. Fire is found within water—how extraordinary! Plant flowers upon the rocks.

Incense is offered. The Iron Ox bellows as the moon sets; the straw dog lies down in the slanting sun. After the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name is perfected, the fields will be full of reeled silk.

As one becomes skilled in reciting the Buddha’s name, wisdom grows ever clearer; every square and round thing is rendered with precision. The heart-painted picture of the Jasper Forest—this is the vow for the Pure Land.

The carving is completed; the jewel throne gathers streams of light, and music resounds through the void. As the master and his disciple wield their chisels, the removal of the plaster is no small task.
The merchant contemplates the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha, whether at home or on the road; for the sake of benefit, he practices virtue, yet remains entangled in the pursuit of wealth.

Sweeping away all emptiness, colored clouds cradle the setting sun; flower-rain scatters amidst fragrant breezes. Uncovered by impermanence, one pays homage at the Golden Terrace to the Awakened Hero.

In learning the Way through the lute, it is like tuning a zither: high and low notes depend upon one’s own mind. When time shortens, the strings snap again; yet where it pauses, the resonance remains.

Returning to the depths, ten thousand sounds fade as the mountain faces the door; all vanish together as the moon fills the forest. Ziqi diligently recites the Buddha’s name—this must surely be one who understands his music.

When the black and white stones have not yet been distinguished on the board, even the immortals do not know the outcome. It is only by observing the moves that victory or defeat is debated, and only at the edge of the lacquered box can the result be discerned.

Males and females are limited; to achieve [liberation] would be a vain waste. The infinite [pursuit of fame] exhausts bitter thought. In this life, transcend to the Pure Land; before the tree-trunk rots, it will be late to reach home.
As for calligraphy, being able to write the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* surpasses a hundred copies of the *Lantingji*. Simply entrust others with writing on the walls; do not indulge in wine.
A full vessel. Massing clouds hang over the great earth; pool waters pour into the vast ocean. Filling [the vessel] with the name of Amitābha, he makes this world of Sahā the model.
He paints blue-and-green landscapes as handed down by the world—Buddha images and immortal deities. He applies his intent to depicting mountains and rivers, fixing his mind upon them.

The Sage and the Seer; Bo Shi excels at painting horses, while Ling Yun delights in planting lotuses. When the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi* manifests, the brush can wield its power, and the jeweled ponds appear all before one.
Let down the fishing line and cease; neither on the bank nor in midstream. In the Lotus Land of the Great Ocean, sentient beings are like lotus roots.
A leaf-boat glides by; the evening sun is red as fire, the new moon curved like a hook. To recite the Buddha’s name is itself the true realm—smoke drifts across the head of an ancient ferry.
The woodcutter lets go of his hand at the precipice; the withered vines are but rotten firewood. Mountains and rivers return to oneself; wind and moon are entrusted to the world.
Equanimous and serene, though bearing a burden of a thousand *qun*, my feet do not stray by even a single thread. Such is true mindfulness of the Buddha; there is no need for prior arrangement.
Plowing the ancient fields that encompass the earth, the mud-man drives the iron ox. Whether one applies the whip early or late, the sowing shall deliver [beings across].
Spring and autumn, ripening and maturing—all are my lot. Returning home, I am spared from seeking elsewhere. I shall simply compare this to plowing and sowing;

how could there be any worry about lacking grain? The cowherd boy has not yet tamed his ox; it easily becomes angry with the sprouting crops. For now, I will pull on the rope-end and let its nose [be guided].

The breath is even; the setting sun lingers over a thousand peaks at evening, while fragrant grasses flourish across the four quarters in spring. To awaken to this Buddha of True Nature, the moonlight upon the thatched gate is ever new.

Officials must maintain a mind of mindfulness of the Buddha; otherwise, amidst the dust of worldly affairs, one squanders the light of time. A single point reveals the Treasury of Radiance, which in turn becomes a source of merit.

Virtue Forest: The curtains hang down, all is silent; leaning on the armrest, the night is deep. This is entirely the ground of cultivation. Lord Yang did not accept gold; until his final breath, he never ceased his diligent efforts.
Reciting the Buddha’s name in secret, he silently upheld the sutras. He was selected as a Buddha and ranked among the "Yellow Tablets. Dwelling amidst the dust, he blended with the world.

The commoner. The moon encircles the lock outside the gate; the wind stirs the bells before the pavilion. One should immediately form the thought of a lotus pond; the spirit’s journey is like awakening from a dream.
The sorceress recites the Buddha’s name—what doubt can there be? She takes up her divine robes at random. Child of the Bodhisattvas in the Pure Land, you are of the highest grade.
The husband and son; the ghostly face turns and changes, while barbarian speech is deployed at will. When facing Yang, he gathers up his wine cup, manifesting the dignified countenance of the Buddha.
The craftsman of the coffin should look back well; man has never died and need not cease. The marvelous and divine become putrid and corrupt; illusory substance is equal [to all].
A floating bubble; gazing long, who remains? Even the Buddha has no place to return, and thus he grieves. The precious name of Amitābha is a wise strategy for the Land of Bliss.

To sever the heart of slaughter is the heart that delivers beings. The principles of the Zen school are profound; receiving a body increases one's evil retribution, while hastening toward death brings [liberation].

Lamenting cries: let go and all become Buddhas; what is grasped is entirely transformed into gold. Amidst a thousand differences, there is but this one phrase: who does not have Avalokiteśvara within their own home?
People commit many transgressions; strive diligently to recite the name of Amitābha. Flowing into the sea of suffering and emptiness, it is transformed into incense.
The rivers of water and the red dust are both swept away; black karma is instantly consumed. Take it for granted that you shall roam in purity and peace; the mind becomes empty in a single kṣaṇa.
When weaving thoughts as one weaves cloth, how could the warp and woof be applied in vain? The great earth is stretched out to form silk, and space is spun [into thread].
Spinning silk: clouds conceal the seamless robe; flowers bloom on branches that never sprouted. With a flick of the arm, he returns home; the lotus opens in the white jade pool.
How could dyeing ever leave the dye-house? The Buddha’s teaching resounds clearly and brightly. Azure and green follow their depths; brocades and silks are left to themselves.
Short or long, they display every kind of color; in various ways, they emit rays of light. Their original nature is pure and free from defilement; golden lotuses fill the world with fragrance.
Bound by their own karma as slaves, people must practice mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded devotion. The "Elder" is none other than Amitābha; one's own body is the Pure Land.

The earth serves as the condition; the waters of the Dharma flow from every pore. Following mindfulness, lotuses bloom from the pond. Amidst billowing clouds of fragrance, the jade verses are proclaimed with clear resonance.
Servants, do not be foolish! How much time remains in this fleeting life? A human body easily grows old; it is difficult to obtain again.

One must know this: one blames oneself for the cheapness of one's skirt and hairpins; others loathe the decay of one's teeth and hair. Go and come while diligently reciting the Buddha’s name, and the five obstacles will be left behind in a single morning.
A courtesan goes from house to house, craving wine and further deluding herself with flowers. By reciting the Buddha’s name, greed and envy are removed; turn the mind back and find peace.
Alas! The irrigation channels are as clear as mirrors; the lotus ponds are as vast as wagons. To cast off the body and become a true man—do not allow a single thought to stray.

Among prisoners, there are none who have committed murder, theft, or lust; yet they groan within the gates of the jail. If one can strike the gong while reciting the Buddha’s name, overturn this place!

Transforming the mind, one follows the teachings as spirits and ghosts howl; when sages and worthies appear of their own accord, the fruit is realized upon the lotus pedestal—Amitābha is not to be sought elsewhere.

When the golden essence emerges from the smelting furnace, the master hand employs tongs and hammers; though the weight in ounces and grams remains unchanged, the vases and basins each take their distinct form.

How appropriate! What a shimmering radiance of auspicious light! How truly rare and wondrous this beautiful resonance is! One should immediately form the thought of Amitābha; his true body is never for a moment departed.
Like silverware forged from silver, he is brought forth and presented face-to-face. This is the same realm as Samantabhadra; it is compared to the Fragrant Elephant.

Radiant light; skillfully fashioning the form of a lotus flower, one shall ultimately return to the City of Ultimate Bliss. Rubbing white snow with black plums—pure karma lies in single-minded diligence.
When the pearl is ready, recite the name of Amitābha; as each single bead passes through, the true Buddha appears. As the thread comes, he manifests; as it is threaded away, merit accumulates.
The merit is great. Ambrosia arises in the throat and tongue; the wild mind repents its finery. Bowing the head before the wish-fulfilling jewel, what can one do but rejoice?
The craftsmanship of jade is not accidental; one must simply maintain firm resolve. One may recite the name of Amitābha, which must be supported by purity.
With the earth as a condition, one is reborn to roam the jeweled realms; opening one's eyes, one beholds the Golden Sage. The tragedy of shedding blood at Mount Jing has been spent in vain;

though the carvings are exquisite and the architectural details are crafted by skilled artisans, and the flowers and grasses appear as if in full spring, look now at the image of Udayana—who was it that wielded the chisel?
The stone is weighed; today the work is perfected. May my vows be fulfilled in this very life. Departing to the side of the Eight Virtues Pond, the lotus shall remain unstained by dust.
Casting and praising the mold of Confucius, the pattern fits within a single kṣaṇa. The poured model is entirely similar; once melted, it is complete.
Trifling! From now on, focus solely on mindfulness; from this point, sever the cycle of rebirth. Turn yourself over in the furnace and go forth; the flowers are so high they cannot be grasped.
Shaping clay and molding sand—playing with earth like a fool. Come out from within my palms; faces and features are fashioned by the mind. Let the mold be cast.
With hands opened, they do not cease holding the Buddha’s name; without interval, they form the lotus-womb. Rising and falling are all due to the ground; from within the flower, a jade child is born.
Adorning the physical frame with golden and azure luster, sculpted with full detail, they take pride in their exquisite craftsmanship, able to manifest the Buddha.
Praise be to the mountains and rivers, the sun and moon, the crimson, white, azure, and yellow! If one obtains a fine golden platform, one may choose freely upon the completion of the task.
To sew the Buddha-remembrance is even more wondrous; with skillful gold scissors, one cuts and shapes it. The ocean boils from within the needle’s eye, and the clouds enter the thread.
The path comes; it covers the body of true emptiness and spreads out a platform of various jewels. With effort uninterrupted, when the flowers close, they immediately bloom.
One embroiders garments with needle and thread; the recitation of Amitābha does not hinder this. A peacock perches upon the branch; beneath the leaves, one sleeps.
Mandarin Ducks. In the courtyard, spring is fair; behind the screens, the day is long. Body and mind have become one whole; throughout the Buddha-land, one may soar at will.

(Shaving the Head) What a distinguished air he has in shaving his head! His name is humble, yet his skill is high. He yields his fertile field to a modest craft; like autumn waters, his true nature is revealed.
A sharp blade. Praise the Buddha without doubt; hold his name without wearying yourself. Suddenly sever the hair of afflictions; within the light, behold the radiant ūrṇā-kośa.
(Miao-di) Like a householder who balances buying and selling, this is a fine livelihood. The measures of grain do not diminish in times of scarcity; the coins and blades are refined.

There is an increase [in merit]. The path leading back to the Land of Bliss is direct; slight attachments to worldly gain cause the conditions to diverge. Chanting the name of Amitābha while sitting or reclining—the lotus pedestal is not far at all.
(The Court Musician): His career is too refined and elegant; it can dispel ten thousand kinds of sorrow. The Prince sings at the ornate banquet; the young nobleman is drunk.
Jade towers—suddenly passing through, the green is hard to tread; Seeking one another, white hair fills the head. One who can proclaim the Dharma of non-self Need not seek it elsewhere.
(The Cook) Not failing the monks' and laymen's midday meal, Diligence accords with their aspirations. With a slight garnish of mushrooms and ginger, The dishes and utensils are artfully arranged.
The arrangements are made: impurities and meat are cleared away; abundance is prepared from the seas and rivers. Amitābha, you must reflect with urgency; from now on, ascend the jade steps.
The mountain recitation is most profound and serene; the clear pool resounds with the warbling of birds in the forest. This is the true realm of the Land of Bliss—excellent for all eternity.

Body and mind compete to shed jade from the tips of branches; they vie to dangle gold beneath the leaves. The light of longevity appears within every dust mote and world-system; what hindrance could there be to seeking it toward the West?
In this city, red dust submerges horses high; yet reciting the Buddha’s name is no mere labor. It pierces the darkness of the mundane path like a torch, and sweeps away the bonds of craving.

The Net-Sword: When ordinary beings ascend to the stage of enlightenment, it is like an elder leading his children; yet without the true public warrant, one has merely endured this Sahā world in vain.
Let the boat of mindfulness take the waters as its neighbor; amidst the dust of long streets and short alleys, the compassionate countenance is like the full moon, and the holy name is grasped.

The jewel-wheel: gathering the sails swiftly at the lotus marsh, rowing the oars repeatedly along the willow embankment. Within this world of blue lapis lazuli, one perfectly realizes the purple-gold body.

This remote village is particularly suited for the practice of *nienfo*; with thatched huts and bamboo fences, its simplicity and austerity are entirely distinct, and its pure sincerity is even more so.
Do not doubt the pure realm of the Land of Bliss; you must lay a foundation for long-lasting stability. This is indeed the Vajrāsana, where the eight-sided Vairambha winds blow.

From the tips of the spring forest trees, the setting sun is ushered away; day after day it exhorts people to return home. When the birds cry out as if their voices were stained with blood, the traveler hears them and sheds tears.
The dripping robe: ancient and modern, it cannot be retained; its coming and going is as swift as flight. Having changed out the hollow interior, may the vow upon the lotus pedestal not be betrayed.
Entering summer after summer, fresh lotuses bloom, causing many to feel deep emotion. Subtle flowers fill the sleeves; the fine birds warble.
The branches of the courtyard trees; the sun sinks in the azure void to the west; the waves of the blue river flow eastward—these all return to the Great Perfect Mirror.
Only do not cling to Saṃsāra. The autumn sky unfolds as a new season; the slender moon is but a single hook. The Master’s entire body is manifested; the land is here.
The mind pervades all: mountain peaks rain down azure topknots; ocean waves wipe away sapphire eyes. Contemplating this, one attains direct vision;
go westward and wander at will.
The winter scene reveals its reward for you to know: the Pure Land is fully manifest when the thousand mountains are all jade trees and the ten thousand ravines—[are all...]

The Jasper Pond is swept clean and empty, free from all obscuration; it is clearly manifest without the need for thought. Heaven’s coldness surely takes pity on me; as the year draws to a close, my tears flow in streams.
I shall soon behold the Buddha before me, his radiance surpassing the sun and moon in the heavens. Layer upon layer, his pupils are pure; tier upon tier, his topknots are arrayed.
A spiral; hanging dewdrops fill the necklaces. A circular canopy of empty clouds; crows cry within the pines and cypresses. This is what is transmitted as the Seal of the Mind.
Abiding is like a pearl rolling upon a platter. How should one contemplate the Buddha’s marks? The moon fills the three thousandfold world system; the wind is clear throughout the ten directions.

The two gates are closed; returning the hearing to hear its source is beyond reach, and turning away from seeing to see its origin is even more difficult. The Great Being should smile; ordinary people are deceived by the burning heat.

The mind of one who sits in meditation is limpid and unshakable; they recite the Buddha’s name from evening until morning. The realm of reality manifests within stillness, while time passes amidst the clamor of the world.

Internally extinguished; the elephant and dragon are all dharma-companions, while the wild ducks and geese each bear the marks of immortals. With plans for return after fifty years, red shoots emerge from jade-green branches.
Lying among the trees, I dream of arriving home—all is white lotus flowers. Extensively praising the Triple Dharma, he transversely divides the five [vehicles].
The colors are like morning mists; precious robes and fragrances are faint and dim. The shadows of pearl trees interlace; just as the dawn bell tolls, the Milky Way slants across the balustrade.
Suffering is immeasurable and entangling; one must return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Worn-out rags meet with rare imperial garments; an empty stomach encounters exquisite silks.

Upon the *raśmi* canopy and the jeweled throne, one pays homage at the three times of day; through a single thought-moment, the Gate of Radiance is perfected. Its brilliance transcends sun and moon, while the sexagenary cycle marks the passing years.
Delight in teaching increases heedlessness; constantly recite the Pure Name with your mouth, and the Buddha-land will manifest according to your mind upon the lotus pedestal.

Recollection ascends like the moon reflected in the void; it is just as fire melts ice. Having already dwelled in the inconceivable stage, one shall only then ascend through transformation in the future.
Do not seek to escape from favorable or adverse conditions; who else could this clearly be? The entire body is Amitāyus—uniformly so.
Contemplate and rightly recollect emptiness to eliminate all delusions; let the wild mind do as it pleases. When thorns pass before one's eyes, they reflect like crimson upon azure lapis lazuli.

When things proceed according to my own whims, they seem lowly or elevated; yet when observed with wisdom, they are actually inauspicious. The Buddha’s name is "Rest from Heedlessness"; follow it and you shall find peace.
It is unconventional. Outwardly it accords with the essence of empty space; within, it flows with the light of the sun and moon. How could this be attained through gradual cultivation?
Right view serves as the ladder and the vessel. May the joyful winds blow in every gale; may we hold one another’s hands and never part. Do not let the mind become lax—this is precisely the Buddha.
Compassion. Butterflies dance as flowers are offered; orioles sing as willows unfurl their brows. In the wondrous samādhi of freedom from sorrow, how could one not be joyful?
Anger first arises because the breath is uneven; it is born within when encountering adverse conditions. Let go and there is nothing at all; upon reflection, it vanishes.
There is contention. When virtuous people gather together and Bodhisattvas practice in harmony, those who are mired in greed and anger are subdued; through gentleness, one nurtures one's own nature.
When decline comes, one does not even realize tears are dampening one's kerchief; enemies become one's own kin. Yet if one merely follows the turns of hatred and love, one has not escaped death.

The wheel of birth turns; in the Pure Land one is free from afflictions, and for long years one is liberated from suffering and bitterness. On the paths beneath Mount Beimang, the wailing of ghosts truly grieves the heart.

Honor, wealth, and nobility are but a fleeting moment—like a single mountain of Sumeru; it has never been heard that such a person has ascended the registers of the dead. There is a medicine that can arrest [the flow of time].

Childlike countenance; the Buddha-land’s countenance has returned. Departing from King Yama, he was granted leave to return. How many sights await in the jade towers? Immortal, one may ascend them at will.
Worthy ones, worthy ones, revered by the world—mindfulness of the Buddha continues unto this day. Within the community is the Great Minister Bai; amidst the mountains is Su.

In the Hanlin Academy, there is little true flavor of the world; my tenure in this office has not yet reached its full term. How many people are there destined for the Pure Land? Seek them carefully within these remaining writings.
That which the fool cannot be parted from for even a moment is itself the foundation of Buddhahood. Beyond the clarity of one's ears and eyes, heaven and earth merge into one.

In the state of primordial unity, the Land of Bliss knows no other thought; do not hold any name other than that of the Sage. Yet one laughs at those who claim to be "awake," for they know nothing of Amitābha.
With great virtue and its corresponding conduct, his benevolence and compassion ensure his words cause no harm; thus he transforms the world into a realm of gold, and from it flows forth jade.
A ray of light; the Buddha bestows the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). The wind wafts the fragrance of the *puṇḍarīka* lotus. Whether sitting or sleeping, all are within the pure realm.

Where else need one seek the Western Land? This ugly form is the very truth of this mind. The jeweled trees and flowered pedestals are close at hand. Even Xi Shi was covered in impurity; as for Mo Mu, her body—
Free from dust, the setting sun is like a suspended drum. To the west is a beautiful woman, adorned with the thirty-two marks. She is the body of a Great Being who has appeared in the world.

Though my body is poor and my path is impoverished, I am not truly poor; I recite the Buddha’s name and exhort others to do so. I use only that treasure which cannot be coveted; it is difficult to forget.

Its value is precious; it is a long eon for the kingdom, yet but a fleeting spring within this realm. Do not say that the Western Land is far away, for it is as close as the bending and extending of an arm.

Though it is said that recollecting the Buddha is difficult when one is wealthy, if food and clothing provide security for this body, one may set aside the golden cauldron and still remain worthy of the image.

Rosewood is swifter than a horse that covers a thousand *li*; it surpasses the Nine-Return Elixir. On the day one achieves merit in the Pure Land, heaven and earth will be viewed as if upon the palm of one's hand.
It is precious to hear the Dharma, for the mind is easily opened; all this comes from reciting the Buddha’s name. Within the three thousand golden worlds and the hundred million jade realms...

The pavilions and terraces are fully endowed with the seeds of Bodhi; they adorn the womb of liberation. Through the root of faith, concentration and wisdom are born, perfecting the treasures of the Dharma King.

Though one may have been lowly and committed many sins in the past, by recollecting the Buddha it is easy to become single-minded and diligent. The seal is directed toward the destruction of the non-mind; the patterns arise from existence.
Visualize that jeweled flowers carpet the ground, and celestial music fills the sky with its resonance. How elegant is this transformation! One is reborn upon a golden terrace of the highest grade.
Sitting in solitary leisure facing the west, one recites the mantra of the wheel without forgetfulness. The Buddha causes the ground of the mind to be pure; the tongue becomes like a lotus root.
The fragrance of flowers; when the sun reaches the mountain peaks, golden light floats filling the chamber. At this moment, free from other thoughts, one personally beholds King Druma.
Busyness steals away leisure, yet it remains with man; who can fulfill a hundred years of spring? In the end, there is no time when it ceases; they are driven on by mutual distress.

Renew yourself daily. Fame and achievement lie solely in mindfulness of the Buddha. Do not worry about poverty in your practice of the Way; even the iron tree will blossom. The Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma.
Mindfulness of the Buddha in old age is the constant rule; do not seek other paths. When the eyes open, there is no different view; when the body departs, [there is...]

Radiant appearance and deportment—Pure Land is entirely dependent on me; as for the mind-king, whom else would you ask? Your name is inscribed upon the lotus calyx; enter the ranks of the sages without doubt.
Do not say that youth is still in its prime; impermanence does not grant anyone respite. When the flower blooms, it meets the rain of donkeys; when the rope snaps, it encounters [the precipice].
The racing wheels whirl on; green hair is still worthy of care, and rosy cheeks are at their peak of vigor. Those of later years must contemplate the Buddha; the aged are dull and lack spirit.
(Retirement) Interest in the arena has already faded; one retires and hangs up the cap and gown. It is better not to have reached this point than to regret it later—what need is there for worry?
The Buddha’s Way is difficult; cease shedding tears at the crossroads. Let the sun and moon roll like skipping balls. Like a single pearl, its radiance is like a bright jade disk.

(Living in seclusion: Whether great or small, the noble person’s body is at ease; in every case, there is no difference between the two. It is easy to dwell by clear springs, yet it is also possible to live in the bustling market.

What difficulty? The place where one attains [realization] is not far; when madness comes, it may be manifold. Mind after mind is the Buddha; sit in silence and contemplate within stillness. (Regarding hardships:
In times of hardship and distress, one must be supported; Amitābha acts as the fundamental teacher. Where a venomous snake lies across the path, a long sword presses close.

While you still have this body, do not regret that your mindfulness of the Buddha is too early; turn the light back within before it is too late. Though the distance be said to be ten million *buddha-kṣetras*, as soon as the thought arises, the Buddha already knows.
(Regarding Illness: It is clear that because there is a body, illness does not spare anyone. Delusive thoughts are nothing but delusion; even the Perfected Immortals have not escaped them.

This is true. When heat comes, one fans the fire; when the bones are cast away, the sinews remain entangled. By reciting the Buddha’s name, one leaves behind birth and death. Jambudvīpa is transformed into dust;
where can one go without being moved by grief? Having lost one's native land to the east and west, though one happens to preserve a wretched life, it is difficult to return to what was once.

At the manor estate, morning and evening I take refuge in the Buddha. When body and mind reach the realm of ultimate bliss, one naturally transcends the defiled and turbid world. The golden palace has halls made of jade.
(Peril and ruin: As peril and ruin approach, tears flow; when will birth and death ever cease? Have you ever seen flowers upon an iron tree? [The station of] the Golden Wheel.

One may remain; together we shall realize the essence of emptiness. This is precisely the point of union. The Buddha Amitābha is one’s own original nature; all people in the human realm are entirely free.

(At ten years of age) Though it is said that the body is small, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha as a provision for the journey. I fear even the green plums will fall; do not boast of your white [hair].

The days grow long; marshy ground becomes a vast flood, and a mere mound rises to the height of a lofty ridge. At eight years of age, she is hailed as a Dragon Girl, sitting majestically upon the site of enlightenment.
(At twenty) when a man reaches his early prime, more than half of a hundred years has passed. To practice mindfulness of the Buddha is not considered too early; to practice compassion—

Weariness is excessive; one must restrain a stubborn temper. The desire to steal gradually diminishes, and one must humble oneself before both the noble and the lowly. Within the body lies the demon of affliction.

(At thirty years of age,) the year my Master attained the Way, I contemplated the Buddha, emulating the Tathāgata. Suddenly beholding the appearance of the morning star, I finally came to know the Right [Dharma].
The eyes open; birds sing and flowers smile of themselves. The mountains are like paintings, the waters like moss. A true man who leans upon the earth—how brilliant is he who turns his light back!
(At forty years of age) "No fame" is what the ancients lamented; mindfulness of the Buddha is the most expedient means. In the bright mirror, three parts are old; on a branch of flowers, one...
Fragments fly away; the Dharma-wheel gives birth to jeweled trees, and merit overflows the golden pond. The cycle of the *jiǎzǐ* year passes like a flash of lightning;

I shall wait for the Pure Land with a broad mind. (At fifty years of age) I am rapidly becoming an old man; my eyes grow dim and my ears are about to go deaf. After contemplating the Buddha and cultivating the self, I shall depart at the time of death.
In the dark, he opens his azure eyes; a single red orb descends. Pure and bright, free from all further thought, a mountain of gold fills the vast void.

(At sixty years of age) Having passed fifty years in declining health, I can do nothing but recite the name of Amitābha. A candle in the wind is easily extinguished; it is difficult to turn back the waters.

The upper waves; the calyxes of the lotus buds appear frequently in dreams. The coral tree’s branches are so beautiful. If one does not make plans for the Western Return, what will become of this head full of frost-white hair?

(At seventy years of age) Long life has always been rare since antiquity. One should recite the Buddha's name while awaiting the Western Return. When black karma is completely eliminated, the crimson sun shall depart.

As if about to fly, one shall immediately roam through pure lands; what need is there to prepare new robes? With clear vision, one beholds the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa; with sincere devotion, one pierces the Iron Ring Mountains.
(At eighty years of age,) how many remain robust and strong? Reciting the Buddha’s name is the most intimate of kin. White hair has become entirely like snow; the clear sky remains—only...
Beholding the sensory objects, he meets the Sage Lord at Panxi; the Pure Land is near to the Able One (Śākyamuni). All are within the radiance, with ten billion bodies upon the tip of a hair.
(At ninety years of age,) preparing his gear for the journey, one does not yet know where he will arrive: the land of neither aging nor death, boundless and without limit.
Measuring the light, five clouds hang down to form a canopy; seven trees stand in rows. The Great Beings and the various Honored Ones dwell together in joy that knows no end.
(One hundred years) When the span of time reaches its end, one remains for but a brief moment within this realm. Quickly recite the name of Amitābha, and together ride upon the *parinirvāṇa*.

Like a boat, at the moment of birth, one is divided into nine grades; with the light of wisdom opening wide the two eyes, one is no longer bound by old age and death, attaining freedom to move in all directions.

(At one hundred and ten years,) a hundred years are even more worthy of reverence; take mindfulness of the Buddha as your path ahead. The temple grounds are vast and unobstructed; it is a dream of the Jade Pond.
It is also pure. The groves of trees all proclaim the Dharma. The necklaces emit radiance; upon the ground are houses of gold. The minds of people transform and become [thus].

(At one hundred and twenty years of age,) a hundred years exceed the full lifespan. Cultivating mindfulness of Amitābha in later life, one’s body dwells in the realm of nirvāṇa. This shore is not birth.
The River of Death. This very mind is itself Buddha. When asked "Who am I?", go straight toward the West. This mountain monk has spoken too much.
*Verses on the Pure Land of the Western Quarters* (Volume Two).
*Western Studio Pure Land Poems*, Volume Three:
The Sixteen Contemplations, Twenty-two Stanzas (The Contemplation of the Sun).
The gate of contemplation is named the "Contemplation of the Sun. The setting sun hangs suspended in the west; It is clearly visible, like a golden drum, Round and full, it hangs [in the sky].
Azure sky. The mind that comes and goes is never obscured; whether eyes are open or closed, it is always present as its object. It is no different from the Buddha; Amitābha appears before one.
(Water Contemplation) This gate of contemplation is called Water Contemplation. After the ice melts, it becomes lapis lazuli, shining with countless pearls; the phenomena are clearly manifest.
Without doubt: ten thousand stories of towers, the moon is bright; the winds of the eight kinds of music blow. How can one speak of "no-self"? Who else could this whole mind be?

(Earth Contemplation) In Earth Contemplation, one contemplates the ground before one. Having contemplated, one knows it clearly. For a moment there is nothing that is not mindfulness; even in the midst of haste, it is the same.

One should contemplate: briefly beholding the Land of Adornment, with the exception of the time for eating, the boundless cycle of birth and death is exhausted; how then could there be any doubt regarding the Pure Land?
(The Contemplation of Trees) The gate of contemplation is named the Contemplation of Trees. Precious trees stand in rows, entirely covered by nets of pearls, their sevenfold radiance intermingling.
Jewel Light: Ten billion youths dwell amidst flowers; a thousand worlds are hidden within fruits. Cultivated from their own seeds, they grow up supporting heaven and earth.
(The Pond Contemplation): This contemplation is named the Pond Water Contemplation; all are formed of the seven treasures and emerge from wish-fulfilling jewels, flowing as golden ravines.
The depths are luminous; the subtle resonance of lotus flowers and the songs of jewel-birds extolling [the Buddha] reach here as mere droplets. All defilements are washed away into purity.

(General Observation) The jeweled towers are named General Observation; five hundred billion stand towering and majestic. Day and night, the various devas play music, proclaiming the Three [Treasures].

The names of the jewels are all inherently present within the minds of the sages; thus, they are not far from initial accomplishment. Although the people of this Saha world are evil, through profound merit they will certainly attain rebirth there.

(The Contemplation of the Lotus Throne) This contemplation is named the Contemplation of the Lotus Throne. Upon the ground of the seven precious jewels are lotus flowers, with petals beyond counting—ten thousand, nay, more than that.

Proudly boasting: "Though the precious jewel may seem illusory, the facial features have never been mistaken. The Great Way transcends truth and falsehood; the person of comprehensive understanding distinguishes the correct from the deviant.

(Contemplation of the Image) The gate of contemplation is named the Contemplation of the Image. Its manifestation is no different from that of the Tathāgata, fully endowed with the golden hue and the marks and signs, seated upon a lotus heart.

The eyes open; the mandarin ducks discourse on the wondrous Dharma. Beholding their majesty, they are arrayed upon flower pedestals. Hearing this, it accords with the True Vehicle; cease using deluded thoughts to conjecture.

(True Body Contemplation) One contemplates that Buddha’s true body, lofty and vast, immeasurable by the world. His ocean-like eyes encompass a thousand realms; the mountain-like hair-tuft between his brows illuminates.

Throughout the ten directions, Śrāvakas serve as his close attendants; his physical transformation radiates a circular halo, and his mind is the very essence of compassion. Amitābha is the Dharma King who perceives all.
(Avalokiteśvara Contemplation) Upon his neck shines Avalokiteśvara; his fleshly protuberance is a body of purple-gold, and atop his crown stands a transformed Buddha, forming a seal of a thousand.

The spoked wheel follows the light through the masses, making it no longer night; the spread of flowers brings eternal spring. Having long lost our Father of Compassion, we shed frequent tears in the wind.
(Avalokiteśvara’s Contemplation: The Great Power-Attainer wears a celestial crown of five hundred fresh jeweled flowers; his *uṣṇīṣa* is especially sublime, and the golden vase is peerless.
Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa. Adorned and pervasive, he sits amidst the borders of the realm, his head frequently nodding. One Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, with bodies as numerous as sentient beings.
(Universal Contemplation) The gate of contemplation is named Universal Contemplation. He sits cross-legged within a great lotus; his illuminating body is like the sun. Opening his eyes, the Sage—

Filling the void, the birds and the forest discourse on the wondrous Dharma; their words and meanings accord with the Sūtras. Who can say there is any separation between them? With single-minded sincerity, one attains penetration in an instant.

(Contemplating the Miscellaneous) First, upon the pond, one contemplates the Buddha, his majestic and dignified body sixteen feet tall. Close by is the lotus seat of Avalokiteśvara, and that of Śākyamitra’s [Mahāsthāmaprāpta] precious...
The light radiates forth; minor marks flow through the motes of lands, while the entire body fills the great void. In the ten directions, all are sovereign; there is neither deficiency nor surplus.
This is the superior grade of contemplation.
(The Highest Grade of the Highest Birth) The three grades are set forth in the gateway of contemplation; each class differs according to its faculties.

If one possesses the complete mind without interruption and practices concurrently without deviation, One will be born in the highest grade in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the royal palace of the Dharma King upon the golden earth. There, one immediately attains the patience of non-arising; how could one worry that Buddhahood is distant?

(Those of Superior Capacity, Middle Birth) Those of middle birth are even more direct: they believe in cause and effect without doubt; they recite various sutras with their mouths and proceed to the ponds of the seven treasures with their bodies.

When the Sage descends to dwell in their place, his platform meets them at the moment of death. Seeing the Buddha, they receive his personal praise; how can they begrudge the delay in receiving their prediction?

(Those of Superior Capacity Reborn in the Lower Grade) Those reborn in the lower grade find practice easy; those of the middle grade do not engage in much contention. Having awakened the mind for the unsurpassed path, they are born within golden lotus flowers.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s various marks and signs of excellence, the wondrous Dharma, and the multitude of his voices, they attain the first stage after three kalpas, accomplishing it without even the effort of a finger-snap.
The Middle Grade Contemplation (Middle Grade Rebirth) contemplates the three grades in their proper order; each class is skillfully arranged. It fulfills the aspirations of all beings.

Furthermore, by observing the Eight Precepts, one is free from the calamities of transgressions; emerging from the depths of the evil realms, one immediately realizes Arhatship and wanders through the pure lands.
Jade Steps.

(Middle Grade, Middle Birth) Regarding the Dharma of observing precepts in a middle birth: if one fulfills them for even a single morning or evening, with a mind examined and free from regret, the Buddhas will come to welcome one with grace.

One shall ascend to the Pure Realm in golden light; amidst the lotus calyxes, one praises the Compassionate Honored One. Realizing the fruit in advance through this middle stage, the true mind penetrates through to the end.

The Source (Middle Grade, Lower Birth). Born as either male or female, you practice filial piety and possess benevolence and compassion. Your spiritual friends speak of the Pure Land; the Bhikṣus are truly your teachers.
Amidst the opening and closing of precious lotuses, and with the bending and stretching of powerful arms, Avalokiteśvara personally guides you; there is no birth that does not [attain liberation].
I regret my delay.

Herein are listed the three grades of the Contemplation Gate for the Lower Grade (Lower Grade Rebirth). I shall offer my critique for each class. Those who commit evil in ignorance feel no shame; may you show them compassion as a friend.

Exhorting one to be born [in the Pure Land]: In a single moment of mind, one receives the names of the twelve divisions of the scriptures; reciting the name of Amitābha with the mouth, the transformed Buddhas from the West come to welcome them.

(The Middle Grade, Lower Birth) Those born in this middle grade have frequently violated the precepts and adorned themselves with evil karma; their spirits and souls are in turmoil within the realm of retribution, and at the time of death, their breath...

The momentum of [your] power is extinguished. The Buddha-vehicle sweeps vast and open like the heavens; it quenches the blazing fires of hell. The assembly of Buddhas comes to welcome you, so that you may partake of the grace of the lotus pond (the lowest of the lower grades).
In this lower birth, one must be intensely vigilant; unwholesome karma brings endless suffering. If you heed the words of the noble sages, you shall depart from evil.

Within the realms of rebirth, the soul flies away and the mind is scattered; the Buddha’s name melts away all sins. Like a lotus blooming under the rising sun, one ascends to the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss.
Eight Verses in Praise of Rebirth by Transformation.

(The White Crane) How could a white crane be of the common sort? Its dark plumage sets its temperament high. To the immortal, it is but a fine steed; yet in the wilds by the sea, it pecks at the rank and putrid.

There is no barrier between this bird and the path to the celestial clouds; why should its feathers on breast and back cause shame? Having heard the Dharma of non-self, it thereby severs all worldly toil.
(Śāri) Śāri is the spring oriole. Its cultivated brows are like dots of lacquer, its eyes are bright; its wings are coated in gold, its voice is struck by jade-green harps.

Above and below are trees of the seven treasures; it rises and falls with the names of the Three Jewels. Turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature, it toils at playing the *nügwa* lute for Guāng Niǔwá.
The peacock is pure and free from dust; it is but a single transformation-body of the Tathāgata. Its tail unfurls at dawn within the golden palace;

its plumage stirs with spring in the jade towers. Let the guardian of sounds cease all confusion; Amitābha’s speech is most true. This numinous bird understands the wondrous principle; those in the world merely pretend to be human.
(Parrot) The parrot is truly able to speak; its tongue remains even after cremation. Having long possessed wisdom and understanding, it shares the same root as I from the beginning.
In vain it reflects the image in the cold pond; in vain it harbors resentment for its former land. How could such a bird as this not soar freely at will in a blissful realm?
The sixty kinds of sounds of the kalaviṅka—by what means could they be depicted? He bellows and sighs beyond the void; he warbles and circles among the trees.

He causes all the female birds to settle in submission and makes the multitude of birds startle in alarm. When the jewel of the mind hears these wondrous echoes, the sphere of the ears becomes vast, penetrating, and clear.
The *jīvamjīvaka* birds share one body with distinct heads; within the Buddha’s garden, they do not differ from human beings in their faces, as all proclaim the Dharma of suffering and emptiness.

The *śāla* trees drink the dew at dawn, and the lotuses chant in the wind by day. In the mutual functioning of sense organs and objects, though conditions differ, their nature naturally interpenetrates.
(Ducks and Waterfowl) Ducks, geese, and variegated mandarin ducks, all together extolling auspiciousness; Dividing one by one across the green marshes, arrayed row upon row at the crimson fords.
A realm of leisure within the trees, a land of prosperity amidst the flowers; I gaze closely with my own eyes upon the precious pond—the great King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels.
(Regarding the Forests: The Pure Land binds my heart. Layer upon layer, the trees cover one another, mutually forming subtle and wondrous colors. Together they proclaim the sound of Nirvana.
Beneath the earth lies frost and swords; throughout the human world are thorns and needles. Sitting here, I contemplate infinite bliss, though I have not yet ascended the towers and pavilions.
An Analysis of the Eight Verses on Nianfo by Master Shandao (Original Verses): Gradually the skin becomes like chicken skin and the hair turns white as cranes;

look at how the gait grows increasingly faltering. Even if gold and jade fill one’s hall, one cannot avoid decay, decline, old age, and illness. No matter how many kinds of pleasures you may enjoy, impermanence will inevitably arrive. There is only the cultivation of the direct path: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.

Gradually the skin becomes like chicken skin and the hair turns white like a crane; the spirit cannot avoid becoming exhausted. Piteous are these aging eyes, blurred and dim, just like the moon shrouded by drifting clouds.

Erroneous thoughts arise with every passing moment; when will this greedy heart ever find rest? It is better to recite the Buddha's name early on, so that you may transcend the sea of suffering from this day forth.
Behold the gait, faltering and frail; head and belly as large as a winnowing basket or a mortar. How can one traverse the distance when strength is exhausted?
How can one ascend the heights when emotion alone is intense? To leave home is a journey of a thousand li; to lean on a staff is to face ten thousand layers of clouds and mountains.
It is better to recite the Buddha’s name early on, so that you may swiftly behold the compassionate countenance upon the precious throne.

Even if your halls are filled with gold and jade, and you are adorned with pearls, emeralds, fine silks, and elegant makeup; even if you constantly dance and sing beneath the flowers, and daily raise your cups before the wine-vases;

though you may contemplate such infinite worldly pursuits, in the end they cannot escape the King of Death. It is better to recite the Buddha’s name early on, so that at the moment of death you will surely proceed to the Western Pure Land.
Decay, old age, sickness, and death are unavoidable; do not boast of your vigorous strength. How long can this rosy countenance last?
Before long, white hair will suddenly fill your mirror. When this finite time has run out, the demon of impermanence will come to collect you.
It is better to recite the Buddha's name early on and awaken to the self-nature of Amitābha.
Though you may possess a thousand forms of happiness, and though you may command ten thousand kinds of skillful means, by what means can this body be made eternally secure?
In vain do you speak of the wondrous elixir of longevity; before long, form and spirit shall part. How could it be permitted to linger for even a moment?
It is better to recite the Buddha's name early on; only the Pure Land is true peace and joy.
Impermanence will inevitably arrive. The sentient beings of the three realms are truly pitiable; it is as if they have entered a mountain of jewels only to return empty-handed.

Amitābha’s entire being is fully revealed, and the Pure Land unfolds in every direction. It would be better to recite the Buddha's name early on, so that upon turning away from this life, one may take a seat upon a lotus throne.
There is only the path of cultivation, which truly arises from one's own mind. Without departing from present mindfulness, one suddenly eliminates the ignorance of kalpas.
Fools still cling to their attachments; how then can turbid defilements be cleared away?
It is better to recite the Buddha’s name early on, so that the fruit of the Bodhi-path may be perfected.
Simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. This mind, in every thought-moment, is the Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no other mind, and outside the mind there is no other Buddha.
Like a single gust of wind blowing open ten-thousand-li white clouds, a radiant red sun emerges.
The jeweled trees and lotus ponds appear before one, beyond the capacity of words or characters to describe.

A Hundred-Verse Poem on Cherishing the Pure Land, Desiring Rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing and Serving King Drum-Sound. Joining the palms, one must face west; bowing the head, one pays homage to that direction.
The gates of contemplation are truly easy to enter; the ritual procedures are indeed immeasurable. The Buddha’s vows are especially deep and vast; the human heart requires long-term cultivation.
Like an infant longing for its nurse, like a traveler afar yearning for home, one receives the new moon with solemnity and sees off the setting sun with earnest devotion.

Clearly, you have received their guidance; do not forget this even in moments of haste. In eating and drinking, take the observance of the fast as your priority; in cultivation, apply yourself with the most excellent diligence.
Completely sever all five pungent roots and forever erect a dam against the ten evil deeds. Do not seek fame or profit; do not trouble yourself to debate right and wrong.
Wearing coarse cloth and skins to ward off illusions, filling my empty bowels with wild herbs and millet; I brush aside the debts of many lifetimes and prop up this sack of nine outflows.
When the spirit is but slightly indolent, joy and anger immediately fall into chaos. A drop of water suddenly fills a vessel; the flow of the Yangtze begins from a single ladle.
Accumulate merit until your practice is complete; take advantage while your physical body is strong. Arrange a thousand-petaled lotus seat within the chamber;

burn a hundred kinds of incense in the burner. Present new robes for the Buddha to wear; prepare exquisite delicacies for him to taste. Do not light torches from leftover oil; instead, boil fragrant water for bathing the image.

The physical frame is as one with earth and wood; the observance of precepts is like ice and frost. Mental conceptions are free from all delusions; sitting cross-legged upon a single couch, in a single kṣaṇa one ascends to the pure realm.
From within the square inch of the heart, a profound light radiates; flesh and bone completely dissolve, and heaven and earth become utterly vast and boundless.
The vast void encompasses both the interior and exterior; the Buddha-field occupies the center. From the lotus, lush and flourishing calyxes emerge;
upon the pond, ripples surge and glisten. Fresh breezes stir and sway them; colorful banners flutter at will. Resplendent is the Golden Hall; tiered and varied are the White Jade Pavilions.

The towers are composed of the four precious gems; the terraces are adorned with the seven treasures. Mirror-like surfaces are spread across the steps and paving; lotus hearts form the inner chambers.
Coral is carved into the railings; agate is fashioned into the beams. The ground is laid out in lapis lazuli; the gardens and groves are spread with brocade and embroidery.
Within, exquisite carpets are spread everywhere; without, silver walls encircle it on all sides. It is covered by a latticed net, and its ground is level without any protruding ridges.
Jade groves stretch out in every direction, and precious trees stand in orderly rows. The fruits are large and as sweet as honey; their sounds are pure and wondrous, like the music of reed pipes.
The tall branches naturally face one another; the luxuriant foliage stands in perfect symmetry. One by one, mynas sing their songs; pairs of phoenixes gather together.

At the Jade Pond there is neither day nor night; the pearl waters naturally harmonize in the *gong* and *shang* scales. The canals are bright at the bottom of the golden sands; the breeze is light beside the jeweled banks.
High and low, the lotuses unfold; deep and shallow, the mandarin ducks sport. Strange forms swallow the flocks of birds; extraordinary blossoms eclipse the multitude of fragrances.

A thousand branches divide into crimson and white; ten thousand clusters intersperse green and yellow. For a moment, inhaling brings refreshment to the body’s faculties; Subtly, it penetrates the sense of smell with coolness.
The *piṅgala* dances before, while the *saṃjīva* soars behind; all day long the oriole modulates its tongue, and the crane draws out its cry toward the clouds.

Having realized emptiness, how could there be a self? Knowing suffering, one understands it is entirely impermanent. The Great Being discourses on the profound principle, and the *śrāvakas* assemble at the Jewel Monastery.
The Sūtras proclaim the twelve divisions; the verses expound hundreds of thousands of chapters. They point directly to the path of Bodhi and together float upon the vessel of Prajñā.

They turn back the seeker of the sword and awaken the frantic one who has lost his head. The nine grades distinguish the coarse from the subtle; the three vehicles alternate between suppression and exaltation.
Refining deeply, the ore is finally exhausted; winnowing thoroughly, how could chaff remain? He manifests as the true Maitreya and consults with Mañjuśrī.
Holy sages gather like dense clouds; celestial music resounds daily. A magnificent and pure youth, he is utterly beyond the maidenhood of the world.
Their speech is skilled in dialogue; their movements are elegant and graceful. The fire-crystal constantly emits its flames, and the mani-jewel further radiates its brilliance.
There is no need to suspend the sun and moon; where could boundaries be set? Their food is celestial delicacies; they do not consume the rice and grain of the world.

A robe of ease hangs upon the shoulders; a bowl held aloft, it naturally provides nourishment. The entire being is exceptionally pure and serene; imbued with radiance, it shines even more brilliantly.

The *kāṣāya* robes envelop auspicious mists; necklaces adorn the celestial garments. One travels everywhere through lands as numerous as motes of dust, circling throughout the fields of Perfect Enlightenment.
With a compassionate countenance, I pay my respects; bearing offerings, I approach. Listening attentively to the teachings of the Muni, I find that what was gained has vanished.
Upon returning in the mere blink of an eye, I laugh at the frantic toil of worldly pursuits. Whenever I receive the joy of walking meditation, who would say it hinders sitting or lying down?

Throughout the heavens, strife and contention are eliminated; across the earth, calamities and misfortunes are stilled. Its majestic spirit pervades the south and north; its virtuous transformation is manifest in the east and west.

Though it has passed through several kalpas of conflagration and the four seas have been turned to fields of plow and loom, this realm remains without loss or damage, and these people merely enjoy the flourishing of longevity.
The census of households and individuals is no longer taken; the registration of ages and ranks is abandoned. My ears hear nothing but the Dharma; for sustenance, I need no grain.

Forever cherishing this grace, it has entered my very marrow; at least I am spared from the poison infecting my sores. If I were to describe the sufferings of this Sahā world, how could I restrain my tears from flowing?
Who among the inner sects can understand this? Their false views are truly pitiable. Bound by greed and anger, they willingly cast themselves into the pits of profit and desire.

Rulers and ministers are as fierce as tigers and leopards; fathers and sons are more savage than jackals and wolves. They heap up money until it fills their houses, yet still long for their granaries to overflow with rice.

In the mountains one encounters pheasants and rabbits; in the wilds, one herds oxen and sheep. Taking life brings retribution in future lives; harboring resentment leads to repayment across generations.
In times of peace one meets bandits; in times of chaos one encounters swords and spears. A fondness for drink leads to an addiction for wine; deluded passions lead to attachment for prostitutes.
The mind-monkey has cast off its tether; the will-horse has been let loose from its halter. Noble ambitions are crushed mid-way; heroic souls hasten to the Northern Mounds.

Weapons and shields have eclipsed rites and music; the yielding courtesy of the era of Yao and Tang has vanished. The constant warfare brings grief to the borderlands; the smoke of burning reaches the highest heavens.
Villages were decimated by slaughter, and bleached bones filled the city moats; ghosts wailed as the heavens grew dark and rain fell, while the people mourned for the nation’s premature deaths.
In years of famine, many perished of hunger; coffins were so precious that few could be buried. Tiles and rubble piled up at the monasteries, and thorny brambles sprouted from the Confucian schools.

Militia levies and taxes are imposed together; the harvests of millet and sorghum have diminished from their former abundance. The conditions for reciting the Buddha’s name remain obstructed, and my pursuit of the scriptures has likewise fallen into neglect.
May your pure spirit soar like a dragon and your lofty stride gallop like a crane. Look back upon your companions as a flock of geese; do not be like a solitary leaping deer.
The holy embryo has been achieved by me; you, my dharma companions, look toward one another. On this jewel ground we share a refined elegance; upon the golden terrace we soar together.

With uplifted diligence, the mountains rise steeply; with accumulated virtue, the ocean flows vast. Through kalpas of eternity, merit becomes ever more manifest; yet even the slightest transgression must be averted.

With three resolves, I look forward to reaching the distant goal; with ten recitations, I prepare my journey for afar. If I am determined to transcend the realm of Māra, from this day forth I shall serve the Buddha-King.

*Fishermen’s Delight*: Sixteen Poems on the Sufferings of the Sahā World.
It is said that the immeasurable sufferings of the Sahā world can cause even the wise to increase their sorrow and fear. A lifespan of a hundred years is like the morning dew;
you must awaken to this truth—that within the cycle of birth and death, there is neither poverty nor wealth. Green hair and rosy cheeks cannot be preserved. O hero...
Where has the hero gone? Turning my head, I see the road beneath Mount Beimang. At twilight, the setting sun; thousands upon thousands of cold crows pass by.
Hearing speak of the immeasurable sufferings of the Sahā world, I suddenly raise my brows before the wind. Greed and desire are like wolves, their rage fierce.
The tiger! The lord of Māra’s army! A man and woman, deluded, draw their bows and set their arrows. The sun and moon pass back and forth through cold and heat;

heaven and earth open and close through clear skies and rain. White bones lie vast and desolate, dissolving into dust. Alas for past and present! Who among men has trodden upon the path of non-arising?
I have heard that the Sahā world is filled with immeasurable suffering; though one calculates it a thousand times over, the mind is weary and distressed.

Earth, water, fire, and wind contend for mastery—what is truly solid? In the end, they all dissolve into fine dust. A single pearl of the mind, free from defilement, is constantly revealed before sound and after form.
Smash open the skull and there is nowhere to find it; this can only be realized through awakening—the golden mouth of the Tathāgata.
Father, you entrusted me to you.
I have heard that the Sahā world is filled with immeasurable suffering; the King of Death presides over all as the lord of saṃsāra, and the six thieves brandish their blades as his companions.
We dwell together; how could we ever part for even a single moment? The Deity of Merit and the Woman of Darkness—these two...
Human beings are most difficult to assemble; a wise host would take none of them. Follow my words: from this day forth, do not again set foot upon my threshold.
Listen to the immeasurable sufferings of this Sahā world: within the casket of the four great elements, a cluster of venomous serpents gathers. The heavy desire to sink, the light desires to float.

They vie with one another in mutual contempt; how much more so when the entire household is empty and without a master? One should early on perceive that the beams and pillars are already out of alignment;

buffeted by wind and rained upon, they can no longer support the structure. In the end, it will collapse due to external forces—this is enough to make one fearful. It would be better to seek a place where one may find security.
I have heard that the Saha world is filled with immeasurable suffering, yet all people are stained by desire and greed for the feasts before them.

With jade-carved pipes and flutes, and drums adorned with gold, they indulge in long songs and dances—the musicians of the Li-yuan and the courtesans of Handan. In winter they wear purple sable furs, in spring white ramie;

they spend their days in cool pavilions and warm chambers to escape the cold and heat. Yet one day, their spirits shall return to the underworld; it will be difficult to reclaim them, leaving nothing but empty tears to fall.

It falls as thick as rain. Listen and hear of the immeasurable sufferings of this Sahā world; for your sake, I shall enumerate them one by one with clarity. Customs are licentious and depraved, and men are overbearing; there are many prisons.
At the end of life, one cannot avoid sinking into the dark underworld. One must examine one’s evil reputation and look upon the registers of transgressions. Because...
This provokes the wrath of Yama; you shall be burned and boiled in glowing coals and cauldrons of boiling water. How could he tolerate you? You yourself created these karmas;
no one else bestowed them upon you.
Listen to the immeasurable sufferings of this Sahā world: you boast of your own abundance while feeling shame before the poor and destitute—those who have neither food, nor clothing, nor shelter.
The eaves hang over the empty cauldron; lifting my head, I see again the red disk at noon. There is only the celery by the stream that can be boiled.

At twilight, I sit listening to the moaning of my hungry bowels. Abundant grain, abundant gold, many sons and daughters—though we gather together in shared joy, look upon it and see it is all but a decree from a previous life.

I have heard that the Saha world is filled with immeasurable suffering; in every household, one cannot avoid becoming a merchant. Moving in and out across mountains and rivers, there are many perils and obstacles—it is not my native land.
With bared fangs and gnashing teeth, one encounters man-tigers who devour flesh. The soul and spirit wish to return home, yet they are lost as to where to go.

Smoke stretches across the northern ridges, clouds hang over the southern hamlets; looking out, the vast expanse reaches to the heavens, all but a wasteland. Who knows where it lies? In the desolate village, the wind whistles through the reeds.
The wind blows and the rain falls;
I have heard that the Saha world is filled with immeasurable suffering. In times of chaos, men join the military; when the enemy arrives, there is no distinction between man and woman.
Their waists and backs are broken—just as the cicada’s song ends with the fall of the mantis’s blade. Even if one possesses talent enough to rise above the ranks of common soldiers, how many...

A man returns to his native land in brocade robes; with a swallow’s jaw and a tiger’s head, he is enfeoffed with ten thousand households. Alas, how mistaken! What can be done? Li Guang met with such strange fortune.
Listen to the immeasurable sufferings of this Sahā world. Martial forces disperse only to gather again. Yesterday they were the Qi, today...
Chu: A captive slave once more. Heaven and Earth ultimately submit to divine prowess. Zhao Kuo’s talent was shallow, yet he vainly presumed upon his own worth;
the powerful Qin used spies to deceive his lord. Four hundred thousand troops entered the earth alive. Alas for antiquity! To this day, ghosts wail beneath Changping.
I have heard that the Sahā world is filled with immeasurable suffering. Its inhabitants dwell in ships scattered like stars across the ocean’s edge.

Looking east toward Fusang, the morning sun emerges; yet one is lost among the islands and shoals. Cannon-clouds arise and the azure sky pours down rain. Lowering the cloud-sails and ceasing the rowing, we meet a headwind as fierce as the dancing of a leviathan.
The surging sound of the tide roars like ten thousand drums, churning the liver and entrails with grief at the onset of such calamity.
Who can rely upon?
Listen to the immeasurable sufferings of this Sahā world: the duties of tea and salt, mines and forges, and granaries and storehouses; the beatings endured when quotas are damaged or missed;
paying fines to the government, exhausting one’s household and selling property to pay off debts for one’s children—how shall one’s mouth and body be sustained by even a grain or a thread? Adrift...
The weeds have no place for me to rest; oppressive rule is more cruel than snakes or tigers. I struggle to find a way to appeal my case. I urge you not to provoke the wrath of lightning and thunder.
Listen to the immeasurable sufferings of this Sahā world; now the karmic debts come forward to be repaid, as thieves plunder wealth and the body is struck.
Captives encounter wolves and tigers; they invoke life or curse death, practicing sorcery and witchcraft. Slaves toil in hardship under cruel masters;

afflicted with black sores, white leprosy, deafness, and blindness, they dwell together in ugliness, folly, and ignorance. Who will pity you? Awaken your resolve and take refuge in the Compassionate Father.

I have heard that in this Sahā world there is immeasurable suffering: people are unjustly beset by lawsuits and detained in government offices. Great clubs strike their bodies before wounds have healed;
heavy lashes inflict such agony that blood drenches the ground and swarms of green flies gather. Legal petitions are filed in profusion, yet all are but false words;
no one dares to beat upon the Drum of Petitions. The celestial immortals govern the lands below; they are capable of soaring lightly—when will they descend once more?

In this place of dark confinement, I hear of the immeasurable sufferings of the Sahā world: the three farming seasons have lost all hope amidst the rains of the plum-ripening season; men labor to pump water for the seedlings, yet the sprouts do not rise.
The scorching heat is unbearable; fanned by the wind, the fields become a mass of withered weeds. After a long drought, digging for springs reveals nothing but dry earth; even the ocean—

The tide enters the reed-filled marshes once more; north, south, east, and west are all salt flats. The grain of millet and sorghum has withered, yet the government still demands taxes from the people’s corpses.
[From] "Sixteen Poems on the Joy of Fishermen" in the Western Regions, set to the tune of *Yújiā'ào*.
I have heard that in the West lies immeasurable bliss, where the Three Sages and Ten Holy Ones alike take refuge. I prostrate to Amitābha, the Perfectly Awakened One; may I long study under him.
Like rivers flowing to the sea or dust accumulating into a mountain, the Buddha-nature resides within one’s own person like a jade rough.

It must rely upon a skilled artisan for diligent carving and polishing. Both ordinary beings and sages are produced by the mind; it is difficult to depict or describe. Within the flower-adorned hall and precious throne...
Pearl necklaces;
hear it said that in the West there is immeasurable bliss. Adorned with the seven treasures as pavilions, with agate, coral, and amber, their radiance is such that one could pluck it by hand.
The paths are demarcated by golden cords—how magnificent and brilliant! Precious trees and numinous birds are all miraculously transformed, filling [the realm].
Ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and cranes; parrots, kalaviṅkas, and peacocks—vying with one another in their cries and leaps. Behold further the blossoming of each golden lotus.
Listen and hear of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land: its ground of lapis lazuli, its walls of golden cities, and its piles of radiant pearls and emeralds.

Falling, the lotus sheds its calyx; how many are blue, crimson, yellow, and white! The Great Beings and Śrāvakas follow wherever they go; celestial flowers fall in profusion, staining their robes and satchels.
Each manifests hundreds, thousands, and ten billions of transformation bodies; by the power of their spiritual penetrations, in an instant they travel throughout lands as numerous as motes of dust.
I have heard that in the West there is immeasurable bliss; the Dharma King governs and transforms, eliminating all evils. Heaven and humanity are fundamentally not separated;
they intermingle, where the holy and the ordinary are equal, all equally perfecting awakened awareness. One constantly sees precious flowers falling through the void;
morning and evening one hears the sounds of music. Clothing and food appear naturally without being contrived; fragrant terraces and pavilions pervade the entire realm.

Ever vast and expansive, one hears of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land. Those of ordinary, shallow wisdom find it difficult to fathom; yet whatever vows or requests one makes, there is nothing not obtained.
Why labor to seek jeweled robes, exquisite feasts, or golden mansions? The ground is as level as the palm of a hand and exceedingly broad—eight [yojanas deep].
The water of merit is not something to be dredged or excavated; within the heart of the white lotus flower, one may find refuge. The pact of three lifetimes—how could it now be lightly cast aside?
Listen to the account of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land: the sovereign himself is the Tathāgata. He does not establish the three luminaries nor the five [elements].
Mountains and valleys are cleared away; crimson clouds and purple mists forever enshroud it. His forty-eight marks and features flash with golden brilliance;

from his alms bowl, exquisite flavors are dispensed according to need. To vow rebirth there is the true supreme strategy. How lamentable are those who, on the path of birth and death, are like drifting weeds.
It is said that in the West there is immeasurable bliss, where the sounds of wind, forests, waters, and birds blend together.
The verses of the Dharma occasionally serve as mutual reminders, thinning out greed and anger, and enabling those in training to become those beyond training.

Unstained by the six sense objects and free from the five turbidities, one sheds the shell of ignorance like a cicada emerging from its husk. Who would willingly accept the bonds of nirvana or birth-and-death? To grasp at them in vain is but empty speculation—mere words and letters.

All are but dregs and refuse. Listen and hear of the immeasurable bliss of the West; once you have heard the wondrous Way, you forget all cognition and perception. Not a single trace of the "original word" remains within the breast.
This is the true bearing: its radiance pervades the world as the crimson sun blazes forth. When the wings of the great Peng are spread wide, the vast blue sea appears narrow. Who—?
One can further ask the sparrow by the hedge: "How many are the ordinary hairs and the holy horns? When all are cast aside, every particle of dust and every world-system returns to non-attachment.
Listen to the talk of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land; long life does not depend on the elixirs of immortals. When the fetus is formed, the eyes open and the flowers are in full bloom.
Unfettered. The mind is manifest and clear; forever a free and easy traveler. Coming to deliver sentient beings from the burning house, at the end of life one escapes the retribution of King Yama.
Like a calf in an open field white as snow, without whip or tether, it leaps and bounds across the golden ground.
I have heard that in the West there is immeasurable bliss; in this Sahā world, I now repent my former errors. The Buddha’s name calls out to me, and I respond to it myself. Reflect upon this:
if the Pure Land is but one's own mind, who says it is separated? The single thread has always been five hundred and two. Infants vainly brandish empty fists to frighten others.
If you hesitate even for a moment, you will receive a blow. All you practitioners of Chan: ordinary sentiments and saintly understandings—[are they not all like this?]
