Once melted away, I have heard tell of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land. Above, below, and in the four directions, the heavens hang like a canopy; it is not like the wretched terrain of this Sahā world.
Boundless and without edges, it is composed entirely of a single expanse of lapis lazuli. It can sweep away the waves of the river of craving and dry them up completely.

The branches and twigs of the tree of suffering are overturned; how could the flames of wisdom allow even a mosquito or gnat to alight? His spirit soars beyond compare, ascending directly to the vast pavilion of Vairocana.
He hears and speaks of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land, and first instructs his shadow and form to deliberate together, gathering his spirit and emotions back into tranquility.

Dwelling in stillness, I grind and polish once more; the hexagonal prism becomes round, yet is further carved back into its original simplicity. Worldly affairs are left to their own course, indifferent and unheeded.
Who can claim both heavenly rank and human honor? Before a single thought arises, who is good and who is evil? Suddenly I awaken: the purple-scaled fish has snapped the golden line.
I have heard that in the West there is immeasurable bliss, yet never before have I heard or seen it; I must now describe it in detail.

Wondrous jewels and rare treasures intermingle their radiance as they dwell together. The Tathāgatas, Great Beings (Mahāsattvas), and Pratyekabuddhas—all these supreme and virtuous ones—have granted their consent.

They discourse on emptiness and explain the nature of suffering, responding to one another like a solitary eagle among a hundred hawks. Soaring through the vast expanse, from this point forward, [all afflictions] shall be forever severed.

Ordinary beings may be wicked, yet they hear of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land. That Land of Bliss is the expansion of my own mind; there, those with impaired faculties and women find no place.
Who is strong or weak? Each person has a single golden lotus calyx. The rows of trees are sevenfold, draped in networks of pearls and jewels.

The wind blowing crosswise chimes the golden bells; celestial music intermingles with them. One must be sincere and earnest, turning the hearing back toward one’s own nature to become equal to those who have awakened first.

Listen and speak of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land; in this Sahā world, one naturally laments that the body drifts like a wanderer. Fix your thoughts and maintain your mind through the darkness.
At dawn, I return to the Imperial Enlightenment; may you not forget our pact as we welcome one another at the Golden Terrace. Our humble dwellings are like those of swallows and sparrows;

the bridge we build stretches afar, following the magpies. Before long, impermanence will come to press upon us; it cannot be pushed away. Westward I travel, swiftly unfolding my wings that reach the heavens.
I have heard it said that in the West lies infinite bliss, where the Holy Lord Amitābha bestows his grace and favor. He washes my Zen mind until it is pure and white;
its traces are difficult to find, as moonlight reflects upon a cool, emerald pool. Old debts and new grievances are all resolved; my entire being transforms into a golden hue.
In a single thought-moment, myriad virtues are perfected—how truly extraordinary! The Buddhas of the ten directions confer their seal of approval.
The Office of the Tathāgata:
A Single Poem with Preface and Postscript on the Subject of the Western Chamber Pure Land.
Day after day, he speaks of the sun at its zenith and the setting sun; The golden drumhead strikes, its resonance deep and rolling (rhyming with *fáng*).
Jue’eng resolves doubts, rejoicing in the repeated explanations; Zelao proclaims the school, fortunate that it is further proclaimed.
A thousand flowers bloom within the Buddha-land of the Dharma-realm; He performs a single song on non-arising, a performance of pearls and jade.
As he was about to depart, he shouted, "I shall kill this fragmented guest! His majestic reputation has suppressed the wildness of the world since antiquity.
Written on the seventh month of the Wushen year by the humble disciple Cheng Shi of Gu Shixi, who bows his head;
he is fifty-one years of age.
The Ten Essentials of the Pure Land,
Volume Eight [Financed by the disciple Cheng Situn, with contributions from] Hu Jingrui,
Wu Jingdi, Wang Jingyu, Xu Zhongxin, Cheng Jingchu, Cheng Chuanchao, Wu Lingqi, and Bi Zhen.
The Venerable Hong Jin-mu and Dai Shixiang each contributed one *liang* [of gold], together carving these "Verses on the Pure Land" for the West Chamber.

We humbly pray that the wondrous realm of the Pure Land may manifest before the minds of each person and all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm at every thought, and that the Dharma-sounds of the Pure Land may fill the ears at all times.
May merit and wisdom increase and flourish in this life, and may we proceed to the Pure Land in the future.
*Shengdeji* (Record of Attaining Prediction). [Also: Jiang Dengguang 2 coins, Yun Yiqian 3 fen; Zhu Chang].
In the ninth volume of *The Ten Essentials of the Pure Land*, selected by the Great Master Ouyi of Lingfeng, it is stated:
The Elder of Lingfeng said, "The ancients' enumeration of the Seven Patriarchs of the Lotus School is far too narrow. For instance..."
The founder of the Tiantai school sat never turning his back to the west and always joined his palms when lying down;
his elucidation of the Pure Land was like a grand military array with its banners held straight—none dared oppose it.

Furthermore, the great-grandson of Fayan recited the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred thousand times day and night, adorning the Land of Peaceful Nurturing with myriad virtues; his elucidation of the Pure Land was likewise peerless.
Is it not the case that all these were the patriarchs of the Lotus School?
For instance, the Master Wujin of Tiantai Youxi took the vows and practices of Ciyun as his daily recitation and lectured on the *Treatise on Birth and Non-birth* he himself had composed.
Whenever he ascended the seat to preach, celestial music would descend from the void; at the time of his death, he drew characters in the air.
When he wrote the title for the *Miaojing*, it suddenly transformed into a lotus; how could one who is the legitimate descendant of the Lotus School feel any shame?

Within the *Jingyao*, I have collected two works by Youxi and now compiled them into a single essential volume. This marks the public emergence of a pioneering tradition among the masters of recent times.
*The Treatise on Birth in the Pure Land as Non-Birth*,
composed by the Tiantai Mountain śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi, prostrating in homage.
I bow my head to the Perfect Wisdom of the Able One (Śākyamuni) and to the Great Teacher, the Awakened Amitāyus, who has expounded the Mahāyāna of the Peaceful Nurturing Land.
The Sūtras of definitive meaning, the most definitive, reaching the Perfect and Sudden; Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the pure great ocean;
Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and Vasubandhu; the patriarchs of the Lotus Society on Mount Lu in this land; Zhiyi of Tiantai and Faxiang;
and all Dharma masters who have propagated the teachings from antiquity to the present—I now take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem, entreating their hidden protection.

Further exerting his supernormal consciousness, he respectfully gathered the secret purports of the sūtras and śāstras to elucidate birth in the Pure Land as non-birth, so that all future beings might universally awaken to this gate, sever doubt, give rise to faith, and advance toward the stage of non-retrogression. In preparing to compose this treatise, he established ten gates:

1. The Gate of the True Dharma-Dhātu; 2. The Gate of the Dependent Origination of Body and Land; 3. The Gate of the Mutual Identity of Mind and Land; 4. The Gate of Sentient Beings and Buddhas... [and so forth].

1. The Gate of Non-duality; 2. The Gate of Mindfulness of the Five Dharma Realms; 3. The Gate of the Mutual Devouring of Objects and Contemplation; 4. The Gate of the Spontaneity of the Three Contemplations;
5. The Gate of the Naturalness of Response and Resonance; 6. The Gate of the Eternal Oneness of Self and Other; 7. The Gate of the Mutual Presence of Present and Future.

Within the single gate of the true Dharma-realm—the one true Dharma-nature—the ten Dharma-realms are fully present. Because the fundamental and the derivative are interpenetrating and harmonious, there is no distinction between the sentient beings of birth-and-death and the Buddhas.
The Treatise says: The One True Dharma-realm is precisely the fundamental mind-nature of sentient beings. This mind-nature possesses immeasurable virtues and receives immeasurable names.
How does it possess immeasurable virtues? It is said to consist of the essence of nature (*xingti*), the magnitude of nature (*xingliang*), and the endowment of nature (*xingju*).

Regarding the essence of nature: this mind-nature transcends the four propositions and is beyond the hundred negations; its essential nature is firm, stable, pure, and unstained, neither arising nor ceasing.

It is eternally abiding and indestructible. Regarding its essential nature and magnitude: this mind-nature extends vertically through the three periods of time and pervades horizontally throughout the ten directions.
While worlds have limits and space is limitless, space has limits while the nature of the mind is limitless. The present has limits while the past and future are limitless;
the past and future have limits while the nature of the mind is limitless. It is inexhaustibly inexhaustible and immeasurably immeasurable; its nature is fully endowed with all.

This nature of mind possesses the ten dharma-realms: namely, the Buddha-dharma realm, the Bodhisattva-dharma realm, the Pratyekabuddha-dharma realm, the Śrāvaka-dharma realm, the Deva-dharma realm, the Asura-dharma realm, the Human-dharma realm, the Animal-dharma realm, the Preta-dharma realm, and the Hell-dharma realm.
These are merely provisional names. Furthermore, there is the primary retribution, namely, the five aggregates of a Buddha, and so forth.
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the hells are real dharmas. Furthermore, there are the dependent retributions, namely the Buddha-lands up to the lands of the hells.

These are divided into three parts for the sake of easy understanding; speaking from the perspective of attaining the meaning, this refers to the nature’s inherent completeness as the substance and magnitude of the nature.

The substance of the nature is free from faults and transcends all that is non-existent; it is precisely the nature’s inherent completeness of the ten realms that is free from faults and transcends all that is non-existent. The substance of the nature is firm.
It is concentrated, pure, and unstained; it is neither born nor extinguished, eternally abiding and indestructible. The nature-inherent ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are likewise so.

The vertical depth and horizontal pervasiveness of this essential measure (*dharmatā-pramāṇa*) are inexhaustible, inexhaustible, immeasurable, and immeasurable. The ten realms inherent in the nature are likewise so.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the primary retribution, being identical in essence to the body of the nature, are pure and all-pervasive; the dependent retribution of the lands (*kṣetra*) is likewise so. This—

The three dharmas are also termed the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*). The nature-essence (*svabhāva-tattva*) is the middle truth; the nature-capacity (*svabhāva-mātra*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

and the nature-endowment (*svabhāva-pariniṣpanna*) is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous primordial mind, is neither mind nor emptiness, and is not earth, water, fire, or wind."
It is not the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; it is not form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomena; it is not the eye-element, and so on, up to the consciousness-element;
it is not ignorance, and so on, up to old age and death; it is not the cessation of ignorance, and so on, up to the cessation of old age and death;
it is not suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; it is not knowledge, nor attainment; it is not generosity, and so on, up to wisdom. It is not...
*Tadāka*. It is not an Arhat; it is not a Samyak-saṃbuddha; it is not permanence, bliss, self, or purity.

This is the measure of its nature, which is without marks; this is the True Dharma. The Tathāgatagarbha is the primordial clarity of the mind’s subtlety: it is the mind itself and it is emptiness. It is earth, water, fire, and wind;
it is the six classes of ordinary beings; it is the two vehicles; and it extends even to the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of the Tathāgata. This...
That the ten realms are inherently complete within the nature is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

That the wondrously luminous mind-source of the Tathāgatagarbha is free from both "is" and "is not," yet is both "is" and "is not," and that this constitutes the comprehensive integration of the essential body of nature, is the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). Furthermore, it is said:
"The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is form as true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form. Pure and naturally so, it pervades the Dharma-realm—earth, water, fire, wind, and space."
Seeing and consciousness are no different from this. Earth, water, fire, wind, space, seeing, and consciousness are the inherent nature (*xingju*).

That they are "pure and originally so" (*qingjing benran*) is the essence of the nature (*xingti*). That they "pervade the dharma-realm" (*zoubian fajie*) is the magnitude of the nature (*xingliang*).

Furthermore, earth, water, fire, wind, space, being pure and originally so and pervading the dharma-realm, refers to the essence and magnitude of the nature as the environment and its receptacle world (*yibao guotu*). Seeing and consciousness are... [pure and originally so].
Pure and fundamentally luminous, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; this is the essential nature and the extent of the five aggregates (*skandhas*) as the primary retribution.

Why is this mind-nature given so many names? This mind-nature may be called the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, or the true suchness (*tathatā*) of Buddha-nature, or the *amala-vijñāna*, or the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), or Bodhi and Nirvāṇa. Such is its essential nature and its extent.
It is called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha. That is to say, the ten realms, the five aggregates, and the lands that are inherently complete within the nature are called the empty Tathāgatagarbha.

Even the essential body and the essential measure of the nature are called Bodhi and Nirvāṇa; that is to say, the ten realms, the five aggregates, and the lands that are inherently complete within the nature are called Bodhi and Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that within the single true Dharma-nature, the ten dharma-realms are fully present. This is the fundamental fusion of the dependent and the primary.

[The Master] said: "It penetrates [all]. There is no difference between the state of birth and that of Buddhahood. Question: "Is the One True Dharma-realm (ekadharmadhātu) the initial mind or the final mind?

If it is the initial mind, there should be no seven names [of the realms]. If it is the final mind, there should be no nine realms. In either case, the initial and final fall into error, and your thesis cannot be established.

Answer: "This precisely reveals the initial mind; therefore, it is the initial mind that is [the Dharma-realm]. Only because the initial mind is so, does the final mind become so. It is like a fruit..."

The environment and its inhabitants are interpenetrated, and matter and mind are non-dual. Manifesting forms throughout the nine realms to skillfully deliver sentient beings is entirely due to realizing this causal mind that is inherently possessed.
Therefore, it is said that the ground of fruition of all Buddhas is characterized by such interpenetration.

By merely realizing the fundamental nature of the principle within sentient beings, one attains the ability to manifest in accordance with that nature without deliberation. Otherwise, how would this differ from the intentional mental activity of the Śrāvakas or the heterodox paths?
Therefore, the Great Master Fazhi said: "The principle of the 'Six Identities' does not apply exclusively to the Buddha.

For all beings—whether provisional or real, belonging to the Three Vehicles or among humans and devas, and even down to dung beetles and those in hell, including their physical forms and minds—one must distinguish their beginning and end through the Six Identities.
This refers to the ten realms, from the 'principle dung beetle' up to the 'ultimate dung beetle,' because all are the nature of reality (dharmatā); there is nothing that is not so."
The Dharma-realm is one and unchangeable; therefore, names are set aside. It does not merely manifest the Buddha, but likewise reveals the nine [stages] as well.

Upon the attainment of the fruit, all ten are brought to ultimate perfection. Furthermore, it is by means of the final mind that the initial mind is truly revealed, for through the final mind on the ground of fruition, one fully realizes the fundamental nature of the principle inherent in the capacities of all sentient beings.
Thus, the seven types of designations on the ground of fruition are entirely the beautiful qualities of the inherent virtues of the nature of sentient beings.
It is so named; however, because sentient beings are deluded, this inherent nature is not manifest. If one examines its intrinsic qualities directly, how could one say they do not exist?
Since it is wholesome both in the beginning and at the end, the established thesis is proven.

In the gate of the dependent origination of the two bodies and lands within the nature of the one true dharma-realm, the unchanging essence is able to follow conditions; thus, the three bodies and four lands all arise through the transformations of the mind.

The Commentary states: The nature of the single true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is precisely what was explained in the preceding text as the essence, the magnitude, and the inherent endowment of that nature.

When the teachings speak of True Suchness (*tathatā*) being "unchanging while following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging," it is precisely because the essence and magnitude of its nature are identical to its inherent endowment.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* translated during the Jin dynasty says: "It can follow defiled and pure conditions and fully create the ten dharma-realms. This refers to the True...
Just as the nine dharma-realms are inherently contained within the nature, so too can the nine dharma-realms of the phenomenal world be produced through defiled conditions;
and just as the Buddha-dharma realm is inherently contained within the nature of *tathatā*, so too can the Buddha-dharma realm of the phenomenal world be produced through pure conditions.

If these were not inherently present in the nature, how could they be said to be "capable" of being produced? It is precisely because they are inherently established by principle (*li-jù*) that they subsequently possess phenomenal function (*shi-yòng*). This is what is meant. Thus, one knows that regarding phenomena...
The ten dharma realms within the middle [of the three realms], the three bodies, and the four lands are all produced through the transformation of True Suchness (tathatā) according to conditions.

Since it is said that "True Suchness is unchanging yet follows conditions, and follows conditions yet remains unchanging," then the defiled and pure bodies and lands within the realm of phenomena are, in their very essence, True Suchness itself;

there is not even a hair’s breadth that can be added to or subtracted from them. In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, "seeing" (the seeing-division of the eighth consciousness) and "that which is seen" (the object-division of the eighth consciousness)—both the seeing and the seen divisions being dependently originated—[are shown to be such].

The nature [of things] and the characteristics conceived by the mind—these arise from the dependent nature through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), yet they are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of bodhi.

If this is so, then the Sahā world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the sentient beings of this world and those to be born in the nine grades, Amitābha who has already attained fulfillment, and the fruition that is my own mind—all are entirely due to the nature of the mind.

That which is transformed and created: when the mind is complete and creates, how could there be a distinction between subject and object? The mind is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself the mind;
the mind is itself the land, and the land is itself the mind; the mind is itself the fruit, and the fruit is itself the mind.

Both the causal conditions that create and the phenomena that are created are, in their very place, entirely the nature of the mind. Therefore, those who clarify this school and seek rebirth in the Land of Bliss are...
Birth and non-birth are the ultimate Dao where both are merged in obscurity.

The gate of the mutual identity of the three minds and the land is the Western Land of Peace and Bliss. Though it lies a hundred trillion *yojanas* from here, it is no different from my own infinitesimal mind; from the very beginning, there is no distinction between self and other.
The Treatise says: The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that from here, to the west, beyond a hundred trillion buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
A single buddha-land consists of ten billion suns, moons, Mount Sumerus, great oceans, and Iron Ring Mountains;
if even one such land is already vast, how much more so are ten million buddha-lands, and how much more so are a hundred trillion? Thus, Sukhāvatī is distant from here.

It is extremely distant. That an ordinary person of the mundane stage (*pṛthagjana*) attains rebirth by merely snapping their fingers through *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is because they are born into the Buddha-land inherent within their own mind.
Because the momentary mind of an ordinary person’s *nien-fo* is so subtle and inferior, it is termed "a mere flicker" (*ji-er*).
Although the lands of ten million billion worlds reside within the "mere flicker" of the ordinary person's mind, this mind itself is the land, and the land itself is the mind.
Therefore it is said that from the beginning there has been no distinction between self and other. Question: The mind, being but a minute fragment, dwells within the square inch of the chest;

how can it encompass such distant Buddha-lands? Answer: As for this minute fragment of the mind, those who are ignorant call it "internal. To the person of great realization, however, the perspective is vast: in truth, neither delusion nor reality has a fixed location.
This deluded mind arises entirely from the nature; yet the nature has no location, and the mind likewise has no location. The nature is like the great ocean, and the mind is like a floating bubble.

The entire ocean becomes the bubble, and the bubble returns to encompass the ocean. Thus, while True Suchness remains unchanging as it follows conditions, that very following of conditions is itself the state of non-change.
Since it follows conditions without changing, how could one distinguish between the true and the deluded by means of size?
The Gate of the Non-duality of the Four Modes of Birth:
Amitābha and the Ordinary Person. Although there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, the Buddha-mind and the sentient-being mind are ultimately no different.

The Treatise says: Amitābha Buddha is one who has attained fruition; he has perfected the merits of the three bodies, the four wisdoms, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and so forth.
Ordinary beings are those who rely on causes; they possess immeasurable afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
One creates immeasurable karma, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and shall undergo immeasurable births and deaths, likewise as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The distinction between delusion and awakening is like that between clouds and mud; yet, to say they are ultimately non-dual means that, according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are two though not-two, while according to their nature (*dharmatā*), they are not-two though two.
This is because the Buddhas awaken to the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings, whereas sentient beings are deluded.
Sentient beings are within the minds of all Buddhas. Those who awaken realize that sentient beings inherently possess the essence, the magnitude, and the endowment of nature;

those who are deluded are confused regarding the essence, the magnitude, and the endowment of nature realized by all Buddhas. How could the wondrous nature of the mind ever be subject to such delusion?
That "deluded yet not deluded" has its basis in this very truth. Therefore, the inherent essence of nature of sentient beings is precisely that of all Buddhas.
The Dharma-body realized is, in its essential nature and magnitude, the Reward-body; in its inherent perfection, it is the Response-body.
This can be understood through the convergence of the four wisdoms, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and other such merits.

An ancient master said: "Within the minds of all Buddhas, sentient beings are in every dust-mote of Sukhāvatī; within the minds of sentient beings, all Buddhas realize the Truth in every thought-moment. Thus, Amitābha is...
"My mind—my mind is Amitābha. Before a single thought is raised, it is already perfected; as soon as a thought is raised, it is immediately fulfilled.
It is because of this principle that the path of resonance and response is established; therefore, for those who recite the Buddha's name, their merit is never in vain.
The five dharma-realms serve as the gateway of mindfulness;
the dharma-realm is the perfectly interfused essence. It constitutes my single thought-moment of mind. Therefore, the mind of my mindfulness of the Buddha is entirely the dharma-realm.

The Treatise says: The practitioner recites the Buddha’s name and performs the contemplative practice of visualizing the Buddha, along with other contemplations regarding the primary and attendant figures, the environment and the inhabitants.

They cultivate the three types of pure karma with a single mind, undisturbed. Even if they recite the name with a distracted mind, it can overcome the vast and turbulent afflictions of view and thought, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All such minds possessing thought arise from the True Suchness (tathatā) remaining immutable while conforming to conditions; they are the entire body of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Therefore, the Great Master Fazhi said: "The inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm constitutes my single thought-moment.

Furthermore, it manifests its entire substance as sentient beings, as Buddhas, as the support, and as the principal. If this is so, even other thoughts are [the Dharma-realm]; how much more so, then, is mindfulness?
This is the Buddha-mind. Therefore, at the time of mindfulness of the Buddha, this very mind is the perfectly interfused and pure precious awakening.
When one uses this wondrous mind to be mindful of that Amitābha, which of his three bodies would not be contemplated? What among his four lands would not be born into?
It depends only on the depth of one’s practice and the level of one’s rank. Question: Are all other minds the Dharma-realm?

"Why must one practice mindfulness of the Buddha? Answer: "Other states of mind are contrary [to reality], whereas mindfulness of the Buddha is concordant. By using what is concordant to overturn what is contrary, one must practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
it is not that there is any difference within the Dharma-realm."
In the sixteen gates of the mutual swallowing of aspects within the six objects, both the phenomenal and the principial modes of contemplation swallow one another, like the Indra’s net.
The Treatise says: "Object and contemplation swallowing one another" refers to the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (shishi wuai).
The reason phenomena and phenomena are without obstruction is that the inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) constitutes my single thought-moment;

furthermore, it constitutes the entirety [of reality] as sentient beings, as Buddhas, as the support, and as the primary object. Since all things are constituted by the entire essence, what single phenomenon is not identical to the Dharma-realm?
Therefore it is said: "A single mote of dust is not small; the ocean of lands is not large. The many are the Dharma-realm; the few are also the Dharma-realm.
Thus, the sixteen realms of the Western Paradise, as well as my own practice of the two contemplations—of phenomena and principle—are each and every one the entire body of the Dharma-realm.
It is like the net of Indra within the palace of Śakra: although each individual jewel appears distinct from its neighbor, they are all but a single pearl.
Yet their reflections enter into the various jewels; although the reflections enter the various jewels, the functions of illumination differ according to whether they face east or west.

The same applies to the object (*ālambana*) and the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Taking the object as the phenomenon (*dharma*), the contemplation becomes the principle (*li*); that the principle can encompass the phenomenon is what is called "contemplation swallowing the object.

Taking the contemplation as the phenomenon, the object becomes the principle; that the principle can encompass the phenomenon is what is called "the object swallowing the contemplation. Whether it be contemplation or the object, or...

One is the phenomenal aspect (*dharma*) and the others are the noumenal aspect (*dharmatā*), or one is the noumenal aspect and the others are the phenomenal aspect; as these mutually encompass one another, they are like Indra’s net.

If this is so, then when I practice contemplation, the environment and its inhabitants of the Western Land are already within my contemplation, and my current body and mind are already within that environment and its inhabitants. To seek birth in An-yang (Sukhāvatī) with a clear realization of this may truly be called—
A wild goose flies across the vast sky, its reflection sinking into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a trace; the water has no mind to retain the reflection.

In the "Gate of the Seven and Three Contemplations as They Are," that which contemplates constitutes the three contemplations, and that which is contemplated is the three truths. Because cultivation arises entirely from within the inherent nature, it is called "as they are" (*dharmatā*).

The Treatise says: The three truths are the ultimate, the conventional, and the middle. The three contemplations are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Regarding the forgetting of emotions and the severing of conceptual understanding, nothing is superior to the ultimate.

Regarding responding to conditions through practical application, nothing is superior to the conventional. Regarding the harmonious integration of emptiness and existence, nothing is superior to the middle.
"Vast, intelligent, and unobscured—my mind is naturally empty. Objects arrive and it responds—my mind is naturally existent.
Emptiness and existence are mutually identical—my mind is naturally the Mean. This is the nature; it is not cultivation. It is the Three Truths; it is not the Three Contemplations."
One who cultivates this realizes it through illumination in accordance with its nature. To realize that this mind is hollow and devoid of substance is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā).

To illuminate that this nature is fully endowed with all phenomena is called "provisional existence" (prajñapti). To harmonize these two extremes as being neither identical nor different is called the "Middle Way" (madhyamā-pratipad).
Thus, it is within this void and spiritual clarity that things respond; it is within responding to things that there is void and spiritual clarity. Emptiness is itself the provisional.

The Middle is the same as the empty within the provisional. The Middle is the same as the empty and the provisional. This is cultivation in accordance with the nature; it is illumination that transcends all dependencies.
It is the inconceivable threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), the compass for the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Such is the detailed discussion.
If one discusses it in general terms, some take the void and numinous nature of one's own mind to be emptiness, and take the myriad phenomena observed therein to be...
The provisional (prajñapti). Taking the non-duality of mind and objects as the middle (madhyama): objects are the objects of my own mind;

how can the provisional not be empty? The mind is the mind of all things; how can the empty not be provisional? Mind is object, and object is mind; how can the middle not be both empty and provisional?

Therefore, when contemplating the environment and inhabitants of Sukhāvatī, one contemplates them with the single contemplation of my own mind—this is the threefold contemplation that illuminates them.

That there is no contradiction between those three truths within a single object, and that there is likewise no contradiction in using the single mind of our threefold contemplation to illumine that single object of the three truths—Master Huxi said: "The object is wondrous conventionality; the contemplation is emptiness;

the simultaneous forgetting of both object and contemplation is the Middle Way. How could forgetting and illumining ever have a sequence? The single mind is fused and transcendent. Thus it is understood.
Since there is no trace [of a self], how could the three contemplations not be in accordance with reality?

In the eighth gate, "Responsive Manifestation Occurring Spontaneously," my mind moves the Buddhas; Amitābha responds immediately. This natural affinity between nature and nature is like a magnet attracting a needle.
The treatise states: All Buddhas and sentient beings share the same source of awakening (*bodhi*). Although delusion and enlightenment differ, their underlying principle is eternally equal.
Therefore, it is said that all Buddhas are the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings, and sentient beings are the sentient beings within the minds of all Buddhas.

Speaking from this perspective, the essential spirit of the minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings is never obstructed; it flows and merges at all times. It is only that the Buddhas... [never cease... *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the extant portion of the passage.)*
I wish to deliver sentient beings. Yet, moment by moment, they wander in delusion and turn their backs on me; thus it is said that one person remembers exclusively while another forgets exclusively.

They may encounter me and yet not encounter me; they may see me and yet not see me. Nevertheless, when sentient beings mindfully remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.
That they are not far from the Buddha is precisely because the single principle of the equal nature of reality connects them. Therefore—

If one can effortlessly uproot suffering and bestow happiness, how much more so for Amitāyus Buddha, who in the midst of his causal practices made forty-eight vows, vowing to take up Sukhāvatī and gather in sentient beings?

Now that he has long since perfected the path and its fruits and long since fulfilled his *saṃnāha* (armor-like resolve), all living beings need not worry that the Buddha will not come to respond to them;
they should simply have deep faith, maintain mindfulness, and repeatedly make the vow to be reborn in the West.

It is like a magnet and a needle that attract each other spontaneously; yet, while a magnet can attract iron, it cannot attract copper, and while a needle can join with a magnet, it cannot join with jade.
This is just as a Buddha can deliver those with whom he has a karmic affinity, but cannot deliver those without such affinity.
Sentient beings are easily moved by Amitābha, whereas they are not so easily moved by other Buddhas. Is this not because the vows of the living being and the Buddha are interconnected? Seek!
For those who are born in the Pure Land, faith, aspiration, and practice must all be present; none may be lacking.
Ninth is the "Gate of Constant Unity":
if, at the time of death, one can maintain right mindfulness without loss—whether seeing light or flowers—one has already received birth in the precious pond.

The Treatise says: In the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Rebirth), it is recorded that Zhāng Kàng served as a Hanlín Academician. He recited the *Dàbēi zhòu* (Great Compassion Mantra) one hundred thousand times, vowing to be reborn in the Western Land.

One day, while suffering from illness in bed, he did nothing but recite the name of the Buddha. Suddenly, he said to his family members: "The Pure Land of the West is right here at the western side of the hall.
Amitābha Buddha is sitting upon a lotus flower, and my father and son are in the golden lotus pond."
On the sand, he performed prostrations and played; after a long while, he passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. Weng’er was the grandson of Kang.
Indeed, the Western World of Ultimate Bliss is but one land within my own mind, and this Sahā world is likewise but one land within my own mind.
Although there is a difference of ten trillion lands between them when considered spatially, when viewed from the perspective of the mind, there is originally no distance at all.
It is near. Since beginningless rebirth, sentient beings have been confined by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) from their true nature (*dharmatā*), failing to accord with the source of the mind.

For one who practices Buddha-recollection, when the fruits of their retribution mature and they are about to cast off the present aggregates to enter the aggregates of the next birth, a lotus flower of the Pure Land suddenly appears before them.
This is a realm of the sole mind, devoid of the characteristics of coming and going or self and other. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "At the moment of death..."

At the time of death, before the sensation of warmth has been relinquished, the good and evil of one’s entire life manifest simultaneously. If one consists purely of pure thoughts, they will immediately ascend and be reborn in the heavens.
If, within that ascending mind, there is a combination of merit, wisdom, and pure vows, the mind will naturally open;

one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the Pure Lands, and be reborn therein according to one's vows. Master Fazhi said: "As death approaches, one sees for oneself that one is seated upon a golden [lotus]."
"Lotus": This means that one’s physical body is already a *kalala* (embryonic stage) born in that land; this is the intended meaning.

In the "Gate of the Mutual Presence of the Ten Manifestations and the Future," the practitioner who now recollects the Buddha does not have their merit go to waste. The fruit already exists within the cause, like a lotus flower in full bloom.

The Commentary states: Those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (yuantun jiao) achieve sudden awakening to the nature of mind, wherein there is cultivation without cultivation. They cultivate that Land of Bliss;

the Ultimate Bliss inherently possessed within the nature is manifested through such cultivation. Furthermore, this nature of mind penetrates vertically through the three periods of time and encompasses horizontally the ten directions of space.

The Buddha-dharma consists of the arising dharma, the true dharma, the dharma of reliance, the causal dharma, and the resultant dharma, all of which are perfectly accomplished in a single thought-moment.
Therefore, mindfulness of the Buddha is called "the complete manifestation of nature in cultivation" and "the complete presence of cultivation within nature.

Although the complete manifestation of nature in cultivation is termed the cause, because the complete presence of cultivation within nature means that the result exists within the cause, the causal dharmas possessed and the resultant dharmas possessed coexist within a single nature.
The nature of the mind is all-pervasive and harmonious, encompassing all phenomena without exception. It is like a lotus flower in full bloom with its fruit already within;

how much more so this mind, which is eternally abiding and devoid of arising, ceasing, coming, or going. Thus, the very mind that recites the Buddha’s name right now is itself the moment of rebirth in the Lotus Pond in the future.

Therefore, for one who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment], the seed of the lotus has already sprouted within the precious pond of Sukhāvatī. If they practice with diligence and do not regress, [rebirth will surely follow].
Day by day it grows and the flower gradually unfolds; according to the magnitude of its merit, it shines with brilliant splendor.
Should one become indolent, retreat, or be mired in regret, it will gradually wither and fade. If one can renew oneself, the flower will once again be fresh and beautiful.

If this is not so, the sprout will scorch and the seed perish. Furthermore, as for this lotus flower, who planted it? It exists both in the present and the future; these words have their basis in truth.
The Old Preface to the *Treatise on Birth and Non-Birth in the Pure Land*:
Master Youxi elucidated the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land through the perfect principle of the inherent nature (*xingju*). He composed this work entitled *Birth and Non-Birth*.
Treatise: This discourse was first expounded at Shicheng Temple in Xinchang. Each time he ascended the seat, celestial music filled the air, heard by the entire assembly;
the occurrence was not false or deceptive. Truly, it is a great bridge across the five turbidities and a supreme expedient for ascending to the nine lotuses.
It is the true spiritual friend of bhikṣus.
I conclude this treatise by taking as its primary principle (the first gate) that within the single thought-moment of the present, there is no dharma that is not fully possessed.

Because such possession necessarily entails creative activity (the second gate), the Buddha-lands and the Buddha-bodies are both identical to my own mind (the third and fourth gates). Now, based on this very principle which cannot be...

The single thought-moment of contemplating the Buddha through the five gates; and how the mutual resonance between the Buddha and sentient beings, the three contemplations of the wondrous perfection of the Western Land’s environment and its inhabitants, and the causes and conditions of vows made over vast eons, are all none other than this single thought-moment of my own present recollection of the Buddha (the sixth, seventh, and eighth gates).
Thus, the ten directions and their respective others, the causes and effects of the three periods of time, and the various, inferior, and deviant seeds [of all beings]— [End of excerpt]
All various doubts can be completely severed (by means of the nine and ten gates). This was composed by the junior disciple Chengshishi when he was still a student.
Proofread by the disciple Zhengzhi of Master Youxi Wujin’s Pure Land Dharma Discourses.
The Dharma-gate of practice is the excellent medicine for the Tathāgata’s personal realization. As medicine varies according to the illness, such methods exceed the sands of the Ganges in number.
Yet, among them, none is as swift and most essential as the recollection of the Buddha and the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land;
it may be called the secret key to swiftly attaining the path of enlightenment. Indeed, escaping birth and death relies upon three powers: first, the power of self-effort.

Second is the power of others; third is the power of innate merit. If one focuses solely on awakening and clarifying the mind-ground, tearing asunder the net of ignorance, crossing out of the river of craving and desire, and becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch, this is called the power of self-reliance.

These are the truly great men of immeasurable capacity, the true Mahāsattvas—such as the various great Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and great patriarchs of the Buddha’s era and the period of the True Dharma.
Such people, in this age of the Dharma’s decline, possess inferior faculties; though they may practice, they do not awaken, and though they awaken, they lack refinement.
Their internal illumination seems to grant liberation, yet they remain deluded regarding external objects. Even if they were not so deluded, they would still be like unbaked earthenware vessels.

Given that Bodhisattvas suffer the confusion of being separated from their physical bodies, and those who have attained the first fruit of the path experience the obscurity of entering the womb—how could ordinary beings at the stage of the "vast ground" avoid drifting along with the current? This...
Self-effort is ineffective; escaping the mundane world through one's own power proves fruitless. A single error leads to a hundred more—a reality truly chilling to the heart.

For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have compassionately bestowed skillful means, providing dharma-gates that rely upon others. These dharma-gates are numerous across the sutras and śāstras;

yet when one seeks those that offer earnest, heartfelt exhortations and praise them with extreme eloquence, it is the patriarchs who have propagated them so that the hearts of people might revere them.
I respectfully submit this. I consider the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss to be the ultimate teaching. Every word elucidates that the Pure Land is solely mind;
every phrase expounds the fundamental nature of Amitābha. Those who awaken to this realize that the mind of birth-and-death and the Buddha-mind are equal.
The mind-ground and the Buddha-land are without distinction. Those who cultivate this attain wondrous contemplation that accords with the wondrous realm;
they are sustained by both self-power and other-power. Moreover, the power of inherently existing merit, which has been nature-endowed since beginningless time, is fully manifested through this;
that which was accumulated over vast eons is suddenly awakened by means of it. Thus, when the retribution of the Sahā world is exhausted, the Pure Land manifests before one.
They are born through transformation within lotus flowers; they are not deluded regarding the aggregates of birth. Upon entering [the path] once, they enter forever and never regress.
Therefore, all who are born there are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive). Their number is exceedingly great.

Compared to those in the Sahā world who have entered the Way—where coarse and powerful sensory objects, perilous difficulties, and evil paths exist everywhere—they are certainly not comparable. Nevertheless, while it is not difficult to speak of this, it is difficult to practice.
It is difficult to practice; it is not the practice itself that is difficult, but the mind that is difficult. This was the warning of those of old, which we should follow.
Yang Cigong said: "If love is not deep, one will not be born in Saṃsāra; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī.

Now, the practice of nianfo—unifying the mind, earnestly holding the name with a focused and undistracted will—is indeed sublime. Yet, there may be times when one forgets and is unable [to maintain it].
One contemplates. Yet one contemplates without being able to achieve singleness of mind. This is due to nothing other than being pulled by emotional attachments.

Indeed, it has long been taught that one should diminish attachment to dispel delusion, severing the root of emotion and escaping the net of love. Nevertheless, there may be cases where one contemplates yet cannot forget, or forgets yet cannot exhaust [the defilements].
This is due to nothing other than the inability of the mind to attain singleness. In this Sahā world, if there is even one instance of attachment that is not light, then...
If one is drawn away by such attachment at the moment of death, how much more so when there is much attachment?

If even a single thought of discordance regarding the Land of Ultimate Bliss can cause one to be turned away at the moment of death, how much more so when there are many such thoughts? Now, attachment may be slight or heavy, thick or thin;
it may concern the primary retribution or the secondary environment. To enumerate its categories exhaustively, they include parents, wives and children, brothers, and friends.

Friends, fame and achievement, wealth and honor, literary works and poetry, arts and crafts, clothing and food, houses and dwellings, fields, gardens, groves, springs, flowers, and precious curiosities are too numerous to enumerate. Some are as massive and heavy as Mount Tai, while others are as light as a goose’s down;
yet there is not a single thing that one does not cherish, nor a single thought that one does not harbor with affection.
Indeed, if there is even a single attachment harbored within the breast, the mind will not be unified. If there is even a single thought that does not return to the One, rebirth cannot be attained.
Alas! If attachment is not profound, one is not born in Saṃsāra; if the mind is not unified, one is not born in Sukhāvatī.

These two phrases are the golden scalpel for scraping away cataracts from the eyes and the sacred medicine for curing chronic ailments of the vital organs. For all who are determined to seek birth in Sukhāvatī...
As for this joy, it should be inscribed upon the walls of one's house and engraved upon one's skin. One should recite it with solemnity from time to time and maintain its presence in every thought.
Day by day, seek to diminish the attachment to this Sahā world; day by day, seek to cultivate the mindfulness of Sukhāvatī.
Lighten it further and further until it gradually approaches non-existence; unify it again and again until it gradually approximates the ultimate. If one can truly do so, [the goal will be attained].

Although one has not yet escaped the defiled land, one is no longer a long-term guest of this Sahā world; though one has not yet been born in the Treasure Place, one is already a distinguished guest of Sukhāvatī.
When right mindfulness manifests at the moment of death, rebirth in Sukhāvatī is certain. Someone asked: "Is there a path for those who have lightened their attachments?

He replied: "There is nothing more essential than a single thought-moment. The questioner asked: "Is there a path for a single thought-moment? He replied: "There is nothing more essential than a single thought-moment."
Regarding this slight attachment, someone might say with a flickering air, "The Master’s words are equivocal; how can students know where to turn? I reply: "It is not a matter of equivocation.
I wish to clarify the source of a single thought. Indeed, thoughts are not unified because the distracted mind pursues diverse conditions.
The distracted mind pursues diverse conditions because it chases after objects as they proliferate. Within this Sahā world, there is a single object..."
Thus, sentient beings possess a single mind; when sentient beings possess a single mind, the Sahā world possesses a single object.
As they gather their conditions, the mind wavers within while it rushes outward; mind and objects race against one another, and cravings are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Therefore, if one wishes to lighten these cravings, there is no better way than to block off their objects. When all objects are empty and all conditions are utterly still, the single thought-moment spontaneously becomes complete.
If a single thought is perfected, then the conditions of craving will be exhausted. Therefore it is said: "To unify one's thoughts, there is nothing better than lightening one's cravings;
to lighten one's cravings, there is nothing better than unifying one's thoughts. Craving and thought cannot coexist; they are like light and darkness, which turn away from each other.
A question was asked: "Is there a way to shut off external objects? The answer was: "What I call 'shutting off external objects' does not mean physically screening them out..."

This means to eliminate the myriad existents. It is also not a matter of closing one's eyes and not observing. Rather, it is to realize their emptiness by engaging with the objects themselves, and to empty the derivative by realizing the fundamental source.

The myriad dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; their appearance as existent is due to the mind’s emotional projections (*qing*). Thus, when emotion exists, the object exists; when emotion is empty, the object is empty.
When the myriad dharmas are empty, the original nature manifests; when the original nature manifests, emotional thoughts cease. Spontaneously...

However, this does not require any forced effort. As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "The seeing, the objects of seeing, and the perceived forms are like flowers in the sky; they have never existed from the beginning.
This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. How could there be 'is' or 'is not' within them?
Therefore, if one wishes to block external objects, there is no better way than to realize that things are empty. Once one realizes that things are empty, [the mind naturally subsides].

Sentiment naturally ceases. When sentiment ceases, craving does not arise; rather, there is only the manifestation of the mind as a single thought. Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To know that it is illusory is itself to leave it;
no expedient means are required. To leave the illusion is itself awakening; this is also not a gradual process. It is simply a matter of one departing and the other remaining.

One cannot even turn over in one's sleep; the swiftness of its efficacy is like that of a drum struck by a mallet. Those who study the Way should apply their whole hearts to this. Furthermore, it was asked:
"Is the lightening of attachment to this world the same as, or different from, the single-minded focus on the Pure Land? He replied:

"One may be able to lighten attachment to the Sahā world, yet not necessarily be able to unify the thought of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. However, if one can unify the thought of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one will certainly be able to lighten attachment to the Sahā world."
This is explained in terms of the distinction between those without aspiration and those with aspiration. In reality, love is not separate from mindfulness, nor is mindfulness separate from love;
the two practices are fundamentally inseparable from the very beginning. He asked again, "I have heard your instructions regarding 'lightening' one's love.
How should one practice 'single-mindedness'? He replied, "The way of single-mindedness has three aspects: faith, practice, and aspiration. Not...

Doubt is the opposite of faith. If one harbors doubt, the mind cannot attain single-mindedness. Therefore, in seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must take the cultivation of faith as the beginning.
One must extensively read the Mahāyāna sutras and study the teachings of the patriarchs in depth.

Regarding all treatises that elucidate the Pure Land, one must investigate each and every one of them. One must realize that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is fundamentally the pure land of one’s own mind. Not...
That [Pure Land] is another land; yet one must realize that Amitābha is originally the true Buddha of one’s own fundamental nature, not some other Buddha.
There are two essential points: first, realizing that wondrous existence (*miāoyǒu*) is all-pervasive and fully endowed, which serves as the basis for rejoicing in purity;

second, realizing that ultimate emptiness (*zhēnkōng*) is perfectly detached and liberated, which serves as the source for abandoning defilement. Second, the practitioner must cultivate faith with the earnestness of one looking with their own eyes, and thus practice.
It is like walking with one's feet. To have faith but not practice is like having eyes but no feet; to practice but lack faith is like having feet but no eyes.

Therefore, once both faith and understanding are complete, one should practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Just as when both eyes and feet are fully equipped, one can reach the Cool Lake (*sītā hrada*), there are two aspects to the gate of practice:

first, the primary (*maula*), and second, the auxiliary (*sahakārin*). Within the primary practice, there are again two: first, the invocation of the name (*nāmoccāraṇa*), and second, the visualization (*bhāvanā*).

Reciting the name as prescribed in the *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, one should maintain the name for seven days with single-mindedness and without distraction. This involves both the "single mind directed toward the object" (*yixin*) and the "single mind in principle" (*yixing*).
If one recites the Buddha’s name orally while binding the mind to that focal point, the sounds will continue in succession and the moments of consciousness will remain undistracted.

If the mind is set upon external objects, gather it and cause it to return. This requires generating a resolute mind to sever thoughts of the future, casting aside worldly affairs and letting go of the攀缘心 (mind that clings to conditions).

Cause the mindful mind to gradually increase, from brief intervals to long durations, and from a small measure to a great one—whether for one day, two days, or even seven days—until you ultimately achieve a state of single-mindedness without distraction. Only after this...
This is the single-mindedness of this practice. If one attains this, the pure cause for rebirth in Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) will be accomplished;

right mindfulness at the moment of death will be assured; the body will be free from the suffering of illness and not beset by evil entanglements; one will know in advance that the time has come and experience joy of body and mind;

one will pass away with auspicious ease, whether sitting or standing; and one will personally behold Amitābha extending his light to welcome and lead one forth, thereby attaining birth in the Pure Land.

It is certainly so. The principle of the one mind is likewise nothing other than this: simply to realize, moment after moment within the one mind of phenomena, that the mind which contemplates and the Buddha who is contemplated are equal throughout the three periods of time and mutually interfused throughout the ten directions.
They are neither empty nor existent, neither self nor other; they neither go nor come, and neither arise nor cease. This very thought-moment before you is precisely that which has never...
When coming to the Pure Land, one recollects while not recollecting, and recollects through non-recollection; one arises from the unborn, and arises as the unborn.
Within that which is beyond recollection, one recollects with fervor; within the unborn, one fervently seeks birth.

This is the "single mind of practice" (saji) within the "single mind of clarity" (myōji). Second, regarding visualization (*vipaśyanā*): it is fully explained in the *Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.

The Sūtra states: There are sixteen objects of focus, of which the contemplation of the Buddha is most essential. One should contemplate the body of Amitābha Buddha as being sixteen feet tall, appearing like an image of purple-golden hue.
He stands upon a lotus pond in the posture of extending his hand to welcome and guide others.

His body possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), and each mark is adorned with eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). For one who forms this visualization, there is also [the attainment of] the objective reality.

Regarding principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*): one binds the mind to the Buddha and the Buddha to the mind. First, one contemplates the flatness of the soles of the feet, which are like the bottom of a casket;
next, one contemplates the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel. Proceeding in this sequence in reverse order, one reaches the *uṣṇīṣa* (fleshly protuberance) on the crown of the head;

then, proceeding again from the *uṣṇīṣa* in forward order, one returns to the soles of the feet. One does so with perfect clarity and without any distraction of thought. As for "single-mindedness according to principle," the Sūtra says:
It is said: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of the Dharma-realm; they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings.
Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha in your mind, that very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.
The ocean of the Buddhas' right and universal knowledge arises from the mind's contemplation. For this reason, you should fix [your attention]..."
"Mindfulness of that Buddha" fully elucidates the subtle and wondrous threefold contemplation, as explained in the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra* (*Guanjing shu*) and the *Miaozong chao*.
However, these two types of correct practice should proceed in mutual dependence: whenever one is walking, standing, sleeping, or lying down, one should single-mindedly recite the Name;
whenever one is sitting cross-legged, one should contemplate with every thought. When walking becomes weary, one should sit cross-legged to contemplate the Buddha; when sitting...

When one goes out, one should practice walking meditation in accordance with the name [of the Buddha]. If one cultivates this without interruption throughout the four modes of deportment, rebirth in the Western Land is certain.

Second, the auxiliary practices also have two parts: first, worldly practices, such as being filial and obedient to one's parents, practicing worldly benevolence and kindness, maintaining a compassionate heart that refrains from killing, and observing all the precepts; if one can dedicate all beneficial deeds...

Turning toward the West, there is nothing that is not a practice to assist the Way. Second, regarding supramundane practices—such as the various merits of the six perfections and myriad practices, the recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras, and the cultivation of various repentance rites—one must likewise employ a mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) to assist in their cultivation;

these are none other than practices for the Pure Land. Furthermore, there is another kind of subtle and wondrous auxiliary practice: it is when one encounters various conditions and objects in daily life.
Regarding the application of the mind: when seeing one's kinsmen, one should conceive of them as the Dharma-kinsmen of the Western Land.

One should guide them by means of the Pure Land dharma-gate, causing them to diminish their attachment so that their thoughts may become unified, and ensuring they become one’s kin in the future state of non-arising.
Whenever feelings of affection arise, one should reflect that the kinsmen of the Pure Land are free from emotional attachment; when shall I be born in the Pure Land and depart from this world?
To be free from this craving: when anger arises, one should reflect that the retinue of the Pure Land is free from provocation and affliction;
"When shall I be reborn in the Pure Land to escape this anger? When experiencing suffering, one should reflect that the Pure Land is devoid of all suffering and consists only of various joys.
When experiencing pleasure, one should reflect that the joy of the Pure Land is infinite and beyond compare. Thus it is throughout all experiences.
One should extend this principle to all objects of perception; thus, at all times and in all places, there is nothing that does not serve as an auxiliary practice for the Pure Land.
As for the third vow: Now, the vessel of the Pure Land must take faith as its rudder, and conduct as its oars, sweeps, mast, and cables, while the vow serves as the wind-sail.
Without a rudder, there is no direction to follow; without oars, sweeps, mast, and cables, [the vessel cannot proceed].
It cannot move forward on its own. Without wind, a sail cannot break through the waves to reach its destination swiftly. Therefore, practice is followed by aspiration to clarify this point.

Furthermore, aspirations may be general or specific, broad or narrow, universal or limited. A general aspiration is exemplified by the "Text for Dedication and Aspiration" established by ancient masters.

Specific aspirations follow one’s own individual intent. A broad aspiration refers to the Four Great Vows of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below; a narrow aspiration refers to a limited scope.
Resolve with vigor to attain birth [in the Pure Land]. This may be restricted to occasional recitation, where one joins the assembly in making the vow;

or it may be universal, where one makes the vow at all times and directs the mind toward this goal in every place. However, the essence must accord with the Four Great Vows and must not be established through arbitrary personal whims.

Generally speaking, a specific vow is superior to a general one. A general vow fears being swayed by the words of others, whereas a specific vow is one that one has personally directed one's own mind toward. Nevertheless...

One gives rise to a resolute vow in accordance with the general [text], which, though general, is specific. If one gives rise to confusion regarding the specific text, then even the specific becomes general.

Furthermore, the broad surpasses the narrow; the broad involves a great resolve for enlightenment and results in a superior fruition, whereas the narrow involves shallow compassion and vows, resulting in an inferior fruition.
Moreover, the universal surpasses the restricted; the restricted is repeatedly interrupted, while the universal is perfected in every thought-moment.
Accomplished. These three methods can serve as a basis for aspiring to birth in the Pure Land and swiftly seeking Amitābha.
Among all the Dharma-gates of the Pure Lands, none go beyond these.

Preface to the *Ten Essentials of Pure Land* selected by the Great Master Lingfeng Ouyi, Volume Ten: It is said that there are two types of people in this world who will certainly be unable to enter the Dharma-gate of Pure Land. First are the Chan practitioners who cling to the gate of awakening and pride themselves on their own power; they regard the practice of nianfo as no more than a dog wagging its tail for scraps, clinging to grass and wood. Second are those who harbor doubts regarding the principle of cause and effect and the reality of rebirth in the Pure Land. These two groups are like a person with eyes who refuses to look at the sun and moon, or one who has ears but refuses to listen to the sounds of thunder and rain. How could they ever attain the path? Therefore, I have compiled these ten essential texts to serve as a guide for those who wish to enter the Pure Land. May all who encounter them take them up and practice them diligently. This is my humble aspiration. May all beings be blessed. Recorded on the twenty-third day of the second month in the year of the Earth-Hare, the first year of the Yongzheng era (1723).
