Alas! The Confucian scholars savor metaphysical principles and revel in elegant discourse; when they see the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, they treat it as nothing more than putrid, leftover food or spittle that they wish to vomit up.
These two groups are alike in that they stare fixedly with deep, piercing gazes, yet fail to see even the fine hairs [between their eyebrows].
It is just like seeking the livers of dragons and the marrow of phoenixes while disdainfully rejecting one's own ordinary tea and soup;

how could one ever gain entry through such means? If you hope for entry, you must settle yourself before this person’s eyes like a crouching hawk, raising your voice in a great shout to cause them to blink in confusion and lose their footing. Or else, wait until they are famished and drooling, and then present it to them.

With a single measure of rice and a bowl of bean soup, he caused those who were famished and hungry to be fully satisfied; yet this is not something that ordinary Chan practitioners, Confucians, or those who recite the Buddha’s name can achieve.
Chan can extinguish the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye—witness clearly the application of Yongming and Chushi.
Confucianism can tear asunder the bonds of words and letters, leading to a thorough awakening to the Way of the Gentleman.
If one begins with the knowledge of husband and wife, and is subsequently able to manifest the Pure Land, one may perhaps succeed in subduing the "thieving mind" of those two types of people.

Yuan Hongdao was a literary hero who could sweep away thousands of troops with his brush, and he was also a Zen master who could leap over the well-railing; thus, he was able to attain realization at the top of the hundred-foot pole.

First, a step back. This is discussed by synthesizing the teachings of the Western tradition to ensure that the two aforementioned types of people cannot fail to humble their pride and subdue their arrogance, bowing down to peer within [the teaching].
As soon as they bow and peer within, their hearts and gallbladders are chilled with fear, and their very vitals are stripped away.
Were it not for relying on the supernatural power of Amitābha, such a thing would be difficult to achieve. Alas! The Altar.
The scriptures’ admonitions have long since vanished; the world hears only talk of refuting the Pure Land.
The teachings of Longxi have perished, and the world bears only the empty title of "seeking monks" and "discussing Chan. In the West, both the sun and the stars are obscured by thick clouds.
This *Heli Lun* (Treatise on the Sun) appeared in an age when the decline of the Pure Land school reached its peak, expounding the Dharma to save the times.
This is its current manifestation. Lingfeng has included it as one of his essential works; it constitutes the tenth fascicle and stands as the culmination of his intent.

Regarding the preface to the *Commentary on the Western Pure Land*, he critiqued that only those who have attained great penetration and great awakening may discuss the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance (*nien-fo san-mei*); otherwise, it is like comparing commoners with [the enlightened].
Knowledge and capability are already far superior. When the benevolent see it, they call it benevolence; when the wise see it, they call it wisdom.
The coming of Dharma from the West was an extraordinary event. Where there is great benefit, there must also be great harm. Alas!
Our predecessors fortunately obtained the great benefit, whereas today we have only the great harm. Who can take the realization of the Way as their vanguard? With...
Taking the recitation of the Buddha’s name as one's final strength is the way to steadily advance upon the path to supreme enlightenment.
Yuan Zhonglang was precocious in his youth and sat firmly upon the tongues of the contemporary Chan masters; those who did not know him took him to be a man of literary talent and spiritual vocation.
Later, he further penetrated the Dharma-realm and turned his heart toward the Land of Bliss, composing the *Western Pure Land Synthesis* in ten fascicles, every word of which arose from the truth.
This is a flow from the gateway of true awakening; therefore, there is not a single character that is a mere imitation, nor is there a single character that is fabricated.

Although he has not yet reached the ultimate depths of the Tiantai school’s inner sanctum, he has thoroughly penetrated the Zen mechanism and fully integrated the teachings and principles of Fǎngshān and Qīngliáng without exception.
Some may doubt this, wondering: "How can a youth have such universal mastery when even the venerable masters who received the transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs could not easily achieve it?"

Section Five: Only after the five desires were not yet eliminated could one finally reach this state. One does not realize that the karmic impressions (*vāsanā*) accumulated over many lifetimes are not accidental.
It is rumored that the Three Yuans are the reincarnations of the Three Sūs of the Song dynasty. Alas! If Zhonglang truly is Dongpo, then the Buddha-dharma will surely advance greatly.
I have often remarked that the achievements of the scholars of the Ming dynasty are far inferior to those of the Han and Tang; as for the Neo-Confucianism (*Lixue*) of the Song, however—

He greatly excelled others. Yangming alone directly continued the heart-lineage of Confucius and Yan Hui. As for the lay Buddhists Tang Liangsu, Song Chen Guan, and Ming Yuan Hongdao—indeed, they cannot be ranked as superior or inferior to him.
When Zhongsu was young, he happened to doubt that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was merely the words of a clay man rubbing a person’s back;
consequently, he was ridiculed by Chan practitioners. Yet, if one were to read his *Sanqian youmen* (The Gate of Three Thousand Existences), [one would see otherwise].
Verse: Can one truly laugh? Even the youthful elegance and refined grace of the Middle Rong (Zhonglang) were disregarded by both monastics and laypeople.
Yet, if one were to read that *Xi-fang-he-lun* (Western Regions Synthesis), could one disregard it again? Alas! People today lack the eye for reading books;
how can we not wonder at those who take their ears for eyes? This collection includes the annotated edition carved in Wumen, along with my own critical commentary.

To commemorate this, we have once again planned its publication to ensure its wide circulation, so that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma realm may, from this point forward, believe and practice this gate of the Buddha-dharma.
Most perfect and sudden, it transcends all Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya;

it encompasses all Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, so that there shall no longer be any sighs of lamentation over a forked path. The fourth month of summer in the year of Xīnmǎo (1811), at Northern Tiānmù.
Written by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu.

Once, when the clergy and laity were reading this preface together, one person was greatly repelled, another held it in his hands and played with it without setting it down, and several people were deeply moved and submitted.
I said to those several people: "A person of great thorough awakening and a hundred [others] who possess both knowledge and ability..."
[The monks] deliberated among themselves as to how far apart their surnames were. I asked again, "If one has not yet attained awakening, what serves as the vanguard? They deliberated once more.
Pointing to the one holding the large whisk (*vīraṇa*), I said, "If this gentleman understands, he would surely be submissive;
he is certainly not like you gentlemen. Then, pointing to the one playing with [the whisk], I said, "This gentleman has grasped its hair; you gentlemen do not even belong to it."
At that moment, the two gentlemen looked at one another and smiled; they brushed [the hair] and played with it, while the two masters remained silent.
Thus, is it not truly difficult to possess the eye that discerns the Dharma? Recorded here by the disciple Chengshi.
Preface to the *Western Pure Land Synthesis* (This preface was also annotated by the Great Master Lingfeng).

While the disciple Xiangguang was cultivating the practice of purity in a mountain hermitage to avoid the clamor of the world, a certain Chan practitioner passed by his dwelling with a wide gaze and stately stride.
Seeing the *Synthesis of Pure Land Teachings* on the table, he read it before finishing the chapter and exclaimed in a loud voice: "The original intent of this Dharma gate..."
This is employed to guide those of middling and inferior capacities. Those of middling and inferior faculties possess slight wisdom and deep-seated karmic forces;

by recollecting the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, they attain birth in the Pure Land, just as a stone attached to a boat can reach the shore. We of our own kind have thoroughly realized the original source:
this mind is the Buddha—where could one seek a Buddha? This mind is the land—where could one see a land? One seeks it within the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of principle.
The phenomena of birth and Buddhahood, coming and going, and the three periods of birth and death—there is not even a single hair’s breadth of these to be grasped.

To say one has "attained Buddhahood" is already a superfluous expression; how could there be any further matter of distinguishing between the pure and the defiled, or abandoning this life to take up another?
One should simply awaken to this and become a free and easy person. Lust, anger, and ignorance are all the equal site of enlightenment (*samabhūmi-dharmadhātu*); they are suchness (*tathatā*).
[The Master] moved. "Why do you abandon your own Buddha to prostrate before a gilded bronze image? Furthermore, you claim that both the enlightened and the unenlightened should practice this;

to create trouble where there is none is something I cannot understand. When Xiangguang heard this, he sighed deeply and said, "If what you say is merely intended to make your speech smooth and clever, you do not realize that with a single step you will fall into a pit of fire. Birth and death are impermanent; in the blink of an eye—"
How can one thoroughly memorize the ready-made, conventional phrases of the Chan school and take them as the ultimate? They all say, "I have already attained Buddhahood;
there is no need to recite the Buddha's name. If one speaks according to principle, every flea and louse possesses the pure awakened body of the Tathāgata.
Whether Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment or sentient beings fall into the three miserable realms, the fundamental substance has never increased or decreased throughout birth and death.
Nirvana and the like are false views. There are no Buddhas and no sentient beings; even in this realization, there is neither a person who realizes nor a dharma that is realized.
When the scope of the mind is extinguished and emotional attachments are transcended, the great earth has not a single inch of soil.
Where, then, can the single word "Buddha" be placed? As for the cultivation of the Dharma-gate, one cultivates and realizes within the state of non-cultivation and non-realization.
Within that which is without distinction, there are distinctions; there are thousands of variations and myriad differences.

Even those who have attained the stage of Equal Enlightenment do not know where the Tathāgata lifts his foot or sets it down. This is why the ancestral masters of old reviled the Buddhas, rejected the teachings, and obstructed everything.

Because people are hindered by teachings, they follow along with words and give rise to interpretations based on them. Failing to awaken to the fundamental essence beyond words, they merely cling to the provisional means within the words.
They speak exclusively of mind, nature, emptiness, and illusion; there is nothing regarding sudden or gradual, cause or effect, that they do not understand.
Yet, when asked about their own original source—the *bǐngmènyuánchén*—they simply counter with scriptures and treatises. Apart from these established verbal expressions, [they rely on...]
The ancients were utterly bewildered. As the saying goes, "One who counts another's money has no share for themselves.

There may be practitioners of true cultivation whose Buddha-nature remains unclarified as they toil in their practice; like a blind person without a guide, they merely attain the fruits of the human or celestial realms and are not born into the family of the Tathāgata.
The Patriarchs, perceiving this flaw, employed their "poisonous hand" to eradicate words and block intellectual understanding.
This path presses upon the emotional consciousness, compelling one to undergo bitter investigation and profound inquiry.

By reversing the flow of birth and death, when the emotions of birth and death are forgotten and the thoughts of grasping and rejecting become still, one finally recognizes the "clothing-jewel" from kalpas past—the innate parents.

Thereafter, looking at treatises and sutras is exactly like attending to affairs within a household. Only then does one practice according to the teachings, purifying emotional conditions through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and bowing to emptiness.
Flower Tathāgata cultivated the Brahma-conduct of the water-moon, ascended the stages of the mirage, and delivered sentient beings who are like echoes.

Not grasping at the realization of quiescence—this is called the seed of the Buddha. (It is precisely after awakening that one should study the sutras and practice; thus it can be seen that awakening to the Way is merely the first step, while studying the sutras and practicing are the post-awakening refinements.

It is not right to follow the common worldly view that regards sutra-study and practice as shallow and proximate, while regarding awakening to the Way as profound and remote, for this constitutes a perverted view. It is just like the bright sun appearing in the sky, traveling upon the Great King’s Road.

It is not the same as wandering through the long night, scrambling over thorns and falling among brambles. How could it be said that from the moment of a single awakening, one immediately attains the ultimate fruit?
Ceng Dachong said: "The nirvana of the fruition has not yet been realized by the good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of the world, because their merit is not yet equal to that of the sages;
however, those who clearly perceive their Buddha-nature may also be called good spiritual friends. Master Hongbian said: "Sudden..."

They clarify their own nature and are of the same rank as the Buddhas; yet, because they possess defiled habits from beginningless time, they must employ provisional antidotes to cause the functioning of that nature to arise accordingly.
It is like a person eating a meal: one does not become full after a single mouthful. Guishan said:

"Those of initial resolve who attain sudden enlightenment into the fundamental principle still possess the habitual tendencies of beginningless, vast eons which cannot be instantly purified. One must teach them to cleanse and eliminate these present [tendencies]."

The flow of karma is consciousness; this is precisely cultivation. There is no separate dharma that can be cultivated or pursued (for whether one studies the scriptures or practices, it is all for the purpose of purifying and eliminating habitual tendencies;

none are separate dharmas). Indeed, the various patriarchs established themselves for the sake of others like a wall ten thousand fathoms high: a mass of fire that burns upon contact, a forest of swords that wounds upon movement.

They never opened their mouths, yet already there were a thousand mountains of separation. When it comes to discussing matters of ordinary reality beyond the realm of karmic conditions, [it is even more so].
There have been those who attempted to bypass the stages of practice; this is clearly and exhaustively detailed in the *Chuan Deng Lu*.

The instructions of Dahui and Zhongfeng are particularly urgent and vital. I urge you with sincere devotion: I fear that empty intellectual understanding may entangle one and cause a fall into demonic activities.

How could it ever be that after awakening one does not rely on cultivation? Those of later generations fail to recognize the intent of the teachings and do not grasp the pivot of the Patriarchs’ function; they seize upon shouts and blows [as the essence].

To revile one's ancestors and break their spirits, taking dangerous phrases as the practice; those of old were obstructed by sutras and treatises, which was like eating a mixture of rice and wheat that could not be digested.
Later people, having memorized the sayings of the Chan school to satiety, reject causes and negate effects, overstepping their bounds and going too far.
This is like taking rhubarb and castor beans for tea and food. To deceive oneself and others—how could the harm have a limit? This is so.
As soon as one enters this gate, one treats the Tathāgatas of the ten directions with contempt, claiming that there is no Buddha to be realized and no practice to be cultivated.
Upon seeing someone recite the Buddha’s name, they say, "The self-nature is itself the Buddha. Upon seeing someone cultivate the Pure Land, they say, "The mind is itself the pure land.

They speak of Zen meditation as being honored above the nine heavens, yet they trample upon the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name as if it were the lowest of the nine earths. They do not reflect at all upon the necessity of cultivation.

In short, both Chan meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name are for the purpose of transcending birth and death. They are equally precious rafts for crossing the sea of suffering and bridges for surmounting the realms of existence.

Since their function is the same as that of one family, how can one be superior and the other inferior? While there are varying depths of realization within the gate of investigation (Chan), there are also differing levels of cultivation in the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name.
How can one dogmatically insist that those who investigate [the mind] possess superior capacities while those who recite the Buddha’s name do not?

For those of inferior capacity, it has been said since the arrival of the Dharma from the West that after two hundred years, those who understand the Way would be many while those who practice the Way would be few;

those who expound principles would be many while those who penetrate the principles would be few. Now, within the *Chuan Deng Lu*, such individuals are as numerous as hemp or millet, yet though they all claim to have attained enlightenment, in reality they are worlds apart.

As for those whose conditions for Prajñā are profound and whose spiritual roots were planted in former lives—such as the Kalaviṅka bird breaking its shell or the fragrant elephant—[they are truly rare].

Cutting off the flow of delusion, one perceives the root and essence in a single phrase; manifesting majestic function through a single shout, one attains great dhāraṇī upon hearing it once and awakening in a thousand ways.
There may be those who harbor the aspiration for world-transcendence and possess the resolve of a true man, who cast aside mundane attachments to investigate the Great Matter.
Do not rely on minor understandings; seek only true knowledge. Taste gall, sleep upon firewood, drink ice, and swallow bitter herbs.

After thirty or forty years, if you encounter an enlightened teacher who pierces you with the needle of painful instruction, the thieving mind will die out and the flower of the mind will finally bloom.

Thereafter, you must continue to practice secretly and cultivate in seclusion to dissolve remaining habitual tendencies. If even views of the Dharma must be abandoned, how much more so those that are not? Zhaozhou removed [the tile].
"Rice porridge and meals involve a distracted mind. For forty years, Yongquan still had movement and fluctuation; for forty years, Xianglin forged it into a single whole.
With every action he was cautious and vigilant, as if protecting his own head or eyes, until smoke vanished and ashes were extinguished, whereupon naturally not a single thought arose.
Karma could no longer bind him; amidst birth and death, he was free and at ease as he wished. If one interrogates what he realized:"
I fear that even this may not yet surpass the highest level of the "Highest Grade of Upper Birth. How is this made clear?
Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was the patriarch of the fundamental school; possessing great wisdom and great eloquence, he upheld the Buddha-dharma.

The World-Honored One bestowed a prediction upon him from afar, which did not go beyond stating that he would realize the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). Yet, in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*...
In the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*, it is stated that one attains the first bhūmi even in a single moment of superior rebirth.

Now, although the various great ancestral masters of the Chan school have seen through and transcended the fetters of delusion, and their words transcend conventional molds, how could they immediately surpass Nāgārjuna? For Nāgārjuna realized the principle of non-arising and signlessness.

Possessing the view that one does not fall into the ranks [of rebirth], one is born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). This is equal to what is realized by those of the highest and highest class;

how then could the realization of a practitioner of meditation alone be superior? Truly, because the understanding of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) regarding birth in the upper or lower realms is identical to the profound awakening of the Chan gate, and because the faith in cause and effect is identical to the cultivation of *śamatha* in the Chan gate, the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth is distinct.

I consider those who have awakened through practice to be such that they neither take the nirvana without remainder to be identical with the Tathāgata, nor are they willing to take the nirvana with remainder to be identical with the followers of the Two Vehicles. They must enter the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices.
Unless they relinquish one body to receive another in order to deliver sentient beings, they shall proceed from one land to another to make offerings to all [the Buddhas].

The Buddha has already seen that those who have attained the various stages of Buddhahood likewise return to be reborn together; ultimately, their superior births are merely on a level with one another, like brothers or peers.
Why, then, do you look down upon the Patriarchs and speak lightly of your fellow practitioners of the Pure Land? Perhaps you have entered the gate of awakening too hastily;
yet if your wisdom does not penetrate the subtle and your Way cannot overcome habitual tendencies, a single unextinguished thought is the very root of birth and death.
Dragged by the winds of karma, one enters the prison of the womb once more—just as the Fifth Patriarch’s precept-mind became that of Su Ziqing, or as Caotang became the Duke of Lu.

After being separated from the shade of the mother’s womb, one wanders through saṃsāra according to conditions; the Way does not increase but rather diminishes, while karma accumulates without ever decreasing.
Even if one’s affinity for Prajñā is deep enough to avoid falling into the three miserable realms, moving from room to room remains far too arduous. Return!

When one observes those of middling and inferior capacity who have attained rebirth [in the Pure Land], heaven and earth are insufficient to describe the disparity between their former misfortune and their present prosperity.

How much more so for later generations, when the ancestral style has declined daily and the faculties of people have grown increasingly diluted? Their resolve is often not genuine, and their practice lacks consistency;
yet, by chance, they may grasp the state of original Buddhahood—the "immediate suchness"—through the verbal sparks of the Buddhas and Patriarchs or the dregs of the teachings of their teachers.
It is a state where the functioning of the mental consciousness cannot reach and where language fails to express; everything is unobtainable, and even that "unobtainability" is itself unobtainable.
When one reconciles this with the words of the ancients, they are without exception identical. Thus it is said: "The frantic seeking has already ceased;
I am a man of no affairs. If one realizes that afflictions are like illusions, then one may let them run their course as one pleases.

This is vexation. Having recognized that the essence of practice is empty, one will recklessly destroy the practice at will, saying, "Generosity (*dāna*) is essentially empty," and thus instead of practicing generosity, one adopts stinginess;

"Patience (*kṣānti*) is essentially empty," and thus instead of practicing patience, one allows resentment to take root. Regarding precepts (*śīla*), they say, "Since there is fundamentally no holding or violating, why not lightly violate them and strictly uphold them?
Regarding meditation (*dhyāna*), they say, "Since there is fundamentally no concentration or distraction, why not abandon distraction and seek concentration?"

In meditative concentration, you listen to circumstances and follow your inclinations; you tread upon existence while discoursing on emptiness. Since it is said that even the Dharma should be relinquished, why do you instead grasp at what is not the Dharma?

Since it is said that even the Truth is not to be sought, why do you abandon it to seek after delusion? Since it is said that the cultivation of contemplation and the practice of concentration both belong to the realm of conditioned effort (*saṃskṛta*), why alone do you covet profit and seek fame, claiming they uniquely accord with the Way of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? [Your] love, hatred, and slander—
The fire of fame rises at the mere touch [of praise]. The wind of birth, old age, sickness, and death stirs upon its slightest breath.

People vie for themselves and others, asserting "right" and "wrong. They go so far as to take the nature of fire for their spirit, pride for their resolve, guile for their skill, deceitful speech for their means, license for their play, and foul words—
To resolve their attachments, they praise those who violate the precepts and lack virtuous conduct, while mocking those who observe the strictest ritual propriety in every step and movement.

Because they exclusively manifest the path of principle, they claim that the profound mysteries and ultimate subtleties are beyond all trace or origin. Because they utterly eradicate the gates of practice, they allow the mind to run wild and follow its own whims, abandoning all rules and regulations.
They claim with their own mouths that rebirth [in the Pure Land] is a teaching of the Lesser Vehicle, leading others to cultivate it only so that they themselves may remain in quiet seclusion.
Yet, some may go for years without prostrating to a single Buddha, without performing a single repentance, and without reciting a single sutra;

instead, they read worldly books that need not exist and engage in conduct unsuitable for those on the Path. They cause younger practitioners to seek only intellectual understanding and indulge solely in their cleverness;
as soon as they acquire some knowledge, they claim to have "transcended directly," becoming frivolous, arrogant, and reckless.
Arrogant, haughty, and unrestrained, their speech was indiscriminate and their conduct devoid of propriety. Moving in packs and bands, they behaved with wild and frantic insolence.
When the father had avenged his grievance, the son proceeded to commit robbery; copying the character for "crow" as "horse," errors were compounded through successive transmission.

They fail to reflect that worldly passions and desires are boundless—were it not for a dam, even a small flood would overflow. How can one, day after day, use smooth and artful words to collectively destroy the causes [of virtue]?

Regarding the gateway of retribution: if one does not breach its barriers and guide oneself toward the inevitable flow [of liberation], yet instead deludes oneself and others, how can one avoid falling into ruin?

If one is not reclaimed by the Maras, one will certainly sink forever into the three miserable realms (*trāya*). There, the sword-trees and knife-mountains shall punish former evils, and the wearing of fur and horns shall requite past calamities.
Do not say that those who have attained awakening cannot be bound by karma; for indeed, karma— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "夫業不" [As for karma...]).
It is capable of binding; it does not mean that what exists is non-existent, but rather that because it is non-existent, it is naturally non-existent.

Since birth follows the objects of perception and one immediately hastens toward death, how could one not follow where karma leads? A single momentary thought of anger before one’s eyes is the form of a monstrous python;
a single momentary thought of greed is the seed of a hungry ghost. The cause, being formless, consists of thoughts that are extremely subtle, yet the resulting retribution takes form.

It is most extravagant. Sentient thoughts are singularly focused, and the field of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) retains them; even after being sifted through for ten million kalpas, they are never lost.
It is like a certain bhikṣu who, by virtue of his wisdom, possessed radiance from his body, yet because of his false speech, maggots flowed from his mouth.
From such a minute word, he obtained this evil retribution; despite his radiant wisdom, it could not ultimately extinguish it. Now, the afflictions and ignorance are blazing fiercely.
Yet they do not sever [the afflictions]. Hoping to eliminate evil karma and escape the three miserable realms through such superficial views and understandings is impossible.

Had these people not considered even a small measure of attainment sufficient, but instead constantly practiced according to the teachings, they would never have claimed for themselves that they had realized "the mind itself is Buddha.
How could they then be compared to those of middle or lower capacity who seek birth in the Pure Land through mindfulness of the Buddha and thereby attain thorough realization?
Although there is fundamentally no birth, this does not preclude the fervent seeking of birth. This very mind is the land; the Lotus Land does not exist outside the mind.

Do not abandon prostration, nor forsake recitation. Only when the two wheels of wisdom-power and practice-power drive side by side will you be able to occupy a lotus pedestal of the highest grade and sit within the jeweled pavilions suspended in space, partaking of the morning meal at the Fragrant Accumulation Hall and wandering through the full moonlight at night. Looking back upon those born from the womb, they appear as mere shadows.

The people linger upon this precious ground, yet they do not hear the Dharma discourse nor behold the Dharmakāya. Elephants and horses cannot herd together; chickens and phoenixes are of different species.
How much less can those who dwell within the jar of the minor fruits of humans and devas—like mosquitoes and gadflies—ever hope for more?

Yet, with empty bellies and haughty hearts, they cling to emptiness and destroy existence. Ultimately, through their deluded interpretations born of biased attachment, they encounter extraordinary and bitter retributions, never to be united with Amitābha.
Having become a son [of man], one is instead made a prisoner of Yama; disregarding the guidance of the pure assembly, one is instead directed by the wardens of hell.

Abandoning the Jewel Grove to wander among the Sword Trees, and forsaking the Brahma-sounds to hear the cries of lamentation, one cannot even rank with those in the world who, though ignorant and sightless, perform small acts of goodness and virtue to be reborn among humans or devas. A hair’s breadth of error leads to a difference in heaven and earth.

The worlds are separated by vast distances; how can one not lament this? Thus, among those within the Gate of the Lineage (Zongmen), those above may not necessarily transcend the superior realms, while those below have already fallen into the three miserable paths.

Therefore, know that this Way is perilous and difficult, not easily traversed. To succeed is to become a Buddha; to fail is to become a Mara. The distinction between king and thief is made by a snap of the fingers;
the difference between a high official and a common cook is distinguished by a twitch of the eye. Such is the nature of suffering and joy.
One should choose [the path] early; otherwise, it will be difficult. In the present age, the single line of the gateway to awakening is as thin as a thread.
Beneath the sounding of the bells and drums, all is silent and desolate, with no one present. There are only two or three men of official rank whose paths are upright;

yet, being worldly men, they differ from the śramaṇas who bind their bodies with the precepts. They place themselves within the midst of a great fire and immerse their minds in the sea of affliction. Although...
Although I have managed to gain a faint entrance into the practice of precepts regarding worldly affairs, my power of the Way is extremely shallow while the power of karma is extremely deep.
Even the coarsest karmas, such as those of sexual misconduct and killing, I am still unable to break through and refrain from physically committing; how much less so for those that are subtle?

How could one possibly achieve liberation from the limits of birth and death? It is merely that those who were wealthy and extravagant like Yu Di, treacherous and evil like Lü Huíqīng and Xià Sǒng, ambitious and impetuous like Zhāng Tiānjué, or refined and elegant like Bái Lètiān and Sū Zǐzhān, all have their names listed in the *Lamp Records* (Chuándēng) and stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the patriarchs.
Consequently, they claim that everything is unimpeded and that there exists a separate source and stream. This is not so.

I know that although these individuals possess right view, if one claims that from this point on they will no longer undergo the retribution of birth and death (*bhavasaṃdhi*) and karma can no longer bind them, I dare not grant such assurance.

They shall still receive retribution throughout the long night of saṃsāra with no foreseeable end. Therefore, one knows that the single gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is especially urgent for laypeople.
When the power of karma is heavy, by relying upon the Buddha’s power, one may avoid being submerged in it forever. As it is said:
Debts are hidden within the royal palace; they cannot be avoided by seeking them out. Once born into the Buddha-land, the understanding attained throughout one's life will not be in vain.
Birth and death urge us on; it is difficult to guarantee that the next breath will remain. Seek the path of return early, lest you fall into chaotic confusion.

Even if your primary intent is to practice Chan meditation, there is no harm in supplementing it with the recitation of the Buddha’s name. In this world, even holding official office or managing a household is said to be no obstacle.
How much more so for those who, morning and evening, perform prostrations and recitations with body and mind in tranquil repose?

Furthermore, by borrowing the mindfulness of the Buddha (nienfo) to alert one’s laxity, one may stimulate diligence in Zen inquiry (can chan); by borrowing the thorough penetration of the Zen gate to strengthen one’s devotion to the Pure Land, these two support each other, which is most stable and substantial.
To not believe this is truly to be as ignorant as the lowest of the foolish. Layman Shitou was young when he first resolved to practice Zen.
His faculties were sharp and keen; within ten years, he had thoroughly penetrated the point of entry. His mental acuity was swift and incisive, his words like pearls rolling across a tray.

Whenever he discussed this matter with others, his brush flowed like a cascading torrent when he took up ink. He did not tread upon the stale expressions of the patriarchs, but let [his words] flow directly from the depths of his own breast.
Like a living tiger or a soaring dragon, there was not a single dead word among them. Consequently, he claimed that he had attained realization and had nothing further to do. Although...
Though worldly affairs have diminished and he no longer enters the dust and toil of the mundane world, he still dandles in the moonlight, mocks the wind, climbs mountains, and wades through waters;
he is indolent within the gardens of literature and wine, and his negligence and recklessness cannot yet avoid indulging his whims. Thus, the aforementioned ailments have not been entirely cast off.

Fortunately, his resolve regarding birth and death is urgent, so that he does not ultimately sink into ruin. He painfully reflects that wherever he encounters obstacles, he becomes stuck, and whenever he perceives an object, a mind arises—floating and wavering.
Because their understanding of the true reality was unable to overcome one another, they first took the view of partial emptiness as their starting point to enter the gateway of Samantabhadra.

Furthermore, they reflected that among the gates of practice, none is more definitive than the recitation of the Buddha's name; yet, they felt that the doubts of those of middling and inferior capacities had not been entirely dispelled through that provisional means.

Later, through extensive study of the sūtras and śāstras, I first realized that this gate originally subsumes the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) and is suitable for cultivation by both those who have attained awakening and those who have not.
Thereupon, I gathered what was proclaimed by the Golden Mouth [the Buddha], expounded by the Bodhisattvas, and set forth by the great spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

Supplementing these with my own understanding, a thousand waves surged up and ten thousand streams flowed across; yet when one investigates where they all converge, they all return to the same source.
This treatise takes the inconceivable ultimate truth as its primary tenet; it takes awakening as its guide;

it takes the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name with single-mindedness and without distraction throughout the twelve periods of the day, with each thought succeeding the next, as its conduct; it takes the six perfections and myriad practices as auxiliary causes;

and it takes deep faith in cause and effect as the gateway for entry. Having just completed this, we shall together participate in the aspiration for enlightenment, uphold the precepts, and recite the Buddha’s name.

These five individuals together desired to circulate [this work] in order to resolve the delusions regarding religious teachings. Xiangguang’s faculties were dull and his consciousness weak; for a long time he had been intoxicated by the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*).
He ran wild with his will and indulged his passions like a mad elephant. Last year, on a night of deep intoxication, he personally visited the Geli Hell where fierce fires blazed;
there he beheld the physical forms of those monks whom he had frequently discussed as being empty [of self], yet who had violated the precepts and perished. Their appearances...
He passed by, emaciated, frail, and with crippled feet; the sound of his wailing shook the earth, almost unbearable to hear.
Upon waking, the hair on my body stood on end, and I subsequently resolved to take refuge in the Pure Land. Later, when I read this treatise, my long-standing doubts were dissolved like ice.
Therefore, today I do not shrink from these harsh words: a sick man knows a physician, and a wayward son pities a traveler. You should completely eradicate all your former views and understandings.
"If you recite and study with an empty mind, you will surely attain entry [into realization]. The matter of birth and death is of great importance; do not delay for long.
At this, the Zen practitioner’s tears flowed with both sorrow and joy. He said, "Had I not met you, I would have almost spent my entire life deceived by empty views. You have brought me to life!

Now, the faults of conditioned phenomena arise from being mired in appearances and deluded in mind; the calamity of reckless nihilism arises from clinging to emptiness to destroy existence. Bodhidharma came to save [us].
Those who cling to signs claim that both sin and merit are empty. Yongming [Yanshou] refuted those of "wild wisdom" by stating that all myriad virtues are complete within it:
water extinguishes fire, yet excessive water brings the calamity of drowning; the sun gives life to beings, yet the sun’s intensity becomes the root of withering and scorching.
The teaching of the Tathāgata is likewise so. Since the Five Patriarchs, the tradition of single-lineage transmission has flourished. By the time it reached...
Today, such狂妄 (reckless excess) has flourished; they erroneously cite "Mind-Only" and are thus no different from the non-Buddhist *asamskṛta* heretics.

Clinging to their words as being all-encompassing, they rush toward the demonic city of the five desires. They do not consider that Ānanda was expelled for his head-shaving practices because he had not yet attained full mastery, nor that Mātaṅga was rebuked by the Venerable One for the slightest trace of fetters.
As thin as a cicada’s wing, their superficial practice keeps them far from the Treasure Place; yet like a towering mountain, their arrogance is immense.
From where do defilement, purity, and pleasure arise? The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was transmitted from Bodhidharma; therein, awakening and cultivation are both esteemed.

At Huangmei, the *Prajñāpāramitā* was propagated; therein, emptiness and existence are both perfected. It has never been heard that the fundamental principles of the One Vehicle reviled the pure precepts. Yet the true heirs of the Five Lamps (the Chan lineage) remain attached to worldly conditions.
