I declined. Those who heard this laughed at me. Today’s scholars have greed, hatred, and false views burning like fire;
yet they wish to untie the bonds of others—how deluded they are! For ten years I studied the Way, only to fall into this madness. Later, upon encountering a catalyst, I gained a slight awakening.
Thereupon, I simplified my worldly toil and turned my heart toward the Pure Land. In the intervals between prostrations and recitation, I took up the works of Nāgārjuna and Tiantai.
The Elder [Hui]yong and others read this treatise with meticulous care; suddenly, their doubts were dispelled.

Having gained deep faith in the Pure Land, they further awakened to the distinct practices of the great Bodhisattvas. Like a poor man who discovers a hidden treasure of gold, they could not contain their joy.
Master Yuan’an and Layman Pingqian requested that I compile various treatises on the Western Paradise.
I have thus taken the essential words of the ancient worthies and bound them into a single volume, entitled the *Western Paradise Compendium* (*Xifang helun*).

It began on the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the Jihai year and was completed on the twenty-second day of the twelfth month. As I lacked sufficient time for review, there are many omissions; I hope only that [it may serve] future generations...

This is the opening of the initial aspiration. Still hoping to attain the correct path through those who possess the Way, I have briefly examined the sages of antiquity and categorized them into ten sections:
First, the Section on Buddha-lands; Second, the Section on Dependent Origination; Third, the Section on Scriptural Categories;
Fourth, the Section on the Characteristics of the Teachings; Fifth, the Section on Principles and Truths; Sixth, the Section on Conforming to Nature.
Chapter Seven: The Gate of Rebirth; Chapter Eight: The Gate of the Net of Views; Chapter Nine: The Gate of Cultivation and Practice;
Chapter Ten: The Gate of Explaining Differences;
Chapter One: The Gate of Buddha-lands.
Indeed, within the single true Dharma-realm, the bodies and lands interpenetrate; throughout the oceans of the ten Buddha-fields, there is no distinction between the pure and the defiled.

It is solely because the karmic actions of sentient beings differ that the manifestations of the Buddhas also vary—whether provisional or real, partial or perfect, temporary or eternal, gradual or sudden.
It is like a single moon reflected in a thousand rivers, where every ripple contains the pure moon; or like ten thousand lamps [illuminating] a single...
The radiance within each chamber individually manifests the entire lamp; in principle, this is the Single Truth, yet in its manifestations, there are a thousand differences.
Were it not for the extensive citation of sacred texts, what standard could sentient beings have to follow? Therefore, drawing from various teachings, I shall briefly set forth ten gates.
1. The Pure Land of Vairocana; 2. The Pure Land of Mind-Only; 3. The Constantly True Pure Land; 4. The Manifested Pure Land; 5.
The Pure Land of Entrusted Retribution; 6. The Pure Land of Emanated Bodies; 7.
The Pure Land of Dependence on Others; 8. The Pure Lands of All Directions.
9. The four kinds of pure lands of the one mind;
10. The inconceivable pure land that gathers in sentient beings of the ten directions.
Regarding the first, the Pure Land of Vairocana: this is the fundamental retribution land of all Buddhas, the Lotus Treasury World.
The ocean of realms: at the very bottom of each Flower Treasury world-system, there are vast lands as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds, adorned with pure majesty.

Each of these vast lands is further surrounded by smaller lands as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds, increasing in size and extent by multiples. Every Flower Treasury world fills all of space, mutually...

Penetrating through, the pure and the defiled are universally contained in layers upon layers of inexhaustibility. According to the Dharma, each single hair and each single speck of dust is fully endowed with this inexhaustible Dharma-realm;

Buddhas and sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction. Some say that because the *sambhogakāya* (retribution body) adornments of these sentient beings differ from those of the provisional teachings which project the Pure Land to another direction, this constitutes the definitive teaching (*nitārtha*). Others say that [the adornments] of the sentient beings...
Although beings possess this true recompense, how can they avoid the fact that True Suchness (tathatā) lacks self-nature and cannot be realized by itself?

Without relying on expedient means to enter the real through the provisional, how could sentient beings ever have a day of realizing Vairocana? Answer: This may be so in terms of the Buddha’s transformative manifestations;
however, within the land of the ultimate reality (dharmatā), such conceptual proliferation does not exist. "Vairocana" is translated here as "Pervading All Places."
To pervade all places is precisely the expressed meaning of Amitāyus; how could there be any distinction of superior or inferior?
When the Tathāgata says that Amitābha is in the West, it is just as the *Mahāmegha Sūtra* records Amitābha Buddha saying that Śākyamuni is in Sahā.
Now, if Śākyamuni is the subject, then Śākyamuni pervades all, while Amitābha is but one place pervaded by him. Amitābha...
When one takes oneself as the subject, Amitābha pervades all things, while Śākyamuni is but one place among those pervaded. It is like a single person:
when he calls himself "self," others call him "other. Thus, when he is his own self, it does not preclude him from being the other of all people;
and when he is the other of others, it does not preclude him from being the self of all people. For this reason, self and other are not mutually exclusive.
It is established that neither self nor other is established. Since both self and other are omnipresent throughout all places, how could one insist that another must necessarily exist?
Therefore, in the Western [tradition], Vairocana is neither self nor other. Why is this? Because there is nothing in which Vairocana is not omnipresent.
If one speaks of him as provisional or as a skillful means, then he would be non-omnipresent; yet to be non-omnipresent contradicts the very meaning of Vairocana.

It is not established [that this is merely provisional] (for if one looks to the West, it is precisely the Pure Land of Vairocana; since Vairocana is the reality, the Western Land is certainly not provisional).
Second, regarding the Pure Land of Mind-Only: to directly realize within oneself that the very essence of the mind is non-mind is itself the Pure Land.

As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The straightforward mind is the Bodhisattva’s pure land. When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who are free from flattery will be born in his land."
The profound mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings endowed with merit come to be born in that land.
The Mahāyāna mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, Mahāyāna sentient beings come to be born in that land.
Thus, if one wishes to attain a pure land, one should purify one's own mind; according as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure. Indeed...
The mind is the very land; the land is the very mind. That the purity of the mind is the purity of the land is the natural law (*dharmatā*).

Is this statement not itself a commentary on the Western Paradise? There are many who, clinging to their own minds, disparage the Dharma-gate of the West as being intended only for those of dull faculties, because they perceive the land as existing outside the mind. Now, mindfulness is itself the mind; how could the recitation of the Buddha’s name...

It is not that the mind is pure; rather, the mind fundamentally contains the lands. How could the Lotus Land lie outside the mind? Therefore, we know that from the perspective of phenomenal appearances, there is no contradiction with the principle of "mind-only.
To say that it accords with the mind truly means that it removes all obstacles to universal salvation.
The "threefold eternal true pure land" refers to the pure land indicated at the assembly on Vulture Peak.

It is intended to lead the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings of the three vehicles to realize that this very land is eternally pure despite its defilement. Although all beings believe it, they do not yet see it.

Now, the nature of defilement is fundamentally quiescent, and conventional appearances are eternally empty; therefore, when bodhisattvas dwell in defilement while remaining eternally quiescent and enter into the mundane while remaining constantly empty, they truly manifest the meaning of purity.

However, sentient beings cling to the ocean [of existence] such that it is difficult to purify; they are bound by the ropes of consciousness so easily. To say that karma is fundamentally empty leads them to act according to their whims;
to say that speech has no substance leads them to wander blindly at will. Thus, they commit the offenses rebuked by Yongjia and fall into the abysses into which Shanxing plummeted.
Consequently, those who encounter royal peril in life and become the retinue of Māra after death are indeed numerous. Alas! Were one to cause the entire earth...

"All are bodhisattvas. These words are indeed beneficial. However, if bodhisattvas were few and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) were many, then the benefit of these words to the world would be slight, while the harm to the world would be great.
(Who would dare to regard the statement that the eternal, true, and pure land is of little benefit and much harm?
Only one who has attained great awakening possesses such courage and insight.)

Regarding the fourth point, the manifestation of the pure land: this refers to the three transformations of the pure land in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where humans and devas were moved to other directions;
and when Vimalakīrti pressed the earth with his toe, the great trichiliocosm immediately became adorned with hundreds of thousands of precious jewels.
This was the Tathāgata’s temporary manifestation, which is also the natural law (*dharmatā*). Yet, even one as wise as Śāriputra was like a blind man; how much more so those of inferior faculties?
Sentient beings have no means by which they may behold it; let alone humans and devas, who are cast outside the realm, they utterly lack the conditions for being guided there.

Though its spiritual power manifests briefly, it vanishes again; how could this be a permanent land? How can it compare to the Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), which endures through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, where the Compassionate Father Amitābha does not abandon even those who commit the ten evil deeds? The superiority and inferiority of these lands are thus clearly evident.

Regarding the fifth point, the "Provisional Reward Pure Land" (kiji-hō-jōdo): within the stages of the four dhyānas, there is the Mahesvara Heaven. It is there that the Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

According to the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Qixin lun*), when a Bodhisattva’s merits are fully perfected, they manifest a body of supreme height and magnitude for all worlds at the Akaniṣṭha (Cloud of Dharma) realm.
Master Fazang stated that this is a provisional reward distinct from the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), corresponding to the tenth stage among the Ten Kings.
Entrusted. At this time, the Heavenly King immediately manifested the attainment of Bodhi there.
Although that heaven is not reached by the three calamities, it is still not equal to the Lotus Land, which directly transcends the Triple World, for it is situated at the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Regarding the six types of pure lands of the divided body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Beyond thirty-two *asaṃkhyeya* worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world named Anabhibhūta (Unconquerable).
I appeared therein and, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, turned the wheel of Dharma in this realm. Furthermore, the Buddha said to Aṅgulimāla:
"I abide at the limit of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmatā*), yet you do not perceive it; go to the east and inquire of the Buddha there."
That Buddha said, "Śākyamuni is my very own body. Da Yi (Dàyì) meant that while that Pure Land is the Buddha’s true recompense (*vipākaphala*), this [world] is a manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Although it reveals the realm of a single Buddha’s recompense, it does not yet fully embody the meaning of gathering and transforming beings; yet, from the perspective of the Buddha himself, it exists.
Within the perspective of ordinary sentient beings, this does not exist and thus cannot be considered particularly sublime.
Seventh, regarding the pure lands of the dependent nature: according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, "I, now as Vairocana, sit upon a lotus pedestal;
around me, upon a thousand petals, there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis. On each petal are ten billion lands, and in each land is one Śākyamuni," and so forth.
As for this: in the first bhūmi, one transforms a hundred lands with flowers having a hundred petals; in the second bhūmi, one transforms a thousand lands with a thousand petals;
in the third, ten thousand petals; and in the fourth, a hundred million petals, increasing tenfold at each successive stage.

This is the realm of retribution manifested by the *paratantra-sambhogakāya*, which is perceived upon entering the bhūmis. It is not like the assembly at the Lotus Pond, where sentient beings with ten recitations suddenly behold the pure Buddha.
Regarding the lands:

as for the pure lands of the various directions, such as the Eastern Medicine Master (Bhaiṣajyaguru), the Southern Sun-Moon-Lamp (Sūryacandrapradīpa), and the Upper Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha), each Buddha has his own pure land.
All of these are adorned with the retribution of reality (*vipāka-saṃbhoga*), or they are manifested through the Buddha’s spiritual power, or through the Bodhisattva’s...
Sāgata went there to make offerings. Because that Buddha had not yet spoken of gathering in sentient beings, beings lacked the necessary conditions to be born there.
Thus, although there were those who attained rebirth in the world of Abhirati, it was not heard that in Akṣobhya’s land there was a universal invitation [to all].
Furthermore, the various mountains such as Sumeru, as well as the malevolent spirits and women, were not as pure and serene as in An-yang (Sukhāvatī). Moreover, in the world of Vaiḍūrya...

Śākyamuni of this realm also exhorts one to be reborn there; however, the primary intent of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* is to assist in rebirth in Sukhāvatī by exhorting people to extinguish afflictions and karma and to achieve the *nien-fo* (buddha-recollection) samādhi.

This accords with the purport of the teachings on the "Gate of Severance" (*zhé mén*), rather than being comparable to the Amitābha Tathāgata’s method of universally gathering all people through *nien-fo* alone to lead them to rebirth in that land.

Regarding the nine types of one-mind pure lands, there are four kinds of pure lands. First is the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages (*prthagjana-ārya-sahavāsa-bhūmi*), which is divided into two categories:

the impure and the pure. Within the impure land, there are two types of ordinary beings and two types of sages. The two types of ordinary beings are: first, evil sentient beings, namely those of the four miserable destinies;

second, virtuous sentient beings, namely humans and devas. The two types of sages are: first, actual sages, namely those of the four fruits, pratyekabuddhas, and the six [stages] of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

Regarding the stages: the ten distinct abodes (*bhūmi*), the perfected ten faiths, and the final mind [of the ten faiths]. Although pervasive delusions are exhausted, the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) still remains;

these are all termed "real. Second, the provisional sages: these refer to the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas and those of wondrous enlightenment within the lands of expedient means, real reward, and tranquil light.

The Buddha manifests birth in the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*) for the sake of benefiting those with whom he has a karmic affinity; all such manifestations are provisional (*upāya*). Because these realms coexist with the four miserable destinies (*catur-gati*), they are called "defiled lands" (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*).

As for "pure lands" (*śuddha-kṣetra*), such as the Land of Supreme Joy (*Abhirati*): although they contain the categories of men and women within the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), they are called "pure" because they lack the four miserable destinies.

Second is the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-avaśeṣa-bhūmi*). [In the following, each of the three lands—Skillful Means and so forth—is divided into pure and defiled; only the Western...]
The Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) horizontally encompasses the four lands, all of which are pure; this is why it is most wondrous (and should be further elaborated upon in detail).

That is to say, the two vehicles and the three types of bodhisattvas destroy the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), realize the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*), and cast off their segmented bodies (*paricchinna-śarīra*) to be born outside the triple world; hence it is called "skillful means.

Yet, because the dust-like secondary afflictions and ignorance (*avidyā*) have not been severed, it is called "having a remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). As the *Śāstra* states: "Outside the triple world, there is a pure land."
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born therein; they receive the dharma-nature body, not the body of segmented birth.

Third is the land of true recompense and non-obstruction, inhabited exclusively by bodhisattvas of the dharma-body who have exhausted the afflictions as numerous as motes of dust and partially shattered ignorance.

One attains the fruit of reality, yet because ignorance is not yet exhausted, it moistens uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*), whereby one receives the *dharmatā-nirmāṇakāya* (the body of the nature of phenomena), which is also called the "land of fruition.

The *Renwang jing* states: "The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages dwell in the land of fruition; by contemplating the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and giving rise to true uncontaminated wisdom, they experience a particularly sublime retribution, and thus it is called 'real.
Because matter and mind are non-dual, and even a single hair and a single pore can contain one another, it is called 'unobstructed.'"

Obstruction. This refers to the Indra’s Net world of the *Avataṃsaka*. Fourth is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, which is the realm of suchness (*tathatā*) illuminated by the ultimate wisdom of wondrous enlightenment;
it is termed a "land" (*kṣetra*) and is also called the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*). It is simply the single true Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*);
it is neither body nor land, yet it is spoken of as body and land. Apart from the body there is no land, and apart from the land there is no body. Thus it is with all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

Regarding the phrase "the place where he comes to dwell," *Miaozong* says: When the sutras and treatises speak of the "marvelous light" (*jiguang*) as being "without marks" (*wuxiang*), they mean that all defiled and obstructive marks have been exhausted;

it does not mean that there is nothing at all, like the great void of space. This is because when the three delusions are ultimately purified, the physical environment (*yi*), the sentient beings within it (*zheng*), and their form and mind (*sexin*) are ultimately revealed in clarity.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "By the extinction of this [conditioned] form, one attains eternal form; by the extinction of sensation..."
The same applies to perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. The Benevolent Kings Sūtra refers to these as the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-skandha*).

This constitutes the ultimate fruit. The names and meanings of the four lands above are distinct from one another; although all pure and impure Buddha-lands each possess these four, they exist within a single mind while their objective spheres differ.
They do not become different through difference. Therefore, the Land of Common Residence is for those who have regressed from the stages, while the Land of Expedient Means...
This is both a stage of regression and a stage of non-regression. That is to say, one may regress and fall into the Two Vehicles, yet not regress and fall into the state of ordinary beings.
The stage of true recompense (*sambhoga-kāya*) is a stage of non-regression; the stage of tranquil light (*śāntaprabha*) is a stage that is neither regressive nor non-regressive.

It possesses only the sense of vertical emergence and lacks the sense of horizontal integration; therefore, at the initial stage of cohabitation (*sahabhū*), there is no inconceivable cause and effect to be discussed.
The inconceivable pure land that gathers sentient beings from the ten directions is the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Within it lies the ocean of great merit, the ocean of great compassionate wisdom, and the ocean of the power of great vows.
To describe them in full detail, even if one were to employ all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas throughout the ten directions, down to the smallest crawling insects...
Moving things such as grasses, trees, tiles, rubble, and even the most subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*)—each possesses immeasurable mouths; each mouth possesses immeasurable tongues;
and from each tongue issue immeasurable sounds. These constantly speak, speak repeatedly, speak fervently, and speak without interruption.
Even after millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they could not be fully exhausted. For now, let us explain this according to five meanings.
This means: first, within the body of one Amitābha there are immeasurable sentient beings; within the bodies of sentient beings there are immeasurable Amitābhas. It is the same with the lands.
Therefore, when one sentient being recollects Amitābha, one Amitābha sees them. When many sentient beings recollect Amitābha, many Amitābhas see them.
When a sentient being recollects Amitābha in every thought-moment, they see Amitābha in every thought-moment. If...
If there is no Amitābha within the bodies of sentient beings, Amitābha is not seen; it is like a sun-crystal (ādityakānta) which can produce fire but cannot produce water.
Therefore, if there are no sentient beings within the body of Amitābha, Amitābha is likewise not seen;
it is like a child in the womb who exists together with its mother, but does not exist with a barren woman. For this reason, the body contains the body; the body contains the body-body; the earth.

The land contains the body; the land contains the land of the body; the body and the land mutually contain one another, layer upon layer without end. This is the meaning of the inconceivable nature of the body and the land.

Second, if one speaks of the land apart from its nature, the land exists outside of the mind; because it would then be a mere illusory transformation, such an illusory transformation is characterized by annihilation, and thus sentient beings would not be born.
If, however, one speaks of the land as being identical to its nature, then since that nature possesses form and is determinate, it would be singular.
Samādhi is itself without change; sentient beings likewise do not arise. It is both nature and appearance, yet neither nature nor appearance.
To exist is not to be non-existent, and to exist is itself to be subject to destruction. This is the meaning of the inconceivable nature and appearance.

"Three" refers to the fact that recollecting the Buddha is itself seeing the Buddha, and becoming a Buddha is itself saving sentient beings—all complete at once. It is like a person who, from age thirty to forty, [remains the same].
Regarding the characteristic of interruption: if one were to go from thirty to forty [years], there would be a limit between them;
however, this body of mine has no such limit. If one were to proceed from thirty to forty, there would be continuity in the interval;
yet, in this body of mine, even such continuity cannot be found. Therefore, the cause and effect of the Buddha’s mindfulness is likewise thus. This is...
The meaning of the inconceivability of cause and effect: Fourth, if Amitābha comes because of mindfulness, then these sentient beings are born because they recollect the Buddha.
That [Buddha] would then have coming and going; having coming and going implies a journey; having a journey implies difficulty and ease. The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* states:
"One does not end one's life here to be born in that other Buddha-field; the Buddha has no [coming or going]."
From the beginning, I have likewise never gone anywhere. As the former masters said: "When born, one is certainly born; when departing, one truly does not depart.
It is like the sounding of a celestial drum, heard equally from far and near, for there is no coming or going. It is like the moon in water: if one moves to the east, it appears in the east.
If one goes west, it is simply west; this is not because of coming or going, for such is the inconceivable meaning of coming and going.
The fifth [analogy] refers to: like mountain reflections in a clear pool; like the hundred grasses in spring sunlight; like the karmic power of sentient beings; like the radiance of the sun and moon;

like the faculties within the womb; like the "self" within the body; like the hardness of the teeth and the softness of the tongue; like the horizontal eyebrows and the long hair. These are ultimately [inexpressible].

Regarding the meaning of the conceivable and the inconceivable: this is why the Buddhas of the ten directions have poured out their hearts and exposed their very guts, speaking only of it as something rare and difficult to believe.
Even with the thousand-spoked tongue-mark of a great chiliocosm, how could one possibly explain even a ten-thousandth part of it?
Confucius said, "The ignorance of a common husband and wife can be made to understand; yet when it comes to the ultimate, even the sages do not know. How profound these words are!
Innumerable Dharma-gates are all unified by a single principle. Second is the Gate of Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpāda).

Now, one who delights in the stench of a fish market does not think of the *candana* sandalwood; it is not that they do not think of it because it is unreal, but rather because they do not find it loathsome. Suppose for a moment one were to lead them away...
In this chamber of encounter, they burn *candana* and incense; before the day is out, they grieve over their former filth and regret that their renunciation was not attained sooner.
Indeed, the stench and filth of birth and death exceed that of a leather tanner’s shop, and the greed and craving of sentient beings surpass those of flies and gnats.
The Buddhas act as merchants of incense, pitying those multitudes of humans and devas who are submerged in the turbid sea. Therefore, Amitābha leads them forth.
The Master extensively opened the shop of Xiangyan; Śākyamuni, the Compassionate Father, firmly pointed toward the gate of the Pure Land.

The entire earth is nothing other than a poor child; even a single invocation of the Buddha's name serves as one’s capital. Do not depart from the ten recitations, for this sufficiently verifies the sincere word.

When the nose is clogged with the stench of the world, one will naturally grow weary of it in time. Now, taking the Western Paradise as the basis for instruction, I shall briefly distinguish ten meanings.
1. Each of the great matters; 2. The profoundness of past causes; 3. The manifestation of the merit of fruition;
4. Relying on the nature of causes; 5. Accordance with sentient beings; 6. The emptiness of defiled appearances;
7. Supreme skillful means; 8. Guiding those of the two vehicles; 9. The power of steadfast endurance.

Tenth, to demonstrate that the True Dharma is the one great matter: sentient beings dwelling in an age of five turbidities are like prisoners in a jail, subject to equal or unequal punishments, with not a single one able to escape.
This is because those who enter prison are all criminals; likewise, those who dwell within the six realms of human and heavenly existence are all bound by karma.

This is because they have received a body subject to the karmic retribution of the *bhavāgra* (the realm of division). Yet, when a person enters a prison, there is not a single moment when they do not seek liberation.
This is truly because the torment of the prison is difficult to endure and impossible to withstand. Beyond the thorny walls, there exists a world of great peace and bliss;
of this suffering and bliss, no one who has entered the prison remains ignorant. Now, sentient beings take afflictions as their home and birth as...
Death is a pen; the mind is bound as a prisoner in the collar and cap, and its emotions are confined within the shackles and stocks of gold and jade.
How could one know that the Great Iron Ring Mountains are my thorny walls, and that beyond the execution grounds of the Three Realms, there exists a home and fields of one's own?
The Buddhas, taking pity on these beings, felt a sorrow that pierced their hearts and bones; they distinguished between the pure and the defiled and pointed out the path for returning to liberation.
Yet, those who have long cast aside their karmic duties find no place of refuge. Therefore, [the Buddhas] further construct vast dwellings to settle them:
one serves as a road for traveling to and from the gates of hell, while the other stands as a guesthouse constantly maintained outside the prison. Thus it is.

How can the grace [of the Buddhas] ever be repaid? Alas! To illuminate the long night and lift up the overturned basin—the Buddhas do not begrudge extending their hands, yet why do sentient beings cling so piteously?
The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata appears in the world for one great matter. This "great matter" is precisely this very thing.
Sentient beings, on the contrary, cling to matters no larger than a hair-tip; they exchange the small for the great and take pleasure in it.
"Dying of emaciation. Why is this? (Qi said: 'To die of hunger and cold while in prison is called dying of emaciation.
Second, those with deep roots of causality have one primary cause: namely, the inherently pure essence of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and all sentient beings.
It is like the myriad phenomena relying on space, mountains and rivers relying on the earth, grain relying on seeds, and flowers and fruits relying on the sapwood. If it did not exist..."
Because of this cause, the fruit of Buddhahood is not realized. All compassion and wisdom are established solely by relying upon this cause.
As stated in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, the Tathāgatagarbha-body and the ocean of wisdom of all Buddhas do not exist apart from abiding therein.

If one does not perceive the Dharmakāya, then all merit, wisdom, great kindness, and great compassion will belong entirely to the realm of birth and extinction. That which is the Dharmakāya is precisely the "True Cause" (the primary cause). Second is the "True Vow."

As stated in the original sutra, when the Bhikṣu Dharmākara made the forty-eight great vows before the Tathāgata Sovereign King (Īśvararāja), he vowed that if even one vow were not fulfilled, he would not attain Bodhi.
This was based on his own nature of immeasurable compassion and wisdom; he thus gave rise to such inconceivable power of aspiration.
It was not that he perceived sentient beings as existing externally to the mind and then made a vow wishing to deliver them, for sentient beings do not [exist apart from the mind].
Because it is external to the mind. Third, the correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*). As stated in the original sutra:

after Dharmākara had made his vows, he dwelt thus in various meritorious qualities and cultivated such bodhisattva practices for incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta kalpas. Furthermore, according to the *Ekānta-bodhisattva-sūtra*:
in the past, when Amitābha was a crown prince, he heard this wondrous Dharma and sat with his side against a wall for seven thousand years.

He did not go to assemblies; he did not dwell on sensual desires or wealth; he did not inquire after the affairs of others; he always remained in solitude, restraining his mind so that it was not swayed.
Furthermore, he transformed eight thousand *koṭi-nayuta* of people, causing them to attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is the practice of his essential nature.
Intrinsic diligence is not a merit produced through effort; though it passes through billions of kalpas, it does not depart from a single thought-moment.
This is because, through the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate, one is detached from all conditioned practices and all kalpas. This is called the right cause, the right vow, and the right practice.

Just as the three dots of the letter *i* cannot form the character if even one is missing, this is neither attained through action nor attained through non-action. As the former masters said: "When the roots are deep, the fruit is lush."
The source is distant and the current is long; since the latent causes are profound, the arising of the teaching is likewise vast. Is this not so?

Regarding the manifestation of the fruit-virtues, there is the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra. All Buddhas and Tathāgatas give rise to great compassion because of sentient beings;
from great compassion arises the bodhicitta; and by means of the bodhicitta, they achieve equal and perfect enlightenment. It is like a vast...
In the wilderness there is a great king of trees; if its roots receive water, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all flourish and grow luxuriantly.
It is the same with the Bodhi-tree-king in the wilderness of birth and death: all sentient beings constitute its roots, while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constitute its flowers and fruits.
By benefiting sentient beings with the water of great compassion, one is able to bring the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to fulfillment.

The flowers and fruits of wisdom. Therefore, those Buddhas who attain the fruit of Buddhahood do so by relying upon sentient beings. If there were no sentient beings, the fruit of Buddhahood would not be realized.
It is like the Han Founder, who waged a hundred battles for the sake of saving the people; because of those hundred battles, he ascended the precious throne;

and because he ascended the precious throne, the common people could enjoy their vocations. If there were no common people, there would be none of the aforementioned matters. This is the ultimate truth.
To discuss this further: generally speaking, if one practices even a single virtue, a single deed, a single benefit, or a single name, none of these can be accomplished without sentient beings.
Therefore, if there were no sentient beings, "I" would not exist; thus, sentient beings are the support for "I," and "I" am the supported by sentient beings.

Sentient beings are the supported and "I" am the support; man and self are equal, and support and supported are non-obstructive. This is because it is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). That which is the nature of phenomena is...

Because it is the fruition of natural virtue, establishing [realities] outwardly does not constitute the meaning of fruition (even if one is deluded regarding the nature of mind and establishes them outwardly, they do not exist outside the nature of mind).
Because the nature of the mind has nothing external to it.
Fourth, regarding the nature as a cause: all sentient beings possess such a pure nature. It is like a single piece of refined gold that is forged into hairpins, bracelets, or a toilet vessel.
The nature of the gold is one and the same; however, the toilet vessel is defiled because it is not the gold itself that is defiled. [This applies to] living beings and Buddhas...
It is likewise so. They share the same pure nature; it is only through their forms as hairpins, bracelets, or urinals that distinctions arise, yet their nature is not different.
Therefore, when an ordinary person of the mundane world attains birth through ten recitations, it is because of this fundamental purity.
When Amitābha Buddha wishes to embrace such beings, he embraces them precisely because sentient beings are fundamentally pure—just like the light within a mirror.

It is not that it is not obtained through polishing, nor is it obtained from polishing itself. For those who are born in the Pure Land, this is not something that can be accomplished merely by the power of their practices, vows, and mindfulness.
Why is this? Mindfulness and practice are like a furnace and a hammer; they can only refine gold, for there is no separate gold produced by them.
Fifth, to accord with sentient beings: for those who delight in childhood, he provides bamboo horses; for those who delight in old age, he provides cane staffs.
Since sentient beings value only jewels, clothing, food, and drink, there appear spontaneously seven-jeweled pavilions, exquisite garments, food, drink, and other such things.
Just as children will not leave the burning house unless they are given carts [like those of] sheep or deer, once they have gone out...
Pure and with great vehicles; the Tathāgata, in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, speaks of the Jewel Land of Amitābha.
Once born there, each being perceives for themselves subtle, wondrous, and pure marks beyond all comparison, only then realizing that lapis lazuli and mother-of-pearl are like mere rubble.
It is as when a high-ranking official describes the splendor of the royal palace to a rustic country boy; he must first resort to things that are extremely precious to him.

The "difference" refers to the intended direction [of the teaching], which is beyond the reach of the cognitive capacity of non-sentient beings; it is like describing colors to one born blind—there is no use for such spatial comparisons.

Regarding the sixth point, the emptiness of the characteristics of the six impurities, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* relates the story of a certain son who delighted in playing among impure things, piling up earth to represent grain.
When grass and trees are treated as birds and beasts, if someone seizes them, one becomes angry and weeps. His father reflected: "This matter is easy to detach from;
once they grow older, they will naturally cease. Sentient beings are attached to their impure and foul bodies and to the various five desires;
yet when the five faculties, such as faith, are perfected, they are able to abandon them. Why is this? If what a small child is attached to were real...

Regarding objects, even if one reaches a hundred years of age, attachment to them only deepens. If the objects to which sentient beings are attached were truly existent, they would be unable to relinquish them even upon attaining the five faculties.
Because all phenomena are empty, deceptive, and unreal, it is easy to transform those to whom sentient beings are attached.
For example, a person may delight in beauty in youth, pursue office in middle age, and crave profit in old age; if these things were truly desirable, such a progression would not occur.
Years change and months pass; because of this constant transformation, all things are merely delusions of the mind, like a person in a dream who awakens as soon as they are called.
If the dream were real, calling out would be of no benefit. Since neither is real, the Buddha has taught the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land for the sake of all sentient beings.
Regarding the seven supreme skillful means: these means rely neither on one's own power nor on the power of another.
Within the ocean of self-nature, such sovereign merits are inherently present and fully manifested. Therefore, a single phrase of the Holy Name requires no further elaboration;

the merit of ten recitations is perfected, instantly transcending many kalpas. It is like ten thousand apertures roaring together, where the power lies in the whirlwind; it is because of the apertures [that the sound arises].

Because it is manifest, the power that illuminates the deep valleys lies in the morning sun; because one perceives through the valley, a single thread from an ant-hole can pierce a dam spanning a range of mountains—this is because the force of water penetrates due to the ants.
A single leaf of reed-matting can move a boat of ten thousand *hu*—this is because the force of the wind acts due to the reeds being spread out.
All of these are, in their totality, the ocean of the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is without action, without conditioning, and beyond thought.
It is manifested through the power of deliberation; it is neither from oneself nor from another, yet is fully possessed by both self and other.

Therefore, there exists such a supreme expedient—this is called the swiftest among the swift and the most direct among the direct. To neglect this and fail to practice it is true folly (a truth unchanging for a thousand ages).
Regarding the eight guides for those of the two vehicles: the followers of the two vehicles avoid sensory objects and pursue quiescence, realizing a provisional nirvana;

they do not attain the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata and continue to undergo the suffering of karma and afflictions. First, because of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), they cannot reach the ultimate extinction of the impurities of the outflows seen through vision and the stench of the habitual tendencies, which is the fruit of the *pāramitā* of purity. Second, because of the ground of ignorance, there exists...

First, because false and delusive practices have not yet been eliminated, one cannot attain the fruit of the *pāramitā* of the self that is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and non-active (*anabhisamskāra*).

Second, because the subtle and delusive arising of outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*) and the various aggregates born of mind (*manomaya-skandha*) have not yet been completely exhausted, one cannot attain the fruit of the *pāramitā* of bliss that is utterly extinguished and far removed.
Third, because the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) continues in a state of intermittent succession...
They continue to flow on, unable to reach the fruit of the *pāramitā* of ultimate immutability and permanence.

Because these four types of karmic afflictions prevent them from realizing the True Principle, the Tathāgata takes pity on them and instructs them to turn back and sever the mind of extinction, to cultivate practices for the Pure Land, and to realize that emptiness is not annihilation and existence is not permanence.
Thus, they may ride upon the wisdom of the Mahāyāna and enter the ocean of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the ninth power, that of firm endurance (*kṣānti*), Nāgārjuna says: When a bodhisattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they always desire not to be separated from the Buddhas.

Why? Because as long as one has not yet entered the bodhisattva stage and has not yet attained the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *avaivartika* [irreversibility], if one were separated from the Buddha, one would destroy all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Immersed in afflictions (*kleśa*), one could not save oneself, let alone save others. It is like a person...
It is like a boat that breaks apart in midstream; wishing to ferry others across, one instead sinks into the water oneself. It is like a small amount of hot water poured into a vast pool of ice:

although it melts a small portion, it instead turns back into ice. Likewise, those with little merit and lacking the power of skillful means, wishing to transform sentient beings, provide only slight benefit and instead fall into ruin themselves.
Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess the benefit of nirvāṇa, they lack...
Because they possess all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they are unable to provide instruction. A bodhisattva is like an elephant sunk in mud; no other elephant can pull it out.
If a bodhisattva enters a non-path, only a Buddha can rescue them, for they share the same Great Path. Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects as follows:
I have not yet attained the Buddha-eye; I am no different from one who is blind. If I were not guided by the Buddha, I would have no direction and would mistakenly enter other paths.
Even if I were to hear the Buddha’s Dharma, those who practice in other places do not know the proper timing for teaching or the extent of the practices to be performed.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees the Buddha—whether through physical sight or the purity of mind—and hears what he teaches, the mind finds joy.
The Dharma. One attains great wisdom and, by practicing in accordance with the Dharma, achieves liberation.
Since such benefits as these are immeasurable and equal to those of meeting a Buddha, how could one not desire to see the Buddha with a single-minded devotion?

It is like an infant who should not be separated from its mother, a traveler who cannot be without provisions, one in great heat who cannot be without cool breezes and cold water, one in great cold who cannot be without fire, or one crossing deep waters who cannot be without a boat.
One leaves the boat, yet the sick person does not leave the skilled physician; likewise, the Bodhisattva does not depart from the Buddhas, surpassing all other matters mentioned above.
Neither parents, nor kinsmen, nor friends, nor kings, nor gods can benefit one as much as the Buddha.

The Buddha benefits all Bodhisattvas by leading them away from places of suffering and establishing them in the stage of the World-Honored One. Question: How is it that one does not depart from the Buddhas? Answer: The assembly...
There are causes and conditions for the sins of immeasurable kalpas arising from birth. Although one may practice merit, wisdom will be meager; although one may practice wisdom, merit will be meager.
A bodhisattva seeking the Buddha-way must necessarily practice the patience toward beings (*sattvakṣānti*) and the patience toward dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).

By practicing the patience toward beings, one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-citta*) toward all sentient beings, thereby extinguishing the sins of immeasurable kalpas and attaining immeasurable merit. By practicing the [patience toward] dharmas...

Because of patience, one destroys the notion that phenomena are non-existent and attains immeasurable wisdom. These two practices are harmonized; thus, one must not be separated from the Buddhas throughout successive lifetimes.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva constantly delights in mindfulness of the Buddha, they always encounter a Buddha whenever they cast off one body and receive another.
Just as sentient beings who habitually indulge in desire take birth in the bodies of lustful birds, and those with much anger are born among venomous insects, so it is for the Bodhisattva.

He does not prize the blessings and pleasures of a *cakravartin* wheel-turning sage king or of gods and humans; he thinks only of the Buddhas. Therefore, he receives a physical form according to what his mind values.

Furthermore, because a bodhisattva constantly and skillfully cultivates the causal conditions for the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha), wherever he is born, he always encounters the Buddhas.
Thus, when Master Tianru was asked whether one who has attained awakening should specifically aspire to seek birth [in a pure land], he replied accordingly.
You have simply not yet attained awakening. Once awakened, this is that toward which the Pure Land proceeds, such that ten thousand oxen cannot turn it back. Furthermore, it says:
"Do you think that after a single awakening, habitual outflows are forever eliminated and one never again falls back?

Is there nothing further to be done—such as extensively studying the Buddha-dharma, practicing, and realizing the fruits of the path? Do you think one can immediately equal the Buddhas and enter life and death without being subject to hindrances?"

Is it because you are distracted by external conditions? To examine this: if those great Bodhisattvas who have cultivated the six perfections and myriad practices for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were all to feel ashamed of you—ashamed of the teachings regarding the delusion of Śrāvakas emerging from the womb and the confusion of Bodhisattvas separated from their physical shells—how much more so should those of recent times with meager understanding and shallow realization, who cannot even save themselves?
Even if their state of awakening were profound and far-reaching, if their practice and understanding were not...

It is indeed so. Yet, how can one who has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and whose power and function are not yet sufficient, dwell in a world of turbid evil and transform those who are stubborn and fierce?

This was not permitted by the former sages; it would be as certain as the principle that a boat which is incomplete and unstable, attempting to ferry many people across a sea of evil, will cause both self and others to drown.
Therefore, the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) states: "Those who wish to sport at the gates of hell must be born in that land to attain the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*)."

Having attained patience (*kṣānti*), one returns to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to rescue suffering sentient beings. For this reason, one seeks rebirth in a Pure Land. As the former sages said:

"Until one has attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), one must not mingle with the mundane world to save beings; until one has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one must never be separated from the Buddha.
It is like a fledgling with weak wings that can only cling to a branch. Now that Śākyamuni has entered parinirvāṇa and Maitreya has not yet appeared...
It has not yet ceased. One is entangled by the causes and effects of suffering in the four evil destinies; distracted by the heterodox and malevolent spirits who stir up disputes;
deluded by the signs of female beauty and licentious sounds; and invaded by the contact with evil conditions and defilements.

With no manifest Buddha to rely upon, and further disturbed by external circumstances, there are few among those of initial resolve who do not meet with failure. For this reason, the World-Honored One was so earnest and diligent.

That the ultimate goal is directed toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss is indeed for good reason. For there, Amitābha currently preaches the Dharma, and the conditions and environment of that Pure Land are manifoldly pure.
If one relies upon that Buddha, the power of patience will easily be perfected; one will attain the high rank of Buddhahood and personally receive the prediction of enlightenment.

Only then do they emerge to transform sentient beings, coming and going without obstruction. I have often observed that many contemporary practitioners of Chan fail to investigate the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Tathāgata and do not understand the profound mechanism of Bodhidharma. With empty bellies and haughty minds, they habitually practice in arrogance;

seeing those who cultivate the Pure Land, they laugh and say, "That is the practice of foolish men and women. I have frequently discussed how such views are not merely base and ignorant, but truly deluded.
This couple is nothing more than those who disparage Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, and others.

Not only have they deluded themselves regarding the True Path, lost their roots of goodness, forfeited their bodies of wisdom, and extinguished the seeds of the Buddha; they have further committed the karma of slandering the Dharma and incurred the calamity of reviling the Sages.
Thus, the Buddhas and Patriarchs regard them as objects of pity. Thereupon, the Venerable Yongming, moved by deep compassion and sorrow, exposed his heart and...

Yongming advocated the Pure Land; he both cultivated it himself and transformed the world. At the time of his death, various extraordinary and sublime signs appeared, and he was directly reborn in the highest grade of the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
Yongming realized the Chan of the direct pointing of Bodhidharma and yet attained the highest grade of rebirth in the Ultimate Bliss.
By this, he resolved the dogmatic attachments of Chan practitioners and exhorted faith for the Dharma-ending age. I say that his intent was profound.
This is what constitutes merit in the religious life. Zen Master Zhenxie Liao said: "In the single school of the Dongshan lineage, all are devoted to secret cultivation.
What is the reason for this? It is because the practice of the nianfo (Buddha-recitation) dharma-gate is a direct path of cultivation that strictly follows the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*).

It directly accommodates those of the highest capacity while indirectly guiding those of middling and lower capacities. He further said: "The great masters of the Chan school have already realized that which is neither empty nor..."

Regarding the Dharma of existence, for those who maintain a diligent resolve toward pure karma (*śukla-karman*), is it not the case that seeing the Buddha through pure karma is even more straightforward than through the Chan school?
It is further said: "Whether Buddhas or Patriarchs, whether in the Exoteric Teachings or in Chan, all cultivate pure karma; they all return to a single source.
Once one enters this gate, one is able to enter all immeasurable Dharma gates. This applies to such masters as Tiantai Yihuai and Yuanzhao.
The great masters of old, such as Ben, Beijian Jian, and Tianmu Li, were all patriarchs of the Chan school.

Upon examining their secret cultivation and public teachings, they unanimously promoted the principles of the Pure Land school; this was not merely coincidental. As detailed in those texts, it is impossible to record it all here.

Therefore, one should know that the esoteric cultivation of the Chan school is not separate from the Pure Land. Those of initial resolve who attain sudden enlightenment have not yet transcended the state of childhood innocence;
only those who enter this path possess the gateway of firmness and non-retrogression.
Tenth, to demonstrate the true Dharma: regarding all dharma-gates, to speak of them as empty or as existing is not yet the ultimate.

This *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) is such that while it is recollection, it is pure; this purity is not non-existence. While it is purity, it is recollection; this recollection is not existence.

To realize that purity has no dependence is the very essence of recollection (*nian-ti*). To understand that recollection is fundamentally detached is the function of purity (*jing-yong*). Therefore, there is nothing outside of purity.
If one thinks that there is purity which can be contemplated by thought, then because there is purity external to thought, that thought would have an object;
since an object is not purity, it is not the case that there is purity external to thought that can purify thought. If there were purity external to thought, then purity would be dualistic;

since duality is not purity, one should know that the Buddhas, in accordance with a mind of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), adorn and purify the lands. When contemplating the pure land, one should enter all gates of quiescent extinction.
The Buddhas adorn and purify their lands in accordance with the mind of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

one should contemplate the pure land as the gateway for entering all doors of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. The Buddhas adorn and purify their lands in accordance with the mind of equality toward all sentient beings;

one should contemplate the pure land as the gateway for entering all doors of equality toward sentient beings. The Buddhas adorn and purify their lands in accordance with the activity of great compassionate wisdom; one should contemplate...

Regarding the Pure Land, one should enter the gateway of all activities of great compassion and wisdom. The Buddhas adorn and purify the pure lands by conforming to their unconditioned, uncreated, and inconceivable activities.
Regarding the Pure Land, one should enter the gateway of all that is unconditioned, uncreated, and inconceivable.
The Buddhas adorn and purify the pure lands by conforming to the very nature of worldly toil and afflictions. Regarding the Pure Land, one should enter...
Regarding all gateways of worldly dust and afflictions, the Buddhas adorn and purify their lands in accordance with the characteristics of a single mote of dust or a mustard seed.
One should contemplate the pure land as entering all gateways of motes of dust and mustard seeds.

Through these aforementioned great Dharma-gateways, one enters realization through a single utterance of "Amitābha Buddha," yet there is neither the characteristic of a subject that realizes nor an object that is realized. If it were otherwise—
This constitutes a purity with remainder. The *Nianfo Samādhi* (Buddha-Recollection Samādhi) is not like this.
Regarding the third category, the gates:

indeed, the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are vast and possess many approaches; some are selected as topics by chance, while others are brought forth due to specific causes and conditions. Only...

The single gateway of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is frequently praised; it stands out like a high mountain rising from the plains, or like a shooting star shining across the desert when the sun reflects its light.

No other dharma-gate is more sublime than this. Now, regarding the great matter of the Western Land as described in various sutras, I have compiled them all together and divided them into two categories:

the "Longitudinal" (*jing*) and the "Latitudinal" (*wei*). The Longitudinal... [is not]... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on a Buddhist text concerning the Pure Land. The final sentence is incomplete, as indicated by the ellipsis.)
Those who speak exclusively of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) are not included; however, those who generally practice the recitation of the Buddha's name (*nianfo*) are admitted.
One may ascend Mount Cong to gather jade from the peaks and harvest sheep’s fat; one may cross the vast ocean to cut fragrant sandalwood and offer up ox heads. These are things never heard before.
I look toward future sages:
[this work is] the warp within a single scroll, the woof within two scrolls, the warp within three woofs,
and the woof within four woofs.
Among the sūtras within sūtras, these are: the *Sūtra on the Immeasurable, Equal, and Pure Enlightenment*; the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*; the *Sūtra of Amitābha*;
the *Sūtra on the Adornments of Immeasurable Life*; and the eighteenth assembly of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the "Assembly on the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life."

The five [versions] are from the same sūtra; the first four translations are somewhat unrefined. The sixth is the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Great Amitābha Sūtra), which the Layman of Longshu compared and harmonized with the previous four translations.
However, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*—a single assembly whose purport is profound and whose diction and dharma are rich—one wonders why the Layman of Longshu did not see it.
Furthermore, there are two others: the *Buddhabhāṣita-amitābha-sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Acceptance*. II.
It is the same sutra, yet at the beginning it is simplified and purified. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Visualization of Immeasurable Life* speaks of the sixteen visualizations;
the dharma-gates for cultivation and practice are fully recorded in this sutra. The three aforementioned sutras are specifically intended to establish the teaching for the Western Land.

Like the God among Gods and the King among Men, one need not exclude or suppress them as being too vast or empty. If even one cannot be attained, how could there be two? Within these sutras, the wondrous [teachings]...

The *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* (*Dharmarāja-dundubhi-svara-rāja-sūtra*), which serves as the warp among the two sūtras that possess the full meaning of other gates, states that by holding the name of Amitābha Buddha, at the time of death,
the Buddha and his assembly of sages will receive and lead one to rebirth in the Pure Land. Furthermore, there is the *Later-Translated Amitābha Gāthā Sūtra*, totaling fifty [verses].

There are six phrases. Both sutras also speak exclusively of the Pure Land, and their terminology and meaning are considerably more concise than the preceding ones. Furthermore, the *Gongyin* (Drum Sound) repeats the dhāraṇī;
since both the gāthā-sūtras and the geya sections are not the fundamental teachings, [they are excluded].

Among the three sets of sutras, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the central thread. When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra made his ten great vows, at the time of the end of life, when all the sense faculties are disintegrating and all majesty and power have been lost, only this King of Vows does not abandon him.
At all times it leads him from before; in a single kṣaṇa, he is reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss. That is to say:
They behold Amitābha Buddha. That person sees themselves born within a lotus flower and receives a prophecy from the Buddha.

After the passage of incalculable kalpas, they universally bring benefit to sentient beings throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds in the ten directions by the power of their wisdom, in accordance with the minds of those beings, even unto the point of being able to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the great ocean of afflictions and suffering.
Those who attain birth in the World of Ultimate Bliss, as well as the householder Vimukta, said:
"If I wish to see the Tathāgata Amitāyus of the Land of Peace and Bliss, I shall see him at will. In this same way, one may see the Tathāgatas of the ten directions whenever one wishes.
I am able to fully comprehend such matters as the adornments of the Tathāgatas' lands and their supernormal powers; they come from nowhere, nor do they go anywhere.

Depart! There is no place of movement, nor any place of abiding. Just as one’s own body has no coming, no going, and no place of movement or abiding, so too it is with this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Upon hearing this scripture and practicing according to its teachings, at the end of one's life, one will immediately go to the dwelling place of Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas.
One shall be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne and attain the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva.

He attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and his faculty of sight became pure. He beheld seven million two hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand-like Buddhas, Tathāgatas.
In the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, Mahāsthāmaprāpta said to the Buddha: "The Buddha Sūryaprabhāsa-virocana taught me the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-remembrance samādhi). It is like this:
suppose there is one person who is single-mindedly intent on remembering, and another person who is single-mindedly intent on forgetting. Thus it was.
There are two people: whether they meet or do not meet, or see one another or not, these two remember each other, and their mutual remembrance is deep.
Thus it continues from birth to birth, like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.
If the child has run away, what can the mother’s remembrance accomplish? But if the child remembers the mother, it is as the mother [remembers him].

When they remember, mother and child do not remain separated throughout successive lifetimes. If sentient beings, in their hearts, remember the Buddha and contemplate the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future;
they will not be far from the Buddha. Without relying on external means, they will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.

One gives rise to great vows, does not forsake sentient beings, and aspires to the great wisdom of all Buddhas.

By purifying the various stages of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*) and thoroughly cultivating all the perfections (*pāramitā*), one accomplishes the vast conduct of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, there are the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) of the highest degree.
Because all aspects are completely pure, and because one realizes the ten powers and fearlessnesses, all Buddha-dharmas are fully accomplished.
Therefore, as I now practice the ten wholesome paths of action, I shall cause all things to be endowed with complete purity.
In this way, the Bodhisattva accumulates roots of goodness, accomplishes roots of goodness, increases roots of goodness, and contemplates roots of goodness.
They fix their mindfulness upon roots of goodness, discern roots of goodness, delight in roots of goodness, cultivate roots of goodness, and abide securely in roots of goodness.
By means of the fruit of reliance obtained through these roots of goodness, they practice the bodhisattva path and, in every thought-moment, behold immeasurable Buddhas.
One should serve and make offerings as is appropriate. Furthermore, it is said: although there is nothing to be done, one should constantly abide in the roots of goodness;
and although one knows that all phenomena have no basis, one speaks of renunciation by relying on wholesome dharmas. I thus exhort those who have attained realization.
Reflect deeply upon the words of the magnanimous Yongjia: seek early the uninvited friends of the White Society;

do not treat the precepts lightly, for there is a Buddha who performs no karma; do not covet empty fame, for there are ghosts that testify against you. The Lotus Land is not far away—please apply the whip immediately.
Regarding the second, the teaching that tends toward quiescence: this refers to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which tends toward the extinction of nirvāṇa.

It does not give rise to joy in adorning the buddha-lands or benefiting others, and thus stands in direct opposition to the Pure Land Mahāyāna teachings. Nevertheless, both the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* mention those from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*.
The former masters have said: "Those of fixed nature in the Small Vehicle are not reborn [in the Pure Land]. However, if they previously generated the Great [Vehicle mind]..."

The mind perfumes [the ālayavijñāna] to form seeds. If one regresses from the Mahāyāna mind toward the Hīnayāna, yet at the point of death turns back from the small toward the great, one will attain birth [in that land].

Because one has long since regressed from the Great Vehicle and has deeply practiced the small, that Buddha, according to their practice, teaches the small and causes them to realize its fruits for the time being.

However, they do not abide in the stage of the small; rather, they give rise again to the Mahāyāna mind, and their progress becomes even more rapid. After five kalpas or ten kalpas, they attain the first bhūmi.
Such gradations are likewise superior; therefore, they differ [from this teaching].
Third, those who follow other teachings realize the truth of the two kinds of emptiness and cultivate the myriad practices to proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood in the Mahāyāna.

They merely do not permit that icchantikas or those of the two vehicles can attain Buddhahood, asserting that icchantikas lack the Buddha-nature and those of the two vehicles possess a fixed nature, such that they can never achieve it.

Because the ultimate truth of the Mahāyāna has not yet been fully exhausted, it is called "with remainder. In this sutra, it is taught that those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) are not born [in the Pure Land];

thus, the teaching and its meaning appear similar [to other texts]. However, the reason those who commit the five heinous crimes are not born there is because they slander the Dharma; they lack faith, but it is not because they lack the Buddha-nature (*gotra*).

In the *Amitābha-sūtra*, it is said that even for sentient beings who have violated the precepts and encounter evil omens at the time of death, if they hear the praise of the Buddha’s merits, the fierce fires of hell will transform into pure water.
A cool breeze blows. Fully endowed with the ten [virtues] that counteract the five heinous crimes and the ten evils, one contemplates and beholds golden lotuses like the orb of the sun;
in a single kṣaṇa, one attains rebirth there. This is the inconceivable merit of self-nature, manifested by relying on the inconceivable power of the Buddha.
If one did not possess the Buddha’s power, how could one—like a block of dull stone—pierce through the moon? One should know that mindfulness can manifest this nature; thus is rebirth attained.
This is the power of the nature. Thus, just as the sun can manifest space, yet space does not depend on the sun, so too all sentient beings attain Buddhahood;
this is unlike other remaining teachings.
The teaching of "nothing remaining" (wu yu) holds that all sentient beings are of one equal nature and shall all attain Buddhahood;
it is the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna. Since its sole doctrinal essence is one's own mind, it is called "without remainder.

In the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, the methods for the environment and the inhabitants—such as faith, vows, and other practices—are ultimately all subsumed within the single mind. Therefore, it is said that through "single-mindedness without distraction," one immediately attains rebirth there.
Regarding birth: furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] states that those born in the three grades all "give rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Bodhicitta is the Buddha-nature. As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "Bodhicitta is like a seed, for it gives birth to all Buddha-dharmas;
it is like a fertile field, for it causes the pure dharmas of sentient beings to grow; it is like the great earth, for it sustains all worlds; it is like pure water, for it..."
Because it is free from the stains of all afflictions; because, like a great wind, it encounters no obstruction throughout the world;

and because, like a blazing fire, it burns away the fuel of all [wrong] views—as explained at length in that sūtra—one should know that the bodhicitta is the sharp medicinal needle within the iron tube, and mindfulness of the Buddha is the medicinal thread.
That one attains perfect awakening at the very moment of first generating the mind in the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra is precisely this.

The meaning is this: the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the five stages of a bodhisattva are merely like a thread drawn through medicine. How could there be any sublime practice that surpasses the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi)?

As for the "five teachings of sudden enlightenment," these are the discourse of the Elder [Vasubandhu]: "When not a single thought arises, one is immediately called a Buddha; it does not depend upon the stages (*bhūmi*)."

Because it is gradual, it is designated as the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*). The *Sāgaramegha-sūtra* states: "Those who have attained the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena do not proceed from one stage to another.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "The tenth stage is the first; the first is the eighth stage," continuing thus until there is nothing at all.
What follows? One should know that "sudden" refers to stages, yet it is precisely not a stage—like the tracks of a bird in the sky, swift and leaving no trace.
From this, all stages arise while simultaneously being non-stages. Therefore, the Sudden Teaching is the fundamental pillar of all teachings;
it is also called the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings. Originally, it cannot be named the "Separate Transmission," and it is especially improper to establish it as a separate category.
Regarding the "One Teaching" (*ekayāna*): if one were to establish distinct names for each, they would already fall into a hierarchy of stages.

Nevertheless, establishing the "Sudden Teaching" (*tongjiao*) as a distinct name is like the method of recording the formation of "living eyes" (*hoekan*) in a go board manual. The *Guanjing chao* states: "In the Dharma of transformation, the Perfect [Teaching] is considered Sudden. Why?

Because the stage of Non-arising Patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is separately located in the first ground (*bhūmi*), whereas the Perfect [Teaching] is in the first dwelling (*vihāra*). In the Separate Teaching, ordinary beings..."
Generally, it takes countless kalpas to reach this stage; only through the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) can one enter it in this very life.

Since both Weiṭi and his attendants were ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) in their current bodies, they are judged as examples of the "sudden" [teaching], for this is the Perfect-Sudden (*yuandun*).

In this sutra, even those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil acts attain non-retrogression in this life simply by holding the name; this perfectly accords with the meaning of the sudden. That which is called "this mind" is...

To become a Buddha is this very mind; this mind is the Buddha. This direct pointing to the essence of the mind leaves no room for detours. Consider, for instance, a single utterance of "A-mi-tuo" (Amitābha):
both right and wrong are eradicated. How direct and straightforward! The ancients called this a "public case of the head. In the depths of boiling cauldrons, how could cold ice be contained?
Amidst the fierce flames of a great fire, how could even a blade of grass find a place? Even if Bodhidharma were to rise again, he would not alter these words of mine.
Furthermore, there may be hesitation regarding ten thousand years or a thousand li.
As for the six perfectly complete teachings, Ci'en states that the former masters categorized the sūtras and śāstras into four schools. The fourth is the School of Revealing Reality (*xiànshí zōng*).
Sūtras such as the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Lotus*, and the *Avataṃsaka* reveal the meaning of the true Middle Way; they cause one to abandon the "transformed city" and return to the "precious city."

Therefore, it is known that the *Amitābha Sūtra* belongs to the fourth school. Furthermore, it is said that when schools are categorized according to their teachings (*śāsana*), there are eight such schools:

first, the school that asserts the existence of both self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ubhaya-satya-vāda*), which is a non-Buddhist (Tīrthika) school and whose inclusion among the orthodox schools is difficult to comprehend;

and so on, up to the eighth, the school of the perfectly realized ultimate truth consistent with reason (*yukti-pariniṣpanna-artha-vāda*). Works such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Amitābha Sūtra* are subsumed under this eighth school. True...
Xie Chanshi and others elucidated the meaning of the perfect interfusion of the Pure Land through the metaphor of the thousand jewels in Indra’s net; this is fully recorded in various texts.

Recently, some have attempted to correlate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with this scripture, claiming that while the former is complete and encompasses the latter, the latter partially encompasses the former, thereby obtaining only a small portion of the perfection.
However, the principle of perfection admits neither "wholeness" nor "partiality. It is like the moon reflected in rivers: every single river possesses the full moon.
Even a single inch of water in a jar or a pond is the complete moon, for there is no partial moon. It is like wind in trees: every tree possesses the complete wind;
even a single inch of leaf, stem, or blade of grass contains the complete wind, for there is no partial wind. If the circle were composed of parts, the circle would then be divisible into segments.
If the parts were not the whole, the circle would not be pervasive. Since both "part" and "whole" are mutually contradictory, the concept of a circle [as a composite] is untenable.

This is not established. Now, according to the ultimate perfection of the Lotus School (*Lianzong*), five kinds of meanings are distinguished. First is the meaning of the mutual containment of the oceans of lands (*kṣetra-sāgara*):
the lands of the reward and transformation bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) of all Buddhas mutually encompass one another; they fully contain both the other and themselves without any obstruction.

If one calculates that they do not enter into one another, this is merely a view based on emotional attachment (*qing-jian*). Emotional views are not reality. It is like space contained within a room: if within it...
Whether it be humans, animals, ghosts, insects, stools, jars, or shelves, all are established in dependence upon space.
When space belongs to humans, then the space upon which ghosts, animals, insects, stools, jars, and shelves depend is entirely subsumed within the category of humans.
When space belongs to animals, then the space upon which humans, ghosts, insects, stools, jars, and shelves depend is entirely subsumed [within the category of animals].
Among the domestic animals, and even down to the ghosts, insects, jars, and shelves—each and every one is thus. They are intermingled yet not mixed; they are distinct yet not divided.
They neither enter nor do they not enter. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The land is radiant and pure, universally peerless.
It shines through immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable worlds, like forms appearing within a clear mirror. One should...

One knows that all pure lands and turbid worlds interpenetrate their light like a thousand lamps in a single room; therefore, the principle of two or three ages occurring simultaneously is established.
Sentient beings, due to their emotional views, cling to the existence of temporal divisions and perceive past events as future ones and so forth.
Within the true reality (*dharmatā*), no essence of time can be found. Why? If one reckons darkness and light to be time, then darkness and light are merely the marks of karma, like a disease.
The vision seen by the eye is not a fixed characteristic. If one calculates time based on "old" and "young," then old and young are illusory substances;
